Galveston’s mayor is warning residents that returning home after a hurricane will offer few basic comforts. Large portions of the island remain without electricity, gas, water, or sewer service, and a nighttime curfew is in force. Many residents stayed through Hurricane Ike, but recovery has been slower than they expected.

Retired General Russel Honore says Haitians should be paid to clear debris and distribute relief supplies rather than treated primarily as a security concern. He argues that international aid is not meeting demand and that the United Nations should prepare an evacuation plan. A second airfield, he says, should have been planned from the first day.

Richard Roberts has resigned from Oral Roberts University, saying in a letter that he loves the institution despite the controversy surrounding his administration. Three professors had accused him of dismissing them after they questioned university spending. Roberts and his wife deny misusing school money, and he had already stepped aside temporarily.

Travelers hoping to attend an Olympic Games should begin planning roughly two years ahead. Tickets generally become available about eighteen months before the opening ceremony, while tours and lodging disappear earlier. Visitors considering Rio must wait until the London planning cycle is complete before buying many official packages.

Everton opened its season by defeating Manchester United, leaving Alex Ferguson’s side to begin with a surprise loss. Robin van Persie watched from the substitutes’ bench after transferring from Arsenal. Deportivo also upset Osasuna in Spain, while Bayern Munich advanced easily in the German Cup.

Robin van Persie scored against Arsenal as Manchester United won 2–1 and moved above Chelsea at the top of the league. Chelsea drew with Swansea after Pablo Hernandez equalized, while Manchester City remained unbeaten despite being held by West Ham. The early table is already separating the likely contenders from the rest.

Roger Federer began his Wimbledon campaign with a victory over Mikhail Kukushkin of Kazakhstan. Novak Djokovic also advanced, as did David Ferrer, Andy Roddick, and Juan Martin del Potro. The grass-court tournament’s opening round brought several established names safely through to the next stage.

The Rolling Stones have reissued “Exile on Main Street” with additional material, drawing renewed attention to one of the band’s most admired albums. Mick Jagger says the record remains special because it captures a period when the group was both competing with the Beatles and learning from them. He believes the timing of the Stones’ rise was unusually fortunate.

Inter Milan remained two points ahead of Roma after beating Chievo in a seven-goal match. Roma kept its title hopes alive by scoring late against Cagliari, while Sampdoria held fourth place with a draw at Palermo. Juventus suffered its fourteenth league defeat, an unprecedented low point for the club.

Roma won the city derby against Lazio when substitute defender Marco Cassetti scored late. Parma preserved fourth place by drawing with Genoa, despite two goals from Jonathan Biabiany. The result moved Roma upward and left Lazio needing points from its remaining fixtures.

Pablo Larrazabal won the Abu Dhabi Golf Championship, finishing one stroke ahead of Rory McIlroy and Phil Mickelson. McIlroy called his result a moral victory after a two-shot penalty, while Mickelson said the tournament helped him regain form before the 2014 season. The finish was decided by a crowded final leaderboard.

India reached 382 for four against Sri Lanka, with Sachin Tendulkar unbeaten on 108 in the second Test at Colombo. He shared a large partnership with debutant Suresh Raina after the visitors lost several wickets in quick succession. India still needed sixty runs to force Sri Lanka back to the crease.

Police in Napa arrested Mark Lugo and accused him of stealing a Picasso portrait titled “Tete de Femme.” The painting is valued at about $200,000, and prosecutors have filed six charges. Investigators say the work was recovered quickly after the theft was reported.

Elephant Nature Park in northern Thailand rescues animals from logging, tourism, and abusive working conditions. It also operates a field clinic for elephants in remote villages. The organization teaches visitors that caring for the animals requires more than providing food after they have been removed from the tourist industry.

Sao Paulo is preparing to pay about $12 million for Brazilian midfielder Ganso. The player calls the transfer a dream and hopes a strong season will restore his place in the national team. He had previously attracted interest from Inter Milan.

Photographers took part in a one-day challenge devoted to shadows, producing images that turned ordinary streets and bodies into abstract shapes. The exercise coincided with Groundhog Day, when Punxsutawney Phil failed to see his shadow and forecast an early spring. Staten Island Chuck offered the same prediction.

A New Jersey town may regulate the appearance of public displays, but a court says it cannot use aesthetic rules to silence union protest. The case involves “Scabby the Rat,” a large inflatable used at labor demonstrations. Officials had banned inflatables, but the court questioned whether the rule was really aimed at the message.

Scarlett Johansson is engaged to Romain Dauriac, who co-owns an independent advertising agency. The actress was previously married to Ryan Reynolds, but that relationship ended in 2011. Representatives have released few details, and Johansson is keeping the new relationship largely private.

Climate scientist James Hansen says preventing catastrophic warming requires stopping the expansion of coal and tar-sands projects. He favors a fee on carbon emissions that would make polluters bear the environmental cost of their products. Hansen says future generations should not inherit a damaged planet because the present one refused to change.

A fisherman reported a six-foot wave off the New Jersey coast, while tidal instruments detected several tsunami-like movements. Scientists are investigating whether the event was caused by weather, underwater activity, or a combination of forces. The National Weather Service says there is no evidence of a destructive tsunami.

Sebastian Vettel celebrated a record-filled season after Red Bull delivered his second Formula One championship. The same awards ceremony honored rally driver Sebastien Loeb, who won an eighth consecutive world title for Citroen. Both men dominated their sports so thoroughly that the competition was often about second place.

Serena Williams defeated world number one Victoria Azarenka in Madrid, winning her forty-first WTA singles title. She struck fourteen aces and twenty-six winners in a match she controlled from the beginning. Williams has not lost on clay this season and is becoming the favorite for the next major tournament.

Michael Schumacher is preparing for his three-hundredth Formula One race at Spa, a circuit he calls the best in the world. The seven-time champion hopes Mercedes can produce a stronger performance than it has managed in most of the season. Schumacher reached the podium at the European Grand Prix earlier this year.

Rain has finally reached a region suffering through drought after the weather pattern responsible for the dry conditions collapsed. The water is welcome, but heavy bursts exceeding an inch per hour have caused fresh concerns about flooding. A cold front is expected to carry the system toward the East Coast.

Passengers were injured in two separate incidents involving JetBlue and Lufthansa flights. Seven people were hurt in the JetBlue event and eleven in the Lufthansa incident. Officials are investigating both cases, but the airlines have not indicated that they are connected.

Terra Jole, who performs under the name “Mini-Gaga,” is an actress and singer with achondroplasia. Her stage persona has attracted a large following, including several well-known entertainers. Jole says she wants audiences to remember her work rather than reduce her career to a medical description.

Sidney Frank left Brown University $100 million shortly before his death. Frank attended the school briefly in the 1930s but left because he could not afford to continue. The gift now funds full scholarships for students with the greatest financial need, and the first recipients recently graduated.

China’s largest microblogging service, Sina Weibo, has introduced a paid membership plan with fifteen additional features. The package costs about ten yuan a month and is intended to create revenue after the company reported a quarterly loss. Weibo is trying to monetize its popularity without driving ordinary users away.

A woman who has food allergies organizes restaurant dinners where managers can discuss ingredients and safe preparation with guests. She advises diners to call ahead rather than assume a menu item is harmless. About twelve million Americans have food allergies, and doctors still do not know why the number appears to be rising.

The investigation surrounding David Petraeus and other senior officials involves four-star generals, roughly thirty thousand documents, and more than twenty current or former CIA directors. The figures illustrate how widely the scandal reached through the national-security establishment. Investigators are examining emails and other records rather than relying only on public statements.

Field Marshal Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has left Egypt’s military to seek the presidency. Analyst Khalil al-Anani says the move reflects the armed forces’ determination to preserve its influence after the revolution. Gulf governments are backing Sisi as a stabilizing figure, while critics fear that his rise will reproduce the insecurity he promises to end.

Central Florida is especially vulnerable to sinkholes because much of the region rests on porous limestone. Homeowners filed more than twenty-four thousand sinkhole-related claims between 2006 and 2010, costing insurers roughly $1.4 billion. State lawmakers are debating how much of the risk should be covered by private policies.

Nokia is promoting the Lumia 1020 as a phone that can replace a dedicated camera, thanks to its forty-one-megapixel sensor. Smartphones have the advantage of sharing images immediately, and future models may combine photographs with information from other sensors. The resolution exceeds that of some professional cameras, though image quality depends on more than pixel count.

David Beckham says his 2011 season was the strongest of his five years in Major League Soccer. The former England captain helped his club win its first championship since 2005 and remains committed to expanding the sport’s audience in the United States. He had considered returning to Europe before the London Olympics.

The Astrodome has stood empty since 2003, but plans are emerging to turn the site into public green space. The building opened in 1965 as the world’s first domed sports stadium and sits beside the home of the Houston Texans. County officials support the concept but have not made a final decision about demolition or reuse.

Some addiction-recovery programs are using virtual worlds alongside counseling and support groups. Patients can experiment with new behavior through avatars, creating emotional distance from situations that feel overwhelming in ordinary life. Psychologists disagree about whether the digital setting encourages insight or simply provides another way to avoid reality.

Brazil’s free antiretroviral program, introduced in 1996, has been praised as a model for confronting HIV/AIDS. As treatment allows more people to live longer, doctors are seeing chronic health problems that were once hidden by early deaths. The government is now trying to adapt its system from emergency care to long-term management.

Sony’s PlayStation Vita has gone on sale in the United States with a touchscreen, two analog sticks, and the ability to run several applications at once. The hardware is more ambitious than most portable consoles, but its success will depend on whether developers produce games worth carrying everywhere. Early reviewers call the machine promising rather than essential.

South Africa defeated Australia by nine wickets in Melbourne to take an unbeatable two-to-nothing lead in the Test series. The visitors had already won the opening match in Perth and now appear to have controlled both contests from the middle of the innings. Australia must change its approach before the final Test.

The South Carolina governor’s office has confirmed the authenticity of emails in which the governor complimented an Argentine woman’s beauty and received an affectionate reply. The newspaper that obtained the messages spent weeks checking them before publication. The correspondence has created a political distraction even though neither writer has described it as an affair.

The United States is tightening financial checks and cargo inspections as it asks allies to strengthen sanctions against Iran. Tehran denies that its uranium program is intended to produce a nuclear weapon, but the International Atomic Energy Agency says the country has repeatedly defied Security Council demands. The dispute continues without a clear diplomatic exit.

Real Madrid leads Deloitte’s annual ranking of football clubs by revenue, with Manchester United and Barcelona following. The decline in the value of the pound has weakened the positions of several English teams even when their match results remain strong. Commercial income now matters nearly as much as trophies in the race to become football’s richest club.

Spirit Airlines is defending a controversial fare policy that lists taxes and fees separately from its advertised price. Senator Barbara Boxer and a consumer group say the airline’s message to customers is misleading and encourages them to accept charges they cannot avoid. Spirit argues that travelers prefer to see the base fare before extras are added.

Riders for Health supplies motorcycles and maintenance services to clinics in rural Africa. The organization manages more than fourteen hundred vehicles across seven countries, with local mechanics keeping them available. Motorcyclists carry blood samples, medicine, and test results between facilities that would otherwise be separated by impassable roads.

Letters written by Stalin, Mussolini, and Hitler reveal different styles of private affection. Stalin told his wife he felt as lonely as a horned owl, while Mussolini asked a lover to repeat that she loved only him. Hitler’s notes to Eva Braun were more restrained, describing her as calm and intelligent rather than using elaborate romantic language.

Actors and politicians remembered Andy Griffith as a performer who made television feel unusually real. Barbara Eden said he created a welcoming atmosphere on set, while President Obama praised the warmth he brought to American homes. Ron Howard, who worked with Griffith as a child, said the actor’s pursuit of excellence shaped his own career.

Health officials are tracing contacts after a passenger infected with measles traveled from Europe to the United States. A separate case in Boston involved a woman who had flown from France. Authorities are asking other passengers to monitor themselves and seek medical advice if symptoms appear.

Steve Jobs’s yacht, named Venus, has been completed at a Dutch shipyard. Jobs worked on the design with minimalist architect Philippe Starck, and his family attended the launch ceremony. As a gift, the builders received customized iPod Shuffles, an appropriately personal detail for a vessel associated with Apple’s founder.

Asian markets fell modestly as investors weighed a credit downgrade against continuing uncertainty over Europe’s debt. Tokyo, Seoul, Sydney, and Shanghai all moved lower, while the G7 promised to take whatever measures were necessary to protect financial stability. U.S. stock futures also declined in early electronic trading.

Archaeologists believe a recently identified stone circle called Bluestonehenge may have marked the beginning of a funeral procession. The monument used Welsh stones whose color gave it its name and stood near the better-known Stonehenge. The discovery adds support to theories that Stonehenge served religious and ceremonial purposes rather than functioning only as an observatory.

Bob Vila advises homeowners affected by Superstorm Sandy to inspect foundations, roofs, wiring, mold, and debris before beginning repairs. He recommends consulting local officials and FEMA about permits and safety standards. Large structural jobs should be left to professionals after the immediate damage has been documented.

Carl Safina says New York and New Jersey have now experienced two hurricanes in two years, forcing residents to reconsider whether rebuilding on vulnerable coastlines is sensible. The alternatives are stronger barriers or gradual retreat, he argues. Federally subsidized insurance can encourage people to place lives and property in danger repeatedly.

Taiwanese taekwondo fighter Yang Shu-chun was disqualified at the Asian Games after officials found extra electronic sensors in her socks. Her country’s immediate appeal failed, and Taiwan’s sports minister threatened to take the case to an international court. The athlete said the equipment was not intended to provide an unfair advantage.

TED has grown from a conference into a global forum where scientists, artists, and entrepreneurs present ideas in short talks. Stephen Hawking and Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie have appeared alongside inventors demonstrating underwater robots and experimental aircraft. The format is designed to make specialized concepts accessible to a general audience.

UEFA has created a Nations League to replace many international friendlies beginning in 2018. European teams will be divided into groups according to their rankings, with promotion and relegation adding competitive stakes. The tournament will also provide another route into the European Championship and World Cup.

Large sections of Nanjing’s Ming City Wall are scheduled to open to visitors after years of limited access. The fortification was built between 1366 and 1386 and remains one of China’s least appreciated historic landmarks. Officials hope the opening will spread tourism beyond the city’s better-known sites.

Paul Donovan argues that the Catholic Church must become more transparent and democratic if it wants to remain relevant. He says the leadership under Benedict XVI moved backward on questions including the role of women and institutional accountability. Reform, Donovan writes, requires more than changing the public tone of the hierarchy.

San Diego Comic-Con has become a major gathering place for cosplayers who spend months recreating characters from films, games, and comics. Certain costumes return every year, but fans continually invent new variations. Organizers are asking attendees to submit photographs from the 2014 convention for an online gallery.

Naturalist David Mizejewski says cleaning oil from birds is difficult, stressful, and no guarantee that the animals will survive their return to the wild. Conservationists nevertheless continue the work because endangered populations may depend on every rescued individual. Humans caused the spill, he argues, creating an ethical obligation to reduce the damage.

The cast of “X-Men” reunited at Comic-Con to discuss “Days of Future Past,” a film built around time travel and conflicting versions of the characters. Peter Dinklage announced that he would play the scientist Bolivar Trask. The panel focused on how the movie would connect the franchise’s earlier and later stories.

Connectomics researchers are attempting to map the brain’s enormous network of connections rather than studying one region at a time. The Human Connectome Project may clarify how structure relates to memory, behavior, and disease. Scientists hope the information will eventually improve treatments for disorders including autism.

King Juan Carlos has apologized after a hunting trip in Africa provoked criticism during Spain’s economic crisis. Animal-rights activists were particularly angry that the trip involved elephants. The king said he had made a serious mistake and would not repeat it.

Bob Greene met a man who has been living almost permanently on cruise ships because the cost is lower than maintaining a conventional home. The arrangement provides meals, beaches, and constant movement, but it also leaves him detached from ordinary communities. Greene calls it a modern version of the beach bum’s fantasy, with a cabin instead of a shack.

Billy Anderson has spent more than a year in the hospital with an unexplained illness that caused him to lose one hundred pounds. Doctors have informally called it “Billy’s Disease” while they continue searching for an answer. His wife says he was once exceptionally healthy and that the uncertainty is harder than the treatment.

Researchers compared four popular weight-loss diets and found no dramatic winner. Programs emphasizing carbohydrates, protein, or fat can all work when they reduce total calories and can be followed over time. The study suggests that adherence matters more than choosing a fashionable theory of nutrition.

Massachusetts is preparing to certify the election of a new senator who will replace the late Edward Kennedy. The winner could be sworn in as soon as Thursday after final returns reach the governor’s office. The special election has attracted national attention because of Kennedy’s long political history.

David Frum argues that Europe’s crisis is fundamentally a problem of currency rather than simply government debt. Countries using the euro cannot devalue their own money or borrow under conditions set solely by national needs. Abandoning the currency would create new dangers for consumers, banks, and financial portfolios around the world.

Michaela Watkins and Casey Wilson have reportedly left “Saturday Night Live” before the program’s thirty-fifth season begins. Watkins called the show a dream job despite the abrupt ending. The new season will open with viewers waiting to see which performers fill the space left by the departing cast members.

The Federal Communications Commission has approved an open-internet plan intended to prevent providers from giving premium service only to customers who pay more. Both supporters and critics say the rules do not go far enough. Congress could still revise the policy or restrict the agency’s authority to enforce it.

Vietnam’s Chapel, designed by a21studio, has been named World Building of the Year. More Asian firms competed for awards than in previous years, reflecting the region’s growing influence in architecture. The winners were announced at a large ceremony in Singapore, the central event of the industry calendar.

Liverpool beat Southampton without Luis Suarez, while vanishing spray quickly became one of the new season’s most popular innovations with fans. Louis van Gaal lost his first league match as Manchester United manager. Monaco also began its Ligue 1 campaign without a point after two games.

Abraham Lincoln delivered the Gettysburg Address while the Civil War was still uncertain, using a brief speech to redefine what the conflict meant. The words spread widely in nineteenth-century newspapers and now circulate through social media. Certain phrases are quoted far more often than the address is read in full.

Five Mexican footballers have been removed from the Gold Cup after testing positive for clenbuterol. Mexico’s football officials say the players ate contaminated meat rather than deliberately taking a banned drug. The case has revived concern about food contamination among athletes who travel for international competition.

Colombia is negotiating a peace arrangement that includes a program for destroying illegal coca crops. The country remains one of the world’s largest cocaine producers, and eradication has often displaced farmers without ending cultivation. Officials hope the broader agreement will address both the armed conflict and the rural economy supporting the trade.

IMF chief Christine Lagarde says Europe must reform in order to produce growth and jobs rather than merely stabilize its currency. The eurozone economy expanded slightly in the latest quarter, but youth unemployment remains above fifty percent in Spain and Greece. Portugal, Italy, and Ireland are also facing severe unemployment among young adults.

A supermoon occurs when a full moon coincides with the moon’s closest approach to Earth. It appears larger and brighter than an ordinary full moon, although the difference is easier to notice in photographs than with the naked eye. Some parts of the United States will see the moon set before the exact moment of closest approach.

China has lost the bronze medal it won in the women’s gymnastics team event at the 2000 Sydney Olympics. Officials determined that gymnast Dong Fangxiao was underage at the time and canceled her results. The United States has been awarded the medal instead.

LZ Granderson says many Americans are already exhausted by the length of the election cycle, with seventy percent wishing it would end. Months of advertising and strategic compromise can obscure the country’s actual needs, he argues. Candidates from both parties, Granderson writes, often protect their campaigns before the public interest.

The Kills are the musical partnership of Alison Mosshart and Jamie Hince, known for sparse rock songs and a carefully controlled visual identity. They design artwork and photographs for their album packaging as well as performing the music. Public interest often follows their personal lives almost as closely as their records.

U.S. officials say Kenneth Bae entered North Korea with a valid visa but is being held for an unspecified offense. Sweden is assisting with diplomatic contact because the United States has no embassy in Pyongyang. Bae was detained in November, and the State Department is seeking more information about his condition.

Former Georgia congresswoman Cynthia McKinney has won the Green Party nomination after defeating three opponents. A party spokesman said every vote she receives will help make the organization more visible. McKinney served six terms in Congress as a Democrat before leaving the party.

Support for same-sex marriage has increased sharply among Americans, especially those under thirty. David Frum says the larger unresolved question is how to strengthen marriage as an institution for children and parents. He argues that stable marriages improve education and economic prospects, though critics dispute his use of marriage as a broad solution to social problems.

Jamaican swimmer Alia Atkinson won the 100-meter breaststroke at the short-course world championships in Doha. Her time equaled the world record held by Olympic champion Ruta Meilutyte. Atkinson became the first Black woman to win a world swimming title, a milestone she said mattered beyond the medal.

Daniel Zarin says the loss of tropical forests contributes roughly a tenth of global carbon emissions, yet countries have struggled to determine exactly where trees are disappearing. A new interactive map tracks forest loss by location and speed. Zarin believes the information will make governments more accountable for promises to end deforestation.

Research in Motion is unveiling BlackBerry 10 as it tries to keep a place in a smartphone market dominated by Apple and Google. The company must satisfy corporations that depend on secure email while persuading ordinary consumers to try a new operating system. Executives describe the launch as a turning point for the struggling brand.

Gulfport Mayor Brent Warr and his wife have pleaded not guilty to federal charges involving more than $222,000. The indictment alleges that the couple received money for which they were legally responsible. They were released on bond and ordered to appear in court in April, where they could face a lengthy sentence if convicted.

Thailand’s national assembly has selected General Prayuth Chan-ocha as prime minister after the military seized power during months of political turmoil. He was the only candidate for the position. The appointment formalizes military control while opposition groups question whether the process represents a genuine return to civilian rule.

Lindsey Vonn suffered a torn ACL, a damaged MCL, and a fractured bone in a dramatic crash. Doctors estimate that recovery could take six to eight months, but Vonn says she will work toward competing in the Olympics. The skier’s determination has become part of the story even as her medical team urges patience.

Femi Kuti has spent twenty-six years extending the political tradition established by his father, Fela. He left his father’s band in 1985 and created the Positive Force, developing a sound that combines protest with dance music. Kuti calls his new album, “Africa for Africa,” his most direct and unpolished record yet.

Supporters of marijuana legalization say a proposal backed by New York politicians could succeed because both Mayor Bloomberg and Governor Cuomo support it. They also argue that an arrest for possession can damage employment prospects far more than the drug itself. Opponents warn that legalization would create health and criminal problems of its own.

Minnesota Lottery customers can now buy tickets at a gas pump and receive the numbers by text message. Officials have imposed a weekly $50 limit to discourage impulsive spending. The system makes gambling more convenient while attempting to signal that convenience should not mean unlimited purchases.

Oil has reached portions of Pensacola Beach and Perdido Key, but Florida’s major tourist beaches remain open. Officials in Alabama are advising people not to swim in affected Gulf waters. Businesses are trying to reassure visitors that the spill’s visible damage is localized even as cleanup continues.

Congress is considering a ban on voice calls during flights after a survey found that most passengers oppose hearing strangers talk from their seats. Bob Greene supports the measure, arguing that a crowded cabin could become intolerable if everyone used a phone. Lawmakers may discover that travelers blame them if the experiment is allowed and chaos follows.

Elisabeth Badinter says the number of women who remain childless has doubled in many countries over the past twenty years. About one in five American women has no children, despite the country’s comparatively high fertility rate. Badinter sees the trend as evidence of an unresolved resistance to motherhood and calls for feminist reforms that would make family life less punishing.

The famous Farrah Fawcett poster may be the best-selling pinup image ever produced. Its appeal came partly from the actress’s expression, which looked confident without seeming distant. A professor calls it one of the last truly iconic pinups, while the photographer says Fawcett herself never understood how striking she appeared.

Nearly seventy percent of the United States is experiencing some degree of drought, according to a climate-monitoring agency. More than half the country is in moderate or worse conditions, the highest proportion since the 1950s. Severe drought has expanded sharply in a single month, threatening crops, rivers, and municipal water supplies.

Turkish police have detained officials from several football clubs in an investigation into match-fixing. The president and vice president of Fenerbahce are among those arrested, shortly after the club won its eighteenth league title. The governing party says the operation is part of a broader effort to dismantle criminal organizations.

Dean Obeidallah argues that public figures who make outrageous statements should not be rewarded with endless attention. Their words matter when they hold power or seek it, he says, but audiences can still refuse to amplify every provocation. Obeidallah’s advice is simple: the next time an attention-seeker speaks, walk away from the spectacle.

Egypt’s defense minister has warned that the country’s conflict could lead to the collapse of the state. Analysts call the language alarming but perhaps overstated, saying the immediate task is to rebuild public confidence. Hillary Clinton also urged the government to restore trust rather than rely on increasingly forceful warnings.

Juventus celebrated its twenty-ninth Italian league title after beating Palermo. Supporters displayed banners claiming thirty-one championships, refusing to accept the removal of two titles during the match-fixing scandal. In the Netherlands, Ajax won its third consecutive championship and its thirty-second overall.

The FDA has approved Ampyra, the first drug specifically intended to improve walking speed for people with multiple sclerosis. It may be used by patients with different forms of the disease, although not everyone responds. Researchers are continuing studies to determine whether the medication improves other neurological functions.

Serena Williams has been eliminated from Wimbledon by Germany’s Sabine Lisicki in a three-set upset. The world number one and five-time champion had been a favorite to win the tournament. Lisicki, seeded twenty-third, is repeating the deep run she made in 2011.

District Attorney Jim Woodall is considering dropping fraud charges against former University of North Carolina professor Julius Nyang’oro. Woodall says the case depends heavily on Nyang’oro’s cooperation. Whistleblowers allege that the athletic department used fake classes to keep athletes eligible, and prosecutors are trying to determine who authorized the scheme.

Karabekir Akkoyunlu describes the aftermath of Turkey’s disaster as a scene in which officials showed little humility or responsibility. He argues that Prime Minister Erdogan treats preventable tragedies as unfortunate side effects of progress and then uses nationalism to avoid blame. That strategy, Akkoyunlu writes, cannot preserve popularity forever.

The son of a former CIA officer convicted of espionage has admitted helping his father resume spying after prison. He cooperated with prosecutors and received five years of probation plus community service. The father remains the highest-ranking CIA officer ever sentenced for espionage, making the family case unusual even by intelligence standards.

New federal rules will require automakers to produce more fuel-efficient vehicles by the 2025 model year. The administration says the standards will reduce oil consumption and pollution while saving drivers money at the pump. Manufacturers warn that meeting the targets will require expensive changes in engines, materials, and design.

Economists disagree about whether the current downturn deserves comparison with the Great Depression. Some say the analogy exaggerates the damage, while historians point to an earlier depression that is now largely forgotten. A survivor of that period remembers not only hardship but also a public determination to endure.

“The Reluctant Fundamentalist,” adapted from Mohsin Hamid’s novel, stars Riz Ahmed, Liev Schreiber, and Kate Hudson. The film follows a Pakistani analyst whose view of America changes after the September 11 attacks. Critics call it thoughtful and well acted, though its political questions are deliberately uncomfortable.

Joplin serves as the commercial center of a four-state region and sits at the intersection of several major highways. Trucking is central to the local economy, while the surrounding area retains a history of lead and zinc mining. The city’s location has made transportation more important than its modest size might suggest.

The television program “Ford Nation” was canceled one day after its debut on Canada’s Sun News Network. The decision followed a Toronto council vote stripping Mayor Rob Ford of most of his powers. Ford has also admitted smoking crack during what he described as a drunken stupor, keeping the controversy in national headlines.

MTV’s “Faking It” has introduced an intersex character whose chromosomes are male but whose physical traits are female. The show follows two friends pretending to be lesbians, but its creator says the new storyline is not a temporary plot device. The character’s identity will develop across the entire series.

Dispersants are used to break oil into smaller droplets during marine spills, and the Coast Guard and EPA say they may be less damaging than leaving crude on the surface. BP plans to test the chemicals beneath the water where oil is gushing into the Gulf of Mexico. Scientists still do not know enough about the subtle effects on deep-water life.

Joe Green predicts that immigration reform will face a difficult vote in the House even after clearing the Senate. The last major overhaul came in 1986, and the political arguments have changed since then. Green says immigrants bring the risk-taking and technical skills a growing knowledge economy needs.

Mario Matt won his fourteenth World Cup slalom in Val d’Isere, tying fellow Austrian Benny Raich’s record. It was Matt’s first victory since 2011. In giant slalom, Tessa Worley defeated Jessica Lindell-Vikarby, while American stars Ted Ligety and Bode Miller failed to reach the second run.

Michelle Wie won the U.S. Women’s Open by two strokes, claiming the first major championship of her career. The Hawaiian golfer finished ahead of world number one Stacy Lewis, who closed with a 66. Wie’s victory answered years of speculation about whether her early promise would become a major title.

The World Health Organization has confirmed nearly nine hundred H1N1 cases worldwide. Mexico reports that infections are declining, but the organization warns that the virus could return in another wave. The United States and Canada are also reporting cases, including an outbreak affecting pigs at a Canadian farm.

“Dungeons & Dragons” is expanding beyond the tabletop with online multiplayer games, webcomics, and other formats. “Neverwinter” offers a digital version of the shared adventure, while “Table Titans” follows the culture through comics. Wizards of the Coast says the different versions are meant to reinforce rather than replace one another.

Lorena Ochoa and Tiger Woods first encountered each other at the Junior World Championships, long before either became a professional star. Ochoa has since won twenty-six LPGA tournaments and began playing at age five. The two golfers remained connected through their shared experience of growing up inside the sport.

Usain Bolt escaped serious injury after crashing a car in Jamaica. The world’s fastest man was taken to a hospital after climbing from the wreck, but officials said his injuries were minor. Bolt had won three gold medals in Beijing and was expected to return to competition soon.

China and India each have populations exceeding one billion, making them the two most populous countries on Earth. The United States ranks a distant third with just over three hundred million residents. At the other end of the list, the Pitcairn Islands have an estimated population of fewer than fifty.

Scott Maney’s Craigslist advertisement for a trampoline attracted attention because he mocked his own children and described the equipment with unusual honesty. The listing went viral and the trampoline sold within a day. Maney says he expected a few local responses, not national internet fame.

New research suggests that losing a job can force people out of professional routines that had stopped satisfying them. Laid-off managers in the United States and Australia often sought work that better matched their values after the initial shock. The researchers caution that the benefits of a career change do not erase the financial damage of unemployment.

Artist Tenzing Rigdol carried sacks of soil from Tibet to India so exiled Tibetans could walk on earth from their homeland. He spread the dirt across a stage for a performance about memory and displacement. Rigdol said his father died without seeing Tibet again, and the project was partly an attempt to give others the contact he had lost.

Boris Becker has supported Bayern Munich for most of his life and has served on the club’s advisory board for a decade. The tennis champion says football is as important to him emotionally as tennis. He believes Bayern’s attack remains strong but worries that defensive weaknesses could cost the team this season.

Previously unpublished photographs of Marilyn Monroe have been found in a New Jersey warehouse. Taken by a Life photographer in Los Angeles, the images show Monroe before the polished public persona was fully formed. Life’s enormous archive occasionally produces such discoveries years after the negatives were filed away.

The baby-boom generation is driving projections that the United States will have 88.5 million people over sixty-five by 2050. Boomers have reshaped every stage of life they have entered, and analysts expect the same influence on retirement, health care, and popular culture. Aging will become a visible social style as well as a demographic fact.

Cosmetic surgeons say mustache implants are increasingly popular, especially among men from the Middle East. Some travel to Turkey or France for the procedure because a thick mustache is associated with maturity and virility in parts of the region. Doctors transplant individual follicles to create a more natural shape than older techniques allowed.

Thierry Henry has returned to Arsenal on a two-month loan from the New York Red Bulls. Arsenal’s record scorer says he expects to serve as a substitute rather than reclaim a regular starting role. He plans to return to Major League Soccer when its season begins in March.

Medical researchers are reconsidering whether curveballs alone explain arm injuries among young baseball pitchers. Little League has introduced limits to prevent overuse, while some doctors say children should avoid the pitch entirely. Roughly 2.6 million young people play Little League worldwide, making the debate a large public-health question.

Defending champion Andy Murray was defeated by Bulgaria’s Grigor Dimitrov in the Wimbledon quarterfinals. Dimitrov dominated the opening set and then held off Murray’s attempts to recover. Novak Djokovic advanced to face Dimitrov, while Roger Federer will meet Milos Raonic in the other semifinal.

An “Inside Africa” program is examining the continent’s role on the United Nations Security Council and the political issues surrounding it. Alicia Keys discusses her humanitarian work, while photographer Tim Hetherington’s images from Liberia are featured in a separate segment. The broadcast also includes the World Food Prize and an interview with Nigeria’s foreign minister.

Caroline Smith DeWaal warns that a government shutdown could interrupt inspections designed to keep contaminated food off store shelves. A recent salmonella outbreak demonstrates how many agencies must coordinate to identify a source and protect consumers. If inspectors are furloughed, dangerous products may remain in circulation longer.

A government study reports that autism diagnoses have increased, but the rise is uneven across regions, genders, and racial groups. Researcher Catherine Lord says those differences may reveal how access to services and diagnostic practices affect the numbers. Families seeking help are being urged to remain persistent while scientists investigate the trend.

Three flight attendants were hurt when severe turbulence struck a plane traveling from Brazil to Miami. The aircraft was carrying 167 passengers, none of whom required treatment, according to the airline. The crew completed the journey after the damaged cabin was inspected.

The United Nations is asking countries to help relocate Palestinian refugees living in camps near the Iraq-Syria border. About two thousand people are in the camps, with several dozen more arriving each week. Aid agencies say medical treatment and safe resettlement are urgently needed as conditions deteriorate.

Representative Steve Israel accused Republicans of ignoring economic problems and abandoning issues important to ordinary Americans. He listed failed proposals, missed opportunities, and policies he believes will hurt the party in the next election. Israel says voters will eventually punish what he calls the GOP’s misplaced priorities.

Germany overwhelmed Argentina 4–0 in Cape Town, scoring early and never allowing the quarterfinal to become competitive. Thomas Muller headed the opening goal, while Arne Friedrich scored his first for the national team. Germany will next meet European champion Spain in the semifinal.

Real Madrid will meet Manchester United in the Champions League knockout round, sending Cristiano Ronaldo back to the club where he became a star. Barcelona drew AC Milan in another meeting of former European champions. Celtic will face Juventus, while Bayern Munich was paired with Arsenal.

Tiger Woods won a World Golf Championship in Florida by two strokes over Steve Stricker. Rory McIlroy’s closing 65 moved him into eighth place. The victory gives Woods momentum heading toward the Masters at Augusta, the first major championship of the year.

Tiger Woods has become one of the most recognizable athletes in the world and can make a credible claim to being golf’s greatest player. In 2008 he was reportedly the highest-paid sportsman, earning about $110 million. His fame extends far beyond the courses where he won his major titles.

Army Specialist Alexis Hutchinson is refusing deployment orders because the childcare arrangement for her son collapsed. She says the child’s grandmother can no longer provide the care promised to the Army. Military officials respond that Hutchinson had enough time to secure another plan and must answer the order.

Cristiano Ronaldo says Real Madrid must win the Champions League despite the pressure created by its history. The club has taken Europe’s top trophy nine times but only once in the past decade. Ronaldo believes Madrid can eliminate his former team, Manchester United, and says he intends to complete his contract in Spain.

CNN is providing extended coverage of the World Economic Forum in Davos, including a final session organized with the forum itself. Former British Prime Minister Tony Blair will lead a panel on the issues dominating the meeting. The broadcast will combine interviews, economic analysis, and the scenery of the Swiss resort.

Tony Fernandes built Asia’s largest budget airline after buying AirAsia for only twenty-six cents in 2001. He had studied in Britain and worked for Richard Branson’s Virgin Records before entering aviation. Fernandes says low fares succeed when the company makes travel feel ordinary rather than luxurious.

An oil spill has turned part of Koh Samet’s shoreline black, threatening one of Thailand’s most popular weekend destinations. Roughly five thousand liters have reached the island, and opposition lawmakers say the damage may be worse than officials first admitted. Cleanup crews are trying to protect nearby beaches and marine life.

Travelers who want to escape Christmas crowds often choose Morocco, where the holiday is less dominant in public life. Iceland offers another alternative for visitors who prefer nightlife and winter scenery, though the parties can be exhausting. Neither destination promises presents, but that is the point for some travelers.

Philippe Cousteau is exploring Sumatra’s rainforest for a CNN special on the island’s shrinking wildlife habitat. Tigers, elephants, rhinoceroses, and orangutans still live there together, making Sumatra unique. Deforestation and the loss of species are transforming a region once treated as nearly inexhaustible.

The Pacific Tsunami Warning Center has canceled its alert after the earthquake near Chile produced only modest waves in the Pacific. Japan’s largest recorded wave reached about four feet, with the first one arriving at Minami Torishima. Officials continue to review coastal measurements even after the immediate danger has passed.

Galatasaray has agreed to sign Didier Drogba from Shanghai Shenhua, while Nicolas Anelka may also leave the Chinese club. In Italy, Juventus was fined after officials said its players and staff behaved aggressively toward referee Marco Guida. The two stories illustrate how quickly high-profile football careers can change direction.

Researchers estimate that browsing the web produces about twenty milligrams of carbon dioxide each second. Data centers are often blamed for the internet’s emissions, but many companies are improving their efficiency. Google argues that moving information electronically can still be cleaner than moving people or goods physically.

President Obama is meeting with the leaders of Canada and Mexico at a summit where conservationists want the monarch butterfly included on the agenda. The species suffered its worst recorded year in 2013, threatening an insect shared by all three countries. Carter Roberts and Omar Vidal say protecting migration routes requires a continental response.

Twitter is changing how it displays conversations so that replies appear in chronological order. Users can share an entire exchange by email or publish individual messages from mobile applications. The update is meant to make long discussions easier to follow without opening each tweet separately.

John Kerry says the United States should gather more information before judging Pakistan’s actions, while Senator Richard Lugar calls the country strategically indispensable. Witnesses before a Senate committee argue that Washington needs a different approach to its complicated ally. The proposed shift would combine pressure with continued engagement.

Researchers say unusually large waves in the Mediterranean can form when wind, currents, and the shape of the seabed interact. The phenomenon is unrelated to the tsunami waves generated by the Chilean earthquake. Scientists are studying historical records to determine whether these storms are becoming more frequent.

Two airplanes were cleared after separate security incidents, one at John Wayne Airport and the other at Phoenix Sky Harbor. Authorities searched the aircraft and questioned passengers before allowing operations to resume. Neither event produced evidence of a continuing threat.

Scientists say they have identified a crucial component of the H5N1 bird-flu virus that could guide the development of better treatments. Since 2003, the World Health Organization has confirmed hundreds of human infections. China reported a possible human-to-human case in 2005, increasing concern about the virus’s potential.

The White House is declining to discuss the details of a letter Barack Obama reportedly sent to Iran seeking dialogue. Iranian sources say Ayatollah Ali Khamenei has not answered the message, which was sent before Iran’s disputed election. He referred indirectly to the letter during a later sermon without describing its contents.

Homeland Security Secretary Janet Napolitano is visiting Mexico, Guatemala, El Salvador, Costa Rica, and Panama on a five-day tour. She says Mexico remains safe for ordinary American tourists despite concerns about violence. The trip is intended to combine security cooperation with support for trade and regional travel.

Secretary of State John Kerry arrived in Egypt shortly before former President Mohamed Morsi’s trial was to begin. The visit is the highest-level American trip since the coup that removed Morsi. Kerry urged political reform and defended the suspension of military aid, saying it was a signal rather than a punishment.

Hungary is asking the European Union and the IMF for assistance as fears grow that its debt could become unmanageable. Debt equals roughly eighty percent of the country’s economic output, and major ratings agencies have reduced its bonds to junk status. A dispute over Hungary’s new constitution is making negotiations with Europe harder.

Ghana’s elections are being watched as an example of democratic continuity in Africa. Since 1992, the country has held five elections that ended with power transferring peacefully. Scholar George Ayittey credits free media and civil-society organizations and says other countries could learn from the model.

Windows 8 is going on sale after midnight, available as a download, on new computers, or in a boxed upgrade. The operating system combines a tablet-style interface with traditional PC functions, which may require existing users to learn new habits. Microsoft is charging forty dollars for the online upgrade.

Walter Isaacson says Steve Jobs regretted waiting too long before undergoing surgery for cancer. Isaacson discussed the authorized biography on “60 Minutes” shortly before the book’s release. The interview presents Jobs as a brilliant but difficult founder who continued working while making deeply personal medical decisions.

CNN journalists have been denied credentials in Venezuela, where President Nicolas Maduro accuses the network of spreading “war propaganda.” The dispute comes during anti-government demonstrations and heightened political tension. CNN says the restrictions prevent it from reporting freely on events already drawing international attention.

Veronica Campbell-Brown has been cleared by Jamaican officials to compete again after testing positive for a banned substance. The IAAF must still decide whether the three-time Olympic champion can return. Other Jamaican sprinters, including Asafa Powell and Sherone Simpson, have also faced positive tests this year.

Australian fast bowler Brett Lee is retiring from Test cricket after a career repeatedly interrupted by injuries. Lee won seventy-six international caps and will remain available for one-day matches. At thirty-three, he says the decision reflects the physical demands of the longest form of the game.

Ernie Els won the British Open at Royal Lytham after Adam Scott bogeyed the final four holes. The one-stroke victory gave Els his second Open title and turned a late collapse into one of golf’s most painful finishes. Tiger Woods shared third after a triple bogey damaged his challenge.

Old footage has surfaced of Susan Boyle singing at a football club social event twenty-five years ago. She appears younger and slimmer, but the voice that later made her famous is already recognizable as she performs a Barbra Streisand song. Boyle became an international sensation after appearing on television last month.

Garrett Billings is regarded as one of Canada’s most promising lacrosse forwards and plays box lacrosse for the Toronto Rock. He is taking the summer away from competition to prepare for his wedding in June. Coaches say the break may help him return with greater focus.

More than ten thousand people sent photographs to a CNN and Instagram project documenting Barack Obama’s inauguration. The images show a crowd that included families, activists, tourists, and longtime supporters. One participant said being present made the ceremony feel both patriotic and historic.

Two hundred guests at a Hong Kong hotel have been released after spending a week confined during a swine-flu scare. Officials wanted to prevent a repeat of the SARS epidemic and kept the building closed for cleaning and disinfection. No large outbreak was linked to the hotel.

Travel analyst Brett Snyder says passengers should receive a refund when an airline fails to deliver their luggage. Delta offers vouchers of $25 to $50 for bags delayed more than twelve hours, while Frontier refunds baggage fees when suitcases miss the flight entirely. Policies vary widely, leaving travelers to study the fine print after a problem occurs.

Picaridin, IR3535, oil of lemon eucalyptus, and DEET all protect against biting insects. Despite its reputation, DEET has been found both effective and relatively safe when used as directed. Experts also recommend long clothing and removing standing water as insect-borne diseases become more common in the United States.

A new Taipei tour lets visitors spend four hours riding in a local taxi wherever ordinary passengers happen to go. The appeal is the lack of a fixed itinerary and the chance to talk with residents. One English traveler was even invited to dinner by a Taiwanese family encountered during the ride.

The Jacksons are scheduled to perform forty shows during their residency at Planet Hollywood in Las Vegas. Meat Loaf will appear in the same concert series shortly before the run begins. The engagement is expected to attract fans of both the family group and the long-running rock singer.

Stephen Colbert won a public vote to name a new space-station treadmill, but NASA chose “Tranquility” for the station node instead. The host joked that the agency had rejected the more playful option after inviting suggestions. The treadmill will still carry Colbert’s name, preserving part of the joke.

Aziz Rana says Republicans have a clear language of freedom built around markets and individual autonomy, while Democrats struggle to connect government programs to liberty. He argues that conservative rhetoric often protects corporate freedom more effectively than personal freedom. Democrats, Rana says, must explain how regulation and social programs can expand people’s choices.

Baku is using oil and gas wealth to transform itself from an energy capital into a broader technology and cultural center. The Azerbaijani government is increasing natural-gas production while encouraging information businesses. The city is also campaigning to host the 2020 Olympics, an ambitious symbol of its new confidence.

The internet’s “check-in” is moving beyond telling friends where you are. New services allow users to announce which websites they are reading and collect badges for their habits. OneTrueFan, Badgeville, and BigDoor Media are competing to make browsing a social activity.

Longtime Comic-Con attendees are complaining that the convention has expanded too far beyond comics and science fiction. Some believe celebrity and mainstream pop-culture panels have displaced the event’s original purpose. Last year, crowds of “Twilight” fans created traffic problems that intensified the argument.

Desertification is affecting hundreds of millions of people, including communities in China that regularly face enormous dust storms. Governments promote tree belts and other “green wall” projects, but critics say local land management is more effective than a single grand solution. The best approach may combine regional planning with careful use of water and soil.

“Just Like Us” follows comedians performing in Egypt, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, and Dubai. Ahmed Ahmed created the tour to show American audiences that Arab humor often depends on the same awkwardness and family experiences found in American comedy. Stand-up is relatively new in much of the region but is growing quickly.

Fans of “Swamp People” have used social media to mourn Mitchell Guist, whose quiet life on the Louisiana waterways made him feel like a relative to many viewers. Commenters say the program offered a version of simplicity rarely shown on television. Guist’s death has made that image seem more fragile.

Mike Rowe has been criticized by viewers who believe his comments trivialized a project to save endangered whooping cranes. Rowe says he was neither bored nor dismissive, but simply questioned how the project was presented. He acknowledges that many people feel a deep responsibility toward animals at risk of disappearing.

Governors will influence how congressional districts are redrawn after the next census. Eighteen states are expected to gain or lose representation, and even a one-seat change can force an entire map to be reconsidered. The process could shift the balance of power long before voters cast a ballot.

Architect Zaha Hadid says the design of new luxury superyachts resembles an anatomical system, with structural frames spreading like veins. The Iraqi-born British architect is also interested in designing Baghdad’s central bank, a project she calls personally meaningful. She argues that governments, not individual designers, must be responsible for construction workers’ conditions.

Don Horton was forty-eight when Parkinson’s disease made it impossible for him to button his shirt in the locker room. The coach describes that moment as the point when the illness stopped being an abstract diagnosis. He has since adjusted his work and daily routines while continuing to lead athletes.

New York and New Jersey are competing for the economic benefits of Super Bowl XLVIII. Organizers predict that the game will generate at least $600 million, though East Rutherford hopes simply to avoid losing money. The stadium’s location has turned a single sporting event into a regional political argument.

Diana Nyad has completed her long swim from Cuba to Florida at age sixty-four, five attempts after she first tried the route in 1978. Her achievement has renewed attention to women who set records in extreme sports, from open-water swimming to high-altitude climbing. Nyad says persistence mattered more than any single day of athletic performance.

Bayern Munich chairman Karl-Heinz Rummenigge says he once feared the club would fall out of Europe’s elite. Bayern’s decision to keep Franck Ribery instead of selling him marked a turning point, he believes. The club is now pursuing another Bundesliga title and hopes to defend its European crown.

Operation Prom collects donated formal clothing for teenagers who cannot afford dresses or suits for school dances. Founder Keren Charles began the nonprofit in New York in 2005 after seeing how much a lack of money could exclude young people from ordinary milestones. Volunteers sort, fit, and distribute the clothing at no cost.

Manny Pacquiao is meeting Juan Manuel Marquez for the third time, years after leaving poverty to earn money as a boxer. Pacquiao now gives part of his fortune to people in need and serves in the Philippine Congress. He says fighting changed his family’s life, but politics may let him change the system that kept others poor.

Tunisian actor Dhafer L’Abidine says censorship has eased since the country’s uprising. He is best known to Western audiences for appearing in “Sex and the City 2,” but his career began at home. L’Abidine believes the new openness will allow local filmmakers to address subjects they previously avoided.

Some Halloween businesses operate all year. Raven’s Grin Inn frightens visitors through the summer, while a Las Vegas Halloween store occupies twenty-five thousand square feet and never closes. For its owners, the holiday is less a date on the calendar than a permanent industry.

Canada won Olympic men’s hockey gold for the second consecutive Games by shutting out Sweden 3–0. Carey Price stopped twenty-four shots. Russia dominated the fifty-kilometer cross-country race and led both the overall and gold-medal tables in Sochi.

Emil Zatopek won the 5,000 meters, 10,000 meters, and marathon at the 1952 Helsinki Olympics, a distance combination no one had previously managed. His wife, Dana, won javelin gold at the same Games. The couple’s medals are preserved in Prague’s national archive.

Tennis is moving into a football setting for an exhibition at Cowboys Stadium, where Serena Williams will face Maria Sharapova and Andy Roddick will play John Isner. The huge venue will be reduced to twenty thousand seats for the event. Organizers at Brussels’ King Baudouin Stadium hope to draw an even larger crowd later in the week.

A majority of mobile users say local information is easier to obtain now than it was five years ago. The survey found especially high use among parents and measured different habits among Hispanic, Black, and white Americans. Weather, traffic, local news, and restaurant information are among the most common searches.

A German startup has designed a pen that vibrates when it detects a spelling or handwriting error. Lernstift contains a computer and motion sensor capable of recognizing the way letters and words are formed. The company is using a Kickstarter campaign to finance further development and production.

Christmas in the Philippines begins as early as September and can continue until January. Families attend traditional masses, hang lanterns made from paper and bamboo, and compete to create the most elaborate decorations. The long season combines religious observance with a strong emphasis on reunions and hospitality.

The United States is sending paratroopers to Poland and other NATO countries as a demonstration of support after Russia moved troops near Ukraine. The exercises are intended to reassure allies without provoking a direct confrontation. Members of Congress call the deployment an appropriate first response, though analysts disagree about its message to Moscow.

Mainz has opened the Bundesliga season with six straight victories, including a 2–1 upset of Bayern Munich in Munich. Young coach Thomas Tuchel has made the club one of the early stories of the campaign. A win against Hoffenheim would give Mainz seven victories, matching a German league record.

Readers of Travel + Leisure have ranked several Southern resorts among America’s best coastal hotels. The Lodge and the Cloister on Georgia’s Sea Island received especially high marks. At the Four Seasons Hualalai, guests can now choose from ten outdoor treatment rooms in an expanded spa.

Japan’s governing party hopes to legalize casino gambling and permit large integrated resorts in major cities. Supporters say gaming revenue could help an economy that has struggled for years. Critics fear the policy would create new social problems and that the economic benefits have been overstated.

Barack Obama will use the same Bible Abraham Lincoln carried at his first inauguration. Lincoln opened the book to a random page in 1861, while other presidents have selected verses that reflected the moment. The object has become a symbol of continuity between two inaugurations shaped by national division.

Apple’s latest quarterly report shows lower profits even though sales exceeded expectations. Analyst Andrew Mayer says the company risks becoming an imitator if it responds only with larger screens and slightly bigger devices. Apple, he argues, needs a genuinely new product rather than another variation on the iPhone or iPad.

France placed two riders on the Tour de France podium for the first time since 1984. Jean-Christophe Peraud finished second and Thibaut Pinot third, behind Italy’s Vincenzo Nibali. The result gives French cycling its strongest finish since Bernard Hinault won the race in 1985.

Mitt Romney says religious conviction and political freedom should strengthen one another, but he does not intend to merge church and state. He acknowledges that his argument will be compared with John F. Kennedy’s 1960 speech about Catholicism and public office. Romney says his beliefs will influence his presidency without becoming official doctrine.

Two men who once hoped to ride every attraction at Walt Disney World failed in 2013 when a storm interrupted them. They returned the following year and completed the challenge in seventeen hours, covering twenty-two miles between parks. The achievement required more stamina than either expected from a vacation.

Radamel Falcao has joined Manchester United on a one-year loan from Monaco as the club tries to revive a poor opening to the season. United has collected only two points from its first three matches. Some supporters are pleased by the striker’s arrival but wonder why the club did not strengthen its defense.

Brazil survived Chile and advanced, while the Netherlands prepared to face Mexico’s disciplined defense. Algeria and Germany have met several times, and the historical record favors Germany. Colombia has become a popular neutral favorite, led by the emerging star James Rodriguez.

Wisconsin’s Republican attorney general is appealing a judge’s decision to delay a law that Democrats say was passed in violation of open-meetings rules. The attorney general argues that the judge lacks authority over the legislature. Senate Democrats insist that public access requirements cannot be ignored for political convenience.

Israel is building taller burial structures as available land becomes scarce and Jewish law rules out cremation. China, India, and Brazil are experimenting with similar vertical cemeteries. The arrangements preserve traditional burial practices while using far less ground than ordinary graveyards.

Developers plan to build an underwater hotel in the Maldives, allowing guests to wake beside coral reefs and passing marine life. The structure resembles three connected saucers and is being designed to limit damage to the surrounding ecosystem. Its futuristic appearance has already drawn comparisons with a James Bond set.

Fewer than two hundred days remain before Euro 2012 begins in Poland and Ukraine. Eight cities will host the tournament, with Warsaw staging the opening match and Kyiv hosting the final. Supporters are arranging travel across two countries whose infrastructure must handle a sudden influx of visitors.

Colorado’s White River National Forest is the most visited forest in the United States. Travelers seeking a different kind of spectacle can see millions of lights at Georgia’s Callaway Gardens or visit Rovaniemi, Finland, promoted as the official home of Santa Claus. The destinations show how varied a “nature trip” can be.

Presidential historians are divided over how George W. Bush will be remembered. Julian Zelizer says historians currently express little goodwill toward him, though Harry Truman’s reputation improved long after leaving office. Another scholar predicts that Bush will be remembered chiefly for incompetence rather than for the controversies surrounding his presidency.

Paris Saint-Germain has won France’s title for the second year in a row, while Monaco was unable to close the gap. PSG nevertheless lost its final home match to Rennes, and Monaco drew with Guingamp. The result shows how a champion can celebrate even after ending the season with an unexpected defeat.

Wolfsburg striker Edin Dzeko expects to leave for AC Milan after informing his German club that he wants a transfer. The Bosnian scored twenty-six goals last season and helped Wolfsburg win the Bundesliga. Milan sees him as a forward capable of providing the scoring power needed for a title challenge.

Roger Federer opened his U.S. Open campaign with a victory as he pursues a sixth title. Andy Murray also advanced, although rain delayed the conclusion of his match in New York. Unseeded American Jack Sock reached the second round when Florian Mayer retired with an injury.

Rafael Nadal reached the final after defeating Roger Federer in four sets. He will face either Novak Djokovic or Andy Murray and has extended his career advantage over Federer to eighteen victories against nine defeats. Djokovic, the defending champion, meets Murray in the other semifinal.

Rafael Nadal is the only former champion still alive at Indian Wells after beating John Isner in three sets. Novak Djokovic was eliminated by Ivan Ljubicic, while Andy Murray advanced when Nicolas Almagro retired. The result leaves Nadal with a clearer route to another title.

Maria Sharapova withdrew from the Pan Pacific Open after twisting an ankle against Petra Kvitova. Novak Djokovic also pulled out of the China Open because of injury. Players have warned that an overfilled schedule is producing exhaustion, and some have discussed striking for a lighter calendar.

Roger Federer began the Kooyong Classic with a straight-set victory over Carlos Moya. Fernando Verdasco and Fernando Gonzalez also advanced. The exhibition gives players a final competitive test before the Australian Open, even though its matches do not affect the official rankings.

David Frum calls Edmund Burke the first conservative but says Burke would reject the radical individualism common in modern American politics. Burke emphasized community, inherited institutions, and responsibility to future generations. Two new books, Frum argues, show why those ideas deserve another hearing.

Sam Waley-Cohen is known both for riding racehorses and for running a multimillion-dollar dental company. He is one of the favorites for the Grand National and rides with his late brother’s initials on the saddle. Waley-Cohen says the tribute is more important than the publicity surrounding his business success.

Wrigley’s caffeinated Alert Energy Gum has attracted the attention of federal regulators. The FDA is asking the company how much caffeine the product delivers and whether consumers understand the risks. Other caffeinated gums remain on the market while officials decide whether broader rules are needed.

An asteroid roughly forty yards wide will pass within thirty-eight thousand miles of Earth. Astronomers say it poses no danger and was discovered by Robert McNaught from a telescope in rural Australia. The close approach offers scientists an opportunity to refine observations of a relatively small space object.

Bo Jackson was disturbed by the tornadoes that struck his home state of Alabama and responded by starting an annual bicycle ride to raise money for survivors. Bo Bikes Bama supports shelters and other community projects. Jackson says the event lets residents contribute long after television crews have left.

Christophe Lemaitre won the 100 meters at the European Championships in Barcelona with a time of 10.11 seconds. Britain’s Mark Lewis-Francis took silver in a close finish, while legally blind runner Jason Smyth reached the semifinal. Lemaitre’s victory made him one of Europe’s most prominent young sprinters.

Hong Kong is running out of space not only for graves but also for storing cremated remains. Private columbaria have appeared to meet demand, though many operate without legal approval. Because ancestor veneration remains important, families are reluctant to scatter ashes and are willing to pay heavily for a permanent place.

Grammy-winning musician Zac Brown has begun serving meals to selected fans at his concerts. Chef Rusty Hamlin prepares food for roughly 150 guests while Brown talks with them and listens without the usual cameras or autograph lines. Brown says removing the performance machinery makes the exchange feel more genuine.

The United States calls Russia’s plan to send long-range patrols near the Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico provocative and potentially destabilizing. Moscow says the flights are a response to American actions in Ukraine and may pass close to U.S. territorial waters. Analysts view the deployment as a deliberate message rather than preparation for an attack.

Jonathan Eyal says the agreement over Ukraine may stop the fighting temporarily without creating a durable peace. He believes Vladimir Putin could be trying to leave the country divided and economically broken, while the western region becomes a failed state. The longer the conflict continues, Eyal argues, the harder it will be for anyone to control the forces released by it.

A Florida man heard a kitten meowing inside the bed of his pickup truck and cut through the metal to reach it. Humane Society workers helped complete the rescue. Donations are now being collected to repair the truck, turning an expensive accident into an unlikely community story.

Ivory Coast remains a popular choice to win the African Cup of Nations, but Guinea scored first in their match through Mohamed Yattara. Ivory Coast was reduced to ten men when Gervinho was sent off, then Seydou Doumbia equalized with less than twenty minutes left. The favorites escaped without losing.

Ghana and Algeria have advanced to the quarterfinals of the African Cup of Nations. Algeria defeated Senegal through goals from Riyad Mahrez and Nabil Bentaleb, while Ghana needed a late strike to overcome South Africa. Both teams are now one victory from the semifinals.

CNN is asking readers to share photographs of their 1960s clothes, from miniskirts and patterned shirts to conservative family portraits. Participants can submit images through iReport and take a quiz assigning them a “sixties personality.” The project invites nostalgia while acknowledging that the decade looked different across social classes.

Low salaries are pushing some talented athletes away from minor-league baseball, while cricket organizers are trying to build a professional game in the United States. Coach Julien Fountain has created a Twenty20 development program for emerging players. One former baseballer says he now dreams of becoming the world’s best cricketer instead.

Social-media users have offered Jon Stewart a wide range of careers after his television show ends, including running for office and replacing Katy Perry’s famous Left Shark. The suggestions mix sincere admiration with jokes about his political commentary. Stewart has not announced what he plans to do next.

CNN’s travel galleries are collecting photographs of Ireland, beaches, and other destinations from readers. Contributors can submit images through iReport and follow the project on Twitter. The editors say the galleries are intended to show places through travelers’ eyes rather than through professional tourism campaigns.

Fans became concerned after “Star Trek” actor Leonard Nimoy was reportedly taken to a hospital. Former castmates sent public good wishes, and viewers shared messages of support online. The incident reminded fans how strongly Nimoy’s portrayal of Spock had shaped several generations of the franchise.

Portland’s mayor says two winter storms arriving close together will make cleanup difficult. Another system may reach Boston and New England on Sunday night, following a fast-moving disturbance from western Canada. Crews are trying to clear roads before the next accumulation begins.

The FAA is reminding Super Bowl spectators that the airspace around the stadium will be a “No Drone Zone.” The temporary restriction is intended to prevent unmanned aircraft from interfering with aircraft, security, or the broadcast. Officials say violations could lead to serious penalties.

Eric Liu remembers becoming absorbed in “Star Trek” as a boy growing up in an immigrant household. The show gave him an imaginative picture of a future in which people from different backgrounds worked together. Liu says that fictional world still resembles the society he hopes to see in real life.

A Dubai construction company has proposed a 540-meter tower in Casablanca called Al Noor. If built, it would be Africa’s tallest skyscraper and a symbol of Morocco’s growing ambitions. The project still requires planning approval and a final site before construction can begin.

Ghana defeated Algeria 1–0 when Asamoah Gyan scored in the final moments. Gyan had recently recovered from malaria, making his return particularly important to the team. The victory keeps Ghana’s hopes alive for its first African Cup title in thirty-three years, while Senegal and South Africa drew in the other group match.

Tina Maze won the Alpine combined at the world championships, adding a third medal at Beaver Creek. The Slovenian has already taken gold in downhill and silver in super-G and is aiming to become the first woman to win five individual medals at one championship. The giant slalom offers another opportunity.

Ford Vox says an outbreak of a drug-resistant CRE superbug requires hospitals and government agencies to coordinate immediately.
