He believes a difficult-to-clean medical device helped spread the infection and accuses the FDA of responding too slowly. The outbreak demonstrates how quickly a hospital problem can become a national health concern.

New images of the “Pillars of Creation” reveal a more detailed view of the famous star-forming region first photographed in 1995. The updated picture shows additional structure inside the clouds of gas and dust. Astronomers say the image is both visually dramatic and scientifically useful.

One couple chose DivorceHotel for a Valentine’s Day separation, hoping to end a twenty-five-year marriage without a prolonged courtroom battle. The company says its process costs less and encourages partners to negotiate in a controlled setting. The couple has four children and wants the breakup to remain as peaceful as possible.

China’s economy is slowing as wages rise and inflation puts pressure on manufacturers. The change may allow Bangladesh, Cambodia, Pakistan, and other Asian countries to attract factories seeking cheaper labor. Economists say the slowdown is painful for China but could open an important opportunity for its neighbors.

Iranian negotiator Abbas Araqchi says Secretary of State John Kerry will meet Iran’s foreign minister on Sunday. Washington has not immediately confirmed the appointment. The proposed meeting comes as the two countries attempt to narrow differences over Iran’s nuclear program.

Adidas is producing sneakers inspired by the distinctive carpet at Portland International Airport just as the airport plans to remove the design after twenty-seven years. The carpet has generated poems, beer, and online tributes. Its popularity shows that even a utilitarian public surface can become part of a city’s identity.

Vladimir Putin’s approval rating has remained near eighty-five percent since last May. Analysts disagree about whether the number reflects genuine support, patriotic response to foreign-policy events, or limits on dissent in Russian media. The stability of the figure is itself becoming a subject of political debate.

Hollywood has announced an all-female “Ghostbusters” reboot, but critics say one diverse cast does not solve the industry’s larger lack of representation. Women and minority filmmakers remain underrepresented both in front of and behind the camera. The announcement has therefore prompted celebration and a renewed argument about who receives major studio opportunities.

Thieves broke into Red Bull’s Formula One headquarters and stole more than sixty trophies. Police say six men used two cars to remove the collection, whose monetary value is limited but whose significance to the team is enormous. Christian Horner called the burglary devastating and asked fans to help identify the missing objects.

King Abdullah has been buried in Riyadh, and Saudi Arabia has quickly named his brother Salman as the new monarch. Salman called for unity and solidarity among Muslims in his first remarks. The rapid succession is intended to reassure the kingdom during a period of regional tension.

World Hijab Day is intended to show that many Muslim women wear the headscarf by choice rather than coercion. Its organizers describe the hijab as an expression of modesty and faith, while asking non-Muslim women to try wearing one for a day. The event has generated both support and debate about representation.

Uber’s reputation is under pressure from criticism of its management and treatment of drivers, but the company continues to expand rapidly. Analysts note that businesses sometimes grow while their public image deteriorates. Uber’s challenge will be deciding whether to change its leadership before the controversy begins to affect operations.

Cloud Cast is a personal cooling system that uses ultrasonic sensors to detect a person and direct a small flow of water toward that individual. The prototype is being shown in Dubai as part of research into alternatives to conventional air conditioning. Designers are also studying wind towers and other traditional methods of moving cool air.

A Norwegian company is designing a cargo ship whose tall sides act as sails. The developers claim the VindSkip could cut fuel consumption by sixty percent and carbon emissions by eighty percent. If construction proceeds, the first vessel may enter service by 2019.

Heart disease remains the leading cause of death for both American women and men, but a study found that women without the disease often shared six basic habits. Exercise, healthy weight, and not smoking were among them. Researchers say the advice is simple, even if changing daily behavior is not.

Prince William and Kate Middleton are spending their honeymoon in the Seychelles, where privacy and environmental standards narrowed the likely choices. North Island is considered the leading possibility, though resorts on Desroches, Fregate, Mahe, and Cousine islands have also been discussed. Officials are keeping the couple’s location secret.

William Petersen is leaving “CSI” after the character’s final episode, ending his run at the top of a successful television franchise. The actor says he was ready for a change rather than forced out. Laurence Fishburne will join the show as it introduces a new central character.

J.J. Abrams’s “Star Trek” earned $72.5 million in its opening weekend, while “Wolverine” fell sharply to $27 million. Total ticket sales were nearly twenty-two percent higher than during the same weekend a year earlier. The week’s ranking reflects both a strong new release and a sequel losing momentum.

Disney’s family comedy led the weekend with an estimated $32.2 million. The sixth “Harry Potter” film followed with $30 million, while “The Ugly Truth,” starring Katherine Heigl and Gerard Butler, opened at $27 million. Several other releases competed for places in the week’s top ten.

Ron Asheton, guitarist for the Stooges, has died at sixty. The band helped shape the aggressive sound of late-1960s and early-1970s rock and was later nominated for the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Asheton’s guitar work influenced musicians who would become central to punk.

Spike Lee’s “Miracle at St. Anna” follows African-American soldiers during World War II and is based on a novel by James McBride, who also wrote the screenplay. A reviewer praises the subject but finds the film diffuse and emotionally distant. The central criticism is that Lee’s filmmaking lacks the energy the story demands.

Chris Brown addressed rumors that he and Rihanna had reunited after she appeared on “Watch What Happens Live.” Rihanna denied that they were a couple but described Brown as “pretty dope.” Their comments revived public discussion of a relationship both performers have tried to define privately.

The cast of “The Big Bang Theory” appeared at a PaleyFest panel that offered few plot spoilers but plenty of stories about working together. Actors described the show’s unusual routines and shared jokes from behind the scenes. The nineteenth episode of the sixth season is scheduled to air that night.

“Sharknado 2” is arriving with a week of related shark programming, and a third film has already been ordered. The franchise’s appeal rests on treating absurd disaster as an interactive joke. Viewers are invited to watch the films while commenting on the increasingly improbable attacks.

Entertainment Weekly imagines where the characters from “Breaking Bad” might be a decade after the finale. Brock becomes a successful student and soccer player, while Skyler survives a battle with lung cancer. The exercise is less a prediction than a way to consider which futures the series denied its characters.

“Jeopardy!” is inviting celebrities including Anderson Cooper, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, and Lewis Black to compete during Power Players Week. Each contestant will raise at least $10,000 for charity, while winners receive a larger donation. The unusual lineup combines journalists, athletes, and comedians who are accustomed to answering questions in public.

“The Closer” ended Kyra Sedgwick’s run as Deputy Chief Johnson with a finale designed to resolve the character’s career. Mary McDonnell will continue the police world in the spinoff “Major Crimes.” The transition gives viewers a new lead while preserving the original show’s institutional setting.

Television networks are filling the weekend with marathons, including two full days of “Harry Potter” films. Comedy Central, BBC America, E!, and other channels are also repeating their most recognizable series. The schedule is designed for viewers who want to spend a rainy weekend inside a familiar fictional world.

Brett Butler will appear as a neighbor on “The Young and the Restless.” The actress is best known for starring in “Grace Under Fire” and recently completed work on “Anger Management.” The soap role gives Butler a return to regular television after several years of less visible projects.

MTV’s “Miley: The Movement” follows Miley Cyrus through the months surrounding her controversial Video Music Awards performance. The program presents her as ambitious, uncertain, and closely attached to her mother. Its central message is that Cyrus is still changing rather than presenting a finished celebrity identity.

Mariah Carey says she was disappointed by “American Idol” because she expected the judging panel to contain three people. She praised the contestants despite her frustration with the production. Carey’s comments add to the tension surrounding a season in which the judges have frequently disagreed in public.

NBC is removing “Animal Practice” from its Wednesday schedule and replacing it with “Whitney.” The network has not announced when “Community” will return. The decision reflects the speed with which broadcasters reshuffle comedies that fail to establish an audience.

Gary Oldman received an Oscar nomination that many expected to go to Michael Fassbender. Ryan Gosling and Leonardo DiCaprio were also notable omissions, while the final “Harry Potter” film was excluded from the major categories. The nominations renewed the annual argument over whether popular films receive enough recognition.

“Madagascar 3: Europe’s Most Wanted” led the weekend with $60.4 million. “Prometheus” opened in second place at $50 million, while “Snow White and the Huntsman” fell fifty-nine percent to $23 million. The figures show how quickly a film’s first-weekend excitement can fade when competing releases arrive.

“The Wolverine” earned $86.1 million in international markets during its opening weekend. “The Conjuring” held second place, while “Despicable Me 2” continued to produce strong profits in third. The results suggest that familiar franchises are still driving audiences across several countries.

The Tony Award nominations have been announced, with “Kinky Boots” leading the field at thirteen. The ceremony will air on CBS in June. The nominations place a new musical about a shoe factory at the center of Broadway’s annual competition.

“The Wolverine” led Friday’s box office, while “The Conjuring” followed with $7.4 million. “Grown Ups 2” landed in fifth place. The weekend’s results suggest that audiences remain willing to divide their money among superhero action, horror, and broad comedy.

Hundreds of thousands of American Facebook users may die this year, leaving behind accounts that families must decide whether to preserve or remove. A study of young adults found that nearly everyone in one age group used the service, meaning digital memorials will become increasingly common. Within a generation, many social-media “friends” may no longer be living people.

India’s refusal to grant a patent for a new Novartis cancer drug has protected the country’s low-cost generics industry. Novartis calls the decision harmful to patients and warns that it may withhold future medicines from the Indian market. Supporters of the ruling say affordable copies are essential in a country where brand-name treatment is out of reach for many.

Japan’s central bank has left its main policies unchanged, continuing a pattern that has lasted since April. Prime Minister Shinzo Abe wants to make the country more attractive to investors, while the bank reports that the monetary base expanded sharply in August. Officials are watching whether the stimulus produces growth or simply raises prices.

People with seasonal allergies should ask their doctors for a management plan before pollen levels rise. Experts recommend limiting outdoor activity during the morning peak and using nasal sprays regularly. Recent flooding may temporarily reduce pollen in parts of Georgia, but it also creates other health concerns.

Apple is expected to introduce software for creating interactive electronic books rather than a new device. The company may also expand the platform used to distribute the books. The tools would let publishers add video, animation, and quizzes to material that once consisted only of static pages.

LG says its new television produces unusually vivid colors because each pixel uses four colors instead of the usual three. Large OLED screens have been expensive and difficult to manufacture, so the company invested heavily in a new production plant. LG hopes the technology will make high-end displays more affordable.

Rovio has acquired “Casey’s Contraptions” and is renaming the physics game “Amazing Alex.” Players build elaborate machines from balloons, boxes, and other objects, creating chain reactions in the style of a Rube Goldberg puzzle. Rovio is using the purchase to expand beyond its “Angry Birds” franchise.

Songza presents itself as internet radio chosen by people rather than algorithms alone. Users select a mood, activity, or time of day and receive a playlist assembled by editors or listeners. The service imposes no limit on listening, betting that curation will keep people returning.

An eBay seller claims to have discovered the legal identity of the anonymous British artist Banksy and is auctioning a piece of paper bearing the alleged name. Bidding has approached one million dollars despite the lack of independent proof. The auction has become a performance of the mystery as much as a sale.

Choosing a music festival involves deciding whether to sleep in a tent or pay for a hotel. Bonnaroo and Coachella reward campers who stay for the entire weekend, but security rules prohibit bringing drugs and alcohol. Experienced festivalgoers recommend planning rest periods rather than trying to see every performance.

Volunteer organizations sometimes provide meals and lodging in exchange for several hours of work each day. Some charge a small fee to cover travel administration, while the Peace Corps offers longer placements for people seeking more than a short vacation project. Applicants should research the host organization before committing.

Several foods that seemed promising to American shoppers failed because they were simply too strange. Chocolate-covered fries, cinnamon fries, coffee-flavored gelatin, and adult versions of baby food all struggled to find a market. Novelty can attract a first purchase, but it does not guarantee a second.

Venoms that evolved to harm people may also provide medicines. Compounds from Gila monster venom can stimulate insulin production, snake venom has helped inspire blood-pressure treatments, and researchers are testing scorpion toxins against brain tumors. Scientists hope to isolate useful molecules without carrying the animals’ danger into the clinic.

In 1806, ice was a luxury that wealthy Boston merchants shipped to the Caribbean. The trade expanded to India before home freezers eventually reduced demand, though the modern ice industry still sells billions of dollars’ worth each year. The story shows how a product once considered absurd can become an everyday necessity.

Henry Ford established a rubber plantation in the Amazon without first determining whether the land suited the crop. Brazilian workers rebelled against the company’s American-style dining hall and alcohol ban, and the project collapsed. Ford eventually sold the plantation at a loss of about $20 million.

Quebec City’s historic streets and compact neighborhoods have earned comparisons with Paris, but the city is also trying to reduce its environmental footprint. Hotels and restaurants increasingly serve local products and promote sustainable practices. Visitors can experience European-looking architecture without crossing the Atlantic.

Katey Sagal’s “Sons of Anarchy” is arriving on DVD, giving viewers another chance to follow the motorcycle club drama. Sagal says motherhood has helped her understand the difficult women she plays. She has heard speculation about returning to “Lost,” but says no one involved has spoken to her directly.

A blunt advice columnist says an apology means little when someone is always late. He also argues that most men would look better in ordinary clothes than in a Speedo. His broader message is that people should risk embarrassment, show genuine feeling, and stop waiting for perfect conditions before pursuing what they want.

Kim Kardashian says accessories should be excessive when the goal is fun. She enjoys wearing jewelry but leaves the larger pieces at home when exercising. Kardashian is especially pleased to have created a jewelry line with her own name rather than merely promoting someone else’s designs.

Kasey Kahl says on Twitter that he will always care about Vienna Girardi, who won Jake Pavelka’s season of “The Bachelor.” Kahl later pursued Ali Fedotowsky on “The Bachelorette,” at one point trying to impress her with a song. Reality television has turned both relationships into public memories.

Retailers are promoting “early Black Friday” discounts as soon as Halloween, spreading the holiday-shopping season across several weeks. Consumers can compare prices online instead of waiting outside stores, but experts advise delaying the largest purchases until the final markdowns. The best deal is not always the first one advertised.

Lenny Kravitz says he accepted the role of Cinna in “The Hunger Games” because the part interested him, not because he wanted to make films simply to expand his résumé. He describes Cinna as quiet and controlled. Music remains his main career, but Kravitz now sees acting as another form of work rather than a celebrity experiment.

Neil Young’s “Le Noise” will be released on CD, vinyl, and iTunes, with later versions planned for Blu-ray and mobile applications. Young recorded the album in a Los Angeles mansion earlier in the year. The multiple formats reflect both his interest in sound and the changing ways listeners buy music.

“Le Noise” has been praised as one of Neil Young’s most intimate records in years. Many of its songs were already appearing in his live performances, where the spare arrangements were easy to hear. The album’s power comes from a deliberately narrow palette: one voice, a guitar, and no desire to disguise age.

Hodor and Bran Stark may not appear in the next season of “Game of Thrones,” according to actor Kristian Nairn. He says the characters are taking a year away from the story while production begins filming in Europe. Their absence will leave viewers waiting to see how the series handles one of its most unusual relationships.

“The Simpsons” will meet the characters from “The Tracey Ullman Show” in a crossover segment for this year’s “Treehouse of Horror.” The episode will use the original voices and revisit the family’s earliest animated form. The meeting is designed as a joke about television history as much as a conventional plot.

Brad Pitt, Shia LaBeouf, Michael Pena, Jon Bernthal, and Logan Lerman lead a World War II film about a tank crew. LaBeouf has drawn particular praise, while Pitt supplies the commanding presence expected of him. Lerman anchors the story by portraying a young soldier learning what the crew’s survival requires.

Fresh Tracks Cafe in Nelson, British Columbia, is known for inexpensive food that appeals to skiers. Utah’s Yurt at Solitude rewards visitors who make the three-quarter-mile trek, while Whistler’s Crystal Hut is famous for waffles. The restaurants prove that a mountain meal can be part of the destination rather than a break from it.

The National Ignition Facility has produced a laser burst containing 1.85 megajoules, more energy than any previous laser experiment. Researchers are studying whether controlled fusion can provide clean energy and improve national security. The result is significant because the facility’s purpose is to make a tiny reaction behave like a miniature star.

Paul Ryan weighs 163 pounds and reportedly has between six and eight percent body fat. He leads early-morning P90X workouts for congressional staff, turning exercise into part of the Capitol routine. The standard home program costs about $120, a small price compared with the political attention Ryan’s fitness attracts.

Hotel restaurants have become more ambitious since the 1990s, offering food that competes with independent destinations. China Poblano in Las Vegas combines Chinese and Mexican flavors, Redd Wood serves Napa Valley visitors, and Southern Art in Atlanta features a bar devoted to artisanal ham. Travelers no longer have to leave a hotel to find interesting cooking.

Copenhagen’s Tivoli Gardens becomes a field of lights during the city’s Christmas market. European advent markets have existed for centuries, selling handmade crafts, regional snacks, and hot spiced wine. The attraction is less about buying presents than about creating a warm public ritual in the darkest part of the year.

A traveler who bought nonrefundable tickets through Cheapoair was told cancellation would cost $535 per ticket. The fee followed company policy, but the amount seemed disproportionate to the customer. After the dispute was publicized, the agency agreed to issue a full refund.

A computer virus has resisted repeated attempts to remove it from systems at Creech Air Force Base. Officials do not yet know whether the malware is sophisticated or simply common software that spread widely. Both classified and unclassified machines were affected, prompting a review of military network procedures.

Tests comparing AT&T and Verizon found that AT&T’s network delivered downloads about twice as quickly, while Verizon provided more reliable voice calls. Verizon’s phone also had a ten-percent advantage when uploading data from a stationary position. The results show why choosing a carrier depends on whether speed or consistency matters more.

The Defense Department is telling troops to stop using CDs, DVDs, and thumb drives on military networks. Officials hope the ban will prevent secret information from being copied or removed. Service members who rely on the devices say the rule will slow routine work, but commanders consider the inconvenience necessary.

Down where the tide has left its lace
I carried a shovel to the sand;
I carved a little harbor there,
But every wave erased the land.
I built it once, I built it twice—
The sea kept all my ships.

Leonardo kept his counsel close,
And trusted neither crown nor throne;
For promises grow thin as smoke
When payment is not shown.

My daughter bends beneath the tree
To find the highest branch;
She looks so long the whole green crown
Seems suddenly to dance.
“The sky has fallen to my feet,”
She whispers through the leaves.

Speak of the truth as evening speaks,
In bands of rose and gray;
The naked sun can blind the eye
That meets it straight at day.
Let understanding find its pace,
Let wonder keep its wings;
The heart receives a guarded light
Before it knows what sings.

Blue wings flicker
Above the grass,
Spring remembered
As rain on glass.
Once we crawled there,
Small and slow,
Now we rise
And go.

I dreamed the moon had learned my name
And carried it across the sea;
I woke beneath a restless sky
That would not answer me.
The dark was deep, the silence wide,
Yet sleep had made me new;
I opened up my empty hands
And found the world come through.

There was an Old Woman of Rye,
Whose hat nearly covered the sky;
When the sparrows came near,
They would borrow her ear,
Then depart with a feather and fly.

Again the wind begins its song,
Five silver notes against the pane;
It urges every word to flee,
To leave the patient page.
But I have fastened language down
With knots the gusts can’t see;
The louder blows the weather comes,
The more the words are me.

I wait beside the stony tide
With your warm fingers locked in mine;
The wind climbs up the water’s face,
The clouds erase the line.
Salt strikes my mouth, the gulls wheel low,
The evening turns to gray;
Yet nothing in the changing storm
Can take your hand away.

The rose is red at break of day,
And red beneath the noon;
The garden calls the apple bloom
Its cousin, and the plum one too.
The pear, the thorn, the cherry tree
All borrow petals’ name;
Perhaps the rose is simply love
That answers when we call it.

The sign said Exit, bright and white,
Above the sleeping road;
I turned away from certain miles
And followed where the dark grass showed.
Past the lamps, past the last known turn,
The night grew wide and slow;
Some doors are marked to leave a place,
Some teach us where to go.

Let rain tap softly on your roof,
Let silver gather in the street;
Let every gutter carry off
The dust beneath your feet.
The clouds have found a lullaby,
The night has learned its tune,
And every darkened window keeps
A little piece of June.

One narrow seat is all we need
To cross the years by rail;
Yet I keep buying every car
As though the world could fail.

What does the opening flower keep?
What does the closing bud release?
What does the bird lift into song?
What does the silent wing decrease?
What does the heart gain when it gives?
What does it lose when it is free?
Perhaps the road is not the thing—
Perhaps the thing is me.

Light slips in
Under the door,
Touches the dust,
Crosses the floor,
Finds a room
That grief had sealed,
Rests on the wound,
And does not leave
Until the wound
Can learn to heal.

I can read the fire for you
If you bring me what is gone;
I will study ash and ember
After every flame has shone.
I will tell you where it traveled,
What it carried through the night,
And which small coal beneath the gray
Still remembers light.

There may be gold beside the green,
Or violet beside the white;
The red may borrow blue at noon,
The yellow change by candlelight.
The painter names the colors—but
The eye decides what stays.

There was a Young Girl of Leeds,
Who planted her garden with seeds;
The beans climbed the wall,
The peas conquered all,
And she harvested more than she needs.

Beneath the moon a swallow cried,
Its dark wings crossed the starry blue;
The sound became a slender road
That led my thoughts to you.
I followed where the night grew thin,
Past roofs and fields of white;
The bird was gone, the stars remained,
But love stayed in its flight.

The child points upward from her bed
And finds the moon between the trees;
She cups its yellow shape in words
And sends them through the leaves.
The branches shake, the window glows,
The brook repeats her tune;
Then sleep arrives, and on her lips
The moon is still a moon.

When sparrows chatter in the hedge,
I think of how you laughed;
When paper skitters down the walk,
I hear the old aftermath.
The world keeps offering little sounds
That carry you along;
I miss you in the quietest ones,
And smile when they are gone.

The tide comes in with one old phrase,
Then folds it in the foam;
It tells the shore what it has told
Since shores and moons were born.
The tide goes out, the tide returns,
Still speaking to the sand.

Willow, wearing April green,
Your branches brush the stream;
Once I watched you from a room
And mistook spring for dream.
Now the door is open wide,
Now the lonely chain is gone;
Shake your leaves and tell the world
I have finally come.

Quick-step!
Leaf-flip!
Branches sway
In bright display.
The orchard drums,
The warm air comes,
And every twig
Begins to jig.

Evening gathers in the trees,
And birds release their shining choir;
The air is blue, the first stars wake,
The roofs grow cool and quiet.
Before the last bird folds its wing,
Before the fields turn black,
Let me add one human song
To the music fading back.

Do you hear the hidden tune?
Can you lend me one bright chord?
Bring me all the colors back
That the gray day has ignored.
Lift me from this narrow room,
Give the clouds a name;
Not every sky is violet—
Not every heart the same.

Rain on the window,
Window on the tree,
Tree holds a bird,
Bird carries me.
Me in the cloud,
Cloud in the stream,
Stream runs to morning,
Morning to dream.

The road is dull beneath the rain,
The broken clouds draw near;
Far cliffs darken into ink,
While white birds disappear.
At the village mill, the grain
Lies fragrant in the sun;
Autumn leaves hold drops of light,
And the work is almost done.

My love’s eyes keep the summer sun
Long after summer’s flown;
Her laughter turns the autumn wind
To music of its own.
No spring can claim her brighter hue,
No winter make her gray;
She stays within the changing year
And warms the longest day.

The spring runs clear beneath the dusk,
And sunset threads its gold;
I watch the ripples join the road
Where travelers pass and hold.
Then I turn toward the rising moon,
And sing before the pines;
The wind replies in needles,
In branches, and in time.

Snow is falling past the door,
Softly whitening stone;
The wind puts winter on my face,
Though I walk alone.
The moon follows above the roofs,
The trees wear crystal crowns;
I step into the quiet land
Where every sound lies down.

Warm summer,
Bee over clover,
Light on the hill,
Day standing still.
Summer, stay near me,
Do not disappear;
The sky is still open,
The evening is clear.

You ask why I sit in the green hills;
I smile, for the answer is light.
Peach petals drift down the water,
And the world does not ask me to fight.

Beautiful river, carry the sky,
Clouds in your moving glass;
You cool the flame, you wake the field,
And teach the stones to pass.
Rain, little bells on the roof,
Rain, bright roots of the plain;
The earth lifts up its thirsty face
And calls you home again.

At the far end of the rainbow
We have stored a little light;
We will carry it through morning,
We will carry it through night.
When the road is rough beneath us,
When the good days turn to gray,
We will meet the next horizon
Side by side along the way.
And when evening folds the hills,
When the last bright colors cease,
We will find, within our hands,
One another—and our peace.

I sit beside the harbor wall
And watch the silver fish;
They leap, disappear, return,
As if the deep were wish.
The evening sky turns rose and blue,
And in that fading glass
I imagine your hand in mine,
The place I want to be.

See my ribbons in the wind,
See the branches bend;
See the flowers lift their heads,
See the rain descend.
Everything is moving now,
Sky above and ground below;
Even quiet things can dance
When the summer breezes blow.

I wandered where the fern leaves grew
And heard a small flower speak:
“I slept below the winter earth,
Then woke to find the spring.
I opened bright to seek the sun,
But someone called me plain;
Still, beneath the morning light,
I bloom through every name.”

Look, look, look—
Spring has come!
Green along the garden wall,
New leaves waking one by one.
Daisy, jasmine, rose, and thyme—
Bring the watering can!
Oh no, the petals turned to ink;
I used the writer’s pan!

When you sleep, the whole room dims
Around your quiet face;
The stars appear more sharply then,
The brook keeps up its pace.
Cars pass shadows on the wall,
The night turns like a book;
I fall in love with you again
Each time I stop to look.

We search the dark for distant life,
Like moths around a flame;
We send our questions through the void
And hope the stars reply our name.
Mars keeps its red and silent face,
Titan storms below;
Perhaps the truest world we seek
Is this one where we grow.

At dawn, when all the garden wakes,
The sparrows fill the air;
I see the light upon your face
And find you waiting there.
The dew has gathered in the cups
Of every folded rose;
My first thought is to call your name,
My last is not to go.

It was a dream without a road,
A spark beneath the rain;
It flashed, it warmed the darkened room,
Then vanished once again.
I woke beneath the paling moon,
Alone beside the glass;
The tears came down like quiet stars
That had forgotten how to pass.

Our thoughts are blossoms,
And the wind knows every name;
It lifts one petal,
Then another, into flame.
With each friend I meet,
I wear a different hue;
The garden changes shape because
I change when I meet you.
Each dance has its own measure,
Each heart its private art;
The many flowers in the field
Are one unfolding heart.

The moon wrote letters in the dark
And sent them toward the sun;
At dawn they shared a violet sky,
Then vanished one by one.
He followed her through evening’s blue,
She crossed his silver shade;
For one brief hour their separate light
Was one bright masquerade.

The spirit opens like a wing,
And rises through the air;
The wind receives its weightless song
And carries it somewhere.
Around me gather feathered dreams,
Their beating makes a drum;
The thunder folds a cloak of rain
Around the day to come.

From this high ridge I watch two birds
Circle and choose the same tree;
Their call becomes a woven song,
A promise carried free.
The morning seems to bless the pair,
The rainbow crowns the air;
Some things are made complete at once
Because two hearts are there.

The trees speak softly.
The shoreline answers.
Thunder folds its heavy hands.
Lightning opens them.
Wind passes over my face.
Birds stitch music through the blue.
Sunset gathers every voice.

The leaves have turned to copper now;
The autumn floor is bright.
They loosen from the highest bough
And settle out of sight.
No leaf complains about its fall,
Or asks the branch to wait;
Its journey ends beneath the tree
And becomes the soil of spring.

Loneliness:
An empty chair beneath the snow,
A lantern burning in daylight,
A boat tied to a forest tree,
A summer bird in winter,
A moon above a roofless house,
A letter with no name,
A road that circles back to me,
Or you beside me,
Still far away.

You carry daylight in your hands;
I keep the midnight sky.
We fold the distance like a note
That neither dares to sign.
Across the dark your window glows,
Across the sea I wait;
The heart can lose its way in light
And still arrive too late.

When love enters the heart,
The feet forget their fear.
The clock says tick, the clock says tock,
And every sound draws near.
Hands that give and hands that hold,
Flowers opening wide;
The smallest acts become a song
With happiness inside.
Tick-tock, the hours wander on,
Tick-tock, the world is bright;
Joy wears no crown but still can dance
In ordinary light.

The garden holds a scarlet rose,
One lantern in the green;
Its color enters every thought
And brightens what has been.
My heart is not a careful thing,
My joy is not an art;
The rose, the garden, and the love
Are mirrors of one heart.
Red rose, red rose,
Remain where spring has grown;
The garden is a lonely place
Until your color’s known.

An angel rests above the door,
The porch is bright with snow;
Beneath the star, the singers raise
A carol soft and low.
Garlands cross the window frame,
The night is feather-white;
The smallest child among the choir
Looks like an angel in the light.

Water finds the open ground,
Air slips through the tree;
Dreams need room to lift their wings,
So let them wander free.
Do not dam the growing stream,
Do not close the sky;
Courage is the river’s art—
It moves because it tries.

I hear the rain upon the leaves,
The leaves above, the leaves below;
The rich ones spill their shining cups
On those that cannot grow.
It is a gentle green applause,
A music near the ground;
Then sunlight fills each waiting drop
With little worlds of sound.
The branches glitter after rain,
The dark leaves turn to glass;
I wait for all that brightens next
To find me as I pass.

Our love rises like morning vines,
Purple against the wall;
It reaches for the patient sun
And will not fear the fall.
The tendrils cross the broken gate,
The roots refuse the stone;
What tries to keep the light away
Becomes the path we own.

Paula turns the garden soil
Around a scarlet flower;
Crabapple petals land like stars
And cottonwood drifts down.
Her hands are dark with summer work,
Her hair is full of spring.

On beaches quiet as a held breath
Warm light settles on the skin;
Turquoise water, amber clouds,
The summer day begins.
Blue glasses shade the watching eyes,
The horizon turns and flies;
Time rolls on beneath our feet,
And every color lies.
The sun returns, the waves repeat,
The sky forgets our names;
We leave the shore, but carry home
Its bright, revolving flame.

My family gathers at the table,
Talking over tea;
We laugh until the plates are bare,
Then sing in harmony.
We dance across the kitchen floor,
We share the evening’s bread;
Whatever happens in the world,
We meet it here instead.
Do you have a room like this,
Where every heart is fed?

The sun lays gold across the day,
The moon turns silver in the night;
Between them stands the tender hour
Where neither owns the light.

The treetops bow into the sea,
Their shadows comb the blue;
A gull writes circles overhead,
The ship cuts slowly through.
One mast rises beyond the rest,
Alone against the sun;
The day is wide, the water calm,
The voyage has begun.

The evening clouds arrange themselves
Above the empty street;
The new moon opens like a book
The dark has come to read.
Its thin light rests on window glass,
Then slips beyond the wall;
The night grows longer as we sleep,
And holds us through it all.

Two red flowers lift their faces
From a rust-colored stem;
They opened with the earliest spring
Before we noticed them.
People pass and talk beside them,
Never looking down;
The blossoms keep their shining watch
Above the busy town.

My children sleep, and in their dreams
They travel with the geese;
The river sings beneath the dawn,
The fish look up in peace.
A pike moves through the green-black water,
Reeds lean with the tide;
Morning holds its quiet breath,
And all the birds abide.
I alone remain awake,
Listening beside them.

In this cold room I think of you;
The window breathes with frost.
The wind moves through the empty street,
Counting all we lost.
Clouds hide the moon, then let it through;
The air remembers spring.
Even winter leaves a trace
Of what your hands could bring.

Rain has covered every path,
And memory walks there;
The leaves lie thick beneath the trees,
The old roads disappear.
Come, stay a moment in the rain,
Before the years depart;
The weather keeps what we once said
And carries it to my heart.

A red kite caught the rainbow’s edge
And tugged against the sky;
The shepherd boy sat in the dust
And watched his paper fly.
He knew the colors could not stay,
Yet mourned the vanishing thread.

Night walks gently through the grass,
And the moon keeps watch above;
Sleep, little one, beneath the stars,
Wrapped in an elder love.
The eagle crosses dreaming air,
The bison moves below;
The wolf calls once beyond the hill,
Then all the dark is still.
Rest, little one; the old tales stand
Around your sleeping door.

Mrs. Moon sits on her cloud,
An old woman in the sky;
She rocks her silver lantern slow
As evening passes by.
With needles made of starlight,
She knits the darkness tight.

The winter sun warmed up the field,
And children ran in play;
Bright butterflies rose over them,
The grass leaned into day.
Small sparrows startled from the shade,
While laughter crossed the lawn;
Two arms went up, a ball flew high,
And everyone ran on.

She calls the school “Shkool,”
And wakes me with a song;
She brings me every small delight
And tells me when things’re wrong.
She waves when I leave home,
Then smiles when I return;
When silence gathers in her face,
I know that I should learn.
My little daughter carries light
Wherever she may turn.

What is happiness?
A laugh across a room,
A hand held out in kindness,
A flower daring bloom,
A quiet act of tenderness,
Or light behind the eyes?

The late sun wears a crimson coat
And stains the western wall;
The colors fade from red to rust,
Then darkness takes them all.
Some hearts rejoice when night arrives;
I listen at the door,
And hope the morning remembers me
As daylight did before.

What a remarkable creature the frog is—
He sits as though he stands,
He leaps as though he flies,
He owns no coat, no hands.
He has no tail to wave hello,
Yet sings when rain is near.

For one brief pulse beneath the skin,
I sat beside the stone;
The wind moved through the broken tree,
And I was not alone.
The world I called inanimate
Had opened like a door.

Blind from birth, I know the spring
By fragrance and by sound;
I hear the lark above the grass,
Though darkness holds the ground.
His song becomes a window,
His bright notes make a view;
One day I’ll see the flowers bloom,
And find the sky is blue.
Until that day, the singing bird
Makes every dream come true.

Above the river’s white ascent,
A violet mountain gleams;
Its waterfall falls through the mist
Like silver torn from dreams.
The torrent drops beyond the cliff,
The stars appear to fall;
The sky has emptied out its light
And poured it down the wall.

The thorn caught hold of everything,
The leaf, the thread, the flower;
One petal fell, then one more fell,
Until the fall was all.
But water keeps another law—
It travels where it can;
It borrows colors from the stone
And gives them back again.
The foam imagines every road,
The river chooses one;
Its unfinished hopes move shining on
Beneath the patient sun.

Like a winter tree, I wait,
My branches bare and wide;
The wind moves through the empty limbs,
And nothing comes to hide.
I smile because the spring will know
The face I kept inside.

When morning wanders through the mist,
The birds begin to sing;
The dew lies bright on every leaf,
And light crowns everything.
I find you in the opening day,
The first thought in my heart;
If youth is ours beneath these trees,
Let love be where we start.

The flowers wake along the lane,
The swallows cross the blue;
The sea has taken on the sky,
And I am walking to you.
The world is made of water, air,
Of breath and turning tide;
Love is the road beneath my feet,
And you are on its side.

Warm light lies across the floor,
And birds call from the field;
The morning opens without end,
Its blue horizon sealed.
The quiet brightness makes me think
Of summers yet to come,
Of days that carry peace like fruit
Beneath a patient sun.

Do you remember porch-light days,
When summer would not end?
We smelled the grass, we talked for hours,
And every dream was friend.
The world was small enough to hold
Inside a single chair;
I wish those evenings could return,
With you still waiting there.
We would speak of all we lost,
Then breathe the open air.

Deep in the woods I have no grave,
No stone to mark my name;
I am the brightness under leaves,
The sudden woodland flame.
Do not bring sorrow to this place,
Or search the roots for bone;
The forest keeps a living light
That shines by being alone.

Salsa!
The harbor swings,
The mast leans low,
The bright fish know.
The oars keep time,
The gulls all rhyme,
The waves lift high,
The boats reply—
Salsa!

Look at the moon,
White in the night;
Look at the sun,
Gold in the light.
Look at the river,
Quick as it runs;
All three are traveling,
All three are gone.

The stars grow faint behind the day,
Yet leave us one last spark;
We spend our borrowed brightness here
Before returning dark.
Our love may burn through every year,
Then scatter into space;
The light we took from distant suns
Will still remember us.

A black cat waits upon the cliff
Where March has stripped the stone;
Its eyes foresee the yellow bloom
That soon will be its own.
The sea below reflects the cold,
The wind becomes a purr;
What joins a household’s quiet breath
To waves that never stir?

Small butterfly, rise through the blue,
Leave the green leaves behind;
You once wore a crawling coat,
Now silver wings you find.
You drift toward one bright flower,
You settle on its red—
But the cat beneath the garden wall
Has made a meal instead.

If I possessed the woven sky,
The blue, the dusk, the dawn,
I’d spread it softly at your feet
Before the night was gone.
But I have only dreams to give,
And dreams are thin as thread;
So walk with care, beloved one,
Across the life I’ve spread.

At dawn I left the city walls,
The clouds were pale and bright;
My little boat moved down the stream
Through a single day of light.
The monkeys called from either bank,
The cliffs stood dark and tall;
The river carried me away,
Yet held the world in all.

She was my lily in the spring,
The fragrance after rain;
Her quiet grace moved through the grass,
Then vanished once again.
I sing her name in drifting wind,
In every pale-green tree;
The flower fades, the song remains,
And keeps her here with me.

The sky has lowered to the fields,
The clouds are heavy, gray;
A single snowflake crosses the road
And wonders where to stay.
The wind complains against the barn,
As though it has been wronged;
Even nature loses its fine crown
When winter lasts too long.

You call the willow love,
The poplar calls it rain;
The branches comb the weather,
Then pull apart again.
I listen, but the country
Has never learned that word.

My love bends over the river,
Watching her image glide;
The ripples break her shining face
And carry it aside.
O water, tell her faithfully
What I cannot make her see:
The picture in your deepest pool
Is steadier in me.

A stranger placed a flower in my hand,
Brighter than May had grown;
I turned away and kept my rose,
The one I called my own.
But when I reached my garden gate,
My rose had closed its door;
Its thorns were all it offered me,
And I desired it more.

The dancers cross the polished floor,
Then turn and cross again;
They join their hands, they break the line,
They gather up the strain.
The old French melody runs on,
The quick feet answer so;
They pause, breathless, as if to ask
Whether we liked the show.

For the blind woman on the train,
Each journey turns within;
She touches my arm, moves one seat,
And lets the dark begin.
Her fingers find a metal ring,
Her face becomes a light;
What worlds are moving through the heads
That crowd this train tonight?

Love is the house I carry,
Affection is its door;
Happiness is the child inside,
Who asks for nothing more.
Friendship is the moving air,
Hope the road we choose;
Life runs bright beneath our feet,
And teaches us to lose.

So many times I thought I’d found
The harbor in the haze;
The wrecked man sees a strip of land
And rows toward it for days.
Then shore becomes another cloud,
Another distant lie;
How many false horizons pass
Before the docks are nigh?

The waves come down along the beach,
Warm sand clings to our feet;
The evening sun becomes a coal,
The air grows soft and sweet.
We skip flat stones, we watch the birds,
We follow crabs at night;
Our footprints scatter through the sand
Like stars beneath the light.

Drink the moonlight from the lake,
Let the dark become your friend;
Write one line upon the bark,
Then let the sentence end.
Keep a room inside yourself
Where no one else can see;
Trust the quiet hand that makes
The art you need to be.

The grass is green,
The sky is blue,
I make a face
At you-know-who.
I laugh at the sea,
I buzz like a bee,
I visit the zoo,
And wave when I see you.

When I look into your eyes,
The old life falls away;
I cannot blame you for the joy
That follows every day.
My laughter has returned again,
My past has lost its claim;
If this is all your fault, then love
Is glad to bear the blame.

The nearest dream retreats from me,
As clover draws a bee;
It dips, it turns, it will not land
Where I would have it be.
I reach, it rises toward the clouds,
A tiny golden ship;
I stand below with empty hands,
And watch the sunlight slip.
What honey waits beyond my reach?
What sweetness will not stay?

She washed the years from every path;
The garden woke in bloom.
Pale roses opened for the bride,
Deep roses filled the room.
The groom stood smiling in the sun,
And time released its gloom.

The white rose trembles in her hand,
So delicate and thin;
Her eyes are paler than the tide,
Yet wonder wakes within.
Fair child of blue-veined morning light,
You bend but do not break;
The frailest things can hold a world
When gentleness is strength.

Now every withheld gift seems near,
The sky is open, wide;
Each bud upon the flowering branch
Has something to confide.
Love gathers courage in the heart,
Joy deepens in the eyes;
The smallest thought becomes a gold
That ordinary hours disguise.
Now.

With poetry
I found a door.
With poetry
The room grew more.
With poetry
Words learned to dance.
With poetry
Thoughts found a chance.
With poetry
The heart can roam.
With poetry
I carry home.

When troubles gather at your door,
You need not stand alone;
An unseen hand may guide you back
Through places you have known.
It keeps a little circle bright,
It watches through the night;
The angel on your shoulder stays
Until you find the light.

Seeds
sleep in dark soil,
Then loosen,
Rise as green thought,
Stretch into branches of language.
The mind bears fruit in sentences;
The page receives the harvest,
And strangers find the crop
Where the writer left it growing.

Flowers open,
Dreams gather,
Stars descend through branches;
Roots below the forest floor
Listen to the earth.
Trees become great sounding boards,
The hidden spirits answer,
And we step beyond ideas
Into the touch of living things.

Sunlight,
Bees,
Pines and wine,
Hares in the grass,
Deer crossing the path,
Cows beneath the hill,
Sheep under moonlight—
Every creature takes its turn,
Every creature breathes;
The world is generous
When we let it be.

At sunrise,
The sunflowers turn
Their open faces east.
The bats retreat beneath the roof,
And morning ends their feast.

The snow has gone,
But cold winds remain;
The forecast promises
More snow, more rain.
Walk slowly over the shining street,
Watch where your footsteps land;
Winter is not finished yet,
So take the weather’s hand.

They plant the message in the child,
They sell the seed for need;
They teach the hungry heart to want
The thing they choose to feed.
They dress the cage in flags and names,
Then call the prison free;
How long before the sleeping mind
Remembers how to see?

You wrote your name upon the sand,
And laughed when waves drew near;
You thought the shore would keep it safe,
Though tides erase the year.
I wrote it deeper in my heart,
Where water cannot run;
The unborn may read it after us
When all the waves are done.

The sun sinks down in liquid gold,
The evening wears a jade;
White mist folds around the trees,
And all the colors fade.
A lonely flute begins to play,
The lanterns fill the square;
We call the feast a joyful night,
But wind may follow there.

Across the prairie, rain has come;
The grass has found its green.
Last year the earth was brown and cracked,
The far hills hard and lean.
Now velvet spreads from field to field,
The clouds move clean and bright;
Montana wears another face,
Reborn in rain and light.

I travel through this world by sight,
By hands that learn the air;
By feet that find the waiting ground,
By lungs that rise and bear.
The body is a borrowed boat,
Its limits mark the sea;
I move through what I understand
And what escapes from me.

There was a Young Poet of Spain,
Who composed in the middle of rain;
He wrote on a wall,
Then forgot it all,
And started the poem again.

Between the dark and blazing day
I walk a narrow road;
The night knows what I cannot say,
The dawn can share the load.
I will not choose the black or white,
Nor turn from either flame;
I carry morning in the dark
And darkness without shame.

Up the slant of the sea she goes,
Her hull a fading gray;
The bow lifts slowly through the fog,
Then sinks beyond the spray.
She has crossed a hundred changing miles,
She will cross a hundred more;
The horizon opens, closes, opens,
Like a half-remembered door.
The night puts green along her side,
And the sea receives her name.

If wisdom can be joyful,
Then joy is not a lie;
If simple hearts can laugh,
Then wisdom may be nigh.
The clouds are light, the sky is blue,
The day has made its claim;
What we call happiness may be
The courage to stay plain.

Look up before the midnight fades,
And choose a star to keep;
The moon has filled its silver bowl,
The world is hushed in sleep.
Make one small wish into the dark,
Then let the darkness hear;
Some hopes are brighter when they rise
Without a witness near.

Behind me stand the patient hills,
Their silence deep and wide;
They carry storms, and snow, and sun,
And never leave my side.
My tears have fed the lower earth,
My sweat has marked the stone;
I climb toward the farther self
That I have not yet known.

I cannot believe you walk alone;
Your laughter makes the morning flower.
Even mirrors lean across the room
To borrow from your power.

When the road refuses you,
Stand up and begin;
Rain has never stopped a heart
That carries hope within.
The race may turn against your feet,
The sky may lose its blue;
Put a smile upon your face
And let the weather through.

I thought a lion crossed the road,
In a golden helmet bright,
With silver running down its sides
And thunder in its flight.
It roared beneath the morning sun,
Then stopped beside the sign;
I saw your Honda, waved my hand,
And knew the beast was mine.

If you can laugh at your own mistakes,
The world grows less severe;
Your laughter gives another heart
A reason to draw near.
One smile can travel through a room,
Then cross a frightened street;
The safest world is built from joy
That makes our neighbors meet.

You can braid it, cut it, curl it,
Let it tumble in the rain;
Part it neatly, leave it wild,
Change it all again.
Fashion lives above the eyes,
But love begins below—
Wear your heart as freely as
The hair you choose to show.

To friends across the distance,
To the lonely and the bright,
To old hands and young faces,
To those who love the light,
I send this small remembrance
From an island of green and blue;
The horizon holds my gratitude,
And all of it belongs to you.

Friend, if you laugh, I laugh;
If you cry, I stay.
If you run, I follow close;
If you jump, I say,
“Please look before you leap!”
But should you leap from stone,
I’ll miss you terribly, my friend,
And wait beside the phone.

Listen—the lark has found the dawn,
And sunlight leaves the hill;
The flowers open cups of gold,
The sleeping fields grow still.
Rise, my love, before the day
Has spent its brightest breath;
The morning is a little song
That vanishes in death.

In every skill, in every breath,
I find a hidden hand;
The flowers rise beside the road,
The sick still learn to stand.
When joy is near and when it leaves,
I trust what I can’t see;
The world is held by quiet care
That keeps on carrying me.

Peace is a window,
Peace is a wing,
Peace is the silence
After birds sing.
Peace is your hand,
Peace is mine too;
Peace is the work
We choose to do.

We belong like dawn and sky,
Like a song that gathers sound;
Through the years we walk together,
Finding common ground.
When the road grows steep or strange,
Love will keep us strong;
Time may turn the world around,
But it will not turn us wrong.

A frog stayed late at the dance hall,
And could not find his way;
A bat swooped down and offered him
An evening taxi ride.

Pink flowers on the eucalyptus,
The branches hum with bees;
Their honeyed scent moves through the yard,
Then settles in the trees.
They are as bright as roses,
Though no rose can claim the name;
The blossoms keep their gentle bells,
And summer sings the same.

I am the king of midnight,
The duke of broken chords;
My kingdom is a smoky room,
My crown is made of words.
The old bluesmen hear me play
And shake their heads in doubt;
I sing so well the moon itself
Must turn its light down low.
I am the king of midnight,
At least until the morning.

Keep swimming,
Keep moving,
The water knows your name.
Through love and peace,
Through salt and foam,
The heart becomes a flame.
Do not stop where waves grow dark;
The farther shore remains.

Love those who wound you,
But do not wound the kind;
To strangers you may vanish,
To one heart, you are the world.

At first there was a word,
Then light broke through the air;
The speaking creature named the world
And found itself in there.
Perhaps the power to make and name
Is more than human art;
Perhaps the animal who speaks
Carries a godlike heart.

Water is the simplest drink,
The answer when we thirst;
It waits beneath the earth and falls
From clouds that break and burst.
Clear water fills the shops in glass—
We pay to hold the rain.

Far star,
Small flame,
You blink
And call my name.
Through dark,
Through white,
You keep
The night alight.

Four ducks drift across the pond,
The spring grass bends behind;
White clouds travel through the blue,
And leave no mark behind.
I will remember this small scene
When other days are gone,
And feel the tears arrive again
For how the light moved on.

My father planted grass seed,
My mother planted flowers;
Their gardens rose in green and red
After only showers.
I planted seeds beside the fence,
And watered every day;
No birds appeared, though I was sure
The birdseed would grow that way.
Perhaps grownups know the secret
That children learn too late.

Sparrows fed through freezing rain,
Which slowly turned to snow;
The flakes slid down an unseen path
From silver into white.
For one brief moment bird and snow
Seemed equally to fall;
Then wings divided them from earth,
And the birds rose above all.

Shake-break!
Feet turn,
Shoulders burn,
Hands roll,
Hips sway,
Green fields flash,
The music plays,
Every branch joins the refrain—
Shake-break!

Cascade after cascade,
The night wheels onward;
Morning waits beyond the dark,
Still unborn and distant.
My monsignor, keep watch—
The cold has filled the hall,
And long pale spirits pass outside
With chants too wise to call.

Water meets fire,
Fire enters air;
Air becomes a river,
Earth receives them there.
Everything is changing,
Nothing stands alone;
The world sings its long living song
In a language without stone.

A trout-colored wind moves through my hands,
And I remember the river;
The trout hid from dinosaurs
That came to drink together.
They sheltered in subways,
In castles, cars, and rain,
Waiting with remarkable patience
For the giants to leave again.

I wrote a poem upon the wind,
With raindrops for my ink;
The forest heard the paper tear,
And asked me not to think.

Wings above the open sea,
Footprints along the sand;
Quiet voices in the breeze,
Balance beneath the land.
No voyage has begun as yet,
No harbor has been named;
The wings are waiting for the road,
The road is waiting too.

Fiddles and riddles,
Riddles and rain;
Poets twist language
To loosen the chain.
Metaphors stumble,
Imagination grows;
Sometimes the coldest world
Is the one a poem knows.

I walked through Ann Arbor alone,
Yet you were at my side;
The students crossed South Main Street,
The bookstores opened wide.
Restaurants spilled their evening light,
The Ark sent music through;
I carried every familiar sound,
And still looked for you.
We remain close in memory,
Though distance keeps us two.

The puppy pulls against the tree,
The leash has caught him fast;
He growls as though the trunk itself
Has chosen him to last.
He blames the hand that holds the rope,
Not knowing what is true:
The leash is tight, the tree is still,
And I am pulling too.

I missed the service by the shore;
The blue tide called me out.
The children chased the foaming waves,
And summer turned about.
The Lord, I think, can understand
How brief a bright day is;
There will be time enough for prayer,
But not always for this.

Hush now, little traveler,
The branches sway above;
The night will rock your dreaming bed
With leaves instead of love.
The bough may bend, the stars may fall,
But morning will come near;
Sleep through the wind, my little one,
I am beside you here.

My mother moves in restless sleep,
Her hands still sort the day;
She murmurs over fields and food,
Though work has gone away.
No crown is placed upon her head,
No trumpet names her worth;
She is the tireless, turning heart
That keeps a household’s earth.

Laughter is a little door
Out of the winter mind;
It does not ask the rich or poor
To leave their grief behind.
It loosens every tightened thought,
It warms the longest day;
Let laughter walk beside you, then—
The blues will lose their way.

The boy I was has left the room;
His springtime crown is shed.
The petals lie along the floor,
The younger days are dead.
Yet love remains the highest god
I ever chose to serve;
If life returned, I’d give it more
Than youth had nerve.

Hills of my childhood, gray and bare,
You heard the northern rain;
The wind once made your heather bow,
Then carried me away.
I thought your slopes were paradise
When Mary walked with me;
Now every path is full of ghosts
That only I can see.

I picture the parking lot,
The row of painted lines;
I repeat the nearest building,
The tree, the yellow sign.
I can return and find the car,
But one question leaves me stark:
I know the place where I am parked—
Where did I leave my heart?

Let me forget the borrowed name,
The rules, the narrow game;
Let me rise beyond the street
And leave the world behind.
No chain, no clock, no watching eye,
No net beneath the sky;
The day is brief, so seize it whole,
And let the self take flight.

Paris, your bridges hold my dreams;
Your lights are in my heart.
The river writes a silver line
Where all my memories start.
I carry you through distant streets,
Through every colored rain;
Paris, you are not far away—
You rise in me again.

There was an Old Man of Peru,
Who painted the ocean bright blue;
He sailed in a shoe,
With a parrot for crew,
And arrived where the sky turned to stew.

The year opens in the flowers,
The day begins at seven;
The dew hangs bright on every hill,
The lark ascends to heaven.
The snail climbs slowly through the thorn,
The morning fills with song;
The world is briefly set aright,
And all the roads seem long.

My memory is a shell washed up,
Its edges worn by rain;
The tide carries its shape away,
Then gives it back again.
One stranger lifts it from the sand,
Closes it in a hand,
Then throws it toward the open sea
Where time will understand.

You found me happier than before,
Though sorrow made me still;
Your love arrived like morning light
Across a frozen hill.
I see a golden world reflected
Clearly in your eyes;
My heart has learned to praise the fate
That brought you to my side.

“I have no name,” the infant said;
“I’ve seen but two dawns rise.”
“Then Joy shall be your name,” I cried,
And kissed her wondering eyes.
She smiled, and all the room grew bright;
The little life began.
Sweet Joy, I sang, and Joy looked back
As only children can.

The shadow of my hand divides
The vanished from the near;
Behind it lies the finished hour,
Before it, comes the year.
One instant stands beneath the line,
No longer lost or gone:
The only time that belongs to us
Is this small breath of now.

I want to laugh with God,
Not whisper in fear;
To teach the sorrowing earth
That joy can still appear.
Let laughter loosen grief,
Let tears become a song;
The heart may bend beneath the world,
But laughter makes it strong.

Scattered dreams became a dust,
Then dust became a grain;
A grain became a brick one day,
And bricks became a wall.
The wall rose higher than the clouds,
Each fragment finding place;
What seemed too small to matter once
Now shelters human dreams.

When night comes down,
The moon goes searching;
Clouds gather slowly,
Thinking together.
Light paints their edges,
Then loses the trail;
The sky keeps moving,
Restless and pale.

The rain falls everywhere—
On pasture, roof, and tree;
It beads upon the waiting coats
Of people passing me.
It falls on ships beyond the shore,
On fields I cannot see;
One weather gathers all the world
Under one gray sea.

Though oceans lie between us,
You have entered where I live;
We trade our daily secrets,
And find more than we give.
Perhaps this small beginning,
A seed beneath the ground,
Will open into friendship
Where two far hearts are found.

Near the ocean, near my heart,
The water keeps its rhyme;
One day calm, the next a storm,
Yet faithful all the time.
The waves break and recover,
The gulls return to land;
Change arrives, then passes on,
And leaves the shore unchanged.

Clear as glass, the water holds
A fish of shifting thought;
It rises toward the light some days,
Some days descends to dark.
No one can predict its path,
No net can make it stay;
The mind, like water, changes shape
Around the passing day.

Carnations fill the garden bed
In white, in red, in gold;
Their clove-sweet fragrance moves at dusk,
Their petals do not fold.
They carry purity and fire,
They catch the passing eye;
Small bright flags of summer bloom
Beneath the open sky.

You offer me a scarlet rose;
I think of little kings.
I hold it gently, heed the thorns,
And breathe what springtime brings.
The flower carries your warm hands
Across the room to me;
A rose can open many worlds
Inside one memory.

At Angkor Wat, an old woman climbs
The sanctuary stairs;
She carries prayers into the stone
And leaves them with the gods.
The corridors still hold their light,
The carved nymphs still dance;
At Angkor Thom, the roots of trees
Have taken back the walls.

At dawn the doves begin their song,
The waking fields grow clear;
Something wonderful seems to wait
In every breath of air.
The spring has opened one more door,
The morning has begun;
I greet the day with both my hands
And turn them toward the sun.

Above the tower hangs a moon
Too large for ordinary night;
It scatters gold on river waves
And makes the roofs look bright.
The empty peaks receive its glow,
The pines release their scent;
Ten thousand miles of darkness shine
As though the moon were meant.

I used to hate my clumsy feet,
Too broad, too hard to hide;
My friend said, “When your head hangs low,
They’re waiting at your side.
They give you something you can see
That makes a smile begin.”
I looked down—and for the first time,
I liked the shape I’m in.

You are my sister, through the years,
My closest childhood friend;
You lift me when the weather turns,
And stay until the end.
You make the darkest room feel bright,
You tell the honest truth;
The love between us changes shape,
But never loses youth.

“Do you remember me?” she asked,
Among the stars she wore.
I said that pride may fade with time,
But memory keeps its door.
Where once your voice had entered me,
It cannot be erased;
The heart remembers every light
That ever touched its face.

She scattered rainbow flowers
Along the avenue;
They leapt behind her skipping feet,
And no one knew why.
Perhaps a birth, a wedding day,
Perhaps a secret cheer—
The road became a waterfall
Of petals bright and clear.

Early autumn waits at the airport,
Where the wide Texas sky turns gold;
The Lone Star state surrounds the gates,
Its distances unfold.
Somewhere beyond the runway lights,
I imagine you smile;
Beauty hides inside beauty there,
And makes the waiting worthwhile.

Let truth defend the smallest voice,
Let every person speak;
Let votes be free, let homes be safe,
Let justice guard the weak.
Humanity is more than words
Recited in a song;
It lives wherever equal rights
Make ordinary lives belong.

Sweet surrender, quiet rest,
The tired soul untying;
Two lives mirror one another,
Neither asks for flying.
Love unfastens every chain,
Across the years and pages;
Together or apart, two hearts
Can meet through all the ages.

Invisible chains hold her fast,
Yet freedom lifts her wings;
She will not bow to borrowed fear
Or wait for what it brings.
Unknown, undaunted, she steps out
To find her private sky;
The world may name her where she stands,
But she decides how high.

There was an Old Man of Japan,
Who balanced a cloud in a pan;
When the cloud drifted free,
He climbed up a tree,
And announced he had captured the rain.

Bring me the dreams you keep concealed,
The songs beneath your breath;
I’ll wrap them in a cloud of blue
And guard them from the world.
The rough hands of the passing day
May reach for what you know;
But hidden melodies can wait
For gentler winds to blow.

I honor the mother who raised you,
But my mother is my own;
She taught me how to stand upright,
And made the earth a home.
No love can be exchanged for hers,
No memory can start;
The woman who first held my hand
Still lives inside my heart.

Many loves have crossed my life,
Some stayed and some moved on;
But yours runs deep and steady still,
Like tide beneath the moon.
It has no shore, it has no end,
It darkens into blue;
The sea could lose its water first
Before I ceased to love you.

Thank you for the patient hand,
For making room and time;
For every laugh, for every tear,
For every borrowed line.
Thank you for the honest words,
The silence and the song;
You gave me more than I could ask,
And helped me carry on.
Thank you.

One silver hair appeared one day;
I plucked it from my head.
It whispered, “You may laugh at me,
But I am not alone.
Soon all my quiet friends will rise
And make your mirror tell
The story that your younger face
Has tried so hard to hide.”

The summer days hang golden-long,
With no command to heed;
The trees lift fires against the sky,
The hours forget to speed.
Time becomes a quiet horse,
The road becomes a cloud;
I drift through every afternoon
And ask for nothing loud.

I hear a name and light begins;
It sounds like silk and wings.
It belongs to angels,
To daughters, queens, and dreams.
If I should ever have a child,
That name would be her sun;
It would make the world more bright
Before her life’s begun.

Graduation, here I come;
The next wide road is near.
College waits beyond the gate,
And freedom fills the air.
I may be known, I may be great,
I may be simply me;
The future opens like a door,
And I am going free.

I’d like to be a bird above,
To wheel across the blue;
But worms are not my favorite meal—
I’d rather steal your fries.
I’d perch beside the picnic table,
And sing for every bite;
Then rise above the laughing crowd
And vanish into light.

What flute is playing in the dark,
Its willow notes set free?
The spring wind carries every sound
Across the sleeping city.
If we should hear that homesick tune,
How could we not recall
The gardens where our childhood lived,
The place we once called home?

We wandered through the younger years,
Then found each other late;
The early summer left the trees,
But love remained to wait.
No false word stands between us now,
No shadow hides the view;
The compass points through every day
Toward me, toward you.

Every family has a shape:
Some loud, some soft, some small;
Mine tells stories over tea
And answers every call.
The kitchen smells of cookies,
The rooms are dressed in light;
I hope that one day I can stay
Within that welcome night.

O world, O life, O turning year,
I climb your final stair;
The spring I loved has flown away,
The winter waits somewhere.
Yet every season leaves a gift,
Each joy survives its flight;
What vanished from the morning sky
Still trembles in the night.

When my breath has left the room,
Will you keep a place for me?
Will my face return in photographs,
Or fade like foam at sea?
If you wish upon a patient star,
Perhaps our warmth will meet;
The sun still finds the sleeping tree,
And love outlasts the heat.

Here where the country opens green,
The old faith still is near;
The morning bell crosses the fields,
The harvest rises clear.
Rain comes down upon the grain,
The soil receives it all;
This is the prayer the farmers know,
And the truest church of all.

Could we pull summer longer,
Stretch the shadows through the trees,
Hold the hours beside us
Like a shawl beneath the breeze?
If love could lengthen daylight,
I would ask the evening stay;
But every season teaches us
To love its vanishing.

Dare to carry hope,
Dare to name the dream;
Dare to trust the little light
That glimmers through the seam.
Follow where the heart leads,
Catch the star before it falls;
Hope is not a distant gift—
It answers when one calls.

Red rose,
Red rose,
Where do you go
When petals fall?
You were my joy,
My bright belief;
Now every garden without you
Feels like grief.

Along Lake Shore Drive,
The towers stand in winter,
Tall and vacant-looking;
Ice drifts below their windows,
While southern gardens wait
For April to remember them.

Words are music
When they strike the water;
They leap from the boats,
They startle the birds,
They scatter among leaves.
Then they sit down to eat
Beside the quiet bank,
Having forgotten
Why they came.

The poet rides sorrow’s waves,
Through pictures made of rain;
He carries language like a lamp
Against the darkened plain.
The gift becomes a burden,
The hermit guards the flame;
He trades his private dreams for words
And gives them human names.

The most important drink is plain,
With neither scent nor hue;
It moves through every living thing,
And keeps the body true.
It washes what the body holds,
It answers sudden thirst;
The simplest gift beneath the sky
Is often needed first.

The river rests inside my hands,
A bowl of moving sky;
I lift it and the water breaks,
And little suns fly by.
I drink, and clouds move into me,
The blue becomes my own.
Which one contains the other now—
The river, or the one?

In spring the earth puts on its green,
And something bright draws near;
The flowers carry signs of grace,
The hidden sky grows clear.
Wherever beauty opens wide,
I feel a careful hand;
The world is not abandoned here—
Love moves across the land.

Strange music turns my head;
Bright colors crowd the street.
I step into another world
Where every drum has feet.
The customs call my curiosity,
The festival calls me through;
I watch, imagine, listen, learn,
And leave changed by the view.

Green mangoes from the tree,
Peeled and cut with care;
Milk and ice inside the glass,
Sugar in the air.
The blender makes a golden storm,
The drink is poured and bright;
One smiling sip of summer
Makes the whole day light.

Professor Griggs once loved the books
And taught the laws of flight;
His children were his daily joy,
His equations his delight.
Now age has turned the tables round:
He studies bills and fees,
While all his former students’ minds
Are sending theirs to college.

We climbed the branch above the pond
And leapt without a care;
The water caught our shouting limbs,
The sunlight filled the air.
No worry followed to the bank,
No future asked our names;
We spent the afternoon as though
The world were made for games.

The fire warms my winter feet,
The old year leaves the room;
The new one carries hidden roads,
Though none of them have bloomed.
I wake and stretch toward morning light,
The ceiling fades from view;
Somewhere beyond the first cold day,
Adventure waits anew.

A butterfly crosses my garden;
I never learn its name.
I do not know its favorite flower,
Its color, or its home.
It pauses once beside my hand,
Then rises out of sight;
The smallest look can make a life
Take wing into the light.

Brilliance lies along the hills,
Where autumn burns the trees;
Gray clouds build a quiet stage,
Blue opens in between.
The horizon holds its breath,
The morning waits below;
Look once, and keep the living scene
Before the colors go.

Day and night, the heart keeps time;
The blood moves through its roads.
The lungs rise like two quiet sails,
The body bears its load.
A morning dove calls through the mist,
We open arms and eyes;
Love grows slowly as we stand
And watch the daylight rise.

January’s afternoon stayed light
For one small minute more,
An unexpected gift delayed
And waiting at the door.
It filled me with a gratitude
The long hot summer hid;
The year had left a little sun
Inside the coldest day.

My little husband sailed away,
The wind returned alone;
It circled once around my door,
Then hurried toward his ship.
If I were light as weather,
I would follow where it went;
But I remain beside the shore,
And wait for its return.

I do not trust the word love;
I know the shape of pain.
I have seen bright endings fade,
And dreams dissolve like rain.
Let other people promise stars;
I sleep beneath the sky.
The heart is safer in the dark,
Where no goodbyes can die.

There was an Old Man of the Pier,
Whose trousers were spotted with beer;
He tore them in strips,
For his nieces’ small ships,
And sailed them away with a cheer.

Open the gate to the one who waits,
With tears upon the stone;
The lock is made of all my sins,
The key is not my own.
Let mercy turn the iron back,
Let grace undo the weight;
I will enter if you call,
Or climb the wall and wait.

If innocence is not ignorance,
And wonder is not youth,
Then wisdom grows from asking why
And staying near the truth.
We do not lose the child inside;
We learn to let it see.
After years of fretful thought,
Wonder becomes a choice.

You say, “Give love when you feel none;
Give what you wish to find.”
That sounds like a beautiful rule,
But what if I am tired?
Is there a better kind of wisdom—
One that lets the heart be still,
Then offers love when strength returns,
By choice and not by guilt?

From every feather, every hue,
The bird wears borrowed light;
It leaps through air, it cannot sing,
Yet makes the sky feel bright.
Its colors tell an ancient tale,
Its wings refuse to stay;
The bird is beauty in motion,
And motion is its prayer.

Clouds of worry gather and break,
Then gather once again;
Thoughts ferment in hidden rooms,
Like weather before rain.
Memory opens old tunnels,
Creativity walks through;
Sorrow holds the heart awhile,
And makes strange work anew.

Sometimes joy flutters
Around my smiling face,
Sometimes it drifts like a bubble,
Light in empty space.
I reach to hold it—
Touch!
The brightness pricks me,
Then rises out of reach.

Your presence turns the room to June,
The summer enters in;
You welcome me beside your door,
And let the day begin.
The life I thought would pass me by
Has opened like a sun;
I had no place for love before,
But you have made me one.

I’m not afraid of thunder now;
I know what lightning means.
The sky is taking photographs
Of all my waking dreams.
So let the storm come rumbling close,
Let silver cross the blue;
Somewhere above the darkened clouds,
The heavens notice you.

Time is short,
The bell is near;
I must be there,
I must appear.
I promise every Sunday,
Then arrive too late;
Perhaps I need to leave my bed
Before the hour has passed.

Self-respect is a quiet love,
The hand that holds you whole;
It teaches care for other lives
By first repairing the soul.
It is control without a chain,
Praise without a throne;
To honor God and honor self
Is not to stand alone.

A thin rain falls through morning light;
It whispers in the trees.
Mist gathers over distant roofs,
Then follows where it please.
The wet roofs darken, cattle shine,
The mountain takes the scent;
By noon the rain has left the hill,
But not the memory.

There is another sky beyond
The one our eyes can see;
Another garden, always green,
Where frost can never be.
Do not regret the fading woods,
Or fields that fall asleep;
Somewhere a brighter orchard waits,
And asks us not to weep.

To my sister on her wedding day,
I bring a heart of cheer;
The man who takes your hand today
Will hold your laughter dear.
May both of you be gentle,
May both of you be true;
I celebrate the life ahead
That opens now for you.

Though branches fill the summer tree,
The root remains below;
Through every season’s false display,
It is the root we know.
I swayed among the leaves of youth,
And now the truth is near;
When flowers fall, the hidden root
Still holds the whole year.

Sleepless sun of sorrow,
Pale star above the night,
You show the dark you cannot warm
With one remembered light.
