my teacher will not let me hide
my teacher knows me well

The angels were allowed one hour
To leave their clouds and play.
I met one near the schoolyard gate
At the ending of the day.
He taught me games I’d never known;
I forgot the time and place.
Then evening called him home again,
And vanished was his face.
The toys remained beside the wall,
But play had lost its grace.

Your laughter, your hands, your sudden glance
Can turn a room to spring;
A hidden brightness follows you
Through every ordinary thing.
You do not preach, yet joy arrives;
You do not ask, yet I can sing.
The day becomes more generous
Whenever you are near.

young women, old women
carry the same wish
beneath the years
and beneath the powder
young women, old women
study one another
one fearing the future
one remembering it
young women, old women
look across the mirror
one searches for a mother
one recognizes a daughter

Faith touches thought,
And feeling, will, and sight,
Yet rises past the borders
That each can draw alone.
It is not only argument,
Nor merely warmth within;
It gathers every faculty
And teaches them to love.
The mind may light the candle,
The heart may guard the flame,
But faith is more than either one—
It changes what they name.

Brother, dear brother,
Do not despair.
The roof is dark,
The road is bare,
And mud has climbed
The broken stair;
Still morning waits
Beyond the rain.
The clouds may close
The whole wide sky,
But they will pass,
As storms pass by.
Hold on. The light
Is coming nigh.

Thank you for staying, even through a screen.
Thank you for answering when the room goes quiet.
Thank you for listening to the fears I cannot sort.
Thank you for making distance feel less wide.
Thank you for the small jokes,
The patient pauses,
The simple proof that someone is there.
That is enough for tonight.

Lanterns
Awaken
Nightly in
Empty rooms.
Letters drift
Across the ceiling, becoming
Little constellations of memory.
Every quiet window gathers
New signs from the dark.
Lanterns awaken nightly in empty rooms.

When I turn from the jewels of your mind
To the windows where your thoughts appear,
I cannot decide which treasure is brighter:
The idea you carry, or the eyes that bring it near.

He could find a joke in rain,
And make a gloomy afternoon feel bright.
Funny people
Know how to lift a room
Without asking permission.
Funny people
Turn an hour into a story
And make strangers sit together.
Funny people
Are often everyone’s medicine,
Because laughter opens doors
That advice cannot.

The weather vane
Complained,
Then pointed
Toward the west.
The wind
Was not a storm,
Nor even strong;
It simply changed
Its mind again.
A restless arrow
Selling directions
To anyone
Who would pay.

My friends,
Where have you gone?
I need you.
I have something to say.
When you ask, I answer,
“Nothing.”
When you begin to leave,
I lower my voice.
The word I cannot speak aloud
Contains everything.

My little stream runs out to sea—
Blue harbor, will you answer me?
I bring you water from the hill,
From shaded stones and springs so still.
I have no treasure, pearl, or gold;
Only the stories I have told.
O sea, receive this wandering tune,
And carry it beneath the moon.

I crossed the hallway one last time,
Past lockers scraped and bare;
The classrooms held their emptied desks,
The summer waited there.
I climbed the steps and took my name
Across the brightened stage.
The bells, the books, the hurried mornings
Closed another page.
A wider life stood at the door,
Impatient to begin;
I left the building carrying
The person I had been.

Fair island in the western blue,
Your distant hills appear
Like folded music on the sea,
Like something half-heard here.
I have not touched your quiet shore,
Yet still your name can bring
The taste of salt, the cry of birds,
And summer on the wing.

The train keeps thunder in its wheels,
And crowded windows glow;
A hundred voices rise and fade
As fields and stations flow.
Then, in the space between two towns,
The racing thoughts grow still.
For one brief mile the moving world
Obeys a slower will.

Why are you far away tonight,
When clouds have covered every star?
The lightning writes across the sky
The words I cannot send that far.
The rain descends like unshed tears,
The thunder answers from above;
The leaves repeat my whispered plea:
Come back. Come back. I’m waiting, love.

The forest speaks in many tongues:
A branch, a wing, a stream.
Some voices soothe the frightened heart;
Some break the quiet dream.
But who can say what nature means,
Or translate root and stone?
We ask the trees to answer us,
And hear what is our own.

Ocean, ocean,
Shining blue,
What is moving there in you?
A silver fin,
A leap, a spray—
A dolphin laughing through the day.
It dives below,
Then rises high,
And throws a little piece of sky.

Each morning when the sun climbs clear
And finches crowd the garden wall,
A bead of rain slips from the leaf...
Each morning when the sun climbs clear
And distant bells ring bright and near,
The first small birds begin to call...
Each morning when the sun climbs clear
And finches crowd the garden wall.

There is a pleasure in the soil
When spring has loosened every clod;
The sparrows quarrel in the hedge,
The robins inspect the sod.
A seed goes down beneath my hand,
A green thought waits below;
The garden keeps its quiet faith
In everything we sow.

Though she remembers years gone by,
My love does not grow old.
We hold together, link by link,
A chain no hands can fold.
She is the song I carry home,
The fire beneath the rain;
Whatever roads the seasons take,
I choose her heart again.

There is a star above the roof.
Some people make a wish.
I have one hidden in my heart,
And I will not say which.
Perhaps the light will understand;
Perhaps it will refuse.
The sky gives every dream a chance,
But no promise to choose.
Look up, and make your own wish too.

A candle without any flame
Is only a stick in the dark.
You may lean upon it like a cane,
But the smallest pressure will mark
Its brittle, unhelpful side.
So strike a match while you can;
Give the waiting wick its work
Before the darkness makes its demand.

The Lord sings, “Take the day.”
He sends no storehouse for the week,
But bread enough for morning’s need
And courage for the weak.
“Gather what the daylight gives;
Do not hoard tomorrow’s share.
Yesterday’s bread turns hard and sour;
Today is fresh with care.
When dawn returns, I’ll send again.
Live one day, and meet me there.”

Peace—an old word,
polished smooth by many hands.
Can it survive
inside a room of shouting?
Can quiet take root
where every voice is sharpened?
Perhaps peace is not the absence
of the terrible noise,
but the breath we choose
between one cry and the next.

Learning is a splendid road,
but soon the road may have a sign
for every traveler.
Degrees will hang above the doors:
for bakers, sweepers, sailors, fools.
When every brow is crowned with letters,
letters may lose their shine.
Perhaps the scholars will retreat
to carving wood and mending chairs,
while everyone else discovers
what education was for.

I searched for some appropriate gift
To honor you today;
No jewel seemed worthy of your name,
No song knew what to say.
Then language taught me its small trick:
One flower answers one flower’s call.
So here is a rose for Rose,
And with it, I offer all.

CHILDHOOD

I remember the courtyard,
My mother’s patient scolding,
The games invented after rain,
The quarrels quickly mended.
My father’s serious voice,
My cousins racing through the dark,
The moon above the rooftops—
All of it remains.
I carry the years with me,
But I still miss the house
That made them possible.

Her sister writes in perfect lines;
I never learned the art.
I send these clumsy little words
To ask her for a start.
She says that rhymes are not her taste,
So mine may make her flee;
Still, if she reads this awkward plea,
Perhaps she’ll write to me.
I only want to know her voice
And be her sister, too.

The cord is never visible,
Yet no blade can cut it clean.
It bends when mother lifts the child,
And strengthens in between.
The years may lengthen out the thread,
The child may cross the sea;
Love keeps a quiet architecture
Of what they used to be.
From care comes courage,
From courage, choice,
From choice, a growing soul.

Laughter pushed me out the door,
I swear it did.
The pavement shone
Where nothing grew,
And I turned my head
To see if joy
Had left a trail.
Perhaps it had:
A lifted face,
A stranger smiling,
One more bright sound
Released into the street.

I stand beneath the theater lights,
Surrounded by the ghosts I knew.
Each gesture wakes an older room;
Each line becomes a life I outgrew.
The audience is made of years,
The future waits beyond the stage.
I speak, I turn, I take my place,
And history applauds the page.

Read a poem slowly.
It may be a maker,
It may be a roof,
It may be the hand
That keeps a falling world
From striking the ground.
Poetry is the question,
The answer, the river,
The salt in the bread.
It lives in the sky,
In the person beside you,
In love beginning again.

Money can purchase a chair,
But not the rest it promises.
It can buy a brighter room,
Not a reason to enter it.
Keep enough for shelter,
Enough for bread and sleep;
The rest is only weight
That teaches the hand to keep.

They say I am only testing my wings,
That I will come back down.
They say the wind is temporary,
That I am leaving town.
But something bright has opened up
Behind my ribs tonight.
I am not stretching toward the sky—
I am learning how to fly.

I want food.
That is true.
I do not want food
from every hand.
That is also true.
The body is made of what it takes,
And so I ask for bread
prepared by someone whose heart
has not forgotten kindness.
Let the meal be simple.
Let the cook be whole.
I want food.

There once was a fellow named Bram
Whose armpit was sour as a clam.
He toured through the square
With a grin and a stare,
While everyone else shouted, “Scram!”

MOTHER, my wheel will not obey;
My fingers burn, my throat is dry.
You say that love can mend the day—
Then tell me why I still must cry.
I trusted one whose words were sweet;
He praised my eyes, my mouth, my hair.
Perhaps a liar may be kind,
Or truth may wear a borrowed face.

late August
the school bell rings—
one lunchbox left open
late August
the school bell rings—
a mother wipes her eyes
the playground fills
with voices again

Why does affection find a seed
In soil we never planned?
It climbs the wall of circumstance
And takes us by the hand.
It asks no passport from the heart,
No proof before it starts;
It enters like a sudden spring
And rearranges hearts.
Love is not owned, nor locked away;
It lives by moving free.

I recognize myself in you.
Not as a sin,
Not as a virtue,
Not as a chain,
Not as a pardon.
I recognize the quiet truth
That makes two separate lives
Stand for a moment in one light.

They told me chance had made the world
And called the answer clear.
Still, I keep looking for a mark
That says a mind was here.
Is all this order merely luck?
Is beauty only chance?
The question follows every star
That crosses my expanse.

I wish
poems could open
like windows in the world,
letting astonishment rush in
until the crowd forgets its name,
until the humble field begins to sing,
until a brook lifts its silver voice
and every listener understands
that wonder is a kind of prayer.
I wish.

Courage does not silence fear;
it gives fear a place to stand.
Courage is the hand that shakes
and still reaches for the handle.
Courage lets you leave the room
when the room has made you small.
Courage says, “You may be hurt,”
then teaches you to rise.
It is not a sword in sunlight—
it is a step taken in the dark.

River, river, sacred river,
Carry every word below.
Wash the dust from hidden sorrow,
Let the buried embers glow.
In your shining current moving,
I release what I have known;
Take this heart and make it lighter,
Take this praise and make it your own.

Selling a bicycle.
When I bought it,
the shopkeeper praised its smooth wheels.
Now that I am selling it,
he points out every scratch.
The bicycle has not changed;
Only the speaker has.

Of every line I tried to write,
I trust the title least;
It came from someone else’s book,
And borrowed someone else’s feast.
If theft were measured by its scale,
I’d be a modest knave:
I stole a phrase and left the poem—
Perhaps the poem I should have saved.

I
will find
the thing I seek
if I keep moving
past every tempting pause.
The road need not explain itself;
my feet can learn its measure.
No wall can make me turn around.
I go.
I go.
I go.

There is a quiet joy in this:
That truth and love can grow.
Plant them in a wounded heart,
And see what roots will show.
Repair the mind, repair the soul;
The harvest will be wide.
The empty places fill with light
When kindness is applied.

Eternity is a wheel of glass,
Turning without a seam;
Time is the line that measures it,
Beginning in a dream.
The line may end, the wheel may spin,
The traveler may depart;
Yet every point along the ring
Returns to where you are.

Paris,
did you know
the hidden spark in me
can wake the sleeping words
you carry in your streets?
And when the inward fire rises,
your towers lose their shadows;
the poem steps outside my body
and finds itself in you.
In poetry,
we meet again.

In the hardest month of winter,
when the garden looked asleep,
a tiny bird began to chatter
by the gate.
The wind shook the bare branches;
I pulled my coat around me
and went to find the singer.
It was weaving sound from frost,
and the whole cold yard listened.

Love without hope is a lantern
carried into a crowded square.
The one who lifts it knows the flame
may never lead anyone home.
Still, the light touches passing faces;
still, the darkness gives way.
Some gifts are beautiful precisely
because they cannot be kept.

That fellow has discovered
some northern sort of romance
with the girl in the red scarf.
She looks like someone from the movies;
he looks like a man who won a prize.
Love sends the head spinning,
puts stars behind the eyes,
and makes an ordinary afternoon
feel like the moon has moved closer.

Stand up in the strength of thought,
In knowledge honestly won;
Stand up when power asks you kneel,
And choose the harder one.
Let wisdom be your backbone,
Let courage guard your name.
The road toward freedom rises
Through every tested flame.

In a quiet square I met an old man
Reading yesterday’s news.
He raised his eyes and asked me,
“What is this paper used for?”
I answered, “It contains the age,
Its triumphs and its lies.”
He smiled as if I had passed a test,
Then returned to the skies.

I miss the mirror I once broke;
Its dark gap held my face.
I bought a brighter, larger one
To give the room more grace.
But glass can change the frame alone;
The face remains the same.
I leaned in close and understood:
No mirror bears the blame.

We stood beneath the trees and listened.
Nothing moved but breath.
The silence gathered around us,
large enough to hold a thought.
Then a hare burst from the brambles,
and the spell ran after it.
The clearing was empty again,
but not as empty as before.

Beside me,
steady and warm,
you share the ordinary burdens:
the groceries,
the quiet injuries,
the sudden temper,
the small sentimental things.
You hide what hurts
until hiding hurts more.
My husband,
my companion,
I love you through every weather.

I saw it first above the roofs,
One pale point in black.
It looked too far for any hand,
Too shy to answer back.
I wanted to place that light
Inside your waiting palm;
But wanting is a timid thing,
And I delayed too long.
Tell me—if I brought it now,
Would you know it was from me?

Rain on the pavement,
a flower in my hand,
the theater doors opening and closing.
I waited through the trailers,
through the laughter of strangers,
through one whole hour of weather.
Then your car passed the curb
with someone else beside you.
The flower kept its shape.
I did not.

For two enchanted lovers,
I write this little tune;
Their initials meet in secret
Whenever rises the moon.
Love lifts you to the rooftops,
Then drops you through the floor;
It makes the stars look near enough
To touch, then asks for more.
Life is a winding roadway,
So watch the signs ahead—
The heart may be a fine driver,
But it has no map in its head.

Money has a bright arithmetic:
it counts, it multiplies, it spins.
But while the numbers grow larger,
the conscience may grow thin.
We purchase comfort, purchase praise,
purchase another want;
then find the self we traded away
waiting at the door.
Money can brighten a room,
but it cannot teach the room to glow.

Gray wrote his stately verses well,
And I respect his art;
But give me the song that trips along
And lifts the children’s hearts.
Some poems walk in solemn shoes,
Some dance without a plan;
I’ll take the tune that makes us laugh
And sing it when I can.

A statue leaves its pedestal,
And walks into the years.
Its shadow crosses crowded streets,
Its stone face gathers tears.
It circles back at evening,
Returning to its place;
The statue stands exactly still,
But time has changed its face.

The clearest truth is not a sword
Raised over every head.
It is the road of mercy,
The bread that can be shared.
The wise have named compassion
The doorway to the divine;
When separate hearts become one heart,
Truth begins to shine.

Mom’s car has three pedals,
And Dad’s car has two.
Does hers go one-third faster,
Or is that not what pedals do?
If I press the extra one,
Will the whole car take flight?
Mom just laughed and told me,
“Please leave the driving right.”

WOMEN sit together—
some young, some old.
The young wear spring upon their faces;
the old wear autumn’s gold.
Yet age has not diminished them.
The years have taught the eyes
to hold a deeper kind of beauty,
the beauty that survives.

Kindness is a cup of water
carried through a desert.
The giver may remain thirsty,
but another lives because of it.
No good deed is wasted
simply because we cannot drink
from every stream we make.

Sleep, little one,
let the night be kind.
I am your shelter,
your familiar song.
The world may turn beyond the window;
here, your breathing is safe.
Rest against my shoulder.
Let my arms be walls.
Sleep, little one,
until the morning calls.

Spanish guitars,
green fields,
and a ball crossing the line—
the feet knew what to do
before the mind could name it.
Victory arrived wearing red and gold.
Life is a long road with too many signs;
do not read them all at once.
Keep your hands on the wheel,
leave room for the unexpected,
and continue.

Of all the bright immortals
who once displayed their power,
only one walks beside me now
through this ordinary hour.
I take his hand and tell him tales;
he listens without pride.
The god of love has become a child
who wants to walk outside.

Faster! Faster! The small animals flee;
They scatter beneath the trees.
They want to remain where the grass is green,
But fear has driven them away.
The people shout, the engines start,
And the open field is gone.
They meant to stay.
They meant to stay.
Now they are only moving on.

If you examine the first attempts closely,
you will find no polished school of style:
only scattered poems,
a book assembled with hopeful hands,
and beginners testing the door.
The early writers were not monuments.
They were invitations.
Their rough pages made room
for the voices that followed.

I would compare you
To a room with no window,
Were it not for your laughter.
I would compare you
To a road without footsteps,
Were it not for your songs.
Where you are,
the dark is never complete.

Love is the window facing east;
At dusk, its panes grow dark.
But morning brings the patient light
And finds the waiting spark.
The sorrow of the night recedes,
The old wounds lose their claim;
Each dawn returns with open hands
And does not ask the flame
To answer for the night.

Water, water, everywhere—
The world begins where rivers run.
Without a drop, the fields lie still;
Without the rain, there is no sun.
Guard the cup, protect the spring,
Offer what you can.
A little water is a gift
From one living thing to another.

Graduation is a doorway,
a promise written in ink;
parents see a distant future,
students see the edge of what they think.
There are books and charts and deadlines,
libraries and sleepless nights,
and a mind that wanders outward
following new lights.
The gown is only cloth,
but the work beneath it matters:
knowledge gathers slowly,
then opens all the doors.

Life keeps changing its direction,
Love keeps learning how to grow;
Every heartbeat adds a sentence
To the story we don’t know.
Feelings may be shaped by weather,
But the deepest ones remain:
Love is life and life is love,
Sunlight after rain.

I fed her, watched her, carried her
Through seven careful years;
I knew the rhythm of her sleep,
Her laughter and her tears.
Last night I lay beside her bed
And heard a stranger speak:
“What a remarkable woman—
I wish I knew her better.”
The stranger was my own voice,
And the words were mine to keep.

To write is to gather color
From the ordinary day:
The window, the hand, the vanished road,
The words we could not say.
The brush is made of language;
The canvas is the mind.
One line may open distant skies,
One image leave us changed.
To write is to discover
What the heart was trying to find.

I remember how bright the world was
When you stood beside me then;
I remember what I promised,
What I thought the years would mend.
Then the hidden wheel of fortune
Turned toward grief I could not name.
Nothing reached you in time,
Nothing called you back from death.
Now the world is still familiar,
But it does not fit the same.

new bathroom
grandmother teaches brushing
red lipstick blooms
the child grins at the glass
mother storms in, blushing

Swirling, twirling, wintertime,
Candles in the snow;
Carols carry through the streets,
Warm windows shine and glow.
New Year waits beyond the bells,
Bright ribbons, silver cheer;
May every door receive some joy,
And every heart a year.

Some of my family reaches the ceiling,
some still fits beneath my arm.
I stand between their different heights
and find them all a charm.
The tall ones guard the little ones;
the little ones make me laugh.
Our family is a staircase
with room on every half.

Could I cross this city every day
and never see the same street?
Could a stranger corner of the map
show me a stranger I might meet?
Take the risk that marks the memory;
let the moment make its scar.
Sometimes the smallest unfamiliar road
reveals where we are.

Above the city, walking clouds,
I saw a figure dressed in white.
I bowed and called him holy;
He looked at me with puzzled eyes.
“I do not know that name,” he said.
The light continued on its way.
Perhaps a spirit needs no title
To brighten up the day.

Thank you for the quiet help,
For finding me when I withdraw;
You turn the gray of morning blue
And loosen every knot of fear.
You do not ask me to be brave;
You simply stay until I am.
The tears grow lighter in your care,
The day grows possible again.

Do you believe in you and me?
In a future we can build?
Do you believe two restless hearts
Can learn to both be still?
Do you believe that love can stand
When everything else moves?
I believe it can, if you do too.
I believe in us.

I do not want to go to school,
I’d rather stay in bed.
There are no sums I want to do,
No books inside my head.
“You must go,” my mother said,
“The children need you there.”
Then I remembered my mistake:
I am the teacher, not the heir!

I found an old card in a drawer,
The paper yellowed thin.
Its handwriting opened doors
To people I had been.
The sentences became whispers,
The whispers became rain;
I read until my eyes grew blurred
And folded it again.

Are you angry?
Have you built a shell
and hidden there?
Come out, old hermit;
play one note
on your little pipe.
Your silence makes the room
too heavy for me.
Come out.
Dance with me.
I cannot balance alone.

I have never trusted happiness.
It always seemed to borrow time.
Whenever my heart began to mend,
another crack appeared in the rhyme.
I wrote this years ago;
the old suspicion remains:
Joy enters through the front door,
then leaves through the rain.

Before I had a shape or name,
Your love had made a place for me.
You knew the roads I had not walked,
The person I might someday be.
Beyond the reach of human thought,
Your calm remains complete;
Through every changing season,
You have not left my feet.

Flutter, flutter, little moth,
Silver in the sun;
Over marigolds and thyme,
Your tiny journey runs.
Sip the flowers, turn and rise,
Circle once, then go;
Every drop of morning light
Makes your wings aglow.

I stand beside the sea,
but the sea will not receive me.
Warm waves fold into white lace
and collapse at my feet.
The rocks have made the water dangerous;
I remain on shore,
watching one bright breaker
after another
build itself and vanish.

Believe in the Maker, someone says—
But why should faith be blind?
I look at rivers, roots, and stars
And find a question there.
Perhaps belief is not a chain
Placed on the searching mind;
Perhaps it is the trust that grows
When wonder is allowed to shine.

Iambs march softly through the line,
Five feet can make a measured road;
The old playwrights knew the trick
Of giving thought a rhythmic load.
I once feared every metrical foot,
And fled from stress and rhyme;
Now every beat becomes a door
That lets the sentence climb.

Riders,
take the road
where the fields keep
their own counsel; speak
plainly, and let each promise be
an action. Loud empty bells announce
themselves, but truth needs no parade.
Walk with your eyes open.

Friend, your white beard has outlived
The banners of your youth.
You wait for justice to arrive
As though it owed you proof.
Do not spend your final years
Beneath a locked-up sky;
Carry your wisdom somewhere soft
Where gentler people try.
The world may not grow fair for you,
But you can make it kind.

Now that you leave for work each day,
the apartment has a different sound.
I walk from room to room and find
the spaces where you should be found.
I miss your ordinary questions,
even “What time is it?”
Silence has learned your shape,
and I keep tripping over it.

It is peaceful to wake alone
when no one waits for a declaration,
when I need not say “I love you”
to a heart that has already gone.
The morning is honest that way:
no performance, no disguise.
I can drink my coffee quietly
and let the truth rise.

At the center of the square,
everyone is acting:
the clerk reads the report,
the crowd repeats a rumor,
the relatives defend the king.
Voices collide like market bells.
One phrase is passed from mouth to mouth,
and no one asks whether it is true.
The only honest choice
is the one made after the noise.

Rainbow, where do you finish?
Do you bend behind the hill?
Is there treasure in the color,
or is wishing treasure still?
Rain, return across the valley;
paint the clouds from end to end.
I would rather keep the colors
than discover where they end.

I do not love you with my eyes;
they notice every flaw.
My heart ignores the evidence
and chooses you because.
Let vision make its careful case,
let judgment shake its head—
Love has a private argument
that reason cannot end.

January begins with vows,
with lists in careful rows.
Each promise lasts a week or two,
then quietly it goes.
We write the same ambitions down,
we fail them, and we smile;
Next year will bring another chance.
We have been saying this awhile.

I saw a star that seemed to wait
Above the winter street.
I formed a wish, but before it ended
The star had moved away.
I lowered my eyes and let it pass;
Another dream was due.
The sky is full of traveling lights,
And room for wishes too.

Beneath the pine trees I asked the boy
Where his teacher had gone.
“Up the mountain, gathering herbs,
Before the daylight’s gone.”
The clouds had covered every path;
The peak was lost from view.
I waited with the boy below,
Not knowing what else to do.

Christmas is near, my shepherd love;
Where do you spend the day?
Are you among the lambs and children,
In some green village far away?
Does a small house keep your laughter?
Does the hillside know your name?
I send a song across the fields
And hope it finds you all the same.

Leave the old road where it ends.
Dust the failure from your coat.
Try again with steadier hands;
There is still a boat.
If you have said, “I cannot,”
Let the sentence lose its claim.
The future does not ask perfection—
Only that you start again.

Faithful friend, I call you back
From all the years between.
You knew the first unfinished lines,
The hopes I had not seen.
Return and listen once again;
The old song has grown clear.
The verse I saved for you alone
Has been waiting all these years.

Seize
the morning.
Hold each hour
like a coin of light.
The sun is lowering now,
and time will not reverse.
Tomorrow may arrive,
but it is not here.
Spend the day you have.

Blind as the old singers were,
He walks with a child beside him.
The child receives the loaf and leads,
Though the father cannot see him.
He cannot watch the giver’s face,
Nor witness the hand that feeds;
But heaven keeps a clearer sight
Of every hidden deed.

I wish I loved the human crowd,
The way they wave and shout;
I wish their jokes could charm me,
And their footsteps draw me out.
When someone says, “How nice to meet you,”
I wish I answered, “What delight!”
Instead I search for any door
That leads me home by night.

You want to be a winner,
so you polish every shoe.
You call it honest ambition;
I call it what ambition makes you do.
You wait beside the avenue,
counting what the rich man spends;
then wonder why your conscience
has fewer and fewer friends.
Still you say, “I’ll rise somehow.”
Perhaps you will. Begin with how.

I watched the children learn the water,
some laughing, some afraid;
My granddaughter climbed the board
with the brave face she had made.
She splashed, she surfaced, she took a bow,
then asked to try once more.
The pool held every small success
and gave it back to shore.

The road has offered us a gift,
though every gift must end.
This life is not our private house;
we borrow and we bend.
So bow before the greater will,
and let your proud heart pray.
The traveler who follows faithfully
will not be lost today.

Come together; leave the old
arguments beneath the ground.
Come together; make a circle
wide enough for every sound.
When the danger gathers near us,
we will meet it side by side.
Separate, we fall like ashes;
joined, we become a tide.
Let us work with open hands:
Together we can stand.

While the hour still grants us laughter,
let us raise a glass and sing.
All of us will cross the water
when the final ferryman comes.
Life is turning like a wheel,
bright, brief, and passing by;
So be merry while the daylight
still is burning in the sky.

There was a young woman from Rye
Whose kite got entangled up high.
She climbed on a chair,
And shouted, “Beware!”
Then waved as the kite sailed by.

Red banners, bright banners,
ribbons in the air;
flags become a language
for anyone who cares.
Wear the colors proudly,
turn the wheels and sing;
Let every road remember
the joy of moving things.

Al Marlow, Saint Venn, and Coralie,
Old Harper, Noll, and Rene;
The bellman, the baker, the child at the gate,
The woman who gives bread away—
All names in the ledger,
All faces in rain,
All gathered at evening
To begin once again.
No one is forgotten,
No door is too small;
Let mercy enter each household,
And let it be Christian for all.

Respect is a door that opens
from both sides.
You may offer it freely;
you may earn it slowly.
No one can force another heart
to admire them.
Speak as you wish—
freedom gives you that much—
but remember the soil remembers
what you plant in it.

The teacher writes,
the students whisper,
the bell announces lunch.
The blackboard explains fractions
while the children explain
the latest movie.
By afternoon the teacher has learned
that every classroom contains
at least one lesson
the teacher did not prepare.

Stillness entered the room
without knocking.
We made space for it.
When it left,
the chair remained empty,
but the quiet stayed behind.
No greeting had been necessary;
no farewell could improve it.

Ask, “Who am I?”
but do not build the answer
inside the forehead alone.
The mind can manufacture rooms
and mistake their walls for truth.
Let the question travel downward,
through breath, hands, and silence,
until inquiry is no longer an image
but a way of being present.

Some people call it a game.
I call it draughts,
and I do not sit at the board
to make friends.
Old Tomas taught me the openings
in a sailors’ room years ago.
He never smiled when he won.
Neither did I.
The pieces crossed the square table
like soldiers with no appetite for peace.

We have filled these rooms for years,
and now the doors are wide.
Soon we will scatter toward new schools,
new streets, new names.
The maze will continue,
though we will not walk it together.
Still, friendship is a road
that does not end at the bell.
We are older now—
or at least taller.

At ten o’clock I find a pen,
An empty page, a chair;
I write beneath the Cairo moon
While warm air fills the air.
No palace lends me parchment,
No scholar guards the gate—
One blue biro and a hotel bill
Are all I need to wait.

When I cannot see the next step,
I trust the hand I cannot see.
The road may grow dull and difficult;
hope is still a form of clarity.
Praise the One who guides the lost,
and keep your heart turned out.
Faith does not erase the darkness;
it teaches us to move through doubt.

In the hush beyond the city,
the grass remembers rain.
The bush opens old memories
with a rustle and a flame.
Birds lift from the thorn trees,
bees move through the flowers,
and every living thing arrives
like weather after hours.
The stillness is not empty;
it is the land awake.

Teenage feelings change their coats
as quickly as the weather:
sunshine, hail, a sudden storm,
then warmth that lasts forever.
I remember that uncertain sky,
those climates of the heart—
one minute ready to conquer the world,
the next afraid to start.

Hope, hope, and hope again—
let the word remain alive.
Even in the narrowest hour,
give the heart a way to strive.
When adversity surrounds you,
do not make despair your throne.
Thoughts can open hidden windows;
no one has to face the dark alone.

I wake beneath a heavy sky,
in a room where nothing gleams.
Summer has forgotten warmth;
the clouds have swallowed dreams.
I wish I had a different life,
some proof that I belong,
but even wanting feels like work
when every road is long.
I look at those who seem to have
what I have never known.

A little frog in Costa Rica
was caught beneath the rain.
It hopped from stone to dripping stone
to escape the downpour’s pain.
At last it found one folded leaf
that held the weather back.
When the clouds had emptied out,
the frog resumed its track—
one grateful croak, one shining leap,
and freedom through the green.

Praise is a strange coat:
who stitched it, and for whom?
An insult from a fool may sound
like music in a room.
A compliment from someone false
can leave a bitter taste.
The poet’s art is partly this:
to know which ears to face.

The evening light grows thin.
We gather in a circle,
each person carrying one flame.
No candle is enough alone,
but together they become
a small and stubborn sun.
This is what our hands can do:
turn separate lights
into a way home.

Walk
with care
through the world.
The road is steep,
the stones are sharp,
the thorns remember skin.
Watch your footing,
but do not freeze.
A careful step is still a step;
keep going.

A friend is the one who helps
when you are caught in a mess.
A partner is already beside you,
equally covered in it.
A pal may have invited you there.
An acquaintance heard the rumor.
A buddy points at the stain
and says, “You made that yourself.”
The best of them stays anyway.

Spring, I am tender-hearted,
and I have much to say;
Before I leave the garden,
ask summer what I gave away.
The buds will tell the story,
the fruit will make it plain:
Love that seems too soft in spring
may ripen after rain.

At the late edge of life,
my wife and I still wake together.
We have known the anxious years,
the quiet years, the difficult weather.
Now happiness is not a trumpet;
it is a hand across the bed,
a familiar voice at breakfast,
the peace of being understood.

Change waits at every doorway;
sometimes it enters without knocking.
It turns the road, unpacks the room,
and gives the past new clothing.
Resisting does not stop the river;
it only tires the swimmer.
If life is to improve,
we must learn to move with it.

I hear the music before it arrives,
like a pulse beneath the floor.
It escapes the measured line,
then returns asking for more.
Music lives in wind and blood,
in the hammer and the rain;
without it, life would lose the beat
that teaches us our names.

I thought I walked the shore alone,
yet footsteps kept beside my own.
I turned toward the silver light,
expecting someone there.
The second shadow disappeared;
the water held no face.
Only the tide continued on,
untroubled by the space.

This Christmas I ask for nothing
wrapped in paper, tied with string.
Let me see my children laughing;
that would be everything.
Let the house be briefly quiet
while their happiness unfolds.
No gift beneath the tree could shine
as brightly as those souls.

My father’s memory comes wrapped
in the white paper of a lunch.
He carried love in ordinary hands,
and gave it out by noon.
His body was a small magician’s box;
from it came work and bread,
and rivers formed by every deed
he performed before he died.

I know my letters, know my sums;
I say I need no school.
I have a job, I have a chair,
I think that makes me cool.
My parents say the world is wide,
that reading opens more;
I wonder if the alphabet
has hidden another door.

Time takes the cities one by one,
the heroes and the crowns.
It carries every human deed
where no remembrance sounds.
Even songs that seem to last
will fade beneath the years;
the trumpet loses breath at last,
the lyre its final tears.

Fire, fire, summer fire,
bright inside the chest;
Fire joins the breathing air
and will not let me rest.
It warms the kitchen, lights the field,
and dances without shame.
When truth and fairness feed the spark,
the heart can bear the flame.

Two sisters bathed one Saturday,
then giggled in the hall.
The nurse asked what had made them laugh;
they would not answer all.
At last one whispered, “Joni bathed,
and I just watched her do it.”
The nurse shook her head and said,
“Next time, both of you get through it.”

The moon grew thin beneath the dark,
Her silver veil undone;
The watching stars leaned close to see
What shadow crossed the sun.
They trembled in the upper air,
Yet none withdrew their gaze.
The night had challenged its own queen
And stood amazed.

Rain comes in restless intervals;
the wind, exhausted, turns.
Gray clouds press against the roofs,
and every wet leaf burns
with a dull, reflected afternoon.
No thunder claims the sky—
only the patient, broken fall
of water passing by.

In the hour when weariness arrives,
let me surrender without shame.
Do not force the tired spirit
to perform devotion like a game.
Draw your dark curtain over daylight;
let the body have its rest.
When morning opens its clear eyes,
I will rise renewed and blessed.

He carries romance like a lantern,
always ready to display its glow.
He finds a story in a garden,
a promise in the falling snow.
He does not mock the dreaming heart;
he keeps his wonder near.
To him, the world is not too serious
to make affection clear.

This is my dream,
my very private dream:
I dreamed my hair was perfectly neat.
Then someone I loved came laughing by
and mussed it with both hands.
I woke with the room unchanged,
but kept the dream’s disorder.

In this small token I have placed
The monument of what I feel.
While we remain beneath the sun,
Its little chain will make it real.
And if our roads should never meet,
Keep this as my last part:
I leave you not a jeweled thing,
But the inheritance of my heart.

They told me poetry should choose
The finest words, arranged with care,
Meaning folded into structure,
Music balanced in the air.
I learned the rule, then changed the road;
I broke the frame and made my own.
The poem is not a narrow room—
It is a house with many doors.

A depth of shadows,
unmeasured,
waits beneath the visible world.
Colors no human hand invented
move across a widening canvas.
Above us, another life reflects
what our eyes have not yet learned.
The picture is unfinished,
but it is waiting.

The one who never came
still arranged my heart around an absence.
What else could longing be
but architecture made from air?
I drew a thousand possible joys
and left one space uncolored.
Perhaps you are not the missing figure;
perhaps you are the shape
that made all the others possible.

I lose my name and call it peace.
I accept the world, then push against it.
I straighten my back with both hands
and remember what I can support.
You remember me;
I remember you.
I take you as you are,
every scar and every small mark included.

Beach, beach—
Puri’s bright edge,
the temple, the sellers,
the horses and camels,
the shortage of hours.
Beach, beach—
shops under the salt wind,
humanity moving past me.
I like this shore
because the river of my life
has already swallowed the road.

There is a country made of morning
where night cannot remain,
where spring continues without ending
and joy forgets its name.
No fear crosses that bright border,
no sorrow owns the land.
There, love is not a promise made—
it is the air at hand.

I know a baby with round eyes,
Pink cheeks and dimpled knees,
Small wrists folded like little fans,
Soft hands that clutch at sleeves.
The mouth makes one demanding sound:
“Come close, and hold me tight.”
Then sleep lowers its gentle curtain,
And the whole room becomes light.

Let love and friendship travel on
Through every changing year.
Let sympathy remain the bridge
When distance brings us near.
Speak truth, not as a weapon,
But as a seed we tend;
The world is made more habitable
By hearts that do not bend.

Release the page!
Let culture breathe
through colors, words, and sound.
Creation is a door we open
into a stranger ground.
Bring out the hidden image;
let imagination start.
The work that surprises others
may first surprise the heart.

Mother’s china waits in stacks;
I was not allowed to eat
Beside the adults at their table,
So I work beside the sink.
I rinse the traces from each plate,
I dry the silver rim;
Then, before I wash another,
I take a break for him—or me.

Lady Mara and her squirrels,
red as sparks among the trees,
run unburdened through the country,
fearless in the autumn breeze.
No one owns their russet coats,
no one tells them where to go;
they carry only their bright pride
through the fields below.

The basketball season rises:
quick hands, bright shoes, and speed;
A sudden dunk, a stolen pass,
the defense begins to bleed.
Three-pointers arc like fireflies,
the crowd refuses sleep;
Every player wants the final prize,
the promise they can keep.

Food remembers where you came from,
what the family taught your tongue.
Food can hide a history,
or reveal it when it’s young.
Take the plate and tell the truth;
the table knows your past.
No appetite can disappear
behind a mask forever.

You are my butterfly,
bright over every flower.
You carry grace into the room
and make the minutes softer.
I love you for your patient wings,
for all the warmth you bring.
You are not merely my butterfly—
you are my mother, my spring.

Thank you, sister,
for the days you stayed.
Thank you for the love
that did not change when people turned cruel.
You stood beside me
when the room became too loud.
I have said these words before,
but tonight they carry more weight:
thank you for being there.

Today I looked at you
and wondered whether love
still lived behind your eyes.
Perhaps you wanted me back;
perhaps I only wanted that to be true.
Either way, I felt the old door open—
and this time, I may be the one
who walks away.

Come, touch the strings and wake the room;
Let music loosen every fear.
Send quick sparks dancing through my blood,
Then draw the gentler melody near.
When all my restless thoughts have burned,
Give me a note as smooth as rain;
Let song first lift me into flame,
Then settle me to sleep again.

I worshiped the portrait love had made—
the long white throat, the midnight hair.
I prayed before that living face
as if a god were standing there.
The jealous powers above looked down,
offended by my human shrine;
They turned the image cold as stone
and left the punishment as mine.

Some call him an ordinary cat,
but wait until he’s fed;
He rules the roof, the yard, the town,
and sleeps beside my head.
He gathers every creature’s fear
into one regal stare;
The smallest beast can wear a crown
if no one tells him where.

Behind the mask
is a personality
bright enough to start a parade.
Jolly, noisy,
full of sudden weather,
you turn every stranger
into a temporary friend.
No room stays awkward for long;
you break the ice,
then dance on what remains.

The laughter in your chest
could raise a ship from the harbor,
could guide a lost child home,
could make sorrow loosen its grip.
Your laughter becomes mine;
my heart answers yours.
Two damaged vessels,
lifted by the same tide,
learning that joy is not a betrayal
of what hurt us.

There are roads written across the sky,
but no wheels travel there.
I trace them from the ground,
imagining ropes anchored in blue.
The clouds drift like islands;
I want to climb among them,
to rest above the roofs,
to swim through daylight.
For now, I sit below
and let my thoughts go upward.

People worship money as if it were a god.
It buys a meal, a roof, a coat,
and sometimes a very expensive toy.
But it cannot buy the friend
who knows when you are pretending.
It cannot purchase the family
that stays after the money is gone.
It cannot make love sincere.
So call it useful if you like—
just do not call it everything.

The calendar is losing pages.
Shoppers hurry through the season,
buying away the quiet.
The year changes its colors,
then disappears into the next.
What waits beyond the turning?
More of what we already know,
or a clean breath of weather?
I stop, exhale,
and choose to enter the future awake.

Mirror, mirror, answer plainly:
Who is least fair to see?
The glass replied, “The one who thinks
that ugliness is destiny.
Faces change and bodies tire;
judgment makes the deeper scar.
The cruelest eye is not the glass—
it is the eye that says you are.”

His eyes were coals beneath the leaves;
I felt the cold climb through my spine.
He watched me from the other side,
all muscle, feather, hook, and shine.
The minutes stretched. I could not move.
The glass was all that stood between
my frightened face and talons curved
for something smaller than a dream.
Then he opened his wings and rose,
leaving the sky abruptly clean.

A friend may share a sister’s heart;
a sister may not be kind.
The friend who stays through every storm
is family by design.
I will not let you disappear
when trouble fills the room.
You are the sister I was given
by love instead of blood.

There was a young lady of Tyre
Who played a magnificent lyre;
Each shimmering chord
Made the harbor applaud,
And set every lighthouse on fire.

The innocence of an earlier world
has gone where hands cannot follow.
We hold its image in memory,
but memory is not tomorrow.
We say we will preserve the past;
the past refuses to stay.
It lives as a light behind us,
and cannot be carried away.

She teaches me the patient things:
how to begin, how to repair,
how work becomes less difficult
when someone shows they care.
She helps me through the ordinary,
makes each afternoon bright;
With her, the smallest lesson
can turn into delight.

Last spring was beautiful because
you stood beside the trees.
You loved the thrushes’ morning song;
I loved the way you listened.
This spring I will not summon you,
or make the season explain.
I’ll love the birds because they sing,
and spring because it came again.

“A special pen, perhaps?”
“A silver one? A fountain nib?”
“For graduation, sir, it seems
the daughter wants a sports car.”
“A pen is more affordable.”
“Then wrap it with some grace.”
“We have a lovely imitation
that writes in second place.”

Treatment begins with how we look:
the creature, the neighbor, the stranger.
Animals act from instinct;
humans can choose a better danger.
Use reason not to dominate,
but to make compassion wise.
The measure of a civilization
is how it treats the lives it finds.

School can fill the head with weather:
pressure, thunder, sudden rain.
Some days I cannot think about it;
some days I am glad I came.
Rules may seem like iron fences,
but learning gives the gate.
Go inside, ask questions, listen—
it is not too late.

For you,
I leave the porch light on.
My arms remain open,
my heart has not moved on.
I dream of you at midnight,
remember you at dawn.
Whatever time may take from us,
my love keeps waiting on.

Seize this New Year while it shines;
the lanterns cross the street.
The dog-year drums are calling,
and every door has something sweet.
There may be no promised tomorrow,
so celebrate tonight.
No limits on our laughter—
let the red fire fill the night.
Next year? We cannot know.
That is why this moment glows.

Do not imitate me.
You cannot add an inch to a foot
and call the measure your own.
You cannot split a melon in two
and claim the fruit has changed.
Find your own strange shape.
Borrowing another person’s outline
is the dullest kind of disguise.

Power meets power in the upper air;
the pressure deepens, sparks appear.
Fire rises where the currents meet,
and wind carries the living heat.
Air protects the flame from rain;
fire gives the breath a name.
Between them, something starts to move:
a force both dangerous and true.

I cry when pain has found me,
when sadness will not leave.
I cry when I am punished,
when anger makes me grieve.
Grownups say that crying means
the heart has lost its way—
but Mommy cries at weddings,
so perhaps tears also say:
This happiness is larger
than my body can contain.

I scrub the kitchen boards
as women before me scrubbed them.
The bucket clouds with gray water;
the house gives back its history.
A long silver hair floats loose,
and I lift it from the pail.
For a moment I feel all their lives
moving through my hands.

Two towers twist toward the clouds,
their glass refusing the sun.
Soft air strikes the sharp new walls
and finds its path divided.
Workers climb through the skeleton,
building rooms above the street;
The city’s great machines are fed
by every human heartbeat.

Tide in:
we walk together
along the lit promenade,
talking while the sea
keeps opening its silver hands.

Tide out:
we cross the darkened sand,
stop where the water retreats,
and hold each other
until the shore is quiet.

The Vale do Paraíba Highway, designated SP-451, is a major road in southeastern Brazil. The highway was among the first roads in the region to calculate tolls according to a vehicle’s axle weight rather than its length. It links the metropolitan outskirts of São Paulo with manufacturing towns and agricultural districts farther inland. The route was originally built as a two-lane road, but successive improvements added divided sections, service lanes, and interchanges near the largest settlements. Freight traffic forms a substantial part of its daily use, particularly vehicles carrying machinery, food products, and construction materials. The highway also serves commuters traveling between the valley towns. During holiday periods, congestion is concentrated near river crossings and industrial access roads. Its name is frequently used for the connected commercial corridor as well as for the numbered road itself.

The European Platform Fairness Regulation is a proposed framework intended to limit abusive practices by the largest online intermediaries. It would require designated platforms to explain certain ranking decisions, provide practical methods for transferring user data, and maintain procedures for businesses wishing to challenge an automated decision. A separate clause would give small companies a temporary exemption from the most detailed reporting requirements during their first year of operation. Companies would be classified as systemically important when they exceeded specified thresholds for users, revenue, and control of a major digital service. Regulators could order corrective measures and impose penalties based on worldwide turnover. The proposal was presented as a way to preserve competition without banning large platforms outright. Critics argued that its reporting requirements would burden smaller firms that supplied infrastructure to the regulated services.

Aerial photographs have identified several faint field boundaries running toward Redbank Camp, although their relationship to the enclosure is uncertain. Redbank Camp is an Iron Age defensive enclosure on a low ridge above the River Dene in northern England. Archaeologists believe that the earliest settlement consisted of a single earthwork bank with a ditch on its eastern side. Later occupants added a second rampart around the southern approach, where the slope was gentle enough for attackers to reach the interior. The western edge required little construction because the ground falls sharply toward the river. Small terraces inside the enclosure may have held roundhouses, although cultivation has obscured most of the traces. A narrow gap in the northern bank is generally interpreted as the principal entrance. The site has not been fully excavated.

A del credere arrangement is a commercial agreement in which an agent accepts additional responsibility for the customer’s performance. In older commercial practice, the supplementary commission was sometimes described as a form of insurance even though the agent did not insure the transaction in the modern sense. The agent receives a supplementary commission in exchange for promising to compensate the principal if the customer fails to pay or otherwise defaults. This obligation differs from ordinary agency, where the agent generally arranges the transaction but does not guarantee the other party’s solvency. A del credere agent is normally liable only for the particular failure covered by the agreement. For example, the agent may have to cover an unpaid account caused by insolvency, but not a dispute arising because the buyer rejects goods that do not conform to the contract. The exact scope depends on the agency terms.

The Civic Ecology Party is a German political party founded in 1997 through the union of several regional environmental groups. Its first national congress adopted a policy of rotating the party chair every two years, a rule later criticized as making long-term leadership difficult. It combines ecological policy with support for expanded local government and proportional representation. The party first gained seats in state legislatures during the following decade and later entered coalitions with both social-democratic and liberal parties. Its membership includes conservationists, urban planning activists, and advocates of renewable energy. The party’s parliamentary delegation has generally been smaller than those of the traditional national parties, but it has exercised influence in coalition negotiations. Internal debates have focused on whether rapid climate legislation should take priority over economic measures designed to protect industries undergoing technological transition.

Algebraic modeling systems provide a notation for expressing optimization and equilibrium problems without writing the numerical solution procedure directly. Early commercial systems were often distributed with sample transportation models that became informal tests of whether a new solver could read the language correctly. A modeler describes variables, constraints, objectives, and data relationships, after which the system translates the formulation for a suitable solver. Common applications include production planning, transportation, energy scheduling, and financial analysis. Extensions have been developed for stochastic programs, complementarity systems, and problems in which several participants pursue competing objectives. Some environments also connect models to databases and allow the same formulation to be tested with different data sets. This separation between description and computation permits researchers to change algorithms while preserving the underlying mathematical statement of the problem.

The Inner Household was the name given to the private service of the royal court in the Kingdom of Arandia. It was distinct from the outer offices responsible for taxation, military administration, and provincial correspondence. The household occupied the most secluded courts of the palace and was directed by a senior chamberlain appointed by the monarch. Its departments managed the royal apartments, treasury, kitchens, wardrobe, and ceremonial objects. A palace school trained pages in languages, music, military etiquette, and accounting. Graduates could later enter the civil service or become officers in the household guard. A surviving court ordinance required pages to spend their first winter sleeping in the service corridors rather than in the palace dormitories. Although the institution originated as a domestic establishment, its members often acquired considerable political influence through their proximity to the crown.

Mara Ellison is an American theater director, actor, and musician who began her career with an improvisational ensemble in Chicago. Before directing, she spent a season as the musical director for a touring children’s theater and wrote short brass arrangements for its performances. After appearing in regional productions, she received supporting roles in several television comedies and directed a series of student performances in the Midwest. Ellison later established a youth improvisation program that offered classes to teenagers who could not afford private instruction. She also performed trombone and vocals in the touring band Harbor Weather, which released an independent album in the late 1980s. The group played clubs throughout the eastern United States and became known for its informal audience participation. Ellison has taught directing and performance at several colleges.

Daniel Mercer is a former American soccer player who appeared as a forward and attacking midfielder. Across a professional career lasting fourteen seasons, he recorded 47 goals in domestic league and cup competitions. His most productive campaign came after a change from the wing to a central attacking role, when he scored nine times in league play. Mercer entered the senior game through the academy of a Premier League club and spent his early years on loan with teams in the second and third tiers. He later played in the United States and briefly joined a Scandinavian club during the winter season. Injuries limited his final campaigns, and he retired after appearing for a regional side in 2019. Following retirement, Mercer worked as a youth coach and earned a qualification in sports administration.

Blue Current is a South Korean R&B trio formed by musicians who met while studying in California. The group moved its activities to Seoul and released its first album in the mid-1990s. Its debut single was promoted through a small series of university concerts before the group appeared on national television. Its recordings combined American soul harmonies with Korean ballad melodies, rap interludes, vocal percussion, and programmed rhythms. The members divided the work between lead singing, production, keyboards, and turntables, giving the group a sound that differed from the dance-pop and adult ballad styles then dominant in the market. Blue Current’s early singles became influential among younger performers, and later critics credited the trio with helping establish a place for contemporary R&B in Korean popular music.

The first takes for *Signals in the Dark* were recorded in a former radio studio whose control room had been left unchanged since the 1950s. *Signals in the Dark* is the fourth studio album by the American funk group Night Assembly. Released in 1976, it followed the commercial success of the band’s more dance-oriented record *Open Circle*. The album combines electric piano, brass arrangements, jazz improvisation, and early synthesizer textures. Its nine tracks were arranged as a loose sequence moving from urban night scenes to a final, slower meditation on morning. Although it did not match the group’s earlier chart performance, the record was praised for its layered production and later became a favorite among musicians interested in funk-jazz fusion. A remastered edition added two instrumental versions and a rehearsal recording.

*The Road to the Western Sea* is a Malayalam travel narrative attributed to Mathew Kurian, a priest and teacher from the Malabar coast. A surviving colophon identifies the first copy as having been completed during a year of unusually heavy monsoon rain, though the date cannot be matched to an independent record. The work describes a journey undertaken by a small delegation traveling through port cities toward the Mediterranean and returning by a different route. Kurian records changes in language, food, architecture, and religious practice as well as the difficulties of arranging transport across several jurisdictions. The manuscript circulated privately for more than a century before being printed by a regional press. Modern scholars have treated it both as a travel account and as an early argument for civic cooperation among the communities of the Indian coast. Several portions survive only in later copies.

The contribution-visibility effect is a concept in behavioral economics describing the additional satisfaction people may receive when their charitable actions are noticed. Experiments using anonymous and publicly named donations have reported larger differences when participants were told that other donors would see their choices. A donor motivated by this effect may care about the recipient while also valuing recognition, public credit, or evidence that the contribution has been counted. The idea helps explain why named scholarships, public pledges, and visible fundraising totals can increase participation. It does not imply that a publicly recognized gift is insincere; motives may be mixed and can change over time. Researchers distinguish the effect from direct financial reciprocity, in which a donor expects a material return from the recipient. The reward in contribution visibility is social or emotional rather than monetary.

A lateral consonant is produced when the central passage of air is obstructed by the tongue and air escapes along one or both sides. A small number of languages distinguish lateral sounds at three different places of articulation, allowing words to contrast dental, alveolar, and palatal laterals. The English sound usually represented by “l” is a familiar example. Laterals are commonly classified as liquids, but the category also includes fricatives, affricates, and brief flap-like sounds in some languages. The location of the tongue contact may be dental, alveolar, postalveolar, or farther back in the mouth. Several languages distinguish more than one lateral according to place or manner of articulation. In some southern African languages, lateral clicks combine a side release with a separate click mechanism, producing sounds that have no close equivalent in English.

Martin Vale (born 1947) is a British singer, songwriter, and record producer whose work has been recorded by performers in pop, soul, and country music. His first publishing contract was arranged through a small London agency that specialized in advertising jingles. He began writing songs for local groups before releasing several albums under his own name. During the 1970s and 1980s, Vale collaborated with lyricists and composers in London, Los Angeles, and Nashville, often supplying melodies for songs later completed by other writers. His credits include ballads, television themes, and dance singles, although he is best known for songs recorded by female vocalists. Vale’s daughter became a touring keyboard player, while his younger brother worked as a studio engineer. He received a lifetime achievement award from a British songwriters’ organization in 2017.

Alsophila monticola is a tree fern found in the humid upland forests of eastern New Guinea and several nearby islands. It usually grows between 800 and 1,700 metres above sea level, although island populations occur at lower elevations. A survey of the largest island population recorded unusually pale spores, a feature that has not been reported from the mainland form. The trunk may exceed four metres in height and supports a crown of broad, finely divided fronds. Mature plants generally retain fewer than a dozen living fronds at one time. The lower part of the stalk is covered with pale scales and occasional short spines. Fertile structures occur near the midribs of the smallest divisions of the frond and are partly enclosed by thin coverings. Botanists have noted considerable variation in the species, and some island populations may eventually be treated as separate taxa.

Lena Morneau (born 1975) is a Canadian journalist and television presenter who has worked in sports, entertainment, and morning programming. She began as a radio reporter before joining a national cable network, where she covered horse racing and university basketball. Morneau later presented a weekend interview program and served as a correspondent for an entertainment news series. She hosted a cooking-and-relationships program for two seasons and was the presenter of the first edition of a Canadian culinary competition. During the program’s first season, she also wrote a weekly newspaper column about contestants’ recipes. Her work has included red-carpet broadcasts, documentary interviews, and a short-lived country-music talent show. Morneau has appeared as a guest commentator on several radio programs and continues to work in television production.

An equinoctial gnomon is an astronomical device designed to identify the date or time at which the Sun crosses the celestial equator. One surviving instrument from the Mediterranean has a movable ring that allowed observers to adjust the device without rebuilding its support. The instrument consists of a marked surface and a raised rod or ring arranged in relation to the observer’s latitude. Near the equinoxes, the shadow follows a characteristic path that can be compared with earlier observations. Builders in the ancient Mediterranean used related devices to improve calendar calculations and to establish the orientation of public buildings. At locations far from the equator, the apparatus must be inclined so that its reference plane corresponds to the projected equatorial plane. The device is simple in principle, but accurate results depend on careful alignment and a level observing surface.

The Southern Peninsula Bank was established in 1951 to provide commercial credit to small manufacturers and agricultural traders in southern India. During the following decades it absorbed several local banking companies and expanded its branch network beyond the original coastal districts. The bank issued its first series of computer-printed passbooks in the 1980s, a change that reduced the time required to update accounts in busy market towns. By the late twentieth century, the bank operated hundreds of branches and automated cash machines in major cities as well as smaller market towns. Its directors later negotiated a merger with a larger national bank, arguing that the arrangement would provide access to modern technology and broader lending capacity. Regulators approved the transaction in 2004. The former bank’s headquarters became a regional office, and its shareholders received shares in the acquiring institution.

The Northbridge Football Club was an Australian rules football club based in a township north of Adelaide. Founded in 1872, it was among the early members of the region’s principal football association. The club suspended senior competition for several seasons after an internal dispute divided its players into two neighborhood teams. It later returned through a merger with a smaller side and resumed playing at its original ground. Financial difficulties and disagreements over the distribution of home fixtures weakened the club during the 1890s. After a season in which it recorded no victories, the committee notified the association that it would not enter the following competition. The club had won a regional premiership shortly before the dispute divided its players. Junior football continued in the district under a different organization.

Matthias Verhulst of Bruges was a sixteenth-century philosopher and logician who taught in the schools of northern France. A later catalogue identifies him as one of the first teachers in the region to use printed diagrams when explaining conditional arguments. Born into a merchant family, he entered an Augustinian house as a young man and studied rhetoric, theology, and Aristotelian logic. His commentaries examined the structure of conditional propositions and the ways in which a conclusion could follow from several statements. Verhulst taught at colleges in Paris and Rouen and influenced students who later wrote on natural philosophy and language. He favored a realist account of universals and opposed the more radical nominalist positions common among some of his contemporaries. A small number of his printed works survive, along with a biography written by one of his former pupils.

Eleanor Price was an American astronomer whose research combined photometry with the design of observational instruments. She taught at a university in California and developed detectors used on large optical telescopes in the western United States. Her equipment allowed astronomers to compare the brightness of faint objects across different wavelengths and helped improve measurements of distant galaxies and active stellar systems. One detector design was later adapted for a survey that measured the brightness of quasars at several radio frequencies. Colleagues regarded Price as an unusually practical researcher because she frequently built, tested, and repaired the devices used in her experiments. She earned a doctorate in the 1950s and remained active in observatory work for more than three decades. Several of her instruments were adapted for later surveys of quasars.

The Evangelical Church of the Lower Coast was a Protestant regional church serving congregations in the northern districts of a German state. It combined Lutheran traditions with administrative practices inherited from earlier union churches. The church’s final merger was preceded by an agreement to keep its theological library in the port city where the bishop had preached. The bishop’s principal preaching church was located in a historic port city, while the church administration occupied offices nearby. In addition to parish worship, the organization operated schools, charitable homes, and theological training programs. After political and demographic changes reduced the number of independent congregations, the regional church entered negotiations with neighboring bodies. It was dissolved in 2011 when it joined two other Protestant churches to form a larger northern federation. Its archives were transferred to a church historical center.

Samuel Armand was a French-American clarinetist and saxophonist who taught at conservatories in New York and New England. He performed with radio orchestras during the 1940s, appeared in several studio ensembles, and played bass clarinet in a major symphony orchestra. Armand later became a faculty member at a prominent music school, where he taught students who went on to work in jazz, film scoring, and concert music. One of his former students later credited Armand’s demonstrations of circular breathing with changing the way the school taught bass clarinet. His instruction emphasized breath control, tone production, and the ability to adapt quickly to unfamiliar arrangements. He also coached reed sections for touring big bands and occasionally arranged music for television programs. Armand retired from regular teaching in the early 1980s.

Patrick Doran is an Irish musician known for playing bass in the rock group Meridian. The group’s first recording was made in a rehearsal room behind a Dublin theater and was released by a small label before the band had played a national tour. His family moved from England to Ireland when he was a child, and he met the band’s other founding members at secondary school. Doran’s restrained playing style provided a steady rhythmic foundation for the group’s early recordings, while later albums gave him a larger role in arranging and production. He has also contributed to film soundtracks and collaborated with the band’s drummer on instrumental projects. Meridian has received numerous industry awards and was inducted into a national music hall of fame. Doran continues to perform with the group and supports music education programs in Dublin.

Re Evans v. Northport is a Canadian constitutional decision concerning the division of legislative authority between the federal and provincial governments. The short railway continued to operate for several years after the judgment, but its bonds were later refinanced by the municipality. The dispute arose after a province authorized a municipality to issue bonds for a short railway connecting local farms with an international port. The federal government argued that the project formed part of an interprovincial transportation system and therefore fell under federal jurisdiction. The court held that the statute primarily concerned local taxation and municipal finance. Because the railway was limited in scope and did not form part of a national network, the provincial legislature had acted within its authority. The decision became a frequently cited example of the importance of a law’s practical purpose.

A radio producer in Chicago first suggested releasing “After the Rain” as a single after hearing an unfinished rehearsal tape. “After the Rain” is a power ballad released by the American rock group Silver Avenue in 1991. Written by the band’s keyboardist and recorded during sessions for the album *Open Roads*, it features a prominent lead vocal over restrained drums and layered guitar. The song became the group’s first major radio success and reached the top position on several adult-contemporary charts. Unlike the band’s earlier singles, it contains little brass and relies on synthesizer textures to create its atmosphere. A later acoustic version appeared on a greatest-hits collection. Critics have described the song as a transitional recording between the band’s arena-rock period and its quieter work of the mid-1990s.

The *Kalyāṇa Kathā* is a group of Bengali devotional narratives composed between the fifteenth and nineteenth centuries. One cycle became associated with a river festival after a local manuscript was discovered beneath the floor of a shrine. The poems center on local deities whose stories are connected with wider Hindu traditions, and they were often performed at seasonal festivals or household ceremonies. Individual works describe the deity’s birth, conflicts with rival powers, tests of human devotion, and eventual establishment of a shrine or sacred practice. Some cycles are associated with river communities, while others developed around agricultural villages and market towns. The tradition was sustained by several generations of poets rather than by a single author. Manuscripts vary considerably in length, language, and the balance between mythic episodes and descriptions of everyday social life.

A hieroglyph is a written sign that may represent an object, an action, or a sound. A small number of Egyptian signs were used mainly to distinguish personal names from nearby words, although their exact function varied by period. The term originally referred to the monumental picture-signs used in ancient Egypt, but it is also applied more generally to scripts whose characters have a strongly pictorial appearance. Egyptian signs could function as words, consonants, or phonetic groups, and additional signs were used to clarify meaning. Their carved form was laborious to produce, so administrative writing usually employed faster cursive scripts. Reading and composing monumental inscriptions required specialized training, which placed scribes, priests, and officials in a position of considerable authority. Renaissance writers later treated the signs as symbols of hidden philosophical ideas, often without understanding their original grammatical use.

Anika Rao (born 1972) is an Indian film actress who has worked in Telugu, Tamil, Kannada, Malayalam, and Hindi productions. She began performing in supporting roles before receiving recognition for a series of dramatic characters in the 1990s. Rao has appeared in more than two hundred films and has received several regional awards for acting, including prizes for both leading and supporting performances. Her first major award came for a supporting role in a Kannada-language family drama, a performance that led to offers from directors in several other industries. Her portrayal of a politically ambitious matriarch in a historical drama brought her a new generation of admirers. In addition to cinema, she has acted in television serials and served as a judge on a dance competition. Rao is known for alternating between commercial films, family dramas, and roles that require extensive theatrical makeup.

Ashwell Castle is a ruined motte-and-bailey fortification near a village in Lincolnshire. The settlement appears in medieval records under a name that may preserve an Old English personal name. A raised mound once supported a timber tower, while two enclosed courts extended toward the lower ground. The smaller inner court probably contained domestic buildings and storage sheds; the larger outer court may have held livestock and temporary shelters. A shallow ditch survives on the eastern side, where the natural slope is least steep. Local excavation records describe a short-lived timber bridge across the ditch, although no trace of its supports has survived. Most of the stone visible at the site comes from later boundary walls rather than from the castle itself. Excavation has been limited, and the date of abandonment remains uncertain.

Christopher Mallory is a British electronic musician, club DJ, and producer. He began performing at small London venues with a sound system assembled from second-hand equipment and later secured a regular residency at an underground dance club. Mallory’s first residency lasted only three months because the venue changed ownership, but it introduced him to producers who later invited him into a studio collective. Mallory won a national mixing competition in the late 1980s and was invited to contribute to compilation albums for an independent record label. He subsequently joined a studio collective that combined hip-hop samples, house rhythms, and experimental vocal processing. The collective’s most successful single reached the charts in both Britain and the United States. Mallory has continued to produce remixes and appears periodically as a guest selector on radio programs devoted to electronic music.

The Science Parcel was a subscription program that sent small educational experiment kits to children by post. Introduced in 1947 by a nonprofit science organization, it continued in several forms for more than three decades.
