A special winter edition included a small prism and instructions for recording the angle of sunlight at noon, and became one of the program’s most requested parcels. Each monthly package contained a short illustrated booklet, a set of inexpensive materials, and instructions for an investigation. Subjects included magnetism, soil chemistry, simple machines, sound, optical effects, and the properties of household polymers. Some parcels supplied components for constructing a pinhole viewer, a balance, or a miniature weather station. Subscribers could also order individual kits for classroom use. The program encouraged children to keep observation notebooks, although surviving records of its circulation are incomplete.

Henry Wainwright was an English cricketer who played as a right-handed batsman and occasional medium-pace bowler. Born in Lancashire, he attended a preparatory school before joining a larger public school whose cricket eleven he captained in his final year. Wainwright was selected for a county second team after making a century in a school fixture against a touring side. He appeared for a county second team during the late 1920s and made his first-class debut for a combined representative side. He later played several matches for Lancashire in the County Championship, scoring steadily without becoming a regular member of the senior team. His final first-class appearance came against a university eleven. In later life he worked in education and served on the committee of a local cricket club.

Marlowe Park is a residential district in north London divided administratively between two boroughs. Much of the area was developed on former farmland during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, when new rail and tram services made commuting more practical. A station on a suburban line remains the district’s principal transport landmark. Older terraces stand near the commercial center, while later housing extends toward a large public playing field. The district’s first public library occupied a converted railway cottage before moving to a larger building near the shops. A railway cutting separates Marlowe Park from a neighboring hill district, although footbridges connect the two areas. An amateur football club once played on land beside the railway; its successor later moved to a ground several miles away.

“The Ice Diary” is the collective title of two episodes from the second season of the animated television series *Beyond the Pines*. The episodes were originally scheduled as a single hour-long broadcast but were divided after the network requested a shorter running time. The story begins when the young heroes discover a collection of recorded messages hidden in a frozen tower. They initially treat the recordings as evidence of a villain’s plan, but the material reveals that the tower’s guardian was once an ordinary scientist who lost his identity after using an experimental device. The guardian attempts to recover the recordings and destroy the evidence, while the protagonists try to understand what happened. The episodes were written as a single story divided for broadcast and were praised for combining comic adventure with a more serious character history.

The surname Mercer may have originated as an occupational name for a person who traded in cloth and other textiles. One early spelling in a northern English register includes an extra vowel that later disappeared from most written forms. Similar forms appear in medieval English and Scottish records, although some families adopted the name from a place or from an earlier personal name. The word was spread through Britain by merchants and later became common in North America, Australia, and other English-speaking regions. Early bearers appear in tax rolls, guild registers, and parish records, making it difficult to determine whether all branches share a single ancestor. Several unrelated families have used distinct coats of arms. In modern usage, the surname is found among people with varied regional and cultural backgrounds.

Velocirhamphus is a genus of small Triassic gliding reptiles known from a partial skeleton discovered in central Asia. The animal possessed an elongated body and an unusual arrangement of skin-supported membranes extending from the rear limbs. A second fragment found near the original specimen may belong to the same animal, but its identification has not been accepted by all researchers. Unlike later flying reptiles, it had no broad wing surface attached to the forelimbs. Researchers have proposed that it moved between trees by spreading the hind-limb membranes and using its long tail for balance. The type specimen was collected from sediments containing fossil plants and other small reptiles. Because only one incomplete specimen has been described, the animal’s exact posture and method of launching remain subjects of debate.

*Afterimage Sessions* is an extended play by a Canadian pop singer released as a companion to her third studio album. The collection contains songs recorded during the album sessions but omitted from the original track list. Its production draws on bright synthesizers, drum machines, and the polished dance-pop sound associated with the 1980s, while the lyrics describe missed chances, late-night calls, and uncertain relationships. Several writers and producers from the parent album returned for the project. The EP received favorable reviews for presenting a coherent set of songs rather than a collection of leftovers. A radio edit of the title track was issued to Canadian stations several weeks before the EP appeared in stores. A later regional edition added an upbeat single that had originally appeared on a film soundtrack.

Westfield Rural is a civil parish in the English county of Berkshire. For several decades after its creation, the parish was administered from the same building as the neighboring urban council, despite having a separate budget. It was created in the late nineteenth century when a larger parish was divided between an urban council and a rural administrative area. The parish forms an irregular band around the western side of the nearby town and includes several hamlets, wooded lanes, and newer housing estates. The northern section remains comparatively rural, while development at the southern edge has connected it with a neighboring commuter settlement. A small parish church, a primary school, and several historic farmhouses are among its notable buildings. A local survey in the 1970s recorded more than a dozen previously unmapped footpaths. Census figures have risen as former agricultural land has been converted to residential use.

A private diary attributed to the expedition’s radio operator describes a disagreement over whether the vessel should winter in the islands or return before the first freeze. The Sokolov expedition was an early twentieth-century Russian voyage to the Arctic. Its public purpose was to survey mineral deposits on a group of islands, but the expedition leader also intended to investigate a possible route across the northern seas. The vessel left a Siberian port in the summer and reached an island chain before sending its last confirmed message. Later searches recovered food tins, fragments of clothing, and a weathered marker on a remote coast. A naval party revisited the marker decades later and found that its inscription had been partly worn away by ice. These finds suggested that the party had traveled farther east than originally planned, although no complete record of its route survives. The disappearance of the ship and its crew remains a subject of polar-history speculation.

The method was refined in the twentieth century after astronomers began comparing pulsating stars with nearby objects whose distances had been measured by other means. The radial-pulsation method is used to estimate the distance to certain variable stars. Astronomers observe how a star’s brightness and surface temperature change during a cycle, then combine those observations with measurements of the star’s motion toward and away from Earth. The velocity data provide an estimate of how the radius changes, while the brightness and color measurements yield a changing angular size. Comparing the physical change in radius with the apparent change in size gives a distance estimate. Modern versions use interferometers to measure angular diameters directly, reducing some of the uncertainty found in earlier calculations. In some observatories, the method is applied only to stars with cycles shorter than ten days. Related techniques apply the same principle to expanding stellar atmospheres after certain supernova explosions.

The small label was initially run from a record shop in Baltimore and used hand-stamped covers for its first releases. *Quiet Animal* is the first solo album by Baltimore musician Evan Mercer, who later became a member of the experimental group Field Notes. Mercer released the record in 2001 through a small label founded with a childhood friend. The label had originally been created to distribute the album locally, but it later expanded into a home for recordings by several related projects. The album’s songs combine drum machines, acoustic instruments, tape loops, and softly sung melodies. Only a limited number of copies were manufactured during the first pressing, and the record quickly disappeared from shops. It was reissued years later after listeners began circulating the original tracks online. A later review described the closing track as the clearest indication of the sound Mercer would pursue with Field Notes. The album is now regarded as an early document of Mercer’s developing sound.

Digital waveguide engraving is a technique for fabricating miniature optical components inside a flat layered structure. Early prototypes were made on glass substrates before the technique was adapted to semiconductor manufacturing. Instead of directing light through a separate three-dimensional object, the method embeds a computer-designed pattern within a thin guiding layer. Light travels through the layer and interacts with the pattern over a comparatively long distance. The guide is formed by placing a material with a higher refractive index between lower-index cladding layers, allowing light to remain concentrated in the central region. Unlike a cylindrical fiber, a planar guide permits movement in two horizontal directions while restricting propagation vertically. A waveguide can be etched with several patterns on the same wafer, allowing filters and splitters to be produced in a single fabrication step. The approach can be used to produce compact filters, splitters, sensors, and other components on a standard semiconductor wafer.

Raven Hall is a coeducational residential college at a large public university in California. Designed in a collegiate Gothic style, it opened in 1931 as the institution’s first purpose-built student residence. The building combines a stone exterior with timber entrances, narrow stair towers, and a central common room. The original dining hall was converted into administrative offices during the 1970s, although its oak paneling was retained. A 1960s renovation added study rooms along the east wing and replaced several original fireplaces with electric heaters. Although it is administered by the university, residents have developed traditions that give the hall a strong community identity. Students organize annual dinners, informal competitions, and ceremonies for new members, while older residents often return to advise the house council. A preservation organization listed the building as a notable example of early campus architecture. Its rooms were renovated several times without altering the original exterior.

Wonder Coast is a family amusement park occupying roughly eighteen acres near a coastal highway in New Jersey. The park’s first admission tickets were printed with different animal illustrations for each day of the week, a practice that collectors later used to date early photographs. Established in 1962 by a married couple who had operated a seasonal toy store, the park uses nursery rhymes and animal stories as its principal themes. A small railway circles the grounds, passing miniature villages, a dragon-shaped play area, and a children’s wheel. The railway was purchased from a traveling exhibition that had toured New England before the park opened. Other attractions include a junior roller coaster, spinning teacups, and a water ride added during the 1980s. During December, the park opens a winter village where visitors can meet costumed characters and attend craft demonstrations. The park remains privately operated and is known for retaining much of its original scale.

Michael Rowan (born 1961) is an English football manager and former midfielder. He began his playing career with a Midlands club before transferring to a major team in Manchester, where he became captain and won domestic league titles, national cups, and a European trophy. Rowan represented England throughout the 1980s and made more than eighty international appearances, captaining the side on several occasions. His first international goal came from a long-range free kick during a qualifying match, although he was better known for creating chances than finishing them. A club program from his final season as a player described him as the dressing room’s most reliable organizer. Supporters gave him the nickname “Captain Row,” referring to his energetic style and willingness to challenge for loose balls. After retiring as a player, he managed clubs in Britain and Asia and worked as a national-team adviser. His career is often cited as an example of a player who combined leadership with technical skill.

The Indian Solar Partnership is a national program intended to increase the generation and use of solar electricity. Its first round of grants favored projects that combined electricity generation with water-pumping systems for small farms, before later tenders placed greater emphasis on grid-scale plants. It was established as part of a wider climate policy and initially focused on utility-scale stations, solar water heating, and village electrification. Later plans expanded the target to include rooftop systems, local manufacturing, and battery storage. State governments administer many of the installations, while the central government provides financing, standards, and grid incentives. A training center in western India was established under the program to teach technicians how to maintain solar pumps during the monsoon season. Capacity increased rapidly after new auction procedures lowered the cost of large projects. Supporters describe the program as a means of reducing fuel imports and extending electricity access; critics have raised questions about land use, transmission capacity, and the uneven distribution of benefits.

“Glass Houses” is a song by the American alternative duo Northbound. Written by the group’s vocalist and a producer from a neighboring rock band, it appeared on the album *Under the Signal* before being issued as a single. The song entered a regional college-radio chart before the band had released a national single, giving the duo its first significant audience outside its home city. A short instrumental passage was recorded with a damaged tape machine, and the resulting distortion was kept in the final mix. The track combines restrained electronic percussion with a chorus built around layered harmonies and distorted guitar. Its lyrics describe creative work as both a refuge and a source of exhaustion, with the narrator comparing inspiration to a chemical that cleans one surface while damaging another. Critics praised the song’s compact arrangement and memorable refrain. The accompanying video follows the musicians through an empty industrial building and was released several months after the recording.

The term stratified frost debris was introduced in a nineteenth-century account of alpine slopes, although later geologists used different names for similar deposits. Stratified frost debris consists of layers of angular rock fragments deposited along the lower slopes of cold-region valleys. In many cases the material begins as bedrock broken by repeated freezing and thawing, then moves downslope through frost heave, seasonal melting, or gravity. The deposits are usually poorly sorted, although their layers may preserve the direction of movement and the conditions under which they accumulated. Some examples occur on slopes steeper than thirty degrees, while finer, more gently inclined sheets can extend across valley floors. Comparable formations have been described in mountain regions of Europe, Asia, and the Americas. Their presence can provide evidence of former periglacial conditions even where glacial ice did not reach. One group of deposits in the Alps has been dated to a period before the last major glacial advance.

An amusement park is a permanent recreational site containing rides, games, food stalls, and spaces for live entertainment. Early parks often relied on admission fees that covered the grounds but charged separately for each attraction, a system that remained common after the introduction of fixed-price tickets. Some parks organize their attractions around a single subject, while others combine unrelated rides and rely on landscaping or seasonal events to create a common identity. Unlike traveling fairs, they maintain fixed structures and operate over many years. Modern amusement parks developed from European pleasure gardens, public exhibitions, and seaside resorts. Early attractions were often mechanical novelties, scenic railways, or dance halls; later parks added roller coasters, water rides, and elaborate themed environments. Several American parks briefly issued guidebooks that ranked attractions by the amount of time visitors were expected to spend in line. The distinction between an amusement park and a theme park is not always precise, although theme parks generally devote more resources to narrative design and architectural detail.

In thermodynamics, conjugate variables are paired quantities whose product represents an increment of energy. The language of conjugate pairs was adopted from analytical mechanics and later became common in textbooks describing thermodynamic potentials. Pressure and volume provide one familiar example, while temperature and entropy form another. A small change in the internal energy of a system can be written as a sum of products involving these pairs, with each intensive variable associated with an extensive quantity. An imbalance in the intensive variable produces a change in the corresponding extensive variable, allowing energy to cross the system boundary or be redistributed within it. Some nineteenth-century laboratory manuals used the term only for pairs that could be measured directly, a restriction that later textbooks abandoned. The choice of thermodynamic potential determines which variables are treated as independent. A change of variables can make the same process appear in a different set of conjugate pairs.

The *Northern Swift* is a high-speed catamaran designed to carry passengers and cars on international routes. Built by an Australian shipyard, the vessel first operated between two Scandinavian ports under a different name. Its original passenger layout included a small observation lounge above the forward vehicle deck, a feature removed during a later refit. The lounge was furnished with locally made wooden panels that were later reused in a ferry terminal café. It was later chartered to companies in the Caribbean and the North Sea, receiving several new names as its ownership changed. The ship uses twin hulls and water-jet propulsion, allowing it to travel faster than conventional vehicle ferries but making it more sensitive to rough weather. After a period in storage, it was refitted for a service connecting a German Baltic port with southern Sweden. Its schedule has varied according to seasonal demand and harbor restrictions.

David Hartwell (born 1974) is an American fiction writer whose short stories often examine work, family loyalty, and the moral pressures of small communities. Raised in the Midwest, he studied journalism before completing graduate degrees in creative writing. His first collection appeared from an independent literary press and received favorable notices from newspaper reviewers and regional magazines. The collection’s title story was adapted for a public-radio drama several years after publication, with Hartwell reading the narrator’s part. Hartwell later donated the notebooks from the collection to a university archive, where they were used in a course on revision. One story from the collection won an award for fiction originally published in a periodical. Hartwell has taught writing at universities in Idaho and the Great Lakes region and has served as a visiting writer at several community colleges. His later work includes a novel and essays on the relationship between local history and storytelling.

The politics of the Republic of Arvania operate under a federal parliamentary constitution. The constitution was revised after a financial crisis that exposed disagreements between the capital and the wealthier eastern provinces. Legislative authority is divided between a national assembly and elected provincial councils, with the provinces retaining powers not explicitly assigned to the federal government. The constitution also gives the western provinces a limited right to delay national infrastructure bills for public consultation. The prime minister directs the cabinet and is responsible to the lower house, while the president serves as head of state and is chosen by an electoral college for a fixed term. Constitutional amendments adopted in the early twenty-first century reduced the president’s discretionary authority and strengthened the assembly’s control over appointments and finance. The courts may review legislation and protect specified civil rights. Political debate often centers on the balance between provincial autonomy and national economic planning.

The 82nd National Film Awards ceremony was held in March 2010 at a theater in Los Angeles and recognized films released during the previous calendar year. The ceremony was moved to Los Angeles after organizers abandoned an earlier plan to hold it in a smaller regional theater. A special tribute reel assembled from footage donated by private collectors opened the broadcast. Awards were presented in more than twenty competitive categories, including acting, directing, screenwriting, and several technical fields. A comedian hosted the televised ceremony, which was produced by a veteran entertainment executive and broadcast nationally. The historical drama *The Long Harbor* won the top prize and several awards for acting, while a science-fiction film received recognition for visual effects and sound design. A separate presentation earlier in the month honored scientific and technical achievements. The broadcast attracted a large audience but received mixed reviews for its lengthy musical numbers.

Melon scoopers are kitchen utensils used to cut rounded pieces from soft fruit. The earliest widely sold versions were marketed as serving tools for formal dessert courses rather than as general kitchen utensils. The tool consists of a small hemispherical bowl attached to a handle, and most examples are made from stainless steel or another washable metal. Some nineteenth-century versions had a hinged scraper that allowed the user to release the fruit without touching it. Cooks press the bowl into a melon and rotate it to form a sphere, which can then be added to salads, desserts, or drinks. Some scoopers have a bowl at each end, allowing the user to make balls of two different sizes. A small opening in the bowl helps release juice and prevents suction. Although designed for melons, the utensil can also portion ice cream, butter, soft cheese, and other foods that hold their shape when cut.

A xerophyte is a plant adapted to survive where available water is limited. Some botanists use the term narrowly for plants that maintain growth through drought, while others include species that survive by becoming dormant. Early botanical classifications sometimes separated xerophytes according to the color of their leaves rather than the mechanisms that conserve water. Such plants occur in deserts, dry grasslands, polar regions, and exposed alpine habitats. Their adaptations may include deep or widely spreading roots, reduced leaves, waxy surfaces, water-storage tissues, and the ability to close pores during the hottest part of the day. Some species survive drought by entering a dormant state in which metabolic activity becomes very low. Cacti and many succulents store water in thick stems, while other xerophytes complete their life cycle during a short wet season. The term describes a set of ecological adaptations rather than a single plant family.

Community health centers, sometimes called polyclinics, were proposed in England as larger facilities offering a wider range of services than a conventional general-practice office. Early planning documents often placed the centers beside public transport interchanges so that patients could reach several services in one visit. Suggested services included routine medical appointments, urgent care, health education, mental-health support, and links to social services. Several organizational models were considered, from networks of existing clinics to new buildings containing multiple practices and diagnostic facilities. Advocates argued that the centers could make care more accessible and reduce unnecessary hospital visits. Critics questioned whether local staff and budgets were sufficient to manage the proposed expansion. A later review found that some pilot centers had attracted patients from outside the districts they were meant to serve. Many early plans were postponed after policy reviews found that projected shifts of treatment from hospitals to community settings had been overstated.

Mapleford is a small village in western New Brunswick, Canada, located near the border with Maine. The settlement was briefly considered for incorporation as a town after a railway spur was proposed, but the plan was abandoned when the line was routed several miles away. It serves as a local shopping and service center for surrounding farming communities and rural settlements. The village contains a grocery store, a hardware shop, a bakery, a post office, and a cooperative bank. Several churches stand within the municipal boundary, along with a hair salon and a small restaurant. A former fuel and convenience store closed after its owner retired, leaving the highway businesses more concentrated near the crossroads. A community hall built beside the crossroads is used for a weekly farmers’ market during the summer. Population counts have remained relatively stable, although the village has experienced gradual changes in the age of its residents and in the number of working farms.

The Willow Creek Caves are a group of limestone chambers in a dry basin of the western United States. The entrance to the largest chamber was widened in the 1950s so that survey equipment could be carried inside, and the alteration is still visible around the outer rim. The caves open onto the side of a low volcanic ridge and were enlarged by water movement during an earlier period of wetter climate. Archaeologists first recorded the site in the 1930s, but systematic excavations began decades later. Researchers recovered animal remains, plant fibers, and several human coprolites whose dates indicate occupation during the late Pleistocene. The findings have been used in debates about the earliest settlement of the region, although the caves do not preserve a continuous record of habitation. A later survey found a second entrance that is accessible only during the driest months. The complex was placed on a national heritage register after additional surveys mapped its underground passages.

The Cedar Valley Quartet was a Southern Gospel vocal group active during the first half of the twentieth century. It was formed by two brothers and two professional singers who performed at revival meetings, agricultural fairs, and regional radio stations. One of the brothers also arranged the group’s four-part introductions and kept a notebook of alternate verses for songs requested by audiences. The quartet’s repertoire consisted largely of hymns and religious ballads arranged for close harmony. Unlike many local groups, its members were experienced musicians who could read notation and adapt quickly to different accompaniment. The quartet recorded several sides for a regional label and later served as backing singers for a well-known country performer. A later compilation restored three recordings that had previously circulated only on damaged discs. Its recordings helped preserve a vocal style that influenced later gospel quartets and church music programs.

Martin Reeve is an English rock guitarist, singer, and songwriter. His first published composition appeared on a local compilation before he had joined a professional touring group. He first performed in a small Cambridge group before joining an experimental band whose records later became influential among alternative musicians. Reeve’s best-known songs were written for a later ensemble that combined bright guitar arrangements with straightforward pop melodies. He has also worked as a producer, studio musician, and occasional composer for television. After a period of touring, Reeve released a solo album under the name Paper Lantern, inviting several singers and instrumentalists to contribute. The album’s cover was designed by a photographer who had previously worked on the group’s tour programs. He continues to perform with different lineups and has taken part in reunion concerts for both of his earlier groups.

Subsistence agriculture is farming primarily intended to feed the household that produces it. In some regions, households reserve a small plot for a crop that is used in local ceremonies rather than eaten or sold. Families may grow grains, vegetables, fruit, or fodder on small plots and keep animals for milk, meat, or labor. Decisions about planting are based first on expected household needs and only secondarily on market prices. Most subsistence farmers participate in some exchange, selling or trading a surplus to obtain tools, fuel, clothing, or building materials that cannot be produced locally. The boundary between subsistence and commercial farming is therefore not absolute. A household may depend largely on its own harvest while still growing one crop specifically for sale. In agricultural surveys, the category is often defined by the destination of the harvest rather than by the size of the farm.

Stenoma pallidella is a moth belonging to the family Depressariidae. The original description was based on a single specimen whose abdomen had been damaged before it reached the museum, making the sex of the type uncertain. It has been recorded from humid forest in western South America, where adults are attracted to light at night. The wingspan is approximately 25 millimetres. Its forewings are pale brown with a darker line along the outer margin and several indistinct spots near the middle. Fine scales give the wings a slightly silvery appearance when viewed at an angle. The hindwings are lighter than the forewings and become darker toward the tip. A later collection from the same valley showed a slightly darker form that some researchers have treated as a local variety. Because specimens vary in color and pattern, the species has occasionally been confused with related moths from the same region.

Jonah Reid is a New Zealand musician who has worked as a bassist, keyboard player, producer, and touring performer. He learned bass from a school music teacher who lent him an instrument for his first year of practice. He began in a Palmerston North ensemble and later moved to Auckland, where he joined an alternative rock group. Reid contributed vocals and arrangements as well as bass and appeared on several of the band’s albums. After leaving the group, he produced recordings for younger artists and released a solo project under the name Soft Harbour. The Soft Harbour project was originally planned as a series of instrumental recordings before Reid added vocals to several tracks. He later joined a trio formed by musicians he met while rehearsing in a neighboring studio. Reid has also played on television soundtracks and taught recording techniques in community workshops.

*Style Report* was a Canadian television program covering fashion, design, and the business of clothing. Its first season was filmed in a converted department store, allowing the production to use shop windows as temporary interview sets. It was broadcast domestically and distributed to stations in several other countries for nearly two decades. The series featured runway reports, interviews with designers, and segments examining the work of stylists, photographers, and retailers. Its original host remained with the program through its first major format change before leaving to work for a fashion magazine. A short reality competition was later produced to select a replacement presenter. The winner hosted several episodes, while other contestants went on to work in fashion journalism and television production. The program’s archive includes several unaired interviews with textile designers.

The Coastal Mathematical Society is an organization serving students, teachers, and researchers in a southern Indian state. Founded in the 1960s, it originally met in the mathematics department of a teacher-training college before expanding its activities to universities in the region. It organizes seminars, workshops, public lectures, and training sessions throughout the region. Its programs address both current research and methods for teaching mathematics in secondary schools and universities. The society publishes a twice-yearly journal containing research articles and papers from its conferences. The journal’s early issues were distributed mainly through member exchanges rather than commercial subscriptions. It also maintains a small grant program for student travel and sponsors an annual lecture honoring a historian of Indian mathematics. Membership includes participants living outside the state and abroad, although most activities are held in local colleges.

Robert Keller was an American football coach who served as head coach at a public university in the Rocky Mountain region during the early 1970s. Before taking the position, he had worked as an assistant at a major Midwestern program. Keller signed a multiyear contract and promised to rebuild a team that had struggled in conference play. His recruiting class included several players from junior colleges, a departure from the university’s previous emphasis on local high schools. His first seasons produced only a handful of victories, and attendance declined as supporters became frustrated with the program’s direction. After another losing season, students and alumni demanded changes in either the coaching staff or athletic administration. Keller resigned the following winter, citing a lack of confidence that the university would provide the resources needed for a successful program. The athletic department later credited his training methods with improving the team’s conditioning standards.

The Redwood Valley Ice Center is an indoor rink in northern California. Its original refrigeration system used equipment adapted from a nearby cold-storage warehouse and was replaced during a major renovation in the 1980s. It was built in the late 1960s by a local cartoonist and his family and was intended to provide year-round skating for the surrounding community. The facility offers public sessions, figure-skating lessons, youth hockey, adult leagues, and private rentals. A summer tournament brings senior hockey teams from several countries to the city for a week of competition. The main rink contains several hundred permanent seats, while temporary bleachers can be installed for concerts and larger events. The center is also used by school teams and a regional figure-skating club. A second, smaller practice surface was added beside the main rink after demand for lessons increased.

Evelyn Carter (1924–2008) was an American mathematician and aerospace engineer who worked for a federal aeronautics laboratory. She began her career as a human calculator in a segregated computing unit, where she checked wind-tunnel measurements and flight tables. A staff newsletter later credited her with creating a card-based system for locating recurring errors in flight tables. After attending evening courses in engineering, Carter became one of the laboratory’s first Black women to receive an engineering appointment. Her first engineering assignment involved testing the accuracy of instruments used to measure airflow around aircraft wings. She later accepted a supervisory position in an equal-opportunity office, where she helped identify barriers affecting women seeking technical promotions. Carter remained connected with the laboratory after retirement and advised programs encouraging students from underrepresented communities to pursue mathematics and engineering. Her career combined technical work with long-term advocacy inside the civil service.

Tornholm is a small island in a Danish fjord, linked to the mainland by a narrow causeway. The causeway was surfaced with stone from a disused quarry on the opposite shore during a reconstruction in the 1950s. The island was once reached only by wading or using a small boat, but a farmer built the road connection in the 1920s to transport shells and agricultural equipment. A survey made before the road was built recorded a seasonal footpath across the western marsh, which disappeared after the causeway altered local drainage. The original processing shed has disappeared, although fields are still cultivated and a modern farmhouse occupies the site of the former dwelling. Only a few people live on Tornholm year-round, and the island is not generally open to visitors. A strip of salt marsh surrounds much of the shoreline, providing habitat for wading birds and protecting the low fields from ordinary tidal flooding.

George Fenwick was an English cricketer who played first-class matches for a county club and for a representative Marylebone side. He began his career in university and club cricket before joining the county staff as a batsman. In his second championship appearance he scored a century, but his later seasons were marked by fluctuating form and occasional injuries. Fenwick’s strongest year came in the mid-1960s, when he was the only member of his county team to reach three figures in the championship. He was also remembered for a determined innings against a touring Australian side, scoring heavily on a difficult pitch. The county later preserved his scorebook from that innings in its ground museum. A newspaper report from the period described him as particularly effective against fast bowling, despite his relatively compact build. After leaving first-class cricket, he coached at a school in the county.

Thomas Harlan was an American athlete who competed in both basketball and baseball during his university career. He became a regular guard after spending his first season as a reserve and helped his team win a national championship in the late 1980s. Before entering university, Harlan had been a high-scoring high-school player in California and was recruited by a celebrated coach who rarely signed athletes from outside the Midwest. Harlan’s role on the championship team was limited, but he contributed important assists in the final tournament. A local newspaper later described his crossover from basketball to baseball as the most unusual transition on the university’s spring roster. A shoulder injury ended his final university baseball season before he could accept an offer from a professional organization. He later played minor-league baseball and worked in sports broadcasting. His unusual combination of sports remains a notable feature of his career.

Pine Ridge Speedway is a motor-racing circuit in the southeastern United States. The track’s first permanent grandstand was assembled from sections of a nearby baseball stadium after the stadium was rebuilt. It hosts weekly stock-car events and has previously welcomed several regional touring series. The track is located beside a county fairground that has operated since the 1960s, and spectators commonly combine race weekends with camping and fair activities. The main grandstand seats several thousand people, while an elevated area along the backstretch allows fans to watch from vehicles. National touring races were held there regularly during the second half of the twentieth century. The circuit also became known for hosting one of the earliest complete stock-car broadcasts on American television. A later television documentary credited the track with introducing several drivers who reached the national circuit.

Thomas Allerton was a nineteenth-century British campaigner who opposed long factory hours and resisted the expansion of the New Poor Law. A pamphlet attributed to Allerton was among the first campaign documents to include testimony from children working in textile mills. Politically conservative in some matters, he nevertheless became an outspoken critic of the conditions faced by children working in mills. Allerton helped organize petitions, public meetings, and pamphlets supporting a ten-hour working day. His influence was greatest during the early years of the campaign, before parliamentary reformers and trade activists took over much of the movement. A commemorative plaque later described him as an agitator rather than a systematic political thinker. Supporters remembered his persistence and his willingness to speak on behalf of workers whose voices were rarely heard in Parliament. A later historian argued that his influence was greatest outside Parliament, where his speeches were reprinted in local newspapers.

The Marigolds were an American girl group from Baltimore that performed briefly during the early 1960s. The group’s first rehearsal took place in the basement of a family-owned grocery store, where the members worked out harmonies between customers. The members were related through two families and began singing as backing vocalists for a local rhythm-and-blues performer. When a dance craze became popular, the group recorded a novelty single intended to capitalize on the trend. The song received invitations to several television programs and reached the lower portion of the national charts. Although the Marigolds did not remain together for long, one former member later joined a major Motown label and another became a session singer. A later reissue paired the single with an unreleased ballad from the same session. Their recording offers an example of the family-based vocal groups common in the period.

The Central Highlands derby is a football rivalry between the national teams of two neighboring Central American countries. The first widely remembered meeting took place in a regional tournament whose final was decided by a late penalty, an incident that became part of the rivalry’s later mythology. Matches between them are marked by large traveling support, strong regional identities, and a history of decisive qualifying games. The rivalry also appears at club level, where teams from the two countries have frequently met in continental competitions. One side has traditionally enjoyed a stronger record in international tournaments, but the balance has shifted from decade to decade. Supporters attach particular importance to matches played during regional championship qualification, and local newspapers often treat the fixtures as more significant than ordinary friendlies. A match abandoned because of heavy rain is still counted in some local records but not in official tournament statistics.

SecureLab is an online community devoted to teaching computer security through legal practice exercises. It began as a university mailing list in the late 1990s before becoming an independent service with its own challenge servers. Its challenges ask participants to analyze simple web applications, inspect code, identify configuration errors, and solve puzzles designed to illustrate common vulnerabilities. The site emphasizes that the exercises are performed in a controlled environment and are not intended to authorize attacks against unrelated systems. Volunteers maintain the challenge servers, discussion boards, and a small online magazine. A rotating group of moderators reviews new challenges before they are made available to registered users. Although the service has attracted a large registered membership, only a fraction of accounts are active at any given time. The most popular exercises are those that can be completed without installing special software. Security students and experienced hobbyists use the site to compare techniques and develop safer testing habits.

Piotr Lewandowski is a Polish conductor, organist, chamber musician, and arts administrator. Before taking up conducting, he worked as an accompanist for a touring vocal ensemble and developed an interest in historical keyboard instruments. A radio interview from his student years describes the restoration of a small positive organ as the experience that first led him toward early music. He studied at music academies in Kraków and Amsterdam before joining early-music ensembles as a keyboard player and conductor. Lewandowski later became artistic director of a historic orchestra and choir, leading performances that combined Renaissance, Baroque, and early Romantic repertory. The orchestra’s first season under his direction included a cycle of rarely performed Polish sacred works. He has recorded solo organ works and directed albums made in churches throughout southern Poland. In addition to concert work, he has organized an international festival and taught interpretation at conservatories in Poland and Austria. His programs often place historically informed performances beside newly commissioned works.

The Horizon Renewal Plan was an automobile company’s restructuring program announced during a period of declining sales. The company initially described the plan as a five-year program, but later shortened the timetable after a sharp fall in orders for large vehicles. It sought to reduce fixed costs, close underused factories, and shorten the time required to bring new models to market. The plan also created a temporary purchasing office intended to consolidate contracts for steel, glass, and electronic components. The company also intended to broaden its profitable product range rather than depend on a small number of trucks and sport-utility vehicles. Executives presented the plan to investors before publishing a revised version that accelerated plant closures and reduced the workforce. A revised production schedule shifted one compact model from an older plant to a newer facility in another state. Some measures produced immediate savings, but the program drew criticism from communities facing factory shutdowns and from dealers who believed the product changes were arriving too slowly. Executives later said that supplier agreements would determine whether the final phase could proceed.

In grammar, a sentence is a unit of language that can express a statement, question, command, request, or exclamation. Some school grammars classify short greetings and interjections as sentences even when they lack an overt verb. Traditional descriptions often define it as a sequence containing a subject and a predicate, although not every sentence follows that pattern explicitly. Syntactic theories may instead treat the sentence as the largest ordinary unit of structure in a particular analysis. In writing, capitalization and terminal punctuation commonly mark its boundaries. In legal drafting, punctuation is sometimes treated as evidence of how a sentence should be divided, although courts do not apply the practice consistently. Speech has no exact equivalent of the period; pauses, pitch, and rhythm may signal a comparable division. A sentence can contain several clauses, while a clause is a smaller structure organized around a process, event, or state. A short sentence may consist of a single word, while a longer one may contain several independent clauses.

Lionel Harcourt was a British tennis player who represented his country in indoor singles and doubles during the early twentieth century. He learned the game at a private club where his father served as groundskeeper and later won a regional junior title. A newspaper profile credited him with introducing a slower, more defensive style to the club’s indoor courts. In a major international tournament, he reached the quarterfinal round after defeating several seeded opponents, but lost a long match to a later finalist. Harcourt also competed at the 1908 Olympic Games, advancing farther in doubles than in singles. His partnership with another British player ended in the semifinal, and the pair were defeated in the bronze-medal match. He was known for a steady baseline game and a preference for long rallies. A surviving tournament program lists Harcourt among the players who favored the heavier rackets then becoming common. Harcourt died while still relatively young, and his competitive record was later reconstructed from tournament reports.

Lowmere Reservoirs are two artificial lakes and a nature reserve in northern England. A former inspection path along the southern bank was reopened to walkers after the water company installed a new fence. The larger reservoir was originally designed with a shallow western margin so that reeds could be established without interrupting water treatment. The site was created as part of a water-treatment complex but has become important for wintering waterfowl. Reed beds, grassland, ponds, and patches of woodland surround the reservoirs, providing habitat for ducks, grebes, waders, and migratory songbirds. The reserve supports several regionally significant species and has recorded more than one hundred bird species over the course of a year. A survey carried out after a cold winter recorded an unusually large number of diving birds in the deeper reservoir. Public access is limited near the treatment buildings, although footpaths and viewing shelters are available around the outer part of the site. Water-company staff and conservation volunteers manage vegetation and monitor bird populations.

Socotra is the largest island in an archipelago located between the Arabian Peninsula and the Horn of Africa. A nineteenth-century survey described the island’s eastern plateau as difficult to cross because wells were separated by several days of travel. An early twentieth-century map labels one of the island’s inland valleys as a possible source of medicinal resin, although the locality has not been securely identified. Its position near major shipping routes has made it politically important, but its isolation has also produced a distinctive natural environment. A substantial proportion of the island’s plant life occurs nowhere else, including trees and shrubs adapted to dry winds, thin soils, and irregular rainfall. The interior contains limestone plateaus and rugged mountains, while the coast includes beaches, salt marshes, and sheltered coves. A botanical expedition later identified a plant community on the plateau that was absent from the coastal valleys. Most residents live in a small number of settlements connected by limited roads. The archipelago was designated a UNESCO World Heritage site in recognition of its biological diversity and unusual landscapes.

Samuel Leighton was an American baseball player who later became a university coach. He began playing as a catcher before moving to the infield after a shoulder injury limited his throwing. During his playing career he was selected for an all-conference team and helped his college win several regional championships. Leighton set school records for hits and total bases in a season and finished his collegiate career with a batting average above .350. He signed with a professional organization after graduation and spent one summer in a minor league before returning to his university as an assistant coach. A former teammate recalled that Leighton kept detailed charts of opposing hitters and used them when preparing defensive drills. He eventually directed the program for several seasons, emphasizing defensive discipline and player development. During his first year as head coach, the team adopted a new practice schedule based on defensive drills. A scholarship established in his name supports students from the rural communities where he began playing.

“Letter to the River” is a popular song written by a composer and lyricist in the early 1960s. The first publisher registered the song under a title that referred to a different kind of messenger, but the familiar title appeared on most later releases. It has been recorded under several titles by singers in the United States, Britain, and Australia. A publisher’s ledger indicates that the lyricist originally imagined the messenger as a train rather than a bird. The verses address a bird or traveler carrying a message to a distant lover, while the narrator remains in a town associated with loneliness and disappointment. One early recording became a modest regional hit; a later version by a British singer reached the national charts and used a different name for the recipient. A soul singer’s interpretation became the best-known American release. A live arrangement later added a small choir that was absent from the original recording. Despite the changes in title and arrangement, the central image of sending a message through nature remains consistent.

Declan Byrne is an Irish journalist, broadcaster, author, and former professional footballer. He played in youth leagues before retiring from the sport and moving into television analysis. Byrne’s first television assignment involved summarizing a domestic cup match from a small studio, where he was asked to explain a disputed offside decision. His first regular contract required him to prepare both the match commentary and the channel’s halftime statistics. Byrne became a familiar voice during coverage of domestic football, European competitions, and international tournaments. He has also hosted a radio interview program, presented a quiz show, and written a regular newspaper column about the game. A collection of his columns was later published with an introduction by a former national-team manager. His broadcasting style combines tactical explanation with outspoken criticism of club management and national selection. Byrne has worked for several competing radio and television networks, sometimes leaving one organization and returning years later in a different role.

*The Comfortable Age* is a six-part television documentary examining prosperity, consumption, and dissatisfaction in modern Western societies. The program’s opening episode was filmed partly in a shopping district that had recently been converted from a railway yard. The production kept a running inventory of discarded packaging gathered during filming and displayed it during the closing credits. The series was produced for an Australian public broadcaster and presented by a journalist known for travel programming. Each half-hour episode considers a different aspect of affluent life, including advertising, work, health, urban development, and the environmental cost of consumption. Interviews with economists, clergy, scientists, historians, and political writers are interwoven with footage from cities and shopping districts. A separate interview with a consumer researcher was recorded but omitted from the broadcast after the series was shortened. The program asks why people may report greater material security while also describing themselves as anxious or unhappy. It was rebroadcast during a season devoted to globalization.

Papilio vanuensis, known as the Vanuan swallowtail, is a butterfly restricted to a mountainous peninsula on a Pacific island. The species was first discussed in a local natural-history newsletter before being described in a scientific journal. Its local name was recorded in two forms by the first field team, with one version referring to the pale markings on the wings. It was described from photographs sent to entomologists after local residents noticed an unusually large swallowtail near a forest road. The species has dark wings marked with pale bands and a small series of red spots near the hindwing margins. Its known range is narrow, and much of the surrounding forest has been affected by farming and road construction. Genetic sampling has suggested that the population may have been isolated from related island butterflies for a long period. Collectors have also increased pressure on the population. Conservation proposals include protecting breeding habitat, monitoring adults during the flight season, and establishing a local program to raise the butterfly in captivity.

World-systems analysis is a historical and sociological approach that treats the global economy as a connected system rather than as a collection of independent nation-states. The approach first gained attention through work that compared long-term trade patterns with changes in political authority. A university seminar in the 1970s helped popularize a diagram that placed financial centers, manufacturing zones, and commodity regions on a single circular map. It commonly distinguishes core regions, which control capital-intensive production and financial institutions, from peripheral regions that supply labor and raw materials. A semi-peripheral category describes areas occupying an intermediate position and sometimes moving upward or downward within the system. The approach emphasizes changes in transportation, technology, trade, and political power over long periods. Critics argue that the categories can oversimplify complex relationships, while proponents use the framework to explain why economic inequality persists across national borders. Some later researchers have used the framework to study migration and ecological change in addition to production and trade.

Milan Petrović is a Serbian filmmaker, screenwriter, actor, and musician who holds citizenship in two European countries. He began making short films with borrowed equipment while studying theater and later worked as an assistant on independent productions. One of his earliest shorts was screened in a railway warehouse after the intended theater lost power shortly before the program began. His films combine surreal humor with naturalistic performances and often focus on communities living at the edge of political or economic institutions. Petrović has competed at major European festivals and has received awards for directing and for the visual design of his productions. A workshop he organized produced a temporary outdoor set that was later incorporated into one of his films. He has also produced music for his films and organized a series of workshops in which young artists build temporary sets and public installations. In addition to cinema, Petrović has performed with a brass ensemble and has been involved in restoring an abandoned industrial district for use by artists.

Kivuli painting is a decorative style that developed in East Africa during the second half of the twentieth century. The name was first used by a gallery owner who wanted to distinguish the paintings from imported tourist prints, although artists later adopted it for their own exhibitions. An early exhibition catalogue divided the style into “market scenes” and “wildlife panels,” categories that later critics found too narrow. Artists traditionally work on hardboard or prepared panels with brightly colored commercial paint. The pictures often depict animals, plants, crowded streets, or humorous scenes in simplified forms with heavy outlines. Small dimensions make the works easy to transport, and many are sold to visitors through galleries, markets, and airport shops. Several early examples were painted on salvaged packing boards from local shops. Critics have debated whether the style should be regarded primarily as popular art, commercial craft, or a distinct regional school. Its practitioners have continued to adapt the format, introducing urban subjects and political satire alongside the earlier wildlife imagery.

Nawagoda is a large suburban settlement on the main road east of Colombo, Sri Lanka. The suburb’s commercial center expanded rapidly after a weekly market was moved from a nearby village to the main road. It grew from several former villages that were gradually connected by housing, schools, workshops, and small factories. The area contains Buddhist temples, Catholic and Protestant churches, markets, repair businesses, and a number of private educational institutions. A bus route introduced in the 1980s still forms the main public connection with Colombo, although newer roads have reduced its importance for freight. Most residents travel toward Colombo for work or study, although manufacturing and logistics provide employment within the suburb. Local government is divided between two administrative councils, which has complicated the coordination of roads and drainage. A cinema built beside the old market operated for less than a decade before being converted into a warehouse. Nawagoda’s population includes a Sinhalese majority as well as Tamil and other communities.

Alasdair MacRae is a Scottish Gaelic broadcaster, author, and scholar of shinty. His first radio series followed the seasonal movement of Highland sporting clubs and included interviews recorded in both Gaelic and English. He grew up in the Highlands and later studied at the University of Glasgow before teaching Gaelic in secondary schools. MacRae joined a Gaelic radio service as a producer and presenter and served on the committees of cultural and sporting organizations. He has written books and academic papers about the history, rules, and social significance of shinty, a stick-and-ball game played chiefly in the Highlands. One of his books includes a glossary of regional terms used for sticks, pitches, and match officials. A recording of MacRae’s first shinty match survives in the archive of a local radio station. MacRae has also worked in communications for a ferry company and appears as a host and quiz presenter on Gaelic television. In his youth he played for clubs in Fort William and Glasgow.

A logarithmic visual-acuity chart is used to measure how finely a person can distinguish letters at a fixed distance. The chart was originally designed for clinical studies in which small changes in vision needed to be recorded numerically. Its rows contain symbols that decrease in size by regular logarithmic steps, and each row is arranged so that the spacing between letters remains controlled. A prototype chart was printed with blue-gray symbols because its designer believed that color reduced the temptation to guess from letter shape. A score is calculated from the smallest line a viewer can read, with individual errors producing small adjustments rather than changing the result by an entire row. The scale is useful in clinical research because it permits more precise comparisons than charts whose letters change by larger increments. A modified version is sometimes used when patients cannot read the standard alphabet, substituting simple symbols with controlled orientation. Ophthalmologists, optometrists, and vision scientists use the chart when testing treatment outcomes or changes in eyesight.

The 68th National Association Cup was the annual season of a major football knockout competition. The competition introduced a separate qualifying round for clubs from the lowest divisions, allowing several teams to enter before the main draw was made. Clubs from professional and semi-professional divisions entered at different stages, with matches normally played at the ground of the first-named team. If a match ended level, the teams met again later in the week at the other club’s ground; further replays were permitted until a winner was found. A replay in the fourth round became the longest match of the season after extra time was added to both meetings. The final was held at the national stadium before a large crowd. The final program included a commemorative page listing every club that had entered the competition since its founding. The eventual champions scored twice after halftime and kept a clean sheet. Weather disruptions caused several early matches to be postponed, extending the schedule into the spring.

South Wind Mother is a Taiwanese pop group whose name combines an image of toughness with the gentleness associated with a mother. The group’s name was chosen after an early rehearsal in which the members compared their contrasting stage personalities to weather patterns. A promotional photograph from the group’s first year shows the members performing in matching white jackets, a costume they later abandoned. The members met through a producer who had written music under a childhood pseudonym, and the group’s early recordings were closely connected with his studio. Each performer contributes to composition and arrangement, although some tracks are led entirely by one member. One of the group’s early singles used a string quartet on its bridge, an arrangement that later became a recurring feature of its live performances. The group received a nomination for a national music award and has appeared in advertising campaigns for consumer electronics. Its songs combine Mandarin pop, dance rhythms, and softer acoustic sections, giving the ensemble a sound that differs from the electronic style common in some contemporary Taiwanese releases.

The Simeon Hartwell House, also known as Hartwell Tavern, is a historic stone building in a village in eastern New York. A survey made before restoration identified a second doorway beneath later siding, suggesting that the building once had a separate entrance for travelers. It was built by a family of German-speaking immigrants who settled in the region during the eighteenth century. The house originally served as a farmhouse, stage stop, and public tavern, and its owners later operated a small restaurant for travelers. A double porch supported by plain columns stretches across the front, while the basement contains a kitchen typical of the period. The tavern’s cellar includes a shallow brick-lined drain that may have been used to wash bottles and food containers. A prominent descendant visited the property during the twentieth century, increasing public interest in its history. A restoration plan proposes to retain the building as a private residence while opening the kitchen to occasional tours. The building was added to the National Register of Historic Places and is undergoing restoration as a private residence.

The Meridian Sovereign was a luxury electronic calculator introduced in the late 1970s. Early advertising presented the calculator as an executive desk object and emphasized its quiet keys rather than its speed. Its pressed-metal case and polished finish were intended to distinguish it from inexpensive plastic calculators aimed at students and household users. The machine performed the four basic operations and several additional functions through a custom integrated circuit, displaying results on light-emitting diodes. A surviving sales memorandum recommends a dark brown version for banks and a white version for schools, although it is unclear whether both were manufactured. High manufacturing costs, import duties on components, and competition from cheaper overseas products limited sales. Its batteries also lasted for a relatively short time compared with later liquid-crystal models. Although the design received recognition from an industrial-design organization, the company soon shifted its attention toward home computers and discontinued the calculator. A later collector’s catalogue estimated that fewer than five thousand examples were produced.

Daniel Bourne is a Canadian actor known for television roles in supernatural, science-fiction, and mystery dramas. Before becoming a regular cast member, he appeared in a low-budget television film about a missing astronomer and later cited the experience as his introduction to genre work. He first appeared in guest parts before joining the regular cast of a long-running series about a family of werewolves. Bourne later played a recurring investigator in a science-fiction program and a government agent in a serialized thriller. A director of one independent drama described his supporting performance as the role that changed his public image. His film work includes supporting performances in independent Canadian dramas, for which he received two critics’ awards. A theater production in which Bourne played a detective was recorded for a regional arts broadcast before its limited run ended. He has also appeared in genre films and provided voices for animated productions. Bourne’s television characters are often described as guarded authority figures whose loyalties become clearer as a story develops.

Paper-process engineering applies chemistry, physics, biology, and mathematics to the production of pulp, paper, and related materials. Early industrial textbooks treated the paper machine as a sequence of separate operations, while later engineers emphasized the interaction between fiber preparation and drying. Engineers study the preparation of plant fibers, the removal or transformation of lignin, the suspension of fibers in water, and the rapid formation of a continuous sheet. Drying, coating, pressing, calendaring, and recycling are treated as linked process operations. Several mills have installed sensors that estimate fiber orientation while the sheet is still wet, allowing operators to adjust the forming process. Modern facilities also recover heat, chemicals, and energy from waste streams. The field has expanded beyond writing paper to include packaging, absorbent materials, composite fibers, and bio-based chemicals. Because the raw material is a complex biological polymer, successful production requires both process control and an understanding of how fiber structure affects the finished product. Researchers have also examined paper mills as possible sources of chemicals made from agricultural waste.

Markus Ellery is an American chemical engineer and university administrator whose research concerns reactions occurring on solid surfaces. Ellery began his career studying the behavior of catalysts under high pressure before moving into university administration. He has held a research chair in chemical engineering and appointments in chemistry at two major universities. Ellery’s laboratory develops catalysts and uses spectroscopy to observe how molecules attach to and transform on surfaces. One of his laboratory’s early projects compared catalysts made from ordinary metals with versions containing small amounts of rare elements. He has served as director of an energy research institute and as a senior vice provost responsible for research strategy. His professional honors include election to national engineering and scientific academies. Ellery has also worked with inventors and industry partners on technologies intended to improve fuel production, pollution control, and the conversion of renewable feedstocks. A university report credited him with establishing a joint laboratory shared by chemistry and engineering students.

An ie fala is a finely woven ceremonial mat associated with Samoan families. Some older mats contain a narrow band of darker fibers that records the village where the weaving was completed. Despite its English description as a “fine mat,” it is not normally used as household flooring; its value is social, ceremonial, and historical. Women make the mats from prepared fibers, judging them by the evenness of the weave, softness, brightness, and finish. A narrow fringe and colored feather strip may identify a particular style. Ie fala are exchanged at weddings, funerals, chiefly title ceremonies, and other events where families publicly acknowledge obligations to one another. A mat presented at a chiefly ceremony may be kept by the receiving family but later displayed at a funeral or wedding. Some mats remain in circulation for generations and acquire names or stories of their own. Completing an important mat may be marked by a communal presentation. In one documented community, weaving a large mat was traditionally shared among three related households.

Leonard Price was an American baseball player, coach, and manager whose playing career took place mainly in the minor leagues. Price signed with a professional organization after being noticed at a regional amateur tournament and began as an outfielder before learning to coach first basemen. He appeared as an outfielder and later served as a first-base coach for a National League club during the early 1990s. Price was part of the staff that helped the team win a pennant and became known for his patient work with young hitters. He had signed with a professional organization directly from high school and spent several seasons in its farm system before changing clubs. During his first season as a minor-league manager, he introduced a daily drill focused on reading pitchers’ movements. After retiring as a player, he managed minor-league teams and settled in the Southern United States, where he remained active in youth baseball. A local sports foundation later named a coaching award after him.

The Wide-Eye Near-Earth Survey Telescope is an astronomical instrument designed to locate small bodies whose orbits may bring them close to Earth. The prototype used a specially coated mirror intended to reduce scattered light from bright stars near the edge of an exposure. Its optical system divides the image from a single wide-field reflector among several cameras, allowing a broad portion of the sky to be recorded at once. The design is inspired by the compound eye of an insect, although the individual detectors produce separate scientific images rather than a single visual mosaic. Automated software compares successive exposures to identify moving objects and estimate their paths. A prototype was built for a European research consortium, with additional telescopes proposed for sites at different longitudes and latitudes. A planned software update would allow the system to compare observations made on separate nights rather than only consecutive exposures. The instrument is intended for surveys of small near-Earth bodies.

Bhands are traditional folk entertainers found in parts of South Asia. Some regional traditions distinguish between performers who specialize in mimicry and those who present longer comic narratives, although the categories often overlap. Their performances may combine acting, dance, music, mimicry, storytelling, and satire, with the exact form varying by region and language. Payment is often collected voluntarily while one performer moves through the audience and the others continue the show. Many performers inherit the occupation through family networks, although contemporary groups also include trained theater artists. In some towns, a bhand troupe traditionally opened its performance with a short exchange about local prices or recent public works. Bhands have historically appeared at festivals, markets, weddings, and household celebrations. In some communities they were invited to bless a newborn child, especially a boy, while entertaining relatives and neighbors outside the family home. The term may refer either to an entertainer or to a style of comic drama. Modern performers have adapted the form for stage and radio without abandoning its satirical purpose.

The Book of Proverbs is a collection of wisdom literature included in the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. Several manuscript traditions arrange the shorter sayings differently, although the broad division into collections remains recognizable. Rather than forming a single continuous narrative, it brings together sayings, poems, instructions, and reflections associated with several periods of composition. Its subjects include work, speech, friendship, wealth, discipline, justice, and the education of children. Wisdom is frequently personified as a woman who calls people away from folly and toward a well-ordered life. The opening sections present the fear of God as the beginning of wisdom, while later chapters contain shorter observations about conduct and consequence. A number of English translations preserve different choices for rendering the same Hebrew terms, especially in passages about discipline and instruction. Medieval commentators sometimes arranged selected proverbs by subject in teaching manuscripts, creating small thematic collections that circulated independently. The book has influenced religious teaching, moral philosophy, and English proverbial language.

Ingrid Solberg is a Norwegian lawyer, academic, public official, and feminist activist. She studied law at the University of Oslo and joined the office responsible for administering national gender-equality policy shortly after its creation. Her first published work examined the treatment of married women in municipal employment contracts. Solberg served as chief adviser to two equality ombuds and filled the ombud position on several temporary occasions. During her years in the ombuds office, she helped design a standard form for complaints filed by workers who could not afford counsel. She later became president of a national women’s-rights organization, where she advocated stronger workplace protections and improved access to public services. Solberg taught law at a university college and participated in planning committees for Nordic women’s conferences. In the 1980s she chaired a committee that compared equality legislation in the Nordic countries. Her career connected legal scholarship with the development of Norway’s early institutional approach to gender equality.

The Omaha are a federally recognized Native American people whose reservation lies primarily in northeastern Nebraska, with a smaller portion extending across the Missouri River into Iowa. A series of nineteenth-century maps places an Omaha burial ground on the Iowa side of the reservation, though its exact location is no longer known. Their language belongs to the Dhegihan branch of the Siouan language family and is closely related to Ponca. An Omaha-language newspaper circulated for several years among reservation communities before the First World War. Omaha communities moved westward from the Ohio Valley and settled along the upper Missouri before the eighteenth century. Political and ceremonial life has historically been organized through kinship, clans, and village institutions. A tribal council established a formal archive of family histories during the middle of the twentieth century.
