The 2014 Ridgeway 500 was a stock-car race held at Ridgeway Motor Speedway in Tennessee. Run over 200 laps, it formed the middle round of that year’s national touring championship. Pole-sitter Aaron Cole led the opening portion of the event, but a late pit-stop decision allowed Marcus Bell to take the lead with 18 laps remaining. Bell held off Cole and veteran driver Dana Whitaker to claim his first victory of the season. The race featured eight caution periods, including one caused by a multicar accident on the backstretch, and 19 lead changes involving seven drivers. Bell’s result moved him from ninth to fifth in the drivers’ standings. The manufacturers’ table remained closely contested, with only a handful of points separating the leading two teams after the race.

The Lanterns were a New York power-pop group active during the early 2000s. Formed by guitarist Lena Ortiz, drummer Paul Raines, and bassist Michael Keene, the band played short, melodic songs that combined bright vocal harmonies with dense guitar arrangements. Their music appeared in several cable television programs, and a track from their first record was used during the closing credits of a reality competition. The Lanterns released the album Paper Satellites in 2003 through a small independent label. A review in a national music magazine praised the group’s sharp choruses while comparing its sound to British beat music and American college rock. Ortiz left the band the following year to pursue studio work, and the remaining members eventually continued under a different name.

In social psychology, an in-group is a group that contributes to a person’s sense of belonging, while an out-group consists of people perceived as outside that circle. The distinction can arise from family, neighborhood, occupation, religion, political allegiance, or an apparently trivial preference. Researchers have found that people may favor members of an in-group even when the group was created moments earlier and has no practical importance. Experiments using arbitrary labels showed that participants were willing to distribute rewards unevenly between invented categories. The findings helped shape social identity theory, which treats group membership as one source of self-understanding rather than merely a description of social organization. In-group boundaries may also change quickly when a larger shared identity becomes more important than the original division.

The Moon Children was a newspaper comic strip created by Finnish illustrator Elina Saarenmaa. It followed three siblings who lived in a lighthouse with their grandmother and encountered fantastical visitors from the sea. Saarenmaa first drew the characters for a weekly cultural paper in 1951, where the strip appeared alongside essays, puzzles, and serialized fiction. A Scandinavian syndicate later purchased the rights and distributed the feature to newspapers in northern Europe. The stories were generally self-contained, although several longer adventures were collected in paperback editions. At its height, the strip appeared in more than thirty newspapers and was translated into six languages. Saarenmaa continued drawing it until 1972, when she retired because of failing eyesight. A Finnish comics organization honored her work with a lifetime achievement award in 1978.

Aristotelia viridimacula is a moth in the family Gelechiidae recorded from northern Botswana. Its wingspan is approximately 13 mm. The forewings are smoky brown with a narrow greenish sheen, crossed by scattered pale scales and several dark wedges near the leading edge. A small ochre patch lies below the first third of the costa, while a broken black line runs from the center of the wing toward the outer margin. Two raised tufts of rusty scales occur along the dorsum, and a cluster of pale dots marks the area immediately before the termen. Near the apex, alternating dark and cream spots form an indistinct fringe. The hindwings are translucent grey, becoming more heavily shaded along the veins and outer border. The species has been collected in dry scrubland after summer rains, although little is known about its larval food plant or seasonal behavior.

North Star Wooden Puzzles is a puzzle company based in Eugene, Oregon. It was established in 2011 by an industrial designer and a former museum educator who wanted to produce small-run jigsaw puzzles using domestic hardwood. The company cuts its puzzles from laminated birch with computer-controlled blades, but the artwork and piece shapes are developed separately for each edition. Some designs use conventional interlocking pieces, while others include silhouettes of leaves, tools, animals, or figures associated with the image. These themed pieces, marketed as “story pieces,” are intended to reward solvers who notice details in the illustration. North Star commissions painters, printmakers, and illustrators rather than maintaining a single house style. Its catalog includes landscapes, historical posters, botanical plates, and reproductions of folk art. The firm has released more than 180 designs and is particularly known for irregularly cut puzzles with dense, decorative imagery.

KQRM (branded as 960 News and Ideas) is an AM radio station serving the greater Tulsa, Oklahoma area. It is operated by Prairie Broadcast Group, which acquired the station in the late 1990s. The main transmitter is located east of the city, while the studios occupy a converted office building near downtown. A low-power translator repeats portions of the schedule on 94.7 FM for listeners who prefer the clearer signal. Weekday programming combines locally hosted news blocks with syndicated political commentary, business reports, and a morning public-affairs program. The station’s weekend schedule includes shows about gardening, home repair, regional history, and personal finance, along with several hours supplied by national networks. KQRM also carries University of Tulsa basketball and selected high-school championship games. During severe weather, it suspends regular programming for extended local updates.

Lydia M. Navarro is an American attorney and politician who served as the attorney general of New Mexico from 2016 to 2022. Before becoming attorney general, she represented Albuquerque in the United States House of Representatives for five terms and held senior positions on committees concerned with commerce and public lands. Navarro was a member of the Democratic Party and briefly chaired the party’s western states caucus. She was born in Las Cruces and studied history at the University of New Mexico before earning a law degree from Georgetown University. After working for a legal-aid organization in Maryland, she returned to New Mexico and became counsel to the state senate. She later served as deputy secretary of the state justice department and advised the governor on consumer-protection legislation. As attorney general, Navarro emphasized privacy enforcement, water rights, and legal assistance for rural communities.

Viktor Andreyevich Malin was a Russian sprinter who specialized in the 400 metres. He represented the Soviet Union at the 1988 European Championships and later competed for Russia at the 1993 World Championships. Malin reached the semifinals of the individual event at his first major championship and ran the anchor leg for a relay team that finished fourth. His fastest 400-metre time, 45.18 seconds, was recorded at a meet in Kiev in 1989. He won three medals at regional competitions, including a relay gold at the 1990 Friendship Games and individual bronze at the 1992 European Indoor Championships. Malin was also a six-time national finalist and won the Soviet title once before taking two Russian championships after the dissolution of the Soviet Union. He retired from international competition in the mid-1990s and later coached junior athletes in St. Petersburg.

La Isla Encantada is the sixth studio album by Puerto Rican singer and composer Mateo Rivera. It was issued in September 1996 and combines salsa, plena, bolero, and acoustic pop. The record includes a slow, orchestral interpretation of a traditional jíbaro melody as well as Rivera’s first song recorded primarily in English, “After the Rain.” Several tracks use hand percussion and brass arrangements modeled on street ensembles from San Juan, while others draw on Brazilian samba and Caribbean zouk. Critics considered the album more varied than Rivera’s earlier dance-oriented releases and frequently singled out “Vuelve a la Mar” and “Calle de Luz” for praise. La Isla Encantada appeared on several year-end lists and received a nomination for Best Tropical Performance at the Latin Music Awards. Rivera later won a composer’s prize for the album’s title track, and three of its singles became radio staples in Puerto Rico and the Dominican Republic.

NBC Screenroom was an online video service introduced by NBC in October 2007. It provided short original programs, promotional clips, and selected episodes from the network’s broadcast schedule to viewers in the United States. The service was folded into NBC.com after two years, when the network reorganized its streaming operations under a single web brand. Screenroom’s initial catalog included comedy shorts, behind-the-scenes interviews, and older episodes licensed from NBC’s television library. Some programs were available without charge through advertising, while premium previews were released to registered users before their television broadcasts. Commercial placements were sold separately from conventional network advertising and could be targeted by program and region. NBC hoped the service would reach younger viewers who watched video on computers rather than through scheduled programming. It also planned live chats with actors and producers, though only a small number were held before the platform was discontinued.

The Mayo County Board of the Gaelic Athletic Association is the administrative body responsible for Gaelic games in County Mayo. It oversees the county’s clubs and selects the teams that compete in the provincial and national championships. Mayo is traditionally associated with Gaelic football, while hurling has a smaller but established presence in the county. The football side reached numerous All-Ireland finals during the twentieth and twenty-first centuries and became known for its running game and strong defensive lines. County competitions are organized across several divisions, with clubs from the larger towns often fielding teams at multiple age levels. The board also supports schools competitions, coaching programs, and the maintenance of county grounds. Its principal stadium, in Castlebar, hosts league matches and championship fixtures as well as county finals. Mayo’s teams play in Connacht and regularly meet Galway, Roscommon, and Sligo in provincial competition.

A dressage judge is a licensed official who evaluates a horse and rider during a prescribed test. Judges sit around the arena and record the execution of individual movements, including transitions, turns, collected work, and the final halt. They consider both technical accuracy and the quality of the performance, then provide marks and written comments that are combined into a final percentage. Officials normally begin at introductory levels and advance only after completing examinations, observation sessions, and supervised judging appointments. The exact grades vary between national federations, although the upper qualifications permit service at international competitions. A judge is expected to score the performance presented in front of them rather than reward reputation or anticipated potential. At the highest level, the Grand Prix, the panel must assess complicated sequences in which small errors can significantly affect the result. Judges may also be required to attend periodic refresher courses.

The Prairie Connector is a divided highway in the U.S. state of Kansas. Built in sections from the 1940s through the 1970s, it linked the older towns along the Cottonwood River with newer industrial districts farther west. The route carries state highways between Emporia and Wichita and crosses the river on a long concrete bridge completed in 1962. Engineers selected a nearly straight alignment across the prairie to shorten travel times and avoid repeated crossings of the river’s former channels. Local residents initially called the road the “air line” because it seemed to run toward the horizon without following an established settlement. Two regional airports were later built near its interchanges, giving the informal name a second association. The highway passes grain terminals, truck stops, and several restored sections of the original county road. During winter storms, the open terrain can make the central portion difficult to keep clear.

A season is a recurring portion of the annual cycle distinguished by temperature, rainfall, daylight, or changes in living organisms. On Earth, the familiar pattern of spring, summer, autumn, and winter is produced mainly by the tilt of the planet’s axis as it travels around the Sun. A hemisphere receives more concentrated sunlight when it is angled toward the Sun and less when it is angled away. The warmest or coldest weather does not necessarily occur at the moment of maximum or minimum sunlight because land and water release stored heat gradually. Near the equator, seasonal differences may be described through wet and dry periods rather than through temperature. Polar communities have also developed calendars based on ice, animal movement, and the return of sunlight. The number of recognized seasons therefore differs among climates and cultures, even though the astronomical cycle is shared across the planet.

Thomas K. Weller was an English-born Australian traveler who crossed the continent by bicycle in 1902. He began at Fremantle and followed a mixture of telegraph routes, stock tracks, and newly surveyed roads toward the eastern coast. Weller had worked as a machinist before emigrating and repaired his own bicycle during the journey, often using parts obtained from railway workshops. The trip took more than four months and included long stretches where water could be carried only in small metal containers. Newspapers in Perth published brief accounts of his progress, and a fuller narrative appeared in a Melbourne sporting paper after his return. Weller later worked as an engineer at a mining settlement in Western Australia. His exact birthplace and family name have been disputed because he used several spellings on official documents. He spent his later years giving public lectures about travel, mechanical repair, and life on the interior routes.

Margaret Elise Horan was a Canadian nutrition scientist, university administrator, and provincial politician. She represented the district of Bay View in the Newfoundland and Labrador House of Assembly from 1987 to 1991. Horan was raised in a fishing family near Corner Brook and studied agricultural chemistry at the Nova Scotia Agricultural College before completing graduate work in food science at McGill University. She joined the federal agriculture department as a research officer and later became director of a laboratory investigating fish-protein preservation and rural nutrition. In the early 1980s she moved to Memorial University, where she coordinated a program linking community health workers with university researchers. As a legislator, Horan served on committees concerned with fisheries, food security, and vocational education. She chaired a provincial review of school meal programs, whose recommendations were adopted in part by the government after her term ended.

Alinghi was a Swiss yacht-racing syndicate created by businessman Ernesto Bertarelli to challenge for the America’s Cup. The team made its first campaign in the early 2000s and won the trophy in its debut appearance, defeating the defending American syndicate in a series held in New Zealand. It later defended the cup in the Mediterranean and developed a reputation for combining large-scale sailing operations with extensive computer modeling. The syndicate’s boats were prepared by an international group of designers and sailors, while its shore base included sailmakers, meteorologists, and composite-material specialists. A dispute over the eligibility of competing yachts led to a separate match before the next full regatta could be organized. Alinghi subsequently lost the trophy and reduced its sailing program, although associated crews continued to compete in other classes. The name remained connected with professional yacht racing for much of the following decade.

A paramagnetic tag is a molecule containing an unpaired electron that can be attached to a protein or membrane component for spectroscopic study. Most tags used in biological work are stable nitroxide radicals, often linked to a selected cysteine residue. When the labeled molecule is examined by electron paramagnetic resonance, the tag reports on the motion and chemical surroundings of the site to which it is attached. By placing tags at several positions, researchers can estimate changes in folding, binding, and distance between parts of a protein. The method is related to isotopic labeling in nuclear magnetic resonance, but it does not require replacing a large portion of the sample with a magnetic isotope. Paramagnetic tags can also alter the relaxation of nearby nuclei, allowing them to be used in paramagnetic relaxation enhancement experiments. Their usefulness depends on the tag remaining sufficiently mobile while still following the behavior of the structure being examined.

Loughan is a small village in County Monaghan, Ireland, situated beside a tributary of the Finn River. It developed around a crossroads on the route between Clones and Carrickmacross and lies among low, rounded hills left by glacial deposits. The surrounding parish contains several lakes, scattered farms, and the remains of a medieval earthwork that gave the settlement its earliest recorded name. A railway once served the village from a halt outside the main street, but passenger service ended in the middle of the twentieth century. The present village includes a church, a primary school, and a community hall built on the site of an older market yard. Drainage work altered the course of the stream through the center during the nineteenth century, creating a narrow green beside the road. Neighboring settlements include Aghabog, Newbliss, and Drum.

Arthur Lionel Fenwick was an English amateur cricketer who appeared in 16 first-class matches for Warwickshire between 1881 and 1890. A right-handed batsman and occasional wicket-keeper, he was born in Birmingham, the son of a manufacturer of agricultural equipment. Fenwick attended Rugby School, where he captained the cricket eleven in his final year, and later studied law at Cambridge. He made his county debut against Gloucestershire at Edgbaston after being invited to replace an injured regular. His appearances remained intermittent because he practiced as a solicitor, but he was regarded as a dependable player on difficult wickets. Fenwick scored his highest first-class innings, 87 runs, against Yorkshire in 1886 and took nine catches during his county career. He continued playing club cricket after leaving the first-class side and served for many years as secretary of a Birmingham cricket association.

Martin Alan Keating was an English professional footballer who played as a right-sided midfielder. He began with Nottingham Forest and made his senior debut in 1983 before joining Carlisle United on loan. After leaving Forest, Keating signed for Grimsby Town, where he became a regular in the club’s promotion campaign and appeared in more than 150 league matches. He later played for Wigan Athletic and Chester City, moving between the second and third tiers of the Football League. Keating was known for accurate crossing and for taking responsibility for free kicks, although injuries limited his appearances during the final years of his career. He helped Grimsby win the Associate Members’ Cup in 1988 and was part of the Wigan side that reached the play-offs two seasons later. He retired in 1996 and subsequently worked as a youth coach and scout in the East Midlands.

Jan Novák is a Czech organist, harpsichordist, and festival director. He studied at the Conservatory of Brno before continuing at the Academy of Performing Arts in Prague, where his teachers included Václav Rabas and Pavel Černý. Novák later attended master classes in Paris and Berlin and developed a repertoire ranging from Renaissance keyboard music to contemporary Czech compositions. He performs as a soloist and regularly appears with chamber ensembles, including a period-instrument orchestra based in Moravia. His collaborations have included programs with violinists, singers, and brass groups, and he has recorded for Czech radio and several independent labels. Novák became resident organist of the St. James Chamber Society in 2006. He also prepares concert programs and lectures on the restoration of historic instruments. In 2014 he was appointed artistic director of the Moravian Early Music Festival, a position through which he promoted performances in churches and small town halls.

Midnight Arithmetic is the second studio album by Chicago rapper Darius Lane, released through the independent label North Loop Records. The album was announced for spring 2012, but its release was delayed after the label changed distributors and several guest appearances had to be cleared. It eventually arrived in August of that year. Most of the production was handled by the duo Glass Office, whose spare drum tracks and looping electric-piano lines give the record a restrained sound. Two songs were produced by Lane himself, and a closing track uses a sample rearranged by Detroit musician Rhea Moss. Promotional videos were filmed in Chicago and posted through the label’s web channel before the album became available for download and on compact disc. Midnight Arithmetic entered the independent album chart in its first week and was praised by local critics for its detailed writing and unusually cohesive sequencing.

Al-Kisa'i was an early Arabic grammarian associated with the scholarly circle of Kufa. He was born in the region of Kufa and traveled widely before becoming a teacher at the Abbasid court. His work dealt with pronunciation, inflection, and the interpretation of unusual forms found in the Qur'an and in pre-Islamic poetry. Al-Kisa'i collected examples from Bedouin speakers and used them to support grammatical rules that sometimes differed from those favored by scholars in Basra. He is also credited with preparing an early reading of the Qur'an that became influential among later reciters. Several books attributed to him were cited by medieval writers but have not survived as independent texts. Much of what is known about his method therefore comes from quotations and disputes preserved in later grammatical treatises. He died while traveling with the court in the early ninth century.

Edward Miles Harcourt was an English cricketer who played first-class matches for Derbyshire during the 1890s. A right-handed batsman and right-arm medium-pace bowler, he was born in Derby and educated at Repton School, where he kept wicket before moving into the county’s bowling attack. Harcourt made his first-class debut against Lancashire in 1891 and appeared in 31 matches over the next five seasons. He took 61 wickets at an average just below 30, with best innings figures of five for 42. His batting was less consistent, although he made a career-best 72 against Sussex after being promoted to number five. Harcourt also played in a handful of minor matches for a combined Midlands side and represented Derbyshire in the county’s early one-day fixtures. He left the county team when he entered the family’s textile business and later served as president of a local cricket club.

The Meridian Four are an American vocal group whose music combines pop, contemporary R&B, and gospel harmony. The quartet was established in Detroit by college friends Calvin Reed, Marcus Hale, Andre Whitfield, and Terrence Price. Unlike many commercially assembled groups, the members had performed together in church and neighborhood talent shows before attracting the attention of a producer. Their first single, “Stay for the Morning,” reached the upper half of the American singles chart, and a later ballad became their only top-ten hit. The group released three albums between 1998 and 2004 and sold several million records internationally. Reed and Hale shared most lead vocals, while Whitfield became known for arranging the group’s layered backing parts. The Meridian Four suspended activity after Price left to work in television production, but they reunited for a series of benefit concerts more than a decade later.

NGC 5189 is a complex planetary nebula in the southern constellation Musca. Its bright central region is surrounded by several loops and arcs that give the object an irregular, almost braided appearance. Spectroscopic studies indicate that the nebula contains knots of ionized gas moving at different speeds, suggesting that the dying star experienced more than one period of intense mass loss. The central star is a compact, very hot remnant with a temperature measured in the hundreds of thousands of degrees. Dust lanes obscure portions of the inner nebula, while faint outer shells extend well beyond the easily visible structure. Astronomers have proposed that a companion star or an unstable magnetic field may have influenced the direction of the outflows. Images from space telescopes have revealed chemical variations across the lobes and have made NGC 5189 a useful target for studying the final stages of stellar evolution.

The Global Price Measurement Initiative is a cooperative statistical program that produces comparable measures of national output and household purchasing power. It is organized by a consortium of development banks, regional statistical offices, and international economic agencies. Participating countries collect prices for representative goods and services, record expenditure weights, and submit information for a common reference year. The program uses these data to calculate purchasing power parities, which permit gross domestic product to be compared without relying solely on market exchange rates. Surveys cover household consumption, government activity, construction, machinery, and other components of the economy. Because prices and patterns of consumption change, the exercise is repeated at intervals rather than treated as a permanent index. Its results are used in poverty research, regional comparisons, and the allocation of some international funds. Methodologists also publish notes describing how unusual products and differing national classifications were handled.

Marjorie Anne Pritchard was an Australian accounts clerk who embezzled more than two million Australian dollars from a regional hardware chain. She controlled the company’s payroll reserve and created false entries that made repeated withdrawals appear to be payments to temporary workers. The theft continued for nearly four years because Pritchard reconciled the cash ledger herself and divided the missing sums among several internal accounts. She spent much of the money on electronic gaming machines at a club where she served on the social committee, while additional funds went toward property renovations, jewelry, and overseas holidays. An internal audit began after a branch manager questioned a series of unusually large cash orders. Pritchard was arrested after investigators found envelopes of company money in her car and later pleaded guilty to dozens of fraud charges. A portion of the funds was recovered through the sale of her house, but most of the loss remained outstanding.

Toni Morrison (born Chloe Anthony Wofford; February 18, 1931 – August 5, 2019) was an American novelist, editor, and professor. She received the Nobel Prize in Literature, the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction, and the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Morrison worked for many years as an editor before becoming one of the most influential American novelists of the late twentieth century. Her fiction frequently examines memory, family, race, and the aftereffects of historical violence through shifting voices and nonlinear narratives. Among her best-known novels are The Bluest Eye, Sula, Song of Solomon, Beloved, Jazz, and Paradise. She also wrote essays, children’s books, and a play. Morrison taught at several universities and served as a mentor to younger writers. Her work has been widely studied for its language, its treatment of collective memory, and its refusal to separate private experience from the larger history of the United States.

The Margulis lemma is a result in the geometry of negatively curved spaces that describes the thin parts of a manifold. Roughly speaking, below a fixed scale determined by the curvature, a sufficiently small neighborhood has a highly organized form rather than arbitrary complexity. In a hyperbolic manifold, a thin region may be associated with a short closed geodesic or with a cusp extending toward infinity. The lemma permits these regions to be separated from the thick part, where the geometry has uniform local control. Its constants depend on the dimension and curvature bounds, and the precise statement varies between smooth and discrete settings. The result is used in the study of finite-volume manifolds, geometric limits, and the behavior of sequences of spaces that degenerate. It also underlies decompositions in which complicated global geometry is analyzed by treating compact and cuspidal regions separately.

The Rio Vista Conveyance is a concrete irrigation canal in central Arizona. It takes water from a regulating reservoir on the Gila River and carries it southeast through agricultural districts before ending near the town of Mesa Verde. The canal is managed by a federal reclamation authority and supplies farms, municipal treatment plants, and several industrial users. Its original design also reserved capacity for a proposed thermal power station, although that connection was never built. The channel has a broad trapezoidal profile, with lined banks and a series of siphons beneath roads and washes. A branch near its western terminus links it to a regional aqueduct that serves communities in the Phoenix basin. Construction began in the 1960s and proceeded in stages as land was acquired. A planned extension into the lower valley remains unfunded, and current operators have concentrated on repairing leaks and improving automated gates.

Raghavendra Prasad (1938–2019) was an Indian politician associated with the Bharatiya Janata Party and its earlier predecessor organizations. He served twice as chief minister of a northern Indian state and later represented the state in the Lok Sabha. Prasad entered public life through the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, joining its student activities while still in school. He was first elected to the state assembly from a rural constituency in 1969 and retained the seat through several changes of party affiliation. His first ministry lasted less than a year and ended after a coalition collapsed over a land-reform bill. He returned as chief minister in the late 1990s, when his government emphasized road construction, irrigation, and the expansion of religious tourism. Prasad left the BJP after a leadership dispute and formed a short-lived regional party before returning to national politics. Supporters remembered him as an effective organizer, while opponents criticized his strongly sectarian campaign style.

Angela Lansbury (1925–2023) was an English-American actress and singer whose career included film, television, and stage performance. She began working in Hollywood as a teenager and received an Academy Award nomination for her first screen role. After moving increasingly toward theatre, Lansbury won Tony Awards for several Broadway productions and became closely associated with musical comedy and character roles. She later reached a new audience as the star of the television mystery series Murder, She Wrote, in which she played a novelist who solved crimes in a small coastal town. Lansbury also appeared in animated films, concert productions, and revivals of classic plays. She received an honorary Academy Award, the National Medal of Arts, and a lifetime achievement award from the Screen Actors Guild. Her long career made her one of the few performers to remain prominent across several generations of American entertainment.

Seafield Road is a residential street in the Dublin suburb of Clontarf, Ireland. It runs from the seafront toward the junction with Vernon Avenue and passes several sports grounds, schools, and late nineteenth-century houses. The road developed as the area changed from a coastal village into a commuter district, and its older buildings include red-brick terraces, detached villas, and a former seaside hotel converted into apartments. A church near the southern end is notable for its pale limestone façade and for the damage caused by salt carried inland from Dublin Bay. The street is connected to a network of cycle paths and is frequently used by pedestrians traveling toward the promenade. Property prices rose sharply during the 2000s, especially for houses with gardens facing the water. One large corner residence attracted attention when it sold for several million euros before being offered again at a considerably lower price during the following downturn.

Amoris laetitia is a post-synodal apostolic exhortation issued by Pope Francis and signed in Rome on 19 March 2016. It followed two assemblies of the Synod of Bishops devoted to family life, marriage, and pastoral care. The document discusses the responsibilities of families, the education of children, the place of tenderness in marriage, and the need for local churches to respond to difficult circumstances with discernment. Its title, translated as “The Joy of Love,” reflects the document’s emphasis on the ordinary happiness and burdens of domestic life. Francis draws on biblical passages concerning creation, charity, and the household, while also engaging earlier papal teaching. The exhortation attracted particular attention for its discussion of accompaniment and the application of general principles to individual situations. It was intended to encourage reflection among clergy and lay Catholics rather than to establish a new code of canon law.

Selin Aydemir is a contemporary Turkish novelist, essayist, and editor. Born in İzmir, she studied sociology at Ankara University and began publishing criticism in literary journals while still a student. Her short story “The Blue Staircase” won a national competition in 1992 and led to the publication of her first collection. Aydemir later worked as an editor at a major Istanbul publishing house, where she specialized in translated fiction and memoir. Her most widely read book, Our Houses at Dusk, reconstructs urban life during the 1970s through linked stories told by several generations of one family. It received a regional literary prize and was translated into Greek, Bulgarian, and Arabic. Aydemir has also written screenplays based on the work of earlier Turkish authors. One adaptation was broadcast as a television miniseries in 2007. Her essays frequently address publishing, memory, and the changing social geography of Istanbul.

Martin Geoffrey Collins was an English first-class cricketer who captained Leicestershire during the late 1980s. A right-handed middle-order batsman and occasional off-spin bowler, he made his county debut in 1978 and remained with the side for more than a decade. Collins scored over 1,000 runs in four seasons and recorded his highest total, 1,246, during the campaign in which he was appointed captain. Under his leadership Leicestershire won the Sunday League and reached the final of the Benson and Hedges Cup. He also played professional football as a young man, appearing for Northampton Town, Peterborough United, and a number of non-league clubs before concentrating on cricket. Collins made one appearance for an England representative side but was never selected for a full international. After retiring as a player, he joined the national cricket board as a logistics manager and later oversaw travel and match operations for touring teams.

Mara Ellison is an American producer and occasional director of independent films. She founded Harbor Light Pictures in Boston and has received two national television awards for documentary production. Ellison’s projects have included the feature dramas Winter Harbor and The Long Return, as well as the documentaries A Map of Home and Glass Children. She served as executive producer on a film about displaced coastal communities that premiered at a major international festival and later received theatrical distribution. Other credits include a period adaptation directed by Celia Hart, a music documentary set in New Orleans, and a television film based on a bestselling biography of a public-health researcher. Ellison has worked with directors from the United States, India, and Ireland and is known for combining commercial financing with small, director-led productions. In addition to producing, she has taught film development and served on the selection committee of a regional arts foundation.

Bishop Iakovos Markou is a Greek Orthodox theologian and hierarch who teaches patristics at the University of Thessaloniki. Born in Piraeus in 1964, he studied theology in Athens and continued his education in Geneva and Rome. He was ordained to the episcopate in 2011 and appointed metropolitan of a diocese in northern Greece, while retaining a part-time university appointment. Markou has represented the Church of Greece in discussions with Roman Catholic, Anglican, and Lutheran delegates and has written extensively on the history of church councils. He has argued that dialogue requires precise definitions of doctrine as well as practical cooperation in matters of social welfare. During preparations for a pan-Orthodox meeting, Markou published a memorandum expressing reservations about several proposed statements and calling for wider consultation among local synods. His comments drew criticism from conservative clergy but were welcomed by theologians who favored continued ecumenical discussion.

The Mazovia encoding was a character set used on Polish personal computers during the 1980s and early 1990s. It was developed for DOS systems whose original video fonts did not include the diacritical marks required by Polish. The encoding retained much of the layout of Code page 437 but replaced selected symbols with letters such as ą, ć, ę, ł, ń, ó, ś, ź, and ż. The replacements were chosen partly for visual compatibility, allowing a document to remain recognizable when displayed on a machine that lacked the customized font. Several keyboard and resident-driver utilities supported the system, and different software packages sometimes implemented slightly different variants. Mazovia was common in offices, schools, and early bulletin-board services before national and international standards became widely available. Text created with it often required conversion before it could be exchanged reliably with later Windows applications.

The Toledo Walleye are a professional minor-league ice hockey team based in Toledo, Ohio. The club plays in the ECHL and holds its home games at the Huntington Center in the city’s downtown district. Practices and occasional preseason games are held at a second rink in suburban Sylvania. The franchise was established in 1991 under a different name and adopted the Walleye identity after moving into its present arena. It has maintained affiliations with several National Hockey League and American Hockey League organizations, most recently serving as a development partner for a club in the Midwest. The team has won multiple division titles and reached the league’s championship series more than once. Its supporters are known for organizing themed game nights and outdoor viewing events. The Walleye are one of the longest-running professional sports franchises in northwestern Ohio and have helped sustain youth hockey programs throughout the region.

Salesian educational institutions are schools, colleges, and training centers connected with the Society of Saint Francis de Sales, a Roman Catholic congregation founded by John Bosco in nineteenth-century Turin. The order developed its educational work around technical instruction, religious formation, and the support of young people who lacked stable family or economic circumstances. Salesian schools are commonly operated by priests, brothers, sisters, and lay teachers working together. Their programs range from primary education to vocational training and university study, and many include boarding facilities or youth centers. By the twenty-first century, Salesian institutions existed on every inhabited continent, with especially large networks in Latin America, South Asia, and parts of Africa. Individual schools often adapt the curriculum to local needs while retaining the congregation’s emphasis on practical skills, recreation, and pastoral care. The order’s name is sometimes confused with that of unrelated Christian teaching organizations.

George Henry Lascelles was an English amateur cricketer who appeared in first-class matches for Yorkshire between 1841 and 1846. He was born near Harrogate, the son of a landowner, and received his early education at Eton. Lascelles played as a right-handed batsman and was occasionally used as a wicket-keeper when the regular player was unavailable. His first-class debut came in a north-versus-south fixture at Lord’s, after which he joined Yorkshire for matches against touring elevens and the Marylebone Cricket Club. He made 18 appearances in total, scoring a highest innings of 64 and taking seven catches. Lascelles also represented Gentlemen of Yorkshire and played for a household brigade team during his military service. He retired from competitive cricket after inheriting an estate in the north and remained involved in the sport as a patron of local clubs. His surviving scorecards provide most of the information about his career.

Harold Dean Mercer was an American sculptor known for monumental works made from welded steel and cast bronze. He lived in Cedar Falls, Iowa, where many of his public pieces were installed in parks, libraries, and civic plazas. Mercer’s best-known commission was a large metal heron placed beside a riverfront museum, but he also produced abstract constructions from farm machinery, bridge cable, and discarded industrial parts. He studied art at a Midwestern college before serving in the military and later completed graduate work in sculpture at the University of Illinois. Mercer taught at a small liberal-arts college and organized workshops in metal fabrication for regional artists. In the 1970s he helped create a downtown sculpture program that brought outdoor works to several towns in the Cedar Valley. His later pieces combined rough welded surfaces with polished bronze elements and often referred to local industry, agriculture, and the changing course of the river.

Acid gas is a natural-gas stream containing appreciable concentrations of hydrogen sulfide, carbon dioxide, or another component that forms an acidic solution when dissolved in water. The classification is based on composition rather than on the gas having a low pH by itself, since pH is measured in an aqueous mixture. Sour gas is a narrower term generally reserved for gas containing hydrogen sulfide at a concentration important to processing or safety. A stream made up chiefly of carbon dioxide may therefore be acid gas without being sour gas. Producers remove these compounds before transportation because hydrogen sulfide is poisonous and corrosive, while carbon dioxide lowers the heating value and can damage equipment in the presence of moisture. Treatment commonly includes amine absorption followed by sulfur recovery or reinjection. The amount removed depends on the sales specification, the reservoir chemistry, and the intended use of the gas.

Frontier Motorsports was a former team in the NASCAR Craftsman Truck Series. It was founded in 1996 by mechanic Alan Rusk and businessman Peter Dwyer and initially entered a single Chevrolet for driver Nolan Pierce. Pierce completed most of the team’s first season and earned a top-ten finish at Mesa Grande Speedway. A regional tool company became the principal sponsor the following year, when Frontier added a second truck for selected races. The team’s first victory came at Phoenix in 1998 after Pierce qualified on the front row and conserved fuel during a late caution. Frontier changed to Ford equipment in 1999 and signed veteran driver Kyle Benton, who won two poles and finished sixth in the championship. Financial difficulties reduced the operation to a part-time schedule, and the organization was sold before the 2001 season. Its final entries were prepared by a neighboring team using the Frontier name and number.

Eleanor Price was an American technical-theatre consultant and author whose work focused on stage machinery and overhead safety. Her handbook, Theatre Flying Systems, was first published by a university press in 1992 and revised several times as counterweight equipment, fall protection, and inspection standards changed. Price founded an independent consulting practice that advised architects, performing-arts administrators, and contractors on the construction or renovation of theatres, concert halls, arenas, and touring venues. She inspected rigging systems in the United States, Europe, and East Asia and helped develop procedures for documenting old equipment whose original plans had been lost. Price also taught intensive courses for stagehands, design students, and venue managers. Her classes emphasized that safe operation depended on routine inspection and clear communication as much as on the strength of individual ropes or battens. She remained active as a lecturer after retiring from regular consulting.

Antaeotricha aurantilinea is a moth in the family Depressariidae known from western Ecuador. The wingspan is approximately 18 mm. Its forewings are pale ash-grey with a warm orange-brown line running obliquely from the costa toward the middle of the dorsum. A second darker band begins nearer the wing base and breaks into small spots before reaching the opposite margin. The central area contains scattered black scales and a faint cream-colored mark at the end of the cell. Near the termen, a row of dusky dots follows the curve of the wing, with a brighter patch immediately below the apex. The costal edge remains nearly unmarked, producing a narrow light border. The hindwings are smoky brown and slightly paler toward the base, with a fringe of fine hairs along the outer margin. Adults have been collected in lowland forest and foothill plantations, but the caterpillar and host plant have not been described.

The dental arches are the curved rows formed by the teeth in the upper and lower jaws. The maxillary arch is ordinarily broader and longer than the mandibular arch, so that the upper incisors and posterior teeth overlap their lower counterparts when the mouth is closed. This meeting of the teeth is called occlusion. Its pattern depends on the size and position of the jaws, the shape of individual crowns, and the way the teeth erupt. In a normal bite, the upper canine lies between the lower canine and first premolar, while the cusps of the molars fit into grooves on the opposing arch. Crowding, missing teeth, jaw growth differences, or habits that alter development can produce malocclusion, including an open bite, crossbite, or excessive overjet. Dentists and orthodontists study the arches through examination, impressions, photographs, and radiographs when planning treatment.

Bolboschoenus maritimus is a perennial wetland plant in the sedge family, commonly called sea club-rush. It occurs around coastal lagoons, river mouths, salt marshes, and alkaline inland lakes across Europe, Asia, Africa, and parts of Australia. The plant spreads through tough underground rhizomes and often forms broad stands in shallow water or saturated mud. Its round, green stems may rise more than a metre and are usually topped by a cluster of brown spikelets supported on unequal stalks. Long basal leaves sheath the lower stem, while one or more stiff bracts extend beyond the inflorescence. The species tolerates salt better than many related sedges and can colonize disturbed shorelines, though prolonged drying reduces its vigor. Dense colonies provide cover for small birds and invertebrates and can trap sediment along the margins of tidal wetlands.

Calocedrus formosana is an evergreen conifer in the cypress family native to the mountains of Taiwan. It is usually a tall forest tree, reaching 20–35 metres, although exposed individuals may remain much shorter and develop a broad crown. Young plants have narrow, pointed leaves, while mature branches carry flattened sprays of overlapping scale leaves arranged in opposite pairs. The foliage is dark green above and somewhat paler beneath, and crushed leaves give off a resinous scent. The small cones mature in a single season and consist of several scales, two of which bear winged seeds. Calocedrus formosana grows in cool, moist ravines and on steep slopes at middle elevations, often with broad-leaved evergreen trees and other conifers. Logging and the conversion of mountain forest have reduced some populations, but the species is also planted as an ornamental in temperate gardens.

The Elmwood Avenue Historic District is a largely residential historic district in Hartford, Connecticut. It occupies several blocks west of the city center and is bounded by Garden Street, Prospect Avenue, and a pair of older parkways. The area was laid out during the 1880s as farmland was divided for suburban construction, with most houses completed before the First World War. Its buildings include Queen Anne residences, Colonial Revival houses, brick apartment blocks, and a small number of Tudor-style homes added in the 1920s. Lots are generally narrow, with mature trees and setbacks that create a continuous leafy streetscape. Several former carriage houses were later converted into garages or apartments. Community institutions include a stone Episcopal church, a neighborhood library, and a private school occupying an early mansion. The district was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1998 because it retains an unusually broad collection of middle-class residential architecture from the city’s expansion era.

The B4176 is a road in southern England connecting the market town of Marlborough with the outskirts of Swindon. Most of the route is a two-lane carriageway, although short climbing lanes were added near the highest part of the downs. It passes through Ogbourne St Andrew, Broad Hinton, and several smaller settlements before meeting the A419 at a roundabout east of Swindon. The road follows portions of an older ridge route used by packhorse traffic and later incorporated into the turnpike network. Roman pottery and fragments of paving have been found near its northern end, though the modern alignment has been altered in several places to avoid villages. During the nineteenth century the road carried farm produce toward the railway at Swindon. Today it serves commuters, agricultural traffic, and visitors traveling to prehistoric earthworks on the surrounding chalk hills.

In astrobiology, the Concordance Principle is a proposed condition of the “zoo” explanation for the Fermi paradox. The zoo hypothesis suggests that advanced civilizations deliberately avoid overt contact with younger worlds, either to preserve independent development or to reduce the dangers of interference. For such a policy to persist, separate civilizations would need to agree on what counts as a protected planet and on the technological threshold at which contact becomes acceptable. Advocates sometimes imagine a council or interstellar association that maintains a shared code of conduct. The principle creates a difficulty for the hypothesis: a larger association would include more members capable of violating the agreement, while a small association could not monitor a wide region of space. Even if the policy began with a single powerful civilization, it would have to be renewed across very different cultures and historical periods. The proposal therefore shifts the paradox from silence alone to the problem of lasting coordination.

Nathaniel Ames Whitcomb (1858–1916) was an American Episcopal priest, lecturer, and writer associated with the Anglo-Catholic movement. He studied at Trinity College and the General Theological Seminary before being ordained in New York in 1883. Whitcomb served as curate of a parish in Newark and later became rector of St. Mark’s Church in Philadelphia, where he promoted daily services, choral worship, and the use of ceremonial furnishings. During his tenure the congregation built a new stone church and established a mission for factory workers in a nearby district. Whitcomb retired because of poor health in 1908 but continued to publish essays on liturgy and church architecture. His best-known contribution was a pamphlet defending the use of incense in Anglican worship, written in response to a debate within the Church of England. He also edited sermons by an earlier bishop and delivered lectures on the relationship between ritual and pastoral care.

Walter “Walt” Danner was an American professional baseball player, coach, and manager. A right-handed infielder, he made his major-league debut with the Cleveland Indians in 1954 and later played for the Kansas City Athletics and Baltimore Orioles. Danner retired as a player after the 1964 season and worked as a scout and minor-league instructor before taking his first major-league managerial position. He led the Baltimore club to two division titles in the 1970s and was known for emphasizing defensive range, aggressive baserunning, and flexible relief pitching. Danner later managed the Milwaukee Brewers, guiding them to their first postseason appearance in more than a decade. He also served briefly as a general manager and developed a reputation for promoting players from the farm system. Danner was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame by a veterans committee in 2008 and was honored by the Orioles with a permanent display at their museum.

College Avenue is a street in Athens, Georgia, that forms part of the commercial and social center of the University of Georgia. It runs from the historic campus toward downtown and connects the main quadrangle with restaurants, bookstores, music venues, and fraternity houses. Many of the buildings along the street are nineteenth- and early twentieth-century structures, although several were renovated for student organizations and retail businesses. The avenue’s northern end is near the university’s oldest academic buildings, while its southern blocks lead toward a courthouse square and a public park. A number of houses once used as private residences now serve fraternities, sororities, or university offices. College Avenue has also been associated with local writers and musicians, and its sidewalks are used for parades, demonstrations, and football-weekend gatherings. Traffic restrictions have periodically been introduced to make the central section more pedestrian-friendly.

“The Missing Passenger” is the ninth episode of the second season of the American mystery series Harbor County and the 31st episode overall. It was written by Marla Keene and directed by Robert Velez, and first aired on a regional cable network in February 2011. The series follows Lena Ortiz, a former prosecutor who investigates minor crimes in a coastal town while caring for her widowed father. In this episode, a commuter van arrives at the terminal with one seat occupied by a suitcase and no sign of the passenger who paid for it. Lena discovers that the missing traveler had been collecting evidence against a shipping company and may have staged the disappearance. Meanwhile, her brother tries to sell the family boat without telling her, and the town council debates closing the old ferry route. The episode was praised for combining a self-contained mystery with the season’s larger corruption plot.

Juniper Canyon is a narrow valley in the western foothills of the San Gabriel Mountains in Southern California. Older maps give the canyon several names, reflecting changes in the surrounding ranches and in the road used to reach the mountain communities. Its upper section lies in Los Angeles County, while the lower slopes cross into San Bernardino County near a seasonal stream. A small elementary school and a fire station serve the residential area at the canyon’s northern entrance. The route connects inland neighborhoods with a pass leading toward the high desert and is used by commuters seeking an alternative to the larger freeways. Hiking trails follow the streambed and climb toward chaparral-covered ridges, although access is sometimes restricted after wildfires or landslides. The canyon’s present road was widened in stages during the twentieth century, replacing an older unpaved track that had been used by ranchers and utility crews.

Rhode Island is a state in the New England region of the United States, bordered by Connecticut to the west, Massachusetts to the north and east, and the Atlantic Ocean to the south. Its official name, the State of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations, reflects the separate origins of the island settlement and the mainland colony founded around Providence. Rhode Island is the smallest state by area but contains a dense network of bays, tidal rivers, and developed coastal communities. Providence is the capital and largest city, while Newport and Warwick are important centers of tourism, education, and industry. The state is divided into five counties, although the counties have no county government. Northern Rhode Island is more urbanized and historically industrial, while the southern and eastern portions include beaches, farms, forests, and islands in Narragansett Bay. Its maritime economy and colonial history have shaped a culture distinct from both Boston and New York.

Classical education is a philosophy that organizes learning around language, history, mathematics, philosophy, and works regarded as foundational to a culture. Its advocates generally argue that students should first develop habits of attention and reasoning before specializing in a profession. The approach is often divided into stages: early instruction in grammar and memory, a middle period devoted to argument and analysis, and advanced study in rhetoric and independent judgment. Classical schools may rely on direct instruction and a common curriculum, but many also use discussion and imitation rather than treating students as passive recipients of facts. The philosophy differs from vocational education, which begins with practical occupational skills, and from progressive education, which gives greater weight to individual interests and experiential projects. Critics have argued that traditional canons can exclude non-Western knowledge, while supporters respond that a shared sequence of demanding texts provides a basis for sustained intellectual debate.

The Bunya branch railway was a narrow-gauge line in southern Queensland, Australia. It was approved in the 1890s to connect timber camps and newly planted farms with the main railway near Dalby. The first section opened to Jimbour Creek in 1898, followed by extensions to Bell and Bunya Creek over the next decade. Construction required several low bridges and a long climb through undulating country, and trains frequently carried grain, livestock, timber, and passengers traveling to regional markets. Settlements grew around the stations, with hotels, stores, and loading yards appearing beside the line. Competition from improved roads weakened the railway after the Second World War, and passenger services were withdrawn before the freight branch closed in stages. Much of the track was removed, though station buildings at Bell and Bunya Creek survive as community halls or museums.

The Montclar Tunnel is a pair of railway bores beneath the western Alps between France and Italy. It forms part of a cross-border high-speed route linking the Rhône valley with the Turin rail network and was designed for both passenger trains and selected freight services. Construction began in 2008 after several years of geological surveys and negotiations over the operating concession. The first bore was completed in 2013 and the line opened to regular traffic two years later. Each bore contains a standard-gauge track, emergency walkways, ventilation shafts, and cross-passages leading to the neighboring tube. The tunnel is named after a mountain pass and a nearby border village rather than after either terminal city. Operation was initially assigned to a private consortium, but responsibility later passed to the two national infrastructure agencies after the concessionaire encountered financial difficulties. Interoperable signaling permits qualifying trains to cross the border without changing locomotives.

Harold James Cotton was an Australian cricketer who represented South Australia as a fast bowler during the 1930s. He played 27 first-class matches and took 82 wickets, but his career was repeatedly interrupted by disputes over the legality of his delivery. Cotton made his debut against Tasmania at Adelaide Oval in 1935 and impressed observers with his pace and steep bounce. During a Sheffield Shield match against Victoria, an umpire called him for throwing twice in the same over, prompting a debate about whether his unusually long arm swing could be corrected. He altered his run-up and delivery during the following season and returned to the side, although he never regained a permanent place. Cotton’s best first-class figures were six wickets for 71 runs, achieved against Queensland. He later coached at a country club and worked as a groundsman after leaving representative cricket.

Advanced air mobility is a broad term for transporting people or goods with small aircraft that operate between cities, suburbs, and remote landing sites. Proposed vehicles include electric vertical-takeoff-and-landing aircraft, hybrid-powered short-haul planes, autonomous cargo drones, and improved versions of conventional helicopters. Developers expect distributed electric propulsion, lightweight batteries, automated flight controls, and digital traffic-management systems to reduce operating costs and noise. Early services are more likely to carry packages, medical supplies, or airport passengers than to replace ordinary urban travel. Most plans assume that aircraft will be operated by licensed companies from vertiports rather than privately owned by individual commuters. The concept overlaps with urban air mobility but also includes regional routes and specialized missions outside cities. Its adoption depends on certification, charging infrastructure, public acceptance, pilot training, and the ability to integrate large numbers of aircraft into existing airspace.

Kooringal was a former railway station on the branch line serving the Riverina town of Kooringal, New South Wales. It opened in 1912 when the line was extended from the main southern route to reach grain silos and a small agricultural settlement. The station had a timber platform, a goods siding, a water tank, and a loop used by mixed passenger and freight trains. Regular passenger service declined after buses began connecting the town with Wagga Wagga, and the final scheduled train ran in 1974. The station was formally closed several years later, although grain trains continued to use the siding during harvest seasons. The platform and the brick foundations of the signal hut remain beside the road, while the former goods yard has been converted into a storage depot. A short section of the branch is occasionally used for heritage excursions and track-maintenance vehicles.

The Springfield Union Station is a historic railway building in Springfield, Illinois. Designed in a Richardsonian Romanesque style by architect William H. Crane, it opened in 1898 as a principal stop on the Illinois Central system. The station served intercity trains and several branch routes, making its waiting room a meeting point for passengers traveling through central Illinois. Declining rail traffic and deferred maintenance led to its closure in the 1970s, after which the building was placed on the state register of historic properties. A restoration campaign repaired the masonry, roof, and interior woodwork and adapted the former baggage rooms for offices and community events. Passenger trains now use a modern platform constructed behind the old building, with a covered footbridge and accessible boarding area. The original station houses a café, a small railroad museum, and the offices of a local preservation organization.

The Invention of the Global West is a study of political thought, economic history, and international development by the Algerian-French historian Nadia Rahmani. The book argues that “the West” should be understood not only as a geographic region but also as a historical story used to organize power. Rahmani traces how ideas about civilization, progress, free trade, and modernity were assembled during European imperial expansion and later presented as universal standards. She distinguishes between the material advantages created by industrialization and the moral claims used to justify unequal relationships with other societies. Several chapters examine the language of development agencies, human-rights institutions, and school textbooks. Critics praised the book for connecting economic history with cultural assumptions, while others argued that it treated internal divisions within Europe too briefly. Rahmani concludes that recognizing the West as one historical formation among many does not require rejecting its intellectual traditions, but does require examining the interests those traditions have served.

Robert Ellis Monroe was an American rower who competed in the eights and coxed fours. He won an Olympic silver medal in 1968 and a gold medal at the 1971 Pan American Games, and he was part of two national championship crews during the same period. Monroe was born in Portland, Oregon, and grew up near the Columbia River, where he began rowing in high school. He attended the University of Washington before transferring to a Philadelphia college, graduating with a degree in civil engineering. Monroe trained with a historic boat club during the summers and represented the United States at several international regattas. After leaving elite competition, he coached at a New England university and later worked as a structural engineer in Sacramento. One of his championship medals disappeared during a house move in the 1980s and was returned years later after being recognized at an estate sale.

Japanese rubber-ball baseball is a form of baseball played with a resilient rubber ball rather than the stitched leather ball used in the standard game. It is known in Japan by several names, including nanshiki yakyū, and is especially common in school, company, and recreational leagues. Some versions use a hollow ball that deforms on impact, while others use a denser semi-hard ball with a rubber covering. The diamond, innings, and basic scoring conventions generally follow ordinary baseball, but the altered ball changes pitching, fielding, and batting technique. Players may use lighter bats and somewhat different gloves, and defensive throws tend to travel more slowly or unpredictably after bouncing. Because the ball is less costly and safer for informal play, the game has been used as an entry point for children and adults who do not belong to formal baseball clubs.

Frederick Augustus Pickering was a colonial administrator who served as president of the Turks and Caicos Islands from 1881 to 1886. He had previously worked as a clerk in the territorial government and was regarded as one of the most prominent local officials of his generation. Pickering’s appointment came during a period of economic decline, when salt exports were weakening and the colonial administration was under pressure to reduce its expenses. He served alongside several elected members of the local council and supported measures intended to preserve the territory’s limited legislative authority. After his term ended, the office of president was left vacant and executive functions were increasingly directed from the larger regional administration. The council was later reorganized under a new constitutional arrangement, with the islands represented indirectly through a wider federation. Pickering remained active in local affairs but held no further senior office.

Amelia Hart is a Canadian politician who has led the Green Party of Nova Scotia since 2012. She represents the district of Halifax Harbour in the provincial legislature, having won the seat in a closely contested election that made her the party’s first elected member. Before entering politics, Hart operated a cooperative grocery business and worked as an adviser on fisheries, food security, and renewable energy. She joined the Greens after campaigning against the closure of a coastal processing plant and became deputy leader before succeeding the party’s founding leader. Hart’s legislative work has focused on public transit, climate adaptation, and support for small farms. In her first campaign she received less than one-third of the vote but prevailed after the major parties divided the urban electorate. She has since retained the district and expanded the party’s presence in municipal and provincial races.

Martin Edward Vale was an English professional footballer who played as a centre forward in the Fourth Division for Port Vale. Born in Coventry, he represented his school at both football and athletics before joining the club’s youth program. Vale made his senior debut in April 1974 as a substitute against Rochdale and scored the winning goal with a late header. It remained his only appearance for the first team. He signed a professional contract that summer but was released after an injury-plagued season and moved into non-league football with Nuneaton Borough and Tamworth. Vale later became a youth coach, directing the academy at a Midlands club for more than a decade. He also worked with local schools to organize girls’ and boys’ development programs and continued to play occasional veterans’ matches after retiring from coaching.

Pine Bluff is a city in Angelina County, Texas, and serves as the county’s administrative center. It lies in the pine forests of East Texas, roughly midway between Houston and the Louisiana border. The settlement began as a railway siding in the 1880s and was incorporated after the arrival of the Angelina and Gulf Railroad. Timber harvesting and sawmills drove its early growth, while later industries included paper production, machinery, and food processing. The city expanded rapidly during the twentieth century as roads replaced railways for regional travel. After the decline of the timber boom, local leaders promoted museums, a public library, and a community college to diversify the economy. Pine Bluff is surrounded by lakes and wooded recreation areas, and its downtown contains several commercial buildings from the period when lumber companies dominated the local economy.

Ravi Menon, known professionally as Ravi, was a Malayalam film director whose only completed feature was The River Carpenter. The film, released in 1994, received favorable reviews for its restrained performances and its depiction of a traditional artisan confronting mechanized construction. Menon won a state award for best first-time director, while the film received a separate prize for popular cinema and was invited to compete at an international festival in Europe. He had initially approached novelist K. Narayanan about adapting a short story concerning a stonemason, but the project was abandoned when the rights could not be secured. Narayanan later agreed to write the screenplay for The River Carpenter after Menon presented a revised outline. Menon planned a second film about a family of boat builders, but illness prevented him from completing the script. His early death left the feature as the sole major work associated with his career.

Eodromaeus is a genus of small dinosaur from the Late Triassic of South America. It was a lightly built biped that probably fed on insects, small animals, and plant material. Fossils assigned to the genus were recovered from red beds in northwestern Argentina, where the surrounding sediments record seasonal floodplains and temporary ponds. The known skeletons include portions of the skull, vertebral column, forelimbs, and hind limbs, allowing paleontologists to compare its body plan with both early theropods and sauropodomorphs. Eodromaeus was less than two metres long and had a long tail, narrow hands, and slender legs suited to rapid movement. The animal lived alongside several other early dinosaurs, rhynchosaur-like reptiles, and small crocodile relatives. Because the fossils occur near the beginning of the dinosaur record, the genus has been used in discussions of how carnivorous and herbivorous lineages diverged.

The end-of-history illusion is the tendency for people to recognize substantial change in their past while treating their current preferences and personality as unusually settled. A person may remember changing friends, values, habits, or ambitions over the previous decade and still expect the next decade to bring only minor adjustments. Researchers have observed the pattern among adolescents, young adults, and older people, suggesting that it is not limited to a particular stage of life. It may arise because the present self feels more coherent than earlier versions and because imagining an unfamiliar future is difficult. The effect can influence decisions about careers, relationships, spending, and long-term commitments. People often choose as if today’s interests will remain stable, even though their own history provides evidence to the contrary. Studies have also found that asking participants to describe possible future changes can reduce the confidence of these predictions.

Rutherford Court is a small residential enclave in the Midtown section of Manhattan, consisting of a paved courtyard and four surrounding buildings. The complex was assembled in the 1930s when architect Helen Rutherford combined several nineteenth-century service structures behind a new entrance on East 52nd Street. A narrow passage leads from the street into the court, which contains trees, benches, and a tiled fountain. The ground floors originally held workshops and small shops, while the upper levels were divided into apartments and studios. Later owners restored the façades and converted most of the commercial space to offices used by cultural organizations. A Spanish-language institute acquired the property in the early twenty-first century and added a small auditorium, library, and gallery below the courtyard. The rear buildings were reconstructed in a simplified version of their original style after a fire, while the entrance and central garden remain largely unchanged.

Southern Herald Media was an American newspaper company that owned regional papers in the Southeast and lower Midwest. It was formed in 2011 when a group of investors purchased the Morning Herald of Savannah from the family that had operated it for nearly a century. The new company soon acquired a chain of daily and weekly papers from a larger publishing group, adding titles in Georgia, Alabama, and Tennessee. It later bought several community newspapers in Florida and a metropolitan daily in Kentucky. Southern Herald invested in digital subscription systems and consolidated printing at two regional plants, while allowing local newsrooms to retain separate editorial staffs. A private-equity firm announced an acquisition of the company in 2016, and the papers were subsequently divided among several holding groups. Some titles were later closed or merged with online editions as advertising revenue declined. The company’s brief expansion was part of a wider period of consolidation in American local journalism.

Elena Marovic is a chemist whose research focuses on nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. She developed a covariance-based method for comparing multidimensional NMR spectra, allowing selected features to be extracted from experiments that would otherwise require lengthy acquisition times. The technique has been applied to protein samples, solid materials, and mixtures used in metabolomics. Marovic received an international award for methodological innovation and has collaborated with researchers in structural biology and magnetic-resonance instrumentation. She is a professor of chemistry at a large public university in the United States and directs a campus facility that provides high-field NMR services to academic and industrial laboratories. Before moving to her present institution, she held appointments at a private university and a national laboratory. Her group also studies the motions of proteins and the use of NMR signals to identify small molecules in biological samples.

The Audio Loop Converter was a companion utility distributed with several Apple music-production applications in the late 2000s. It converted ordinary AIFF and WAV recordings into tagged loop files that could follow the tempo and key of a project in GarageBand or Logic. Users could assign an author, instrument, genre, and descriptive comments, then search for the resulting loops through the host application’s browser. Early versions were released with Logic packages and later made available as a separate download from Apple’s developer site. Version 2.0 added batch conversion and improved compatibility with Intel-based Macintosh computers, while a final maintenance release corrected problems with metadata saved in projects created on newer operating systems. The utility was eventually discontinued as its functions were incorporated into Apple’s main audio applications. Older loop files remain usable in some versions of GarageBand and Logic, although the standalone program is no longer supported.

Leonard “Lefty” Marston was an American professional baseball outfielder who spent most of his career in the minor leagues. In 1931 he hit 54 home runs for the El Paso Texans of the Class C Arizona State League, earning a late-season trial with the Philadelphia Phillies. Marston appeared in nine major-league games, collected two hits in 18 at-bats, and returned to the minors after the club decided that his throwing accuracy was insufficient for regular outfield work. He batted left-handed and threw right-handed and was known for an unusually powerful swing. During a 15-year minor-league career he won four batting titles and led his league in runs twice. Marston was born in Arkansas and worked as a railroad clerk before turning professional.
