He later managed a small-town club, taught hitting at a winter camp, and remained a popular figure in the Texas and Oklahoma circuits.

The Newlywed Game is an American television game show in which married couples answer questions about one another. Created by Bob Eubanks and produced by a company associated with Chuck Barris, the program first aired in the late 1960s. One spouse was separated from the other contestants while the host asked questions about habits, memories, and domestic disagreements; the answers were then compared for matching responses. The original network run ended after several years, but the format returned in syndicated versions during the 1970s, 1980s, and 1990s. Different hosts introduced variations in scoring and prize structure, while the central game remained largely unchanged. A later cable revival added newly married couples and occasional anniversary episodes featuring earlier contestants. The show became known for revealing affectionate or embarrassing differences between spouses and for the host’s repeated use of the phrase “how well do you know your mate?”

The Mekong Gateway Airport was a proposed international airport in southern Laos intended to supplement the existing facilities at Vientiane. Planning began in 2003, but land acquisition and financing delays repeatedly postponed construction. The proposed site covered a large tract of former agricultural land east of the capital and was designed to handle domestic flights, regional passenger services, and air cargo. A consortium led by a Japanese airport operator was selected to prepare the terminal, runway, and access roads under a long-term build-operate agreement. Initial plans called for capacity of eight million passengers per year, with later phases intended to double that figure. Negotiations broke down after the government and consortium disagreed about passenger forecasts, ownership of the surrounding commercial zone, and the length of the concession. The original contract was cancelled, and a new feasibility study reopened the project to competing investors.

Keisuke Matsuda is a Japanese politician and member of the House of Representatives. Born in Hakodate, he represents Hokkaido through a proportional-representation block and is affiliated with a center-left opposition party. Matsuda first sought national office in 2005 as a candidate in a Saitama constituency, but lost to the incumbent. He entered the Diet the following year when a party colleague resigned a proportional seat to contest a local by-election. Matsuda was defeated at the next general election and spent several years working as a policy adviser before returning to parliament in 2010. During an opposition administration he served as parliamentary secretary in the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry and later advised the prime minister on regional development. His committee work has focused on ports, energy policy, and the economic needs of northern municipalities. He has retained his proportional seat through several changes in party leadership.

Paul Brown (1908–1991) was an American football coach and administrator known for introducing systematic preparation and several innovations in the organization of the sport. He coached at Massillon Washington High School, Ohio State University, and the Cleveland Browns, where he helped establish a professional team that bore his name. Brown emphasized written playbooks, filmed opponent analysis, timed practices, and clearly defined assignments for every player. His teams won multiple championships in the All-America Football Conference and National Football League, and many of his former assistants later became head coaches. Brown also supported the use of facemasks, specialized position coaching, and regular testing of players’ knowledge of formations. After leaving Cleveland, he founded the Cincinnati Bengals and served as their first head coach. He was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1967 and remained involved in team management until late in his career.

Daniel “Danny” Rusk was an American college football quarterback who played for Prairie State College in Illinois. He had been an all-state athlete at a high school near Peoria, where he also competed in baseball and wrestling. Rusk began college at a small Nebraska institution whose football program lasted only a few seasons before the school closed for financial reasons. As the team’s starting quarterback in its final year, he directed an option offense to a 7–2 record and a victory over a larger state university. The team was invited to a regional bowl, but the school could not afford to accept the place and another club took its invitation. Rusk transferred to Prairie State the following autumn and became a team captain. His former coach described him as a precise passer and an unusually calm leader in the huddle. After graduation he worked in insurance and coached high-school football.

The Workers’ Tent was a Swedish musical-theatre production that toured the country during the summer of 1982. Staged inside a large traveling tent, it combined actors, folk musicians, community choirs, and performers associated with the progressive music movement. The production traced the history of Swedish labor organizations from the late nineteenth century through the contemporary political debates of the early 1980s. Historical figures appeared alongside fictional workers, factory owners, and organizers, while a narrator moved between scenes and addressed the audience directly. The project included anarchists, social democrats, communists, and independent theater groups, whose disagreements were incorporated into the performance rather than concealed. Each presentation lasted several hours and was followed by music and discussion. Most of the songs were newly written for the production, although traditional workers’ anthems were also used. The tour visited industrial towns, agricultural districts, and university cities before ending with a final performance in Stockholm.

Vincent D. Lacava was an American football coach and general manager who led the Hartford Giants during the 1927 season. The club had been assembled from players of the Hartford Blues, a professional team removed from the National Football League during a league-wide reduction in membership. Former owner George Mulligan organized the Giants as an independent semi-professional team and appointed Lacava to handle both coaching and contracts. Hartford finished the regular season with seven wins and one loss, but was defeated by New Britain in a state championship series. A later championship game was cancelled when the two organizations disputed gate receipts and player eligibility. The Giants continued to practice during the winter but lacked the money to schedule another full season. Most of the players returned to local clubs, and the organization dissolved soon afterward. Surviving scorecards provide the only complete record of Lacava’s coaching career.

A sky anchor is a balloon arrangement designed to keep a zero-pressure balloon at a more stable altitude. The lifting balloon contains helium or another buoyant gas, while a second, sealed superpressure balloon is attached below or beside it as a ballast element. In a passive configuration, the anchor maintains a fixed volume; an active configuration includes a valve or pump that allows its internal pressure to be adjusted. As sunlight warms the lifting gas during the day, the system rises and the anchor displaces less dense air. At night, the lifting balloon contracts and begins to descend, but the anchor enters denser air and supplies a greater upward force. This counteracting behavior can reduce the large daily altitude changes that occur in ordinary scientific balloons. Launching the tandem system is technically difficult, and the two balloons can interfere with one another in wind. Several flight tests have succeeded, but failures during inflation and separation remain common.

Robert Andrew “Bob” Long was an American football wide receiver who played in the National Football League during the 1960s and 1970s. He attended a high school outside Pittsburgh and later played college football at Wichita State, where he earned all-conference honors. The Green Bay Packers selected Long in the fourth round of the 1964 draft, and he spent the first part of his professional career as a reserve and special-teams player. He later became a regular receiver for the Washington Redskins. Long was a member of the Green Bay teams that won the NFL title in 1965 and the first two Super Bowls, although he was used primarily in supporting roles. After seven seasons he retired from professional football and returned to Kansas, where he worked in construction management. He was inducted into the Wichita State athletic hall of fame and later received recognition from a sports organization in western Pennsylvania.

The olm, or proteus, is a long-bodied aquatic salamander native to underground streams and lakes in the limestone caves of the Dinaric Alps. It spends its entire life in darkness, feeding, resting, and reproducing beneath the surface rather than returning to land as many amphibians do. The animal has pale skin, small eyes covered by tissue, and external feathery gills that remain functional in water with little light. It can survive long periods without food and uses smell, vibration, and electrical sensitivity to locate prey. Populations occur in Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the karst region near Trieste, while several colonies have been introduced elsewhere. Local traditions once described the salamanders as young dragons washed from caves after storms. Naturalists began recording the species systematically in the seventeenth century, but pollution and changes to underground water flow now threaten some of its habitat.

Cetrelia borealis is a foliose lichen in the family Parmeliaceae. It was described from the northern Ural Mountains after specimens were found on the bark of mature birch and fir trees. The species has since been reported from several cool, humid forests in Scandinavia and western Russia, generally at middle to high elevations. Its leafy thallus is grey-green and forms overlapping lobes that may spread several centimetres across the substrate. The upper surface is slightly glossy and bears pale pores, powdery soralia, and occasional raised pustules. The lower surface is dark near the center and more lightly colored toward the margins, with short rhizines anchoring it to the bark. Apothecia are uncommon in the collected material, and identification often depends on the chemistry of the lichen substances as well as its shape. The species grows slowly and is sensitive to prolonged exposure to polluted air.

The Sea Wanderer, Opus 41, is an orchestral and choral setting of a poem by the German writer Friedrich Schiller composed by the Austrian composer Emil Hartmann. Hartmann began sketching the work in 1874 while staying on the Baltic coast, but revised the final movement repeatedly before completing the score in 1878. His uncertainty concerned whether the poem’s bleak conclusion should be followed by a return of the opening theme or by silence. During the delay he completed a set of songs for mezzo-soprano and orchestra, which later supplied several ideas for the choral work. The premiere took place in Lübeck in March 1879 under the composer’s direction. The piece is performed less often than Hartmann’s symphonies but has been praised for its restrained orchestration and unusual treatment of the chorus. A typical performance lasts approximately twenty minutes.

Mary Tahoma was a Yakama woman who challenged the exclusion of Native children from a public school in central Washington. In 1919, Tahoma and several other families petitioned to enroll their children at a newly constructed school near their reservation, but the district directed them to a separate federal day school. The Indian school offered only a limited elementary curriculum, had fewer teachers, and lacked the laboratory and library facilities available at the public school. Tahoma’s family argued that the arrangement violated the state constitution and denied the children an equal education. The district claimed that a state law authorized separate instruction whenever a federally operated school stood nearby. After the families brought suit, a county judge ordered the district to admit the children, but the school board appealed and delayed implementation. The case became an important local example of Native resistance to unequal education.

In probability theory, a normal variance-mean mixture is obtained by allowing the mean and variance of a normal distribution to depend on a second, positive random variable. If the mixing variable is denoted by (V), a conditional observation can be written as (X mid V=v sim N(mu+ eta v,; vsigma^2)). The resulting distribution is generally more skewed or heavy-tailed than a single normal law, depending on the density chosen for (V). It can be interpreted as a population made up of many normal subpopulations whose locations and spreads vary together. The same construction describes the position of a Brownian particle observed at a random time, with the mixing variable supplying the elapsed time and the coefficient of the mean supplying drift. Several important families arise from this framework. When (V) follows a generalized inverse Gaussian distribution, the mixture produces the generalized hyperbolic class, which includes commonly used models for financial returns and other asymmetric data.

Slack is a workplace communication platform that provides direct messages, persistent group channels, file sharing, and integrations with other software. It developed from an internal messaging system used by a game company and was released as a separate product in 2013. Organizations can create public or private channels, search older conversations, and connect services such as calendars, code repositories, and cloud storage. The platform was initially marketed to technology companies but was later adopted by schools, nonprofits, newsrooms, and large corporations. A free plan limits message history and some administrative features, while paid plans add larger archives, identity management, and compliance tools. Slack introduced voice and video calling through its own interface and through integrations with other providers. The company expanded internationally before being acquired by Salesforce, after which the service was incorporated into a wider collection of business collaboration products.

David Michael Hargreaves was an English professional football midfielder who played in Britain and the United States. He began with Sheffield Wednesday and later represented Carlisle United and Bristol Rovers before joining an American Soccer League club in California. Hargreaves spent part of the 1977 season on loan to a North American Soccer League team and returned to England for winter training. He then moved into indoor football, appearing for the Baltimore Comets and the Cleveland Force before being traded to the New Jersey Rockets. The shorter indoor game suited his close control and passing, while he continued to play outdoor matches during the summer for clubs in the American Soccer League. Hargreaves finished his career with a second-division team in Ohio and later coached youth players in Pennsylvania. He was one of several British midfielders who moved between the emerging indoor and outdoor leagues during the period.

Donald S. White was an American basketball player and coach. He grew up in Indiana and led his high-school team to two state championships before enrolling at Purdue University. White played both basketball and baseball, and in his final basketball season he led the Western Conference in scoring while helping Purdue win the conference title. He was selected to several All-American teams and entered coaching after graduation. White served as head coach at Washington University in St. Louis, Connecticut, and Rutgers, where his teams won or shared seven regular-season conference championships. He favored disciplined half-court offense and frequently used a rotating defense that kept opponents from settling into a single matchup. White’s college coaching record was 301–332, and he remained involved in basketball after retirement as a regional tournament official. A university athletic hall later named an annual coaching award in his honor.

The St. Louis United were an amateur American soccer club founded in 1948 by German and Austrian immigrants. The team entered regional competition under a different name before adopting its present identity and winning the Missouri State Cup in 1954. It captured the National Challenge Cup in 1959 and again in 1965, defeating clubs from Philadelphia and New York in the final rounds. During the 1960s the organization absorbed two smaller teams whose players and supporters expanded its youth program. United also reached the national final in 1962 but lost after a replay. The club’s strongest period ended when many players moved into professional leagues and local factories that had sponsored the team closed. It later merged with a Scandinavian cultural association and briefly competed under a combined name. The surviving organization now operates youth teams and an adult amateur side using the St. Louis United name.

The Capital Services Relocation Act was a German federal statute governing the division of government institutions between Berlin and Bonn after reunification. It followed the parliamentary decision to make Berlin the seat of the Bundestag and the principal center of federal government while preserving Bonn as a major political and administrative location. The act specified which ministries would move, which agencies would remain in Bonn, and how federal property and employment would be managed during the transition. It also promised investment in Bonn’s scientific, international, and communications infrastructure and formally recognized the city as the Federal City. Some departments were divided between the two locations rather than transferred entirely, creating a long-term system of dual offices and regular travel between them. The legislation was adopted in the mid-1990s and served as the administrative framework for the government move that followed over the next decade.

The Chelmsford built-up area is an urban settlement in Essex, England, consisting of Chelmsford and adjoining suburbs. Statistical authorities define it by the continuity of developed land rather than by municipal boundaries, so the area includes some neighborhoods governed by neighboring parishes and excludes nearby villages separated by open fields. Its principal subdivisions are Chelmsford, Great Baddow, and Springfield. The settlement lies at the meeting of the Chelmer and Can rivers and grew rapidly after the arrival of the railway and the expansion of London commuter services. Census data record a population of more than 110,000, with a majority identifying as White British or other White ethnic groups and sizeable Asian and mixed-heritage communities. Christianity remains the largest reported religion, although a substantial minority identifies as non-religious. The built-up area forms only part of the wider City of Chelmsford local-government district.

The Adventures of Tintin universe is a fictional setting shared by the comic albums created by Belgian artist Hergé. Its central character is the young reporter Tintin, who travels with Captain Haddock, Professor Calculus, Thomson and Thompson, and the dog Snowy. Many stories begin in Brussels but move through invented countries, real cities, and imagined versions of historical events. The setting includes the port of Moulinsart, the moon rocket program, and recurring criminal organizations, although the continuity changes slightly between albums. The comics are the primary source of the universe, but the characters have also appeared in animated television series, radio plays, feature films, stage productions, and video games. Different translators and adaptations have altered names and dialogue while retaining the basic relationships among the characters. The series’ fictional geography allows adventure stories to combine travel, espionage, science fiction, and comedy.

Nino Kapanadze is a Georgian politician and former member of the parliament of Georgia. Born in Batumi, she studied law at Tbilisi State University and later earned degrees in European studies at universities in Germany. Kapanadze entered the regional legislature of Adjara in the late 1990s and became associated with a political movement led by the territory’s then-dominant local leader. She was elected to the national parliament on a party list in 2003, but the result was annulled after the government changed during the Rose Revolution. Kapanadze therefore never took her seat. She later represented Georgia in a Council of Europe working group and served as a visiting scholar at an American university. After moving to the United States, she worked on programs concerning democratic institutions and regional security. Her political career ended before she could return to elected office, although she continued to publish commentary on Georgian constitutional reform.

The Riverside Arts Centre is a performance and conference complex in Croydon, London. It opened in 1968 with a main theatre, a concert hall, exhibition rooms, and meeting spaces designed to serve both professional companies and local organizations. The concert hall has hosted orchestras, touring musicians, comedy performances, and recordings for radio and television. Community groups use the smaller rooms for amateur drama, dance classes, school concerts, and religious gatherings. The center closed for a major redevelopment in 2017, during which the seating, backstage facilities, and public circulation areas were rebuilt. It reopened two years later with a new studio theatre and offices for a resident touring company. A cinema screen was added to the concert hall as part of the renovation, allowing the venue to show films as well as live events. The complex remains one of the principal cultural spaces in the borough.

Henri Vever was a French jeweler, collector, and writer on Japanese art. He inherited and expanded the family jewelry business, which became known for Art Nouveau ornaments and finely worked enamel. Outside the workshop, Vever collected prints, illustrated books, paintings, and historical documents from Europe and East Asia. He began purchasing Japanese ukiyo-e during the 1880s, when dealers in Paris were making large quantities of prints available to European collectors. Vever belonged to a circle of artists and scholars who met to discuss Japanese publishing and image-making, and he frequently lent pieces to exhibitions. His collection eventually numbered many thousands of prints, including works by major artists as well as rare publisher’s editions. European researchers used his holdings when preparing early histories of Japanese printmaking, and he contributed essays and illustrations to several of those studies. Parts of the collection were sold after his death, while other groups entered museums and university libraries.

Alicia Morgan is an American hurdler and bobsled athlete who competed in the 60-metre and 100-metre hurdles. At Louisiana State University she won two national collegiate titles and earned numerous All-American selections. Morgan took national indoor championships in three consecutive seasons and won a gold medal at a world indoor meet in 2011. She narrowly missed the Olympic final after clipping the second-to-last hurdle in a qualifying race, but later defeated the season’s leading hurdler at an international grand prix. Morgan also joined the United States bobsled program as a brakewoman and won a world championship medal with pilot Kara Humphries. Her best indoor time of 7.73 seconds stood as the American record for several seasons. After retiring from regular competition, she worked with youth athletes and appeared as a commentator during national track championships.

An Iron-distance triathlon is a long-course race made up of an open-water swim, a bicycle ride, and a marathon-length run completed in that order. The format is associated with the Ironman brand and is widely regarded as one of the most demanding single-day endurance events. Organizers commonly allow between 16 and 17 hours for the full course, although the limit depends on the venue and weather conditions. Athletes must reach the end of the swim within a little more than two hours and usually face a separate cutoff for completing the bike leg and the second transition. Some races impose intermediate deadlines at aid stations, mountain passes, or road closures. A competitor who finishes before every required deadline receives an official result, while anyone arriving after a cutoff is removed from the course even if the remaining distance is short. The races generally begin early in the morning so that roads can reopen by evening.

Barantola rubrifascia is a moth in the family Depressariidae recorded from northeastern Queensland and the lowland forests of New Guinea. Its wingspan is about 16 mm. The forewings are charcoal-grey with a narrow crimson streak along the basal portion of the costa and a pale ochre line beneath it. A broad yellowish band crosses the middle of the wing, interrupted by dark scales near the cell and bordered with reddish brown toward the rear. Near the outer third, a silver-white mark begins below the costa and bends toward the apex before continuing as a broken line along the termen. The tips of the forewings are sharply pointed. The hindwings are nearly white, with a faint grey wash along the veins and fringe. The species is known from a small number of specimens collected in wet forest, and its larval food plant has not been identified.

Madison is a city in northern Alabama that extends across Madison and Limestone counties. It forms part of the Huntsville metropolitan area and lies between the Tennessee River and the communities surrounding Redstone Arsenal. For much of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries it was a small settlement centered on a railway stop and farms. The expansion of the arsenal, NASA facilities, and nearby research parks brought new residents and industries after the Second World War. Suburban neighborhoods now surround the older downtown, and many residents commute to engineering, defense, and aerospace employers. Madison is among Alabama’s fastest-growing municipalities and has attracted a large number of technology and professional-service firms. The city maintains parks, schools, and a public library system while preserving several houses associated with the former farming community. Its population has increased sharply since the late twentieth century.

The Fagaloa River is a major stream on Upolu in Samoa. It flows from the island’s central volcanic highlands toward the eastern coast and passes through forest, plantations, and several villages before reaching Fagaloa Bay. The river has an upper branch rising near a crater ridge and two smaller tributaries that join it below the mountain settlements. A coastal road follows part of the eastern valley and crosses the lower river on a concrete bridge. Water from the catchment supplies village systems and is also used for a small hydroelectric installation that operates during periods of heavy rainfall. The surrounding slopes contain waterfalls, gardens, and remnants of older footpaths linking the interior with the coast. Flooding can damage roads after tropical storms, but the river remains an important source of fresh water and a landmark in the cultural geography of eastern Upolu.

Old Serowe is an archaeological and heritage area in Botswana near the modern town of Serowe. The two places are treated separately by local residents: the present town is a large contemporary settlement, while Old Serowe preserves traces of an earlier capital and surrounding villages. The site contains stone foundations, pottery, grinding stones, rock shelters, and paintings from several periods of human occupation. It became especially important after the Bangwato established a major settlement there during the nineteenth century under Kgosi Khama III. The community later moved to a new location as wells and springs became unreliable, leaving behind the remains of compounds, meeting places, and defensive walls. Visitors are drawn to a perennial spring, seasonal cascades, and the scattered foundations of round houses. Archaeological work has also identified tools and artifacts associated with earlier Stone Age activity in the surrounding hills.

Harlan Fiske Stone (1872–1946) was an American lawyer, jurist, and statesman who served as the 12th chief justice of the United States. A Republican, he had previously been dean of Columbia Law School, attorney general of the United States, and an associate justice of the Supreme Court. Stone was born in New Hampshire and studied at Amherst College before earning his law degree at Columbia. He practiced in New York and became known for his support of administrative regulation and professional legal education. President Calvin Coolidge appointed him attorney general, and President Herbert Hoover later placed him on the Supreme Court. As chief justice, Stone presided during the Second World War and participated in cases concerning civil liberties, federal power, and the rights of wartime defendants. His opinions often emphasized the importance of judicial review while recognizing the practical authority of elected institutions.

Susan L. Beck is an American geophysicist whose research concerns earthquakes, crustal deformation, and the tectonic history of mountain belts. She studied geology at a western state university, completed a master’s degree in structural geology, and earned a doctorate in seismology from a Michigan institution. After postdoctoral work at a national laboratory, Beck joined the faculty of the University of Arizona, where she later served as chair of the geosciences department. Her field projects have examined active faults in the Andes, the Rocky Mountains, and the western margin of North America. Beck has also used regional earthquake networks to study how the crust thickens beneath rising ranges. She is a fellow of major geophysical and geological societies and has chaired an international consortium that coordinates university seismology research. Her honors include a medal recognizing contributions to the study of the crust and lithosphere.

The Nordic Literature Library is a public research library established by a national academy to support committees that evaluate literary prizes and other cultural awards. It occupies rooms in a historic exchange building in the old center of Stockholm and maintains a collection of novels, poetry, criticism, and literary journals in dozens of languages. The library was founded at the beginning of the twentieth century, when the academy began acquiring foreign-language works for its reading committees. Its holdings now include more than 150,000 volumes, along with manuscripts, translators’ correspondence, and reference materials on world literature. Although much of the collection serves scholars and prize juries, members of the public may request books for use in the reading rooms. The institution also lends selected materials to libraries in neighboring countries and offers lectures, exhibitions, guided visits, and seminars on literary history.

The Tay Bridge is a railway bridge crossing the Firth of Tay in eastern Scotland. The present bridge was completed in 1887 after an earlier structure collapsed during a storm, and it carries the railway between Dundee and the northern shore. Engineers used a series of steel lattice spans supported by masonry piers, producing a long, low profile across the estuary. Construction required extensive work in deep water and was carried out in stages as foundations were strengthened against tides and shifting sediment. The bridge became an important link for trains traveling between Edinburgh, Perth, and Aberdeen and remains one of the most recognizable structures on the east coast. Its length and exposed setting have made maintenance a continuing concern, especially during high winds. A parallel road bridge and later transport improvements changed the surrounding landscape, but the railway crossing continues to carry passenger services.

Shinui was an Israeli political movement that combined secularism, economic liberalism, and opposition to the political influence of religious parties. It emerged from an earlier civil-rights organization and entered the Knesset in several different electoral alliances. At its strongest, the party became one of the largest opposition groups and campaigned for civil marriage, public transportation on the Sabbath, and changes to the system of religious jurisdiction. Internal disputes over economic policy, coalition participation, and the balance between social liberalism and free-market reform repeatedly produced defections. A later surge in support gave Shinui a substantial parliamentary bloc, but most of its members left to create new factions after disagreements with the leadership. The formation of a centrist rival party removed much of its remaining constituency, and the movement failed to cross the electoral threshold in the next election. Several successor groups continued to use parts of its platform without restoring its former national influence.

Barton is a suburb in the metropolitan borough of Salford, Greater Manchester, England. It lies on level ground beside the Manchester Ship Canal and forms a continuous urban area with neighboring districts to the west and south. The main road connects the suburb with Eccles and the industrial estates around Trafford, while a railway station provides service toward Manchester and Liverpool. Before the nineteenth century, the area consisted largely of farms, mossland, and scattered hamlets. Drainage projects reclaimed peat ground and made possible the construction of new roads, factories, and canals. The opening of the ship canal transformed Barton into an inland port and encouraged the development of warehouses and worker housing. A local urban district council administered the area for much of the twentieth century before municipal reorganization incorporated it into the City of Salford. Modern Barton combines older terraces with later estates and commercial parks.

A fineness-of-grind gauge is a metal instrument used to determine whether pigment, powder, or another solid has been dispersed into a liquid without leaving oversized particles or agglomerates. The device consists of a polished block containing one or more channels whose depth decreases gradually from one end to the other. A small amount of the test material is drawn along the channel with a straight scraper. The point at which particles or streaks become visible is compared with graduations marked on the block, commonly expressed in micrometres or Hegman units. Paint manufacturers use the result to monitor milling, color strength, surface smoothness, and the stability of a finished coating. The gauge must be cleaned carefully between tests, since residue can alter the reading. It is useful for quality control but does not replace microscopic examination when the shape or chemistry of individual particles matters.

The Fukuoka International Marathon was a men’s road race held in Fukuoka, Japan. Founded in the late 1940s, it became one of the country’s principal marathon competitions and attracted leading runners from Japan, Europe, Africa, and the United States. The course traditionally began and ended at a municipal stadium and passed through streets along the Hakata Bay area. For many years the race served as a trial or championship event for Japanese teams preparing for the Olympic Games and world championships. Its fast route produced several national records and encouraged organizers to invite large fields of elite athletes. The competition was sponsored by a national newspaper and broadcast throughout Japan. Rising operating costs, changing selection procedures, and the growth of other international races eventually reduced its role. The final edition was held in the early 2020s after more than seven decades of annual competition.

Phantom Investigators was a short-lived animated television series about four middle-school students who solved supernatural mysteries in their town. The thirteen episodes were broadcast during a Saturday-morning programming block in 2004. The series combined cutout animation for the children, stop-motion sets for houses and streets, and live-action footage for ghosts and other apparitions. Each protagonist had a different unusual ability, such as sensing hidden rooms or hearing memories attached to objects. Cases ranged from a haunted amusement park to a missing school portrait, and most episodes paired the central mystery with a personal problem involving friendship, family, or school. The program was created by a puppeteer and experimental filmmaker who had previously worked on short-form television comedy. Its unusual mixture of techniques drew attention from animation critics, but the series was cancelled before a second season could be produced.

Circuit Breaker is an extended play by the English electronic duo Neon Method, released in 1997. It reached the lower half of the United Kingdom singles and albums charts and remained there for two weeks. The title track combines distorted synthesizer patterns with a heavy breakbeat and became an early example of the sound the duo developed on later records. A vocal sample in “Get Loose” was taken from a late-night radio broadcast recorded in the 1980s, while the phrase repeated in “Pressure Line” came from the same program. The EP’s opening track was licensed for a futuristic racing game and appeared on its soundtrack. It was later reissued on a retrospective compilation and used as a B-side in Japan. Because the final track flows directly into the following song, compilations have treated its ending differently: some fade the piece early, while others preserve the abrupt stop and record-noise effect of the original release.

“The Perfect Alibi” is the twelfth episode of the third season of the American television comedy series City Desk. It was written by Marissa Cole and Peter Lang and directed by executive producer Dana Ruiz. The episode first aired on a cable network in April 2012 and featured guest appearances by a television anchor, a former governor, and an actor playing the mayor of a fictional city. In the story, newspaper editor Nora Bell discovers a handwritten confession in the office coffee machine and assumes that it was left by her anonymous admirer. Meanwhile, the paper’s publisher learns that a rival company is planning to purchase the building and tries to stage a publicity stunt to make the newsroom appear indispensable. The staff photographer organizes a mock awards ceremony for a colleague who wants to win a prestigious journalism prize. The three plots converge when the confession is revealed to be part of a marketing campaign for a new legal drama.

“Afterglow” is a song recorded by South Korean singer Min-seo for her second extended play, also titled Afterglow. It was released as the record’s lead single in July 2017 by a Seoul-based entertainment company. The lyrics describe the desire to leave a difficult relationship without losing the memories associated with it. Producers combined electronic dance percussion, smooth R&B harmonies, and a light tropical-house rhythm, giving the song a brighter sound than the singer’s earlier piano ballads. Critics praised Min-seo’s controlled vocal delivery and the gradual expansion of the chorus. The single reached the top ten of South Korea’s digital chart and appeared on an international streaming chart devoted to Korean pop. Its music video followed the singer through an empty hotel, a night market, and a seaside road, using changing colors to represent the stages of separation. The song became her first major commercial success as a solo performer.

Torvald Tu was a Norwegian poet, playwright, novelist, and humorist who wrote primarily in Nynorsk. He was born in a farming district of Jæren and retained the rhythms of the local dialect in both his poetry and dialogue. Tu made his literary debut with a short play in 1916 and published his first collection of poems the following year. His most successful stage work was the musical comedy The Wedding at Håland, which opened at Det Norske Teatret in Oslo during the 1920s. The production toured two Norwegian regions at the same time and became a favorite of amateur companies. Tu collaborated with several composers and wrote additional comedies for theaters in Bergen and Trondheim. One of his plays ran for more than a hundred performances during a single season. His works remained popular in Nynorsk drama clubs because they combined rural settings, broad humor, and sympathy for characters negotiating marriage, work, and social expectation.

The word-frequency effect is the finding that readers and listeners usually identify familiar words more quickly than rare words. Frequency can be estimated from speech, books, or a particular person’s experience with a language, so the same word may not have the same status for every participant. Experiments have observed the effect in alphabetic writing and at the level of individual characters in languages such as Chinese. Researchers also distinguish lexical frequency from the frequency of a spelling pattern or sound sequence. Low-frequency words often show a larger improvement after a single repetition, whereas high-frequency words are already recognized rapidly and gain less from additional exposure. The effect has been used to study visual word recognition, memory, vocabulary development, and the interaction between spelling and meaning. It is generally measured by reaction time, accuracy, or the speed with which a reader names a displayed word.

Udea geminipuncta is a moth in the family Crambidae recorded from the Lesser Antilles. The wingspan is approximately 20 mm. The forewings are pale olive-brown and densely marked with darker scales, especially along the costa and outer margin. A faint wavy line crosses the wing before the middle, followed by a small pair of dark spots in the central cell and a larger kidney-shaped mark below them. The postmedial line bends inward near the fold and then curves outward again before becoming broken among the veins. A row of blackish terminal dots follows the edge. The hindwings are translucent white with a brown tint toward the apex and a small discoidal stigma. Their outer line is thin and interrupted, while the inner half is almost unmarked. The species has been collected in dry woodland and coastal scrub, but its caterpillar and preferred host plants are unknown.

Fahsa is a traditional Yemeni dish consisting of slow-cooked meat served in a thick, highly seasoned broth. The base is usually prepared from beef or lamb simmered until it can be pulled apart, then enriched with fenugreek foam known as hilbah. A green or red relish made from chilies, tomatoes, garlic, and herbs is added at the table or stirred into the stew. Some cooks include potatoes, beans, eggs, or shredded vegetables, although recipes vary between regions. Fahsa is commonly served hot in a stone or earthenware bowl and eaten with flatbread, which is used to scoop up the meat and sauce. It is especially associated with communal lunches and family gatherings. The dish shares ingredients and techniques with other northern Yemeni stews, but its distinctive texture comes from pounding the meat and mixing it with the thickened broth before serving.

Kafi is a form of Sufi devotional song associated with the Punjab, Sindh, and other parts of South Asia. It is built around short mystical poems, often attributed to poets such as Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, Bulleh Shah, or Khwaja Ghulam Farid, and may be performed by a solo singer with a small ensemble. The texts describe longing for the divine, the collapse of worldly distinctions, and the search for union with a beloved who is both human and spiritual. Kafi is heard at shrines, festivals, and private gatherings as well as on radio and recorded albums. Performers commonly use harmonium, dholak, hand clapping, and a repeated refrain that allows the audience to participate. During the late twentieth century, prominent singers brought the form to urban concert halls and international festivals. Regional pronunciation, melody, and instrumentation vary widely, and the same poem may be arranged as a quiet song or an energetic communal performance.

The Austral Inland Railway Authority was created by the governments of the Northern Territory and South Australia to oversee completion of the railway between Alice Springs and Darwin. Established in the late 1990s, it held infrastructure interests, negotiated access to the existing southern line, and supervised the lease of track and terminal facilities to a freight operator. A consortium of construction and transport companies received the contract under a build-own-operate-transfer arrangement, with the operating concession extending for several decades. Federal and state governments supplied a mixture of grants, subordinated loans, direct equity, and contingent financing for the project. The railway opened after construction across remote desert and tropical terrain, but the operating company later experienced financial difficulties and entered restructuring. Ownership of portions of the line and responsibility for maintenance were subsequently divided among public agencies and private contractors.

Occitanie is a region in southern France whose musical life combines traditions from the Mediterranean coast, the Pyrenees, and the inland valleys of the former Languedoc and Gascony. Toulouse and Montpellier host major orchestras, opera companies, conservatories, and summer festivals, while smaller towns organize outdoor concerts in June and July. Traditional music uses instruments such as the cabrette, hurdy-gurdy, violin, accordion, fifes, and regional bagpipes. Dance repertories include circular and line dances performed at village fêtes and cultural gatherings. Contemporary musicians have adapted these forms to jazz, rock, and electronic music without abandoning the older melodies. Regional institutions offer classes in Occitan song, instrumental performance, and dance, and touring ensembles regularly perform in Spain and Italy as well as throughout France. The mixture of languages and local customs has made Occitanie a center for both revivalist folk music and experimental interpretations of southern French traditions.

Cerconota rubrolineata is a moth in the family Depressariidae recorded from eastern Panama. The wingspan is about 21 mm. Its forewings are warm ochre at the base and become darker, almost chestnut brown, toward the outer margin. Three broken bands of violet-grey scales cross the wing at irregular angles. The first begins on the costa before the middle and bends toward the dorsum, while the second encloses a small dark mark at the end of the cell before descending toward the lower edge. The third is shorter and curves outward near the termen. The bands are faint in some specimens and separated by patches of shining orange-brown scales. A line of small grey spots follows the fringe, with a darker dot near the apex. The hindwings are dull ash-brown and slightly paler toward the base. Adults have been collected in humid lowland forest, but their larval biology remains unknown.

Peter Pianto was an Australian rules footballer who played for Geelong in the Victorian Football League and later represented Claremont in Western Australia. A rover recruited from a country club, he chose Geelong after receiving offers from several metropolitan teams. Pianto played 121 senior matches and kicked 144 goals during seven seasons with the Cats, helping the club win premierships in 1951 and 1952. He was known for quick movement around stoppages, accurate handball, and the ability to drift forward when matches tightened. In a semi-final against Collingwood he kicked five goals, the highest total of his career. Pianto won Geelong’s best-and-fairest award, represented Victoria, and was selected as an All-Australian. He later moved to Claremont, where he became a senior player and coach before returning to Victoria to lead Geelong. He finished near the top of the Brownlow Medal count on more than one occasion.

Kon Tum is a city in Vietnam’s Central Highlands and the capital of Kon Tum province. It lies near the meeting of the Đăk Bla River and several smaller streams, in a region historically inhabited by Bahnar, Jarai, and other highland communities. The modern city is now largely Kinh in population but retains distinctive village architecture, communal houses, and craft traditions associated with the older groups. National Route 14 connects Kon Tum with Pleiku to the south and Đăk Glei to the north, while a second highway leads east toward the coastal provinces. Coffee, rubber, cassava, and other crops are produced in the surrounding district. The city contains schools, a provincial hospital, markets, and a football stadium, and it is served by an airport outside the urban center. Its location makes it a commercial and administrative gateway between the highlands and the central coast.

Antonio Varas de la Barra was a Chilean lawyer, educator, and political leader of the nineteenth century. He began as a conservative parliamentarian and later helped establish the National Party, which supported administrative reform and a strong civil service. Varas held several ministerial posts, including portfolios concerned with the interior, justice, and education. He was born in Cauquenes to a family whose property had been confiscated after Chilean independence because of his father’s royalist sympathies. His older brother supported his education at the Instituto Nacional, where Varas became a teacher, vice-principal, and eventually rector. During his tenure he revised the curriculum, raised examination standards, and expanded instruction in science and modern languages. Varas remained closely associated with former students who entered public life and used the school as a base for broader educational reforms. He continued to serve in government until declining health limited his activities.

Marina Crescent is a luxury residential development on an artificial island in the Broadwater near the Gold Coast, Queensland. The project was built by a partnership between two Australian property companies and occupies roughly ten hectares of reclaimed mangrove and tidal flats. A bridge more than 300 metres long links the island to the mainland, while internal roads divide the site into a northern residential precinct and a southern area of salt marsh left largely undeveloped. The master plan was intended to give every apartment a view of open water. The developed section includes a marina, several apartment towers, a restaurant, and a group of detached houses facing the channel. The largest building rises more than ten storeys, and the marina provides berths for private boats and visiting yachts. Landscaping and dredging created additional beaches and canals, making the island recognizable from the air as a curved crescent.

Night Rooms is a two-hour public-radio program devoted to ambient, electronic, space, and experimental music. Hosted by broadcaster Maya Ellis, the program combines long-form artist interviews with quiet live performances recorded in studios, homes, and small concert spaces. Guests have included composers, sound artists, jazz musicians, and performers associated with new-age and contemporary classical music. The program has issued a series of compact-disc collections drawn from its sessions and later made the performances available through online archives. It is distributed by a public-radio exchange and heard on dozens of stations in the United States and Canada, with continuous streaming available through its website. Ellis created Night Rooms with producer David Kline in 1991 after the pair completed a documentary series about independent electronic music. Their earlier work received awards from broadcasting and arts organizations for its use of interviews, field recordings, and music history.

Teresa M. Lewis is an American former professional basketball player who competed in the Women’s National Basketball Association and in international tournaments. She was a member of the United States team that won an Olympic gold medal in the late 1980s and later became one of the early high selections in a professional women’s draft. Lewis played two seasons as a forward for the Sacramento Monarchs before finishing her career with the Los Angeles Sparks. She became known for her rebounding, physical defense, and work with youth basketball programs. Lewis’s son later played in the NBA, while her daughter was selected in a professional women’s draft, making the family one of the few in which a former Olympian had children drafted into both leagues. Her career was profiled in a documentary about the pioneers of women’s basketball, and she was inducted into a national women’s basketball hall of fame.

Arthur James Wellman was an English-born farmer and political representative in Saskatchewan. He immigrated to Canada in 1910 and settled on a homestead near the developing town of Rosetown. Wellman served on the board of a local wheat cooperative, represented farmers at provincial grain meetings, and helped organize rural credit and school services. He was elected to the Saskatchewan Legislative Assembly for a west-central riding in 1948 as a member of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation. During his time in the legislature he supported public ownership of utilities, agricultural marketing boards, and improvements to roads connecting isolated farms. Wellman also served on the council of a rural municipality and was active in the Methodist and later United churches. He became deputy speaker near the end of his career and retired from the assembly after three terms. He continued farming until his death.

Fleetwood Mac are a British-American rock band whose career has included more than a dozen studio albums, live recordings, compilations, and numerous singles. The group’s lineup changed repeatedly during its early blues period before settling into the combination of guitar rock, pop melody, and layered vocal harmonies associated with its best-known records. The album Rumours became an international bestseller, produced several major singles, and remains the band’s most commercially successful studio release. Fleetwood Mac also recorded Tusk, Mirage, Tango in the Night, and The Dance, while individual members pursued solo projects between tours. The band has placed multiple songs in the upper levels of the American and British charts and has sold many millions of albums worldwide. Its history is marked by strained personal relationships, changes in membership, long periods of inactivity, and repeated reunions for recording or concert tours.

The Brooklands was an English cyclecar manufactured for a short period in the early 1920s by the Northgate Motor Company in Birmingham. Designed by engineer Alfred Pritchard, it used a light wooden body attached to a tubular steel frame and carried its small air-cooled engine behind the passenger compartment. The two-cylinder motor produced roughly nine horsepower and drove the rear wheels through a three-speed gearbox and chain final drive. A movable rear axle allowed the driver to adjust chain tension, while a lever combined the functions of an exhaust release and starting mechanism. The car’s narrow body and low weight were intended to keep licensing and running costs below those of a conventional automobile. Braking operated on the rear wheels through external contracting bands. Production ended when the company failed to secure a reliable supply of engines, and only a few complete examples are known to have survived.

Brad Paisley is an American country music singer, songwriter, and guitarist who has released more than a dozen studio albums and numerous singles. He began recording in the late 1990s and built his early reputation through a mixture of traditional country guitar, humorous lyrics, and polished radio production. Several of his albums have received platinum certification, while songs such as “Mud on the Tires,” “Whiskey Lullaby,” and “Then” reached the upper positions of the country charts. Paisley has recorded duets with other country performers and has appeared as a guest on songs by artists from outside the genre. His singles have earned multiple number-one placements and awards from country-music organizations. In addition to recording, he has hosted televised award programs and served as a mentor to younger musicians. His guitar playing often incorporates bluegrass runs and references to older Nashville styles.

George Alfred Mercer was a Canadian farmer and politician in Nova Scotia. He represented the rural district of Cumberland East in the provincial House of Assembly during two nonconsecutive periods between the late 1970s and the 1990s. Mercer was born near Amherst and operated a mixed farm specializing in cattle and forage crops. Before entering provincial politics, he served on the county council and chaired a regional agricultural society. He first won his legislative seat by a narrow margin, lost it at the next election, and returned several years later after campaigning on roads, farm credit, and rural health services. Mercer was appointed minister of agriculture near the end of his career and remained in the cabinet after his party won a subsequent election. He retired from public life rather than seek another term and was later inducted into an Atlantic agricultural hall of fame.

Trademark stuffing is a form of search-engine manipulation in which a website repeatedly uses another company’s trademark or service name to attract users and ranking signals. The practice can involve hidden text, misleading page titles, copied product descriptions, or paid advertisements that imply an affiliation that does not exist. It differs from legitimate comparative advertising, news reporting, or the use of a mark to describe a genuine review or resale listing because the objective is to divert traffic rather than identify the subject of the page. A successful campaign may cause a search engine to display an unauthorized site when users look for the trademark owner. The practice can expose the operator to claims involving trademark infringement, unfair competition, or deceptive advertising, depending on the jurisdiction. Search engines may also remove pages, lower their ranking, or suspend advertising accounts when they detect the behavior.

Riverland Air was an Australian regional airline that operated scheduled and charter services until the early 2000s. It was founded in 1956 by brothers Thomas and Edward Riverland with a single Auster aircraft based on a farm outside Wagga Wagga. The company moved to a larger airport at Albury and began carrying passengers on regular routes to Canberra and Sydney during the 1970s. Its fleet later included Cessna twins, Piper Chieftains, Embraer Bandeirantes, Shorts 360s, and agricultural aircraft used for seasonal spraying. During the 1990s Riverland withdrew from several western New South Wales routes and sold its smaller piston aircraft to another regional carrier. A national airline acquired a controlling interest as part of a strategy to feed passengers into its major hubs. By the time Riverland ceased trading, it operated only turboprop aircraft, including Saab 340s and Metro airliners.

Trinity Chapel is a historic Episcopal church in the Rockaway section of Queens, New York. The small wooden Gothic Revival building was designed by architect Richard Upjohn and completed in 1860 on a brick foundation. It began as a mission chapel supported by a larger parish in nearby Nassau County and served a growing coastal community of summer residents and fishermen. When it became an independent parish, the congregation adopted the name St. John’s and added a vestry and parish hall. Membership declined during the twentieth century, and the church was later merged with another Episcopal congregation. The building was sold to a Pentecostal church, which retained the steep roof, timber belfry, and lancet windows while adapting the interior for new forms of worship. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places because of its age, architectural integrity, and association with the early development of the Rockaway peninsula.

Charles J. Hanlon was an Oregon legislator who won election as an independent after defeating a long-serving party leader. He represented a coastal district in the state senate for three terms before joining the Democratic caucus. Hanlon was known for refusing to follow the timber industry’s position on forest regulation and for supporting a proposal to permit self-service gasoline stations. He introduced a constitutional amendment that would have lengthened legislative terms while imposing a cumulative service limit, although the measure did not pass. Much of his reputation came from constituent work rather than from high-profile leadership. In one case he persuaded a state licensing board to provide an oral examination for a barber who could not read the written test. Hanlon continued to vote independently after joining the Democratic Party and retired from the senate at the end of his final term.

Central Valley Television is a regional infotainment network serving the Central Luzon region of the Philippines. Its studios and administrative offices are located in San Fernando, Pampanga, while a high-power transmitter operates from a tower in the Clark area. The station broadcasts local news, public-affairs programs, entertainment, agricultural reports, and educational features each day from morning until late evening. It is owned by a regional broadcasting company associated with a larger family business group and distributes some programs through cable and online video platforms. Central Valley Television has received awards from national broadcasters’ organizations and regional media festivals for its news coverage and community programming. Surveys have periodically ranked it as one of the most watched free-to-air stations outside Metro Manila. The network also produces election debates, disaster updates, and cultural programs about towns and provinces in the Central Luzon plain.

In computer programming, a union is a data type whose storage can represent one of several alternative members. Unlike a record or structure, which reserves separate space for each field, an ordinary union overlays its members in the same memory region. Writing one member therefore replaces the bytes previously used for another, and the program must keep track of which interpretation is currently valid. A union might allow a value to be treated as either a floating-point number or an integer, or as one of several pointer types. Some languages provide tagged unions, in which an additional discriminator records the active case and makes pattern matching safer. Low-level languages often expose untagged unions for compact layouts and communication with hardware or binary file formats. Their flexibility is useful, but reading a member that was not most recently written can produce implementation-dependent results.

“Bulan di Jendela” is a song written by Malaysian singer-songwriter Arif Nordin and recorded as a duet with vocalist Nadia Karim. The lyrics describe a woman who is cautious about beginning another relationship after an earlier betrayal. Her new partner acknowledges that he is not the first person she loved but promises to remain patient and loyal. The recording was made at two studios in Kuching and later included on Nordin’s 2018 album Jalan Pulang. It became the album’s second most successful single and received airplay on regional radio stations in Sarawak and Brunei. The pair performed the song at a state music awards ceremony, where it won a prize for best vocal collaboration and finished as runner-up in the song of the year category. Its arrangement combines acoustic guitar, restrained percussion, and a chorus supported by traditional string instruments.

Railway police are officers or specialized agents responsible for protecting rail infrastructure, employees, passengers, revenue, and freight. Their powers differ greatly between jurisdictions. Some railway police are sworn public officers with authority to investigate crimes, make arrests, and patrol areas beyond railway property, while others function primarily as security personnel employed by a transport company. In North America, large freight railroads commonly maintain their own police departments, and some passenger systems operate similar agencies. Elsewhere, national or regional police forces handle railway work as part of a general transportation command. The United Kingdom uses the British Transport Police to police railways, stations, and certain other transit systems. Typical duties include theft prevention, trespass enforcement, accident response, counterterrorism, and coordination with local police during major events.

Edward Gustav Trinkler was a German-born American metalworker whose decorative ironwork appeared in California houses, churches, and civic buildings. He immigrated to the United States after completing an apprenticeship and established a workshop in Los Angeles during the 1890s. Trinkler produced gates, balcony rails, grilles, lanterns, fireplace screens, and small household objects, often combining forged iron with bronze or hammered copper. Architect Julia Morgan employed him for an important commercial building and later recommended him for work on a large coastal estate. Between the 1920s and 1930s he supplied door fittings, window grilles, lighting fixtures, and ornamental gates for the project. One set of gates included small profiles of the craftsmen who worked there, with Trinkler’s own likeness placed among them. Other clients included oil executives, film directors, and the owners of prominent Los Angeles residences.

The Varzob River is a river in central Tajikistan that joins the Kofarnihon north of Dushanbe. Its headwaters lie in the Hissar Range, where snowfields and mountain springs feed a narrow upper valley. The river descends through a steep gorge before entering a broader corridor occupied by villages, orchards, and the main road toward the capital. Several tributaries bring water from side valleys, and seasonal floods can carry large quantities of rock and sediment downstream. The river is used for irrigation, drinking water, and small hydroelectric installations, while its upper reaches are popular for hiking and rafting. A road and power line follow much of the lower valley, but some high settlements remain accessible only by rough tracks. The surrounding mountains historically limited movement between communities and helped preserve local dialects and customs.

Anglesey Aluminium was a large aluminum smelter operated near Holyhead in North Wales. It was established as a joint venture between an international mining company and a North American metals producer and began production in the early 1970s. The plant employed hundreds of people and was one of the largest single users of electricity in Britain. Alumina and carbon materials arrived by ship at a private quay in Holyhead Harbour and traveled to the smelter through enclosed conveyors and service tunnels. A rail spur connected the works with the North Wales Coast Line, allowing raw materials and finished aluminum to be moved without relying entirely on road transport. At full capacity the plant produced more than 100,000 tonnes a year. Rising power costs and changes in the aluminum market eventually made the operation uneconomic, and the smelter closed after several decades of production.

A personal seat license is a contract that gives its holder the right to purchase season tickets for a particular seat at a sports stadium. The license is separate from the tickets themselves and may be transferable, subject to the rules established by the team or venue operator. If the holder stops buying season tickets, the license may expire or return to the team, depending on the agreement. Prices vary according to seat location, and newly constructed arenas often sell licenses before opening to help finance building costs or repay loans. Supporters may value the arrangement because it guarantees a familiar view and location for every home game. Critics argue that it turns access to ordinary season tickets into an additional expense and can exclude fans who cannot afford the initial fee. A license generally lasts only while the team uses the specified stadium.

Jonathan Blow is an American independent game designer and programmer best known for the puzzle-platform game Braid. He studied computer science and worked in software development before becoming dissatisfied with the commercial game industry. Blow founded a small studio and developed Braid over several years, writing both its code and much of its design. The game was released in 2008 and became one of the earliest prominent titles distributed through a digital console marketplace. Its time-reversal mechanic and densely written visual style received widespread critical attention, while its development was discussed in essays and conference talks about independent games. Blow later founded a programming and game-development company and worked for many years on The Witness, a first-person puzzle game released in 2016. He has also spoken publicly about authorship, software tools, and the economic conditions faced by small game studios.

First Draft is the debut studio album by American rapper Marcus Reed. It was released independently in 2002 after recording sessions at a small Detroit studio shared by several local producers. Reed handled much of the writing and worked with the production team Northside Audio on the drum tracks, while guest vocals came from neighborhood rappers and a gospel singer. The album was issued in a limited run of compact discs and cassettes, which Reed sold at shows and through a local record shop. It was not initially available through online music stores, although the title song later appeared on a digital compilation. Critics gave the record mixed reviews, praising its detailed autobiographical verses while finding the production uneven. Fewer than 1,000 physical copies were pressed, and surviving copies became sought after after Reed signed to a national label several years later. A remastered version of the title track was released for the album’s anniversary.

Marianne Ellis was an American lawyer who became a senior partner at a national plaintiffs’ firm and helped establish its first office in Boston. Born in Brooklyn, she grew up in New Jersey and studied political science at the University of Michigan before earning a law degree from Georgetown. While still a student she worked for a federal legal-services program and represented tenants in housing disputes. Ellis joined a large corporate law firm after graduation but left after deciding to focus on consumer and employment cases. She later helped expand her new firm’s practice throughout New England and served on its committee for pro bono work. In interviews she described being one of only a few women in her law-school classes and recalled being asked by a professor to stand so the class could “see the future of the profession.” Ellis argued major wage and disability cases and mentored younger women entering trial practice.

Ikat is a textile technique in which threads are dyed in sections before they are woven, producing patterns that appear slightly blurred at their edges. Indonesian ikat traditions vary by island and may use resist-dyed warp threads, weft threads, or both. Artisans tie or wrap portions of the yarn to prevent dye from reaching them, repeat the process with additional colors, and then arrange the threads on a hand loom. Motifs can represent plants, animals, ancestors, geometric forms, or scenes connected with local ceremonies. The materials, color combinations, and complexity of the design differ according to regional customs, available dyes, and the intended use of the cloth. Some ikat garments are reserved for weddings, funerals, or exchanges between families, while others are made for everyday wear and contemporary fashion. Indonesian weaving cooperatives and museums have worked to preserve the knowledge as mass-produced imitations become more common.

Baba Dioum was a Senegalese forestry engineer and advocate for sustainable land management. He became widely known after presenting a conservation paper to an international environmental organization in the late 1960s, where he argued that successful protection depended on teaching people to value the living world around them. His professional work focused on agricultural development, soil conservation, and the management of woodland resources in the Sahel. Dioum was born in a rural community near Dahra and spent part of his childhood helping his family cultivate crops and care for livestock. He attended schools in Linguère and Dakar before studying natural sciences at the University of Dakar. He later traveled to France for advanced training in forestry and received an engineering diploma from a national forest school in Nancy. Dioum worked with government and international development agencies and continued to write about the relationship between rural livelihoods and environmental stewardship.

Calvin Thomas Bruton was an American-born Australian basketball player and coach who became a prominent figure in the National Basketball League. He won a championship with the Brisbane Bullets in 1985 and later earned All-NBL honors while playing for the Geelong Supercats. Bruton served as a player-coach in Geelong and received the league’s coaching award before moving to the Perth Wildcats, whom he guided to another championship in 1990. He became an Australian citizen during the 1980s and represented the national team after giving up his American citizenship. Bruton was among the first group inducted into the NBL Hall of Fame. His son later played professionally in Australia and developed a separate career as a successful guard. After retiring from coaching, Bruton worked in basketball administration and youth development.

Antaeotricha pallidilinea is a moth in the family Depressariidae known from Guatemala. Its wingspan is approximately 22 mm. The forewings are pale cream-ochre with a wash of grey-brown scales along the dorsum and three broken diagonal bands crossing the surface. The first begins near the basal fifth of the costa and reaches the lower margin just before the middle. The second runs from the center of the costa toward the dorsum before the tornus and leaves a small dark spot visible near the outer cell. The third is shorter and lies between the second band and the apex, where it curves slightly toward a row of seven dark marginal dots. The lines are irregular and less sharply defined than those of related species with similar coloring. The cilia remain light brown and the hindwings are dull grey, becoming darker toward the outer edge.

Julieta Venegas is a Mexican singer, songwriter, and multi-instrumentalist whose music combines pop, rock, folk, and electronic elements. She began performing in Tijuana and later moved to Mexico City, where she released her first solo album in the late 1990s. Her songs have earned Latin Grammy awards and nominations, as well as recognition from Latin music and film organizations. Venegas plays piano, accordion, and guitar, and her arrangements often place a direct vocal melody over bright keyboard or string parts. Albums such as Sí, Limón y Sal, and Otra Cosa produced singles that reached radio audiences throughout Latin America and Spain. She has also written songs for other performers, contributed music to films, and appeared in theatrical and television projects. Her work has been praised for joining accessible pop structures with lyrics about independence, memory, and complicated relationships.

Massimo Vignelli was an Italian-American graphic designer whose work included corporate identities, packaging, books, exhibitions, and public information systems. He studied architecture and design in Milan and Venice before moving to the United States, where he established a design office with his wife, Lella. The firm worked for airlines, department stores, publishers, museums, and transportation agencies. Vignelli was known for reducing complex visual systems to a small number of typefaces, colors, and geometric forms. His clients included a major coffee company, a furniture manufacturer, and the New York subway system. He also designed posters, glassware, furniture, and books, treating typography and industrial design as parts of the same discipline. Vignelli taught and lectured internationally and received awards from professional design organizations. His work influenced later generations of designers through its emphasis on consistency, legibility, and restraint.

RuralLink Towers Limited is an Indian telecommunications infrastructure company that builds and manages mobile towers, fiber routes, rooftop sites, and shared network equipment. It supplies services to several national carriers and regional internet providers, allowing multiple operators to use the same physical structures. The company began as a tower division within a major mobile network and became an independent infrastructure business after a restructuring. It later combined with a rival tower operator through a joint venture in which the parent carrier retained a controlling interest. RuralLink manages tens of thousands of sites across India, including installations in remote districts where a single mast may serve several competing networks. Its revenue comes from long-term leasing, maintenance, power management, and the installation of new equipment. The company has also invested in fiber backhaul and small data centers near major transport corridors.

The Hank Williams Center is a music museum and performance venue in Montgomery, Alabama, devoted to Hank Williams and the musical traditions of the American South. It occupies a former railway warehouse renovated by the city in the 1990s. The permanent collection includes handwritten lyrics, stage clothing, recording equipment, photographs, and instruments associated with Williams’s career. Additional galleries examine country music, blues, gospel, and the musicians who worked in Alabama and neighboring states. The center contains a small theatre for concerts and lectures, a rotating exhibition space, and a research library. A replica of the singer’s childhood home was moved to the grounds and opened to visitors as part of an expansion project. The museum also hosts a yearly songwriting festival and educational programs for local schools.

Westfield Horticultural Products was a British manufacturer and marketing company that employed several hundred people in the production of household gardening supplies and agricultural formulations.
