Its main offices and laboratory were located in Hertfordshire, with a distribution warehouse near Ely. The company sold liquid plant foods, weed treatments, insect controls, and products for commercial growers in Britain and overseas. It became especially well known for a small bottle of indoor plant fertilizer marketed under the name Greenleaf. Westfield also published a series of brightly illustrated gardening guides written by a horticultural consultant who later became chairman of the firm. The books covered vegetable gardens, houseplants, greenhouses, and lawn care and were designed to provide practical advice to inexperienced gardeners. Their combination of simple instructions, photographs, and product information became a model for the company’s packaging and advertising.

Ritchie Aidan Sutton was an English football defender who played primarily in the lower divisions and non-league competitions. He came through the youth system at Crewe Alexandra but did not make a senior appearance for the club, spending loan periods with Leek Town and Stafford Rangers. After his release, Sutton played for Northwich Victoria, Halifax Town, and Nantwich Town before joining Port Vale. He later moved to Mansfield Town, where he helped win the Conference National title and was named the club’s player of the season. Sutton signed for Tranmere Rovers in 2015 and was loaned to Barrow during the following campaign. He helped Tranmere return to the English Football League through the National League play-offs and subsequently played for Morecambe. After leaving the professional game, he returned to part-time football with Altrincham and spent a season on loan at Alfreton Town.

The 2015 Rally Finland was a motor-racing event for World Rally Championship cars held over four days in late July. Based around Jyväskylä, it used fast gravel stages through forests and over broad jumps and covered more than 300 kilometres of competitive driving. The rally was won by Jari-Matti Latvala, driving for Volkswagen Motorsport, who secured his third victory in Finland. His teammate Sébastien Ogier finished second after recovering from an early puncture, while Ott Tänak completed the podium for Ford. Latvala won by less than half a minute, and the result narrowed the gap in the drivers’ championship. The supporting WRC-2 class produced a close contest between two Škoda crews, with the winner taking the category by only a few seconds. Large crowds gathered at the roadside stages despite heavy rain before the final day.

In philosophy of mind, emergentism holds that a system can possess properties that arise from the organization and interaction of its parts without being properties of any single part. The view is often presented between strict reductionism and forms of dualism. An emergentist may accept that cells are made of chemicals and brains are made of neurons while arguing that life or consciousness cannot be explained adequately by listing the behavior of individual molecules or neurons. Stronger versions claim that higher-level properties introduce genuinely new causal powers; weaker versions treat emergence as a practical description of patterns that are difficult to derive from lower-level equations. Examples are often drawn from chemistry, biology, cognition, and collective behavior. Emergentism is generally naturalistic because it does not appeal to supernatural substances, but its critics question whether the word explains anything beyond complexity and limited human knowledge.

Mtaa Sauti is a Tanzanian hip-hop duo from the Temeke district of Dar es Salaam. The group consists of rapper Juma “Kiongozi” Hamisi and producer-vocalist Baraka Mussa, who began performing together in the late 1990s as Swahili rap was gaining a national audience. Their name refers to the neighborhood voice and to the direct, street-level style of their lyrics. The duo’s first popular single, “Mambo ya Mtaa,” was followed by the album Hadithi za Usiku, which included the radio songs “Kivuli” and “Moyo wa Chuma.” A later record, Nje ya Ukuta, produced their most widely recognized track, “Asali ya Maisha.” Their songs address romantic loyalty, unemployment, neighborhood politics, and the pressure to succeed without abandoning one’s community. Mtaa Sauti has collaborated with artists from Kenya and Uganda and has received awards for stage performance and songwriting.

The Lahore Collegiate Institute is an independent boys’ school in Lahore, Pakistan, serving day students and boarders from the primary grades through advanced secondary education. Its program combines academic courses with cricket, athletics, debating, music, and community service. Senior pupils prepare for international secondary and pre-university examinations before applying to universities in Pakistan and abroad. The school was founded in the late nineteenth century as a college for the sons of regional chiefs and was later reorganized as a modern boarding school. Its alumni include civil servants, judges, athletes, writers, and several national political leaders. The campus contains historic red-brick buildings, playing fields, laboratories, and a library named for one of its former principals. Administrators describe the institution’s purpose as the development of independence, public responsibility, and disciplined study rather than examination success alone.

Vijay Nair is an Indian film director, music composer, playback singer, actor, and producer working primarily in Malayalam cinema. He entered the industry as an assistant director during the late 1990s and studied Carnatic vocal music with teachers in Kerala and Chennai. Nair later sang backing tracks for several composers before recording his first original song for a Malayalam fantasy film. He made his acting debut in the same production and received attention for combining live performers with animated and three-dimensional sequences. Nair’s first film as director and music director was a romantic comedy set in an urban arts college. The film was released after several delays and became known for its ensemble cast and songs performed in multiple languages. He has continued to alternate between directing, composing, and producing small independent films.

A decommissioned highway is a road that no longer carries an official national, state, or provincial route designation. The change may involve closing the road entirely, transferring it to a local authority, removing only one of several route numbers, or abandoning a section after a replacement is built. Many former highways remain open as local streets, farm roads, scenic routes, or access roads for properties that would otherwise be isolated. Others are demolished when bridges, interchanges, or unsafe grades have no practical use. A road can therefore remain physically visible long after it disappears from official maps. Decommissioning is often associated with bypass construction, changes in traffic patterns, municipal boundary adjustments, or the conversion of a route to a limited-access freeway. The former alignment may retain historical importance even when it no longer carries through traffic.

The lunar crater von Braun is located near the northwestern limb of the Moon, along the western edge of Oceanus Procellarum. Because of its position, observers on Earth see the crater at a pronounced angle and cannot easily judge its full circular outline. The rim is somewhat elongated and has been altered by later impacts, including a smaller crater attached to the western wall. Several craterlets mark the eastern and southeastern rim, while terraces and slumped material interrupt the inner slopes. The floor is comparatively level and contains only a few small impact scars. A low ridge crosses part of the interior, and portions of the rim become difficult to distinguish from the surrounding basin when the Sun is high. The crater was named for the German-American rocket engineer Wernher von Braun and has been examined in photographs from lunar orbiters.

Minisupercomputers were a class of scientific computers developed during the 1980s to provide vector processing and limited multiprocessing at a price below that of large institutional supercomputers. Universities, engineering firms, and government laboratories used them for fluid dynamics, seismic modeling, weather research, and other calculations that benefited from operations on long numerical arrays. Their manufacturers combined specialized vector hardware with relatively compact cabinets and lower operating costs, often targeting departmental budgets rather than national computing centers. The machines varied widely in architecture, but software environments were frequently more standardized than the underlying electronics. Advances in very-large-scale integration made it possible to build powerful systems with fewer components, while falling memory prices broadened the market. The category declined as workstation clusters, high-end minicomputers, and inexpensive parallel systems became capable of similar workloads.

Hours-of-service regulations govern how long commercial motor-vehicle drivers may work, drive, and remain on duty in the United States. Federal rules apply to interstate trucking and many passenger carriers, while drivers operating solely within one state may be subject to additional state requirements. The regulations establish limits for daily driving, weekly duty cycles, required off-duty periods, and longer rest breaks intended to reduce fatigue-related crashes. Drivers must record changes in duty status, including driving, loading, waiting, and sleeping. Historically these records were kept in paper logbooks; most covered vehicles now use electronic logging devices that automatically capture motion and transmit or store the driver’s hours. Carriers are responsible for maintaining records and scheduling trips within the limits, while federal and state inspectors review logs during roadside inspections and audits. Emergency and adverse-driving provisions allow limited extensions in specific circumstances.

The Gaudiya Mission is a Vaishnava religious organization founded in Bengal during the early twentieth century to spread the devotional teachings associated with Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. Its monastic branches maintain temples, publish theological works, train religious teachers, and organize public chanting and lectures. The movement grew from an earlier monastery established in Mayapur by Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati, who later created a wider network of preaching centers. Its leaders emphasized accessible devotion rather than birth-based privilege and accepted followers from different religious and social backgrounds. The organization’s publications explained Sanskrit texts, ritual practice, and the history of the Bengali bhakti tradition in several languages. Branches were established across India and later in Europe, North America, and other parts of Asia. Although the movement has experienced divisions over succession and administration, its institutions continue to combine monastic discipline, congregational worship, publishing, and missionary work.

Dumitru Țepeneag is a Romanian novelist, essayist, short-story writer, and translator who has lived for much of his career in France. He was associated with the Oniric literary movement, which used dream logic, shifting identities, and discontinuous narrative as alternatives to socialist-realist conventions. The Romanian government revoked his citizenship during the 1970s because of his dissident activities, after which he became an important figure in the country’s literary exile in Paris. Țepeneag has translated French experimental and philosophical writers into Romanian and has also rendered the work of younger Romanian poets into French. He founded a magazine devoted to Eastern European literature and wrote criticism influenced by libertarian socialism and anarchism. His wife, Mona Țepeneag, is a translator and essayist. The couple’s work helped maintain intellectual connections between Romanian writers abroad and readers in France.

Grant management software is used by organizations that award grants, apply for funding, or administer projects supported by outside money. Systems designed for grantmakers can accept and route applications, record eligibility checks, monitor budgets, schedule payments, collect reports, and evaluate the results of funded work. Applicant-oriented systems focus instead on finding opportunities, assigning writing tasks, preparing budgets, storing attachments, and tracking deadlines. Some products combine both functions, while others are built for a particular field such as medical research, education, or the arts. Programs may be installed on an organization’s own servers or delivered as cloud services accessed through a browser. Common features include role-based permissions, electronic signatures, automated reminders, audit trails, and dashboards summarizing awards and expenditures. By bringing correspondence, financial records, and performance measures into one system, the software reduces the administrative work required to manage a grant from proposal through closeout.

Dysoxylum australe is a large evergreen tree native to rainforests and moist coastal forests of eastern Australia. It occurs from northern New South Wales into southern Queensland and is often planted along streets or in parks because its broad crown provides substantial shade. Mature specimens can exceed 40 metres in height and develop a straight trunk with rough, aromatic bark. The species grows on volcanic soils, near mountain ranges, and in sheltered valleys, although established trees can tolerate short periods of drought, salt exposure, and light frost. It is slow-growing when young but responds strongly to warm temperatures, reliable moisture, and fertile ground. The timber has been used for furniture, interior joinery, and construction, while extracts from the fragrant bark and leaves have been examined for possible commercial uses. The tree also provides food and shelter for rainforest wildlife.

Robert Michael Bender is an American basketball coach and former college player. He attended Bloomington High School in Illinois, where he became an all-state guard, and later played for Indiana and Duke. Bender was part of Indiana’s undefeated 1976 championship team before transferring to Duke, where he appeared in another national title game. He was selected in the NBA draft but did not play professionally. Bender began coaching as an assistant under Mike Krzyzewski and later became head coach at Illinois State and the University of Washington. His teams were known for disciplined half-court defense and for using multiple ball handlers rather than relying on a single scorer. He subsequently served as an assistant coach in the NBA with the Philadelphia 76ers and Memphis Grizzlies. Bender is unusual for having participated as a player in championship games for two different universities.

The PEN/International Writers Prize is a biennial award presented by PEN America to a living writer whose work has made a significant contribution to literature across national or linguistic boundaries. The prize is supported by a private literary foundation and includes a cash award, a public reading, and a program of events with writers and translators. It was originally established as a fiction prize and named for a major twentieth-century novelist, but its scope was later broadened to include poetry, nonfiction, and bodies of work written outside the United States. A revision of the award rules also changed the eligibility requirements and increased the prize money after several years in which no award was given. The selection committee considers literary achievement, formal ambition, and the relationship between a writer’s work and international readership. The prize is regarded as one of the organization’s most prominent honors.

Lila Karp was an American activist, novelist, teacher, and feminist associated with the second-wave women’s movement. Her best-known novel, The Queen Is in the Garbage, was written during a decade she spent in London and published after she returned to the United States. Karp joined a radical feminist collective in New York and appeared in a documentary about women’s organizing during the 1970s. She later helped establish women’s studies as an academic field, directing a university women’s center and developing courses on literature, labor, and gender. Karp presented a widely discussed paper on the resistance faced by women’s studies programs at a national scholarly conference in 1979. She subsequently became co-director of an institute devoted to the study of women and men at a California university. Her writing and teaching connected feminist theory with fiction, education, and the practical work of building institutions.

Emerald City Comic Con is a multigenre popular-culture convention held annually in Seattle, Washington. It began in the early 2000s as a smaller comic-book gathering organized by local retailers and artists and later expanded to include film, television, games, animation, and publishing. The event usually occupies several days at the Seattle Convention Center and includes an exhibition hall, panel rooms, autograph areas, screenings, workshops, and a large cosplay program. Professional guests and exhibitors often arrive for a preview period before the public opening, allowing dealers to prepare displays and attendees with full passes to enter early. The convention has hosted comic writers, actors, game designers, illustrators, and voice performers. As attendance increased, organizers added satellite events and moved some programming into nearby hotels and theatres. It is one of the largest annual gatherings of its kind in the Pacific Northwest.

Aurora Field are a British alternative-rock trio based between Belfast and Brighton. The group was formed by filmmaker and guitarist Daniel Kerr, bassist Michael Hume, and drummer Sophie Lane, and became known for performing in churches, galleries, market halls, and other spaces not normally used for rock concerts. Their first EP, Low Tide Signals, was released by a small Belfast label in 2009. Hume left soon afterward to join another band, and was replaced by former Cutaways member Chris McRory. The new lineup issued the single “Glass Horizon” and began recording its first album at an independent studio in Belfast. Walk Through the Weather was released in 2011 and combined heavily processed guitar with quiet instrumental passages. The trio later appeared at a Berlin art festival and at several outdoor music events in Northern Ireland before taking an extended break.

Thomas William Borrer was an English amateur cricketer whose date of birth is uncertain but who was baptized in Sussex in 1819. While studying at Oxford, he played first-class matches for the university against the Marylebone Cricket Club in 1839 and 1840. He also appeared once for Sussex against Kent, batting low in the order before being promoted in the second innings when the team needed a more experienced opener. Borrer made another first-class appearance for a local gentlemen’s side at Lord’s several years later. His scores were modest, and surviving scorecards do not identify a regular bowling style. He was stumped in one innings by a prominent wicket-keeper and remained not out in another. Most details of his life outside cricket are unknown, although later records suggest that he returned to Sussex and became involved in estate administration.

Marco Bellini was an Italian professional footballer who played as a full-back and wide midfielder on both sides of the pitch. He began with a provincial club in northern Italy before earning a transfer to Bari, where his speed and crossing attracted the attention of larger teams. Bellini joined Juventus in 2000 and spent six seasons there, winning domestic league and cup titles and reaching a European final. He later played in Spain for Valencia, returned to Italy with Roma, and finished his career at a Swiss club, where he moved into coaching. Bellini was known for overlapping runs, accurate long passes, and the ability to switch from defense to attack during the same match. He represented Italy at international tournaments and won more than 50 caps. After retiring as a player, he coached the Swiss club for one season and worked as a technical adviser.

Meir Sternberg is an Israeli literary critic and scholar of biblical narrative. He teaches comparative literature and poetics at Tel Aviv University and is associated with a literary approach to the Hebrew Bible. His influential book The Poetics of Biblical Narrative examines how biblical stories use omission, repetition, pacing, and shifts in perspective to guide the reader. Sternberg argues that the narrator controls the distribution of information and creates interpretive tension by leaving important details unstated until later scenes. He treats biblical narrative as simultaneously aesthetic, historical, and ideological, rather than as a transparent record of events. Sternberg’s work has been discussed alongside the studies of Robert Alter, Adele Berlin, and other scholars who analyze characterization and plot in literary terms. His emphasis on narrative gaps has influenced both biblical criticism and broader theories of how readers infer motives from incomplete stories.

Poolish is a liquid pre-ferment used in breadmaking, especially in French and Central European baking. It is made by combining flour and water in roughly equal weights with a small amount of baker’s yeast, then allowing the mixture to ferment before the final dough is mixed. The long fermentation develops aroma, acidity, and extensibility and can produce a loaf with a thin crust and open crumb. Unlike a stiff starter, poolish is loose enough to stir and usually forms bubbles across its surface as it matures. Bakers may prepare it for several hours at room temperature or refrigerate it overnight, adjusting the yeast according to the schedule and the strength of the flour. The fermented mixture is combined with additional flour, water, salt, and sometimes more yeast. Poolish can improve flavor and keeping quality without requiring a sourdough culture.

In audio electronics, a bridging connection is one in which the input impedance of a receiving device is much higher than the output impedance of the source supplying it. The arrangement allows the input to measure the source voltage while drawing very little current, so connecting the two devices causes only a small change in the original signal. Mixers, amplifiers, recording interfaces, and measuring instruments commonly use voltage bridging at their inputs. The opposite design goal is impedance matching, in which source and load impedances are made equal or related as complex conjugates to maximize power transfer or suppress reflections on a transmission line. Bridging is preferred for most audio voltage signals because preserving the waveform matters more than extracting maximum power. A poorly chosen low-impedance load can attenuate the signal, increase distortion, or alter the behavior of the preceding circuit.

Anchiornis is a genus of small, feathered paravian dinosaur known from Late Jurassic rocks in northeastern China. Fossils preserve a lightly built animal with long feathers on the forelimbs, hind limbs, and tail, giving it a four-winged outline when viewed from above. The type species was less than a metre long and probably weighed only a few hundred grams. Its bones and feather impressions have been used in debates over the origin of powered flight and the relationship between early birds and other maniraptoran dinosaurs. Some specimens preserve evidence of a dark body, a crest, and contrasting feathers, although interpretations of coloration remain dependent on the quality of fossilized melanosomes. Anchiornis lived in a forested environment containing lakes, volcanic ash beds, insects, and other small vertebrates. Its exact position on the dinosaur family tree has changed as new fossils and analytical methods have become available.

FuboTV is an American streaming television service that began as an internet platform for live soccer broadcasts and later expanded into a broader virtual cable package. Subscribers can watch sports, news, and entertainment channels through smart televisions, web browsers, phones, and dedicated streaming devices. The service offers several tiers with different channel lineups, cloud-based digital recording, and optional add-ons for international or premium networks. It was introduced in the mid-2010s and initially concentrated on football and other sports that were underserved by American streaming products. As the catalog grew, the company added entertainment channels and regional sports coverage while retaining its original sports identity. FuboTV has operated in the United States and Canada and has periodically changed its pricing and channel packages. Its business competes with satellite, cable, and other live-streaming distributors.

The Columbia Law Review is a scholarly legal journal edited by students at Columbia Law School in New York City. It publishes articles by professors, judges, practicing lawyers, and students on constitutional law, administrative law, criminal justice, corporate regulation, and international affairs. The review was established in the early twentieth century and became one of the principal journals associated with American legal education. Members of the editorial board select submissions, edit manuscripts, and prepare shorter notes and comments for publication. Alumni of the journal have included federal judges, government officials, law professors, and attorneys in major public-interest and private practices. The publication also maintains an online companion that allows shorter essays and responses to appear between print issues. Its editors periodically collaborate with other law reviews on symposia devoted to major questions in legal policy.

Rhythm Avenue is the debut album by the American funk group Brass Avenue, released in 1977 by an independent label. The record combines horn-driven funk with Latin percussion, jazz harmony, and repetitive vocal hooks designed for live dancing. Most of the songs have one-word titles and use short lyrical phrases rather than extended narratives, leaving room for the rhythm section and brass arrangements to carry the structure. Recording was delayed while the group’s leader completed work as a session musician, but the album became an unexpected success after a regional radio station began playing its first single. It reached the upper portion of the American soul chart and later appeared on the British album listings during the disco boom. Critics praised the tight ensemble playing and the clarity of the horn section. A European reissue in the 2000s introduced additional mixes and renewed interest in the group.

Social history is a field of historical study concerned with the experiences and relationships of ordinary people as well as with institutions and political leaders. Researchers may examine family structure, work, migration, religion, health, education, consumption, crime, or popular culture, often using sources that earlier historians overlooked. The field expanded rapidly in the 1960s and 1970s alongside labor history, women’s history, and the study of marginalized communities. Social historians frequently combine census records, diaries, court files, oral histories, newspapers, material objects, and quantitative methods. One central problem is connecting broad changes such as industrialization, war, or state formation with the decisions and constraints faced by individuals. Critics have sometimes argued that social history can lose sight of political power, while its practitioners respond that institutions become meaningful only when their effects on daily life are examined.

The SD40T-2 is a six-axle diesel-electric locomotive built by Electro-Motive Division for railroads operating in the mountainous western United States. It is known as a tunnel motor because its cooling-air intake was placed near the walkway rather than high on the locomotive roof. The arrangement reduced the amount of hot exhaust air drawn back into the radiator fans when the locomotive worked inside tunnels or under snow sheds. The design used the manufacturer’s Dash 2 electrical equipment, high-adhesion trucks, and a turbocharged diesel engine. More than 300 examples were produced during the 1970s for the Southern Pacific and its subsidiary railroads. Many were later rebuilt with updated controls and new designations, while others passed to short-line and excursion operators. The locomotives were especially useful on steep grades where long trains demanded sustained power at low speed.

Armenians are an ethnic group and nation historically associated with the Armenian Highlands and the southern Caucasus. The Armenian homeland lies between Anatolia, the Caucasus, and Mesopotamia, and Armenian communities have also developed in Russia, Iran, Lebanon, Europe, North America, and Australia. The Armenian language has its own alphabet, created in late antiquity, and the Armenian Apostolic Church has played a major role in preserving literary and religious traditions. Political borders and repeated migrations divided Armenian populations among several empires and modern states. Major cultural centers have included Yerevan, Tbilisi, Istanbul, Jerusalem, and Beirut, while communities abroad established schools, newspapers, churches, and charitable organizations. Armenian history incorporates periods of independent kingdom, imperial rule, trade, artistic production, and mass displacement. Contemporary Armenians maintain strong connections through language, family networks, religious institutions, and cultural associations.

Galveston Bay is a shallow estuary on the upper Texas Gulf Coast, east of Houston. It is formed by several rivers and tidal channels and opens to the Gulf of Mexico through Bolivar Roads and the channel between Galveston Island and the Bolivar Peninsula. The bay includes waters bordered by Harris, Galveston, Chambers, and Brazoria counties and is connected to the Houston Ship Channel, one of the busiest industrial waterways in the United States. Marshes, oyster reefs, mudflats, and barrier islands surround portions of the estuary and provide habitat for fish, birds, and migratory wildlife. Indigenous communities used the bay long before Spanish exploration, while later settlements grew around fishing, shipping, and port industries. Modern Galveston Bay supports petroleum refining, chemical manufacturing, container traffic, commercial fishing, and recreation. Pollution, shoreline development, subsidence, and storm damage have made conservation and restoration major regional concerns.

The River Lanterns were an indie folk and alt-country band from Johnson City, Tennessee. The group was founded by singer-songwriters Hannah Quinn and Jesse Andrews, who met while working at a summer camp, and initially performed as a duo with dobro player David Ritchie. Over time the lineup expanded to include electric guitar, fiddle, drums, pedal steel, and keyboards. The River Lanterns combined Appalachian balladry, bluegrass, rock, and country into a lively stage sound that drew attention from regional music magazines. Quinn’s song “Power Lines” won a songwriting prize at a North Carolina festival, while “Anywhere but Here” was selected for a national public-radio feature. The band performed at Bonnaroo, the Bristol Rhythm and Roots Reunion, and several touring roots-music festivals. Its growing profile made the group a representative act of the alternative-country revival, although the members continued to release records through small independent labels.

Nadine Coyle is an Irish singer, actress, and model who became widely known as a member of the British girl group Girls Aloud. The group produced numerous top-ten singles, several successful studio albums, and a major award-winning single before taking an extended hiatus. Coyle launched a solo career with the album Insatiable, released through her own imprint in partnership with a large retail chain. The title track entered the British singles chart, while a later digital EP reached the top of a download store’s album list. She returned to major-label promotion with the single “Go to Work” and subsequently released songs including “Fool for Love” and “All That I Know.” Coyle has also appeared in theatre and television programs and participated in reunions with Girls Aloud. Her solo recordings have generally charted below the group’s peak but have attracted a dedicated audience through online releases and live performances.

Taja Cheek, known professionally as L’Rain, is an American experimental musician, composer, multi-instrumentalist, and curator. Her first album introduced a collage-like approach that combines sung passages with field recordings, distorted instruments, fragments of conversation, and abrupt changes in rhythm. A later record, Fatigue, received critical recognition and appeared on several year-end lists devoted to experimental music. Cheek has collaborated with visual artists, dancers, and musicians working in ambient, noise, free jazz, funk, gospel, and electronic pop. She has performed in museums, galleries, clubs, and concert halls, sometimes using the stage as a site for improvisation rather than presenting a fixed band arrangement. Cheek describes her practice as approaching song without accepting conventional limits on melody or form. Reviewers have compared her work to psychedelic pop, post-punk, musique concrète, and avant-garde R&B.

“Silver Promise” is a country duet recorded by American singers Ruth Collins and Wade Harper. Released in 1971 as the lead single from their joint album, the song follows two former partners who meet again and discover that the relationship has not entirely ended. Its arrangement combines a moderate country rhythm with strings, steel guitar, and alternating verses before the singers join in the chorus. The single reached the top five of the American country chart and became a number-one hit in Canada. It was Collins’s largest recording success at that point and Harper’s first major chart appearance in several years. The pair made a second top-ten duet the following year, but neither performer matched the commercial impact of “Silver Promise” until Collins recorded a later solo ballad and Harper returned to the charts with a gospel album.

Upward Bound is a computer-animated adventure film released in 2011. Directed by Mara Ellison from a screenplay written with Peter Cho, it features the voices of Helen Mirren, Jacob Tremblay, Alan Tudyk, and Regina King. The story follows an elderly cartographer who launches a balloon-powered house to fulfill a promise made to her late partner and is accidentally joined by a young wilderness volunteer. Their journey carries them over a remote South American plateau, where they encounter a talking river dog, a brightly colored flightless bird, and a former explorer determined to capture the bird. The director developed the idea after imagining a house that could travel away from an unpleasant neighborhood, and the production team spent several days studying cloud forests and tepui landscapes. The film was rendered in stereoscopic 3D and was noted for its stylized character designs and detailed cloth simulation.

Umklapp scattering is a process in a crystal lattice in which the sum of the participating wave vectors lies outside the first Brillouin zone. Because reciprocal lattice vectors represent equivalent points in a periodic solid, the resulting vector can be folded back into the first zone. The crystal momentum is therefore conserved only up to a reciprocal lattice vector, even though ordinary momentum conservation is not violated when the lattice is included in the calculation. The process can occur when two phonons combine, when a phonon is split, or when electrons interact with the periodic potential and lattice vibrations. In a simple picture, waves traveling in the same general direction can produce a folded result that appears to point in the opposite direction. Umklapp events are especially important at high temperatures, where they provide a major channel for limiting heat transport in crystals along with scattering from defects, boundaries, and impurities.

The sirilla is a traditional dance from Chiloé in southern Chile. It is performed by couples or by groups arranged in lines and is accompanied by guitar, accordion, and singing. The dancers move through short turns, crossings, and changes of place that follow the repeated verses of the song. Some traditions describe the dance as having arrived through contact with travelers from the mainland and Argentina, while others treat it as a local development of older Chilote forms. At the beginning of a performance, the dancers enter slowly and take their positions opposite one another. They then lift the edges of their skirts or move their handkerchiefs while marking the rhythm with small steps. Because the figures are easy to learn, the sirilla is often taught to children and used at school festivals as well as community celebrations. Larger groups may add playful variations between verses.

“Tell Me Again” is a song from the musical Sunday Letters, with music by Andrew Lloyd Webber and lyrics by Don Black. It was first recorded as a duet for a concept album and later received a new lyric when the stage production was revised for a different singer. The melody had appeared earlier in an instrumental variation, and portions of that composition were reused in the dance material for the musical’s second act. A solo recording by British singer Sarah Brightman was issued as a single and reached the lower part of the United Kingdom chart. The song’s narrator asks whether a broken relationship can be repaired, shifting between quiet verses and a more expansive chorus. Critics praised the melody and Brightman’s performance, although some considered the production dated compared with the electronic pop surrounding it. Later revivals restored sections of the original lyric and altered the orchestration.

The Ubuntu Edge was a proposed high-end smartphone designed by Canonical as a demonstration of a device that could operate as both a phone and a desktop computer. The project was announced in 2013 and sought funding through a month-long crowdfunding campaign. When connected to a monitor, keyboard, and mouse, the handset was intended to run a desktop version of Ubuntu while retaining ordinary phone functions. The planned hardware included dual operating-system support, substantial memory, and a high-capacity battery intended to serve both mobile and desktop use. Canonical hoped to produce an initial run of approximately 40,000 devices, but the campaign raised only a portion of its unusually large funding target. Although tens of thousands of backers pledged money, the goal was not reached and the phone never entered commercial production. The project nevertheless influenced later discussions about converged mobile and desktop computing.

The Enchanted Island is a two-act comic opera with a libretto by Edward Morton and music by Charles Villiers Stanford. The story takes place in a realm where fairies observe human beings and decide that mortal love must be the source of their happiness. They bring several men from Earth into the fairy court, expecting the visitors to teach them virtue and romance. The experiment produces jealousy, rivalry, and a series of comic misunderstandings before the mortals return home and the fairies reject the emotional turmoil they have witnessed. The opera premiered at a London theatre in 1911, with the composer supervising the score and a well-known actor-manager producing the staging. Reviews praised the music but criticized the uneven libretto and the first production’s principal performer. A replacement cast improved the reception, yet the work closed after a short run and was never followed by another opera from the composer.

Maple Grove Park is a neighborhood park and playground in the Queens borough of New York City. It occupies a block between 81st and 82nd Streets and runs along the southern side of 35th Avenue. Much of the site is paved for basketball, tennis, handball, and seasonal community events. A children’s play area includes climbing equipment, benches, and a spray feature shaped like leaves and vines. The park also contains restrooms, a small picnic space, and bicycle racks. A section of the adjacent street was converted into a permanent plaza, and part of a nearby school’s sports yard was later incorporated into the park. Mature trees shade the edges, but the site has little open lawn and almost no uninterrupted green space. It is heavily used because the surrounding community has relatively few public recreation areas.

The Martu are an Aboriginal Australian people associated with the Western Desert cultural region. Their traditional country extends across parts of the Great Sandy Desert and the lands surrounding several salt lakes in Western Australia. During the twentieth century, many Martu families were moved or traveled to settlements and missions far from their desert homelands. In later decades, groups returned to country and established or reoccupied communities such as Parnngurr, Punmu, and Kunawarritji. The return movement supported the maintenance of Martu languages, hunting practices, ceremonial knowledge, and relationships with sacred places. Some Martu people continue to live in regional towns while maintaining ties to remote communities and outstations. Population counts and the number of speakers have changed as families reunite and younger people participate in cultural education, art programs, and ranger work.

“Chromatic” is a song by American singer Lena Vale from her third studio album, also titled Chromatic. Vale co-wrote and co-produced the track with electronic musician David Blair and producers Nick Mason and Dino Zane. It was one of the first pieces created for the album and established the record’s interest in combining dance music with theatrical pop. The song uses a steady techno beat, piano chords, processed guitar, and bursts of synthetic noise between the vocal lines. Its lyrics have been interpreted as describing a romantic attachment, a relationship between an artist and an audience, or the merging of commercial pop with visual art. Critics responded favorably to the restrained arrangement but disagreed about the imagery and the deliberately retro production. The track was not released as the album’s main single but became a frequent subject of fan remixes and live performances.

The Blue Meridian are a Swedish rock trio influenced by late-1960s blues rock, psychedelic music, jazz, and folk. The group was formed in Gothenburg in 2010 by vocalist-guitarist Elias Faraj, bassist Oskar Lind, and drummer Christian Eriksen. Their first album, Road of Echoes, was issued as a double vinyl set by a small Scandinavian label and featured extended guitar passages alongside lighter acoustic interludes. A short single followed, and the band released a second record, Open the Circle, two years later. A Dutch distributor arranged a wider European reissue of the debut, allowing the trio to tour Spain, Germany, and the Netherlands. The Blue Meridian became known for reproducing the atmosphere of 1970s album rock without abandoning contemporary recording techniques. A Spanish music magazine included them in a list of notable revivalist bands, and the group appeared at several European roots and psychedelic festivals.

Tengrism is a historical religious and political tradition associated with Turkic and Mongolic peoples of the Eurasian steppe. Its central figure is Tengri, a sky deity connected with order, fate, sovereignty, and the well-being of the people, while local spirits, ancestors, earth, water, and mountains also occupy important places in ritual life. The tradition was practiced in forms that varied across nomadic confederations and imperial courts and coexisted with Buddhism, Christianity, Islam, and other religions. Medieval rulers invoked Tengri to justify authority, military victories, and the continuity of the ruling line. Modern movements using the name Tengrism range from cultural revival projects to explicitly monotheistic or nationalist interpretations. Scholars disagree about whether the older religion should be described as polytheistic, monotheistic at the imperial level, or a flexible form of animism and shamanism.

Jenson is an old-style serif typeface based on the roman types cut by the Venetian printer Nicolas Jenson in the fifteenth century. Modern versions were developed by several designers for book printing and later adapted for phototypesetting and digital composition. The face is characterized by a low contrast between thick and thin strokes, a broad lowercase form, and an angled stress that gives paragraphs a warm, humanist texture. Its italic is designed to complement the roman rather than imitate a separate handwriting style. Jenson has been used for literary books, scholarly editions, magazines, and identity systems that seek a historical but readable appearance. Type designers have produced different weights and optical sizes, since the details that work well in a small footnote may appear too delicate at display scale. The typeface remains a common choice for publishers interested in Renaissance-inspired typography.

Arthur Rackham was an English illustrator known for his imaginative drawings and color plates for fairy tales, legends, and children’s books. He studied at the Lambeth School of Art and worked as a newspaper illustrator before receiving commissions for illustrated editions. Rackham’s figures often combine delicate line work with grotesque faces, twisting branches, winged creatures, and theatrical costumes. His books included versions of Grimm’s fairy tales, Rip Van Winkle, Peter Pan, and stories from Norse and medieval traditions. He produced hundreds of illustrations during a period when advances in color printing made elaborate book plates commercially viable. Rackham was influenced by Pre-Raphaelite painting and by the visual language of late Victorian fantasy, but his work developed a distinct atmosphere of unease and humor. His illustrations influenced later fantasy artists and remain widely reproduced in books and exhibitions.

“Fireline” is a hard-rock song recorded by the British band Red Voltage and written by its guitarists, Alan and Martin Cole. It appeared on the group’s 1991 album Edge of the Night and was released as a single later that year. The recording opens with a repeated guitar figure before the full band enters with a driving rhythm and a shouted chorus. The lyrics use images of gambling, speed, and unstable relationships, and the song became one of the band’s most recognizable concert numbers. It reached the upper half of the British singles chart and entered the top forty in Australia and the United States. A live version recorded during the album tour appeared on a concert album two years later. The accompanying video combined stage footage with scenes of the band performing in an industrial warehouse. Red Voltage later retired the song from its set after its original drummer left the group.

Claude Debussy was a French composer and pianist whose music helped shape modernist approaches to harmony, timbre, and musical form. He entered the Paris Conservatoire as a child and won the Prix de Rome in 1884, although he remained skeptical of academic rules and later rejected many of the conventions associated with the prize. Debussy worked as a pianist, accompanist, and critic before gaining attention for orchestral works, piano pieces, songs, and chamber music. His music often uses whole-tone scales, modal melodies, parallel chords, and instrumental colors that suggest light, water, or changing atmosphere. He collaborated with poets and painters and wrote the music for the ballet Jeux and the opera Pelléas et Mélisande. Although sometimes associated with Impressionism, Debussy preferred to describe his work through its sound rather than through a borrowed visual label.

Sarayköy is a town and district in Denizli Province in western Turkey. It lies in the Büyük Menderes valley and borders the districts of Honaz, Pamukkale, Buldan, and Güney, with the Aegean coast several hours to the west. The district center developed around agricultural villages and later expanded after the railway and highways connected it with Denizli and Aydın. Cotton, grapes, olives, and other crops are grown in the surrounding plain, while the hills contain pine woodland and seasonal streams. Sarayköy became a municipality during the twentieth century and was later organized as a district with several dependent villages. The name is associated with an old settlement and a former estate said to have served travelers on the valley route. Protected forests and hot springs in the wider district attract visitors, while irrigation and textile production remain important to the local economy.

Climate change feedbacks are internal responses within the climate system that strengthen or weaken an initial change in temperature or another forcing. A positive feedback reinforces the original shift, while a negative feedback opposes it. For example, warming can reduce snow and ice cover, allowing darker land or water to absorb more sunlight and causing additional warming. Increased atmospheric moisture can also amplify warming because water vapor is itself a greenhouse gas. In contrast, some changes in clouds, vegetation, or atmospheric circulation may counteract an imposed temperature change. Feedbacks are distinguished from forcings, which are external influences such as altered solar output, volcanic aerosols, or increased greenhouse-gas concentrations. Several feedbacks operate at the same time and interact across the atmosphere, ocean, land, and cryosphere. Their combined strength is one of the main reasons estimates of climate sensitivity include a range rather than a single fixed value.

The Wind Singer is a science-fantasy novel by the American-Irish writer Mara McCaffrey. Published in 1978, it was the first book set on the planet Aster and introduced the young musician Elian, who lives in an isolated coastal settlement threatened by recurring storms from a distant red star. The novel was marketed to young adults and later became the opening volume of the Songs of Aster trilogy. Its story takes place several centuries after human settlement, during a period when the planet’s climate cycles have begun to change and older technologies are treated as magic. Aster’s central cities appear in later books, while The Wind Singer focuses on a remote sea-hold and the communities that depend on it. Near the conclusion, Elian is rescued by an airship navigator and carried toward the capital, where the plot joins the political events introduced in the second volume.

Oleksandr Mykolayovych Hrytsenko is a Ukrainian politician who served as prime minister from 2017 to 2020. He previously was mayor of Poltava, vice prime minister for regional development, and minister responsible for construction and municipal services. Hrytsenko entered national politics after winning a parliamentary seat on the list of a pro-presidential coalition and became speaker of the Verkhovna Rada during a period of political realignment. As prime minister, he promoted decentralization, road construction, and reforms intended to give cities greater control over local budgets. His government resigned after a new parliamentary majority formed following the 2019 election. Hrytsenko later led a party called Civic Renewal, but it failed to win representation in the next legislature. He has remained active as a commentator on regional government and infrastructure policy.

The River Bridge Trust is a charitable foundation administered by the Corporation of London. It originated in medieval funds collected to maintain a crossing over the Thames and was formalized by royal charter during the thirteenth century. Tolls, donations, and income from property gradually gave the trust an endowment large enough to finance the repair and replacement of several bridges. Over the centuries it contributed to the construction of Blackfriars Bridge, acquired Southwark Bridge, and helped pay for the Millennium Bridge. Its investment properties in the City of London now generate income used for maintenance, administration, and charitable grants. A grant-making arm supports projects involving community development, education, health, culture, and the environment. The trust is managed separately from the city’s general funds, although the Corporation oversees its governance and appointments.

Lim Kean Chye was a Malaysian lawyer and political activist from a prominent Straits Chinese family. His father was a Cambridge-educated lawyer and legislative councillor, and several of his siblings also studied law in Britain. Lim attended Cambridge University and was called to the English bar before returning to Malaya. He helped found the Malayan Democratic Union in 1945, one of the first political organizations in Singapore to demand representative self-government. The group was composed largely of English-educated professionals who opposed continued colonial rule and debated the form of a future Malayan federation. Lim’s family history reflected the movement of Chinese communities through colonial Southeast Asia, their participation in the legal profession, and the emergence of new national identities after the Second World War. He later practiced law and remained involved in public discussions about constitutional development.

The Rembrandt was an international passenger train linking Amsterdam with Frankfurt and later with cities in southern Germany. It was named after the Dutch painter Rembrandt van Rijn and operated as part of the European Trans Europ Express network. The service initially replaced a shorter train that ran between Amsterdam and Bonn, then was extended eastward in response to requests from passengers and government officials. A later timetable connected the train with onward services to Nuremberg, although the late arrival made the journey inconvenient for some travelers. Railway administrations revised the schedule and restored a direct Amsterdam–Frankfurt service with timed connections to the south. In 1979 the train was converted from a first-class TEE into a two-class InterCity service. It continued as an international route for several years before being assigned to domestic German services and eventually withdrawn.

West Eyreton is a rural settlement in the Canterbury region of New Zealand’s South Island. It lies north-west of Kaiapoi and near the farms and small communities of the Waimakariri district. The settlement was named for Edward John Eyre, a nineteenth-century colonial administrator, and developed around agriculture and transport links across the Canterbury plains. A branch railway was built in the 1870s after poor roads made it difficult to move grain and livestock to larger markets. The line opened from a junction near Kaiapoi and was extended to connect with another branch at Bennetts. Passenger traffic was light, and sections of the route were closed during the twentieth century before the remaining line was abandoned. Little survives except the earthwork, a loading bank, and traces of the former station. West Eyreton remains a small farming community with scattered houses and local services.

Jaljala is a market settlement in a rural municipality of Achham District in western Nepal. The present municipality was created by combining several former village development committees, including Jaljala, Mangalsen, and neighboring hill communities. A national census recorded roughly 2,800 residents in the settlement during the 1990s, living in several hundred households, while a later count found that fewer than half of the population was literate. The village lies on a steep ridge above a network of seasonal streams and is reached by roads that become difficult during the monsoon. Dasain and Chaitra festivals are celebrated by families from several castes and communities. The main shrine is dedicated to a local form of Kalika Mata and stands near the center of the settlement. Many younger residents work elsewhere in Nepal or abroad, but return for religious festivals and agricultural activities.

Yaron Israel is an American jazz drummer and educator. He began learning organ and trumpet as a child before concentrating on percussion while in secondary school. Israel studied at a Chicago university and later completed graduate work in New Jersey. He became the house drummer at a Chicago jazz club, where he worked with visiting musicians and developed a reputation for attentive accompaniment. After moving to New York in the late 1980s, he performed and recorded with artists in hard bop, free jazz, and contemporary composition, including saxophonists, guitarists, and vocalists from several generations. Israel has also toured with popular singers and large ensembles and has appeared on numerous jazz albums. He joined the faculty of Rutgers University in the 1990s and later became a professor at Berklee College of Music. His teaching emphasizes listening, rhythmic flexibility, and the history of small-group improvisation.

Reading Through Stories was an educational television program broadcast in Israel during the 1980s and repeated in later decades. It was designed for children in the early primary grades and used songs, short sketches, animated inserts, and recurring characters to introduce reading and writing. The program was developed with the education ministry and accompanied by workbooks, teacher guides, and enrichment booklets prepared by a national educational-technology center. Each episode demonstrated the relationship between sounds, letters, words, and sentences through stories that were acted out in a colorful studio setting. Several well-known Israeli performers served as hosts, while guest actors appeared as a detective, a newspaper seller, and other characters who returned throughout the series. Clay-animation segments introduced two letter-shaped figures who solved simple problems. The show was used as a supplement to classroom instruction and became familiar to a generation of young viewers.

Klaus-Christian Kleinfeld is a German business executive who has led companies in the metals, engineering, and industrial-technology sectors. He served as president and chief executive of Siemens before becoming chief executive and later chairman of the aluminum producer Alcoa. During his tenure he oversaw expansion into emerging markets, reorganized several business units, and helped separate the company’s aerospace and transportation operations from its traditional metals business. Kleinfeld resigned from the chairmanship of the successor company in 2017 after a dispute with the board. The following year he was appointed to lead an international development project in Saudi Arabia and later became an adviser to the country’s crown prince. His corporate career has included senior roles in Europe and the United States and has often involved large-scale restructuring, acquisitions, and infrastructure investment.

The preservation of flowers has been practiced for both ritual and decorative purposes since antiquity. Archaeologists have found pollen and dried plant remains in burial sites in the Middle East and Egypt, where flowers may have been placed as offerings or memorials. Later cultures used pressed, dried, waxed, and artificially colored flowers in medicine, household decoration, jewelry, fans, and clothing. During the Renaissance, ornamental nosegays became more common, and the Victorian period developed an elaborate language in which particular flowers communicated affection, mourning, secrecy, or apology. Bouquets were arranged to convey messages that could not be spoken openly. Modern preservation methods include air-drying, pressing, glycerin treatment, freeze-drying, and embedding flowers in resin. The practice continues in memorial arrangements, wedding bouquets, botanical collections, and craft work, although the symbolic meanings attached to individual flowers vary across cultures.

Degrassi: New Generation is a Canadian teen drama series and part of the long-running Degrassi franchise created by Linda Schuyler and Kit Hood. It follows students at a Toronto secondary school as they deal with friendships, family conflict, romance, bullying, identity, and social issues. The series introduced a new group of characters while retaining connections to earlier Degrassi programs, and it was filmed at a studio complex in Toronto rather than on the street that inspired the franchise’s name. The program was produced by a Canadian television company and broadcast domestically before being distributed internationally through cable networks and streaming services. Its first season premiered in the early 2000s and ran for more than twenty episodes. Later seasons changed the cast and tone as the characters advanced through school, while continuing the franchise’s tradition of addressing difficult subjects in serialized storylines.

Kličevac is a village in eastern Serbia in the municipality of Požarevac. A census in the early 2000s recorded a population of about 1,300 people, most of them ethnic Serbs. Agriculture, small trade, and seasonal work abroad are the principal sources of income, and many residents maintain homes in the village while working in Austria, Germany, Switzerland, or Italy. Kličevac has a primary school serving children from nearby settlements and a community center used for local celebrations. One tradition connects the village’s name with the Serbian word for “key,” claiming that an Ottoman official lost a set of keys while passing through the area and ordered the inhabitants to search for them. Another explanation derives the name from a verb meaning “to shout,” referring to the commotion of the search. Neither story is considered a certain historical origin.

The Quebrada Formation is a fossil-bearing geological unit in the eastern Andes of Colombia. It crops out along a river valley in the northern part of Huila and consists of dark micaceous shale interlayered with siltstone and fine sandstone. The beds were deposited during the Early Ordovician on a shallow marine shelf near the northern margin of Gondwana. Graptolites and fragments of other marine organisms have been recovered from the finer sediments, providing evidence for the age of the formation and the changing depth of the ancient sea. Pyrite occurs in several horizons, and weathering gives some exposures a rusty surface. The depositional basin opened toward deeper cold-water regions associated with the Iapetus and Rheic oceans. Because relatively few Early Paleozoic fossil localities are known from Colombia, the formation has been important in reconstructing the country’s early marine environments.

Estádio Governador Magalhães Pinto, commonly called Mineirão, is a football stadium in Belo Horizonte, Minas Gerais, Brazil. It was opened in 1965 and became the principal home ground for major clubs in the city, as well as a venue for national and international matches. The original stadium held more than 100,000 spectators, but redevelopment before the 2014 FIFA World Cup reduced the capacity and added modern seating, hospitality areas, improved circulation, and a roof over much of the bowl. Mineirão is owned by the state of Minas Gerais and operated under a long-term concession. Its name honors a former governor who supported the construction project. The stadium stands beside an indoor arena and a university campus and is reached by major roads and public transport. Cruzeiro uses it for many home matches, while other clubs in the city play there for important fixtures.

Vilnius Airport is the largest civil airport in Lithuania and the principal international gateway to the country. It lies south of central Vilnius near the railway line and serves passenger, charter, cargo, and general-aviation traffic. The airport has a single paved runway capable of handling large narrow-body and selected wide-body aircraft, together with several taxiways and a terminal complex divided into arrival and departure areas. It functions as a base for Lithuania’s national and low-cost carriers and is also served by airlines connecting the Baltic region with Western and Northern Europe. Earlier airport buildings were expanded and modernized as passenger numbers increased, and a new terminal project was proposed to address congestion during peak travel periods. The facility was formerly known by a geographic name associated with the surrounding district and was later renamed for a prominent Lithuanian political figure.

Alexander Wellford was an American amateur tennis player who competed in national and international tournaments during the 1950s. At the age of 42 he entered the Wimbledon singles draw and lost in four sets to the British player Ivor Warwick, who advanced several rounds before meeting a leading Australian competitor. Wellford had won the Tennessee state championship earlier that year and traveled to Europe with limited professional support. At the French Championships he lost a close match to a player who later took a set from one of the tournament favorites. Before leaving the United States, Wellford played Vic Seixas in Florida and briefly led the first set by attacking the ball early and passing his opponent at the net. His results illustrate the openness of amateur tennis during the period, when strong regional players could sometimes face the world’s leading competitors.

“Good Vibrations” is a song by the American rock band the Beach Boys, written by Brian Wilson and Mike Love and released as a single in 1966. The recording combines several contrasting sections rather than following a simple verse-and-chorus structure. Its lyrics use the language of attraction and intuition, while the arrangement layers voices, electric instruments, percussion, and a distinctive electronic keyboard sound. The single became one of the group’s largest international successes, reaching the top of the charts in the United States and several other countries. Wilson assembled the track from sessions recorded in different studios, an unusually expensive and time-consuming process for a pop single of the period. Critics praised its inventive production and vocal harmonies, and later musicians cited it as an example of the recording studio functioning as an instrument. A touring musician participated in the sessions before becoming an official member of the band.

Pujon County is a mountainous county in South Hamgyong Province, North Korea. It lies among the Pujon and Hamgyong ranges and borders several counties in South Hamgyong and Chagang. The county was reorganized during the administrative changes of the early 1950s and includes broad upland valleys separated by steep ridges. Much of the terrain stands more than 1,000 metres above sea level, while the highest peaks rise well above 2,000 metres. The climate is cold and continental, with long winters, heavy snow in exposed areas, and frosts that may continue from early autumn into late spring. Forests cover much of the county, and residents cultivate potatoes, grains, and other crops in the lower valleys. Roads and settlements follow the river corridors, while the higher mountain areas remain sparsely populated.

Jimmy Graham is an American football tight end who entered the NFL after playing college basketball. He spent four years on the basketball team at the University of Miami and played only one season of college football before being selected in the third round of the 2010 draft by the New Orleans Saints. Graham quickly became a major receiving target because of his height, leaping ability, and experience positioning himself near the basket. In his second professional season he caught 99 passes for more than 1,300 yards and 11 touchdowns, earning Pro Bowl and All-Pro honors. He later played for the Seattle Seahawks, Green Bay Packers, and Chicago Bears. Graham set several New Orleans receiving records and became one of the first tight ends in franchise history to exceed 1,000 yards in a season. He also worked with youth basketball and football programs during the offseason.

Michael A. Shevchenko is a former American competitive swimmer who won a bronze medal in the 200-metre backstroke at an international championship in the late 1990s. At Harvard he became one of the university’s most decorated individual-medley swimmers, earning repeated first-team All-American honors and winning several Ivy League titles. Shevchenko received the conference’s award for swimmer of the meet on multiple occasions and was later inducted into the Harvard Varsity Club Hall of Fame. After completing his swimming career, he entered sports business and joined a media-rights advisory firm at its founding. He has worked on negotiations and strategic projects involving professional football, baseball, motorsport, tennis, mixed martial arts, hockey, youth sports, video games, and digital platforms. His deals have been valued in the billions of dollars, and a sports-business publication named him to its annual list of promising executives.

The magnetosheath is the region between a planet’s bow shock and magnetopause. Solar-wind plasma is compressed as it crosses the bow shock, then flows around the planet through the sheath before encountering the stronger magnetic boundary that separates it from the magnetosphere. The magnetic field in the sheath is weaker and more disordered than the undisturbed interplanetary field, and its density is higher than in the upstream solar wind but lower than in many regions inside the magnetopause. Spacecraft observations show that the region is not merely a passive layer produced by two boundaries. It contains waves, turbulence, vortices, current sheets, and changes in particle temperature that can influence the shape of both the bow shock and magnetopause. The magnetosheath may also control how energetic particles cross into or escape from a planetary magnetosphere.

Cylia Vabre is a French swimmer who specialized in the individual medley. She represented France in the 200-metre event at the 2008 Olympic Games and trained with a Lyon club under coach Richard Martinez. Vabre earned her Olympic place after finishing second at the national championships, recording a time below the qualifying standard. In the Olympic heats she swam strongly during the butterfly leg and held an early lead, but lost ground during the breaststroke and freestyle portions. She finished seventh in her heat and twenty-first overall, missing the semifinals. Vabre had previously won medals at domestic championships and was regarded as one of the country’s promising medley swimmers. She remained with her club after the Games and later worked with junior swimmers while completing studies in sports management.

Picada is a finishing mixture and cooking technique used in Catalan and Valencian cuisine. It is not usually served as an independent sauce; instead, a small amount is added near the end of cooking to thicken a dish and combine its flavors. Garlic, parsley, saffron, and toasted nuts are common ingredients, which are ground together in a mortar before being loosened with stock, wine, or cooking liquid. Other versions include cinnamon, bread, chocolate, herbs, or the cooked liver of a chicken or rabbit. Picada can be stirred into stews of meat or fish, rice dishes, beans, vegetables, and soups. The mixture helps emulsify the juices and gives the finished dish a concentrated aroma. Recipes differ between households and regions, and cooks may prepare a rough or smooth paste depending on the texture desired.

Dalí Jewels is a permanent exhibition of jewelry and designs associated with the Spanish artist Salvador Dalí. It occupies a building attached to the Dalí Theatre-Museum in Figueres, which was redesigned by architect Òscar Tusquets to provide separate galleries and an independent entrance. The collection includes gold and gemstone jewelry commissioned from the former Owen Cheatham collection, later additions, and drawings and paintings that show how Dalí developed the pieces. The works date from the 1940s through the 1970s and include brooches, pendants, watches, crosses, and objects with moving parts. The Gala-Salvador Dalí Foundation acquired the collection from a Japanese organization and prepared it for public display with advice from gemologists and conservators. The exhibition presents the jewelry alongside Dalí’s sketches, emphasizing the relationship between his surrealist imagery and the practical work of fabrication.

Brandon Michaels is a Latin freestyle and pop singer from San Jose, California. He led a vocal and dance group that became known on American radio during the early 1990s. The group’s best-known single, “Kisses in the Night,” was released by an independent label distributed through a major company and reached the lower half of the Billboard Hot 100. The track used layered background vocals and a polished dance arrangement, with session musicians contributing guitar and additional production. Michaels followed it with the club single “Destiny,” which received strong play on regional dance stations even though it did not match the chart performance of the first hit. The group performed in California and on touring packages with other freestyle acts before its members moved into separate projects. Michaels later worked as a songwriter and vocal coach.

Midtown Sacramento is a historic neighborhood immediately east of downtown Sacramento, California. Its commonly recognized boundaries extend from R Street to J Street and from 16th Street toward Alhambra Boulevard, although residents use a broader definition that includes parts of the original city grid. The area is largely residential and contains tree-lined streets, Victorian houses, apartment buildings, and converted commercial spaces. Midtown has become a center for restaurants, galleries, music venues, boutiques, and neighborhood bars, and it hosts a monthly art walk that draws visitors from across the metropolitan area. A small winery and several craft businesses operate among the older buildings. The southern portion includes a historic Asian American community and businesses associated with generations of immigrant residents. Midtown’s combination of preserved housing and active nightlife has made it one of Sacramento’s most recognizable districts.

Kobi Libii is an American comedian, actor, and writer from Fort Wayne, Indiana. He became known as a correspondent on a Comedy Central news-satire program, where he appeared as a fictional citizen journalist who investigated politics and popular culture. Libii has also acted in television dramas and comedies and performed in theatre productions in New York and Chicago. He helped create the documentary-style play Boiling Pot, which premiered at the Cherry Lane Theatre and explored race, identity, and public argument through interviews and staged scenes. Other stage credits include a production of Really Really and several improvisational performances. Libii graduated from Yale University, where he studied theatre and performed with an improv troupe, and later trained at Second City. His television appearances have included ensemble roles in series about law, college life, and political offices.

Internal devaluation is a policy intended to lower a country’s domestic costs and restore the competitiveness of its exports without changing the official exchange rate. Governments may pursue it through wage reductions, lower employer contributions, public-sector cuts, tax changes, or reforms that reduce the cost of production. The approach is most often discussed when a country belongs to a currency union or maintains a fixed exchange rate and therefore cannot use a conventional currency devaluation. Supporters argue that lower costs can improve trade balances and public finances, while critics contend that the policy places the burden of adjustment on workers and can deepen unemployment and recession. Internal devaluation became a prominent subject during the European financial crisis of the late 2000s and early 2010s. Its results depend on the speed of adjustment, the condition of domestic demand, and whether other members of the currency area provide fiscal support.

A license is an official authorization that permits a person or organization to perform an activity, use property, or exercise a right that would otherwise be restricted. A public authority may issue a license after an application, examination, inspection, or payment of a fee. A private owner or rights holder may grant one through a written contract between a licensor and licensee. The document often identifies the permitted conduct, its duration, geographic limits, conditions, and the consequences of breach. In legal shorthand, a license is sometimes described as a promise not to sue because it permits an act that might otherwise violate a property, copyright, trademark, or regulatory rule. Driving, fishing, broadcasting, copying software, and manufacturing patented products can all require licenses, although the legal effects differ between public permits and private agreements.

Matteo De Luca is a Belgian professional footballer who plays as a forward or winger. He developed in the youth systems of Leuven, Anderlecht, and Gent before making his senior debut on loan to a third-division club. De Luca moved to the Netherlands in 2007 and spent several seasons with a first-division side, where his pace and ability to cut inside attracted larger clubs. He transferred to Utrecht and later joined PSV Eindhoven with a teammate for a combined fee. After winning a domestic cup and super cup, he signed for Napoli and became a regular in the attacking rotation. De Luca has scored more than 100 goals for the Italian club and has represented Belgium in European and World Cup competition. He was selected for the league’s team of the year after a season in which he combined goals with a high number of assists.

IPA Braille is a system for representing the symbols of the International Phonetic Alphabet in braille. Early versions were developed for blind language students in the 1930s, but the notation became difficult to maintain as the printed IPA changed and different countries adopted incompatible conventions. A revised system was issued in North America during the 1990s, while a later international revision returned to the older consonant and vowel mappings and redesigned the treatment of diacritics. In the current notation, many marks follow the base letter rather than preceding it, making sequences easier to read and type consistently. The system allows detailed descriptions of speech sounds, but support for tone and some unusual diacritics remains incomplete. Braille authorities continue to revise the standard as the printed alphabet gains new symbols and as teachers develop more practical ways to represent phonetic transcription.

Dolph is an unincorporated community in Tillamook County, Oregon, near the border with Yamhill County. It lies along the Little Nestucca River where two state routes meet in the Northern Oregon Coast Range.
