The settlement began as a toll gate and travelers’ stop on a stage road linking the Willamette Valley with the coast. A toll road constructed in the late nineteenth century brought freight wagons, timber workers, and settlers through the mountain pass. The post office opened in the 1880s, followed by a school and a small collection of businesses. At its busiest the community included a hotel, store, sawmill, barrel factory, livery stable, blacksmith shop, and campground. Some of the original townsite later fell on the opposite side of a revised county boundary. The area is now surrounded by forest and is used mainly by travelers, recreationists, and residents of nearby rural properties.

The Jones Cup is an international basketball tournament held annually in Taiwan and organized by the Chinese Taipei Basketball Association. It was established in the late 1970s and named for Renato William Jones, an early administrator of the International Basketball Federation. Separate men’s and women’s competitions are held, and the field may include national teams, professional clubs, university teams, and representative selections. The tournament is not equivalent in prestige to the Olympics or the FIBA World Cup, but it attracts teams seeking preparation for continental and world competitions. Asian teams form the largest part of the field, while clubs and national sides from North America, Europe, Africa, and Oceania have also participated. The men’s event has frequently been won by American teams, while the women’s title has been shared among teams from South Korea, Taiwan, and the United States.

Path tracing is a Monte Carlo rendering technique that estimates the light reaching each pixel by following many possible paths through a three-dimensional scene. A ray is sent from the camera into the scene, where it may reflect, refract, or be absorbed by a surface. At each interaction the renderer samples another direction according to the material’s reflectance and eventually connects the path to a light source or terminates it. Repeating the process produces an estimate of global illumination, although too few samples create visible noise. Because the method treats direct and indirect light within the same framework, it naturally produces soft shadows, reflections, refractions, depth of field, motion blur, ambient occlusion, and caustics. Physically based materials and cameras can yield images that closely resemble photographs. Volumetric path tracing extends the method to fog, smoke, clouds, and other media in which light is scattered through a volume rather than only at a surface.

Antarctica is the southernmost continent and surrounds the geographic South Pole. Almost all of its land lies south of the Antarctic Circle, and a vast ice sheet covers the underlying mountains, plateaus, and basins. The continent is bordered by the Southern Ocean and is nearly twice the size of Australia. Most precipitation falls near the coast; the interior is an extremely cold polar desert where snowfall accumulates slowly and remains frozen for centuries. Research stations operate throughout the year, although their populations decline sharply during the long winter night. Penguins, seals, seabirds, microscopic invertebrates, and hardy algae are among the native organisms, while vegetation is concentrated along the milder coast and Antarctic Peninsula. Antarctica contains a large share of the world’s fresh water in the form of ice, and changes in its ice shelves and glaciers influence global sea levels and ocean circulation.

Göran Bertil Lagerberg is a Swedish musician and songwriter known for playing bass and sharing lead vocals in the rock band Tages. He joined the group in the early 1960s when it was still a skiffle ensemble and changed from washboard to bass as the members adopted beat music. Lagerberg became one of the band’s principal songwriters and contributed many of its original recordings, including material on the album Studio. He was the only member to remain with the group throughout its changing names and lineups until its dissolution around 1970. Lagerberg later played with the progressive rock group Kebnekajse and joined the Swedish supergroup Grymlings during the 1990s. His work with Tages has been cited as an important contribution to Swedish rock of the 1960s, particularly for combining British beat influences with more ambitious studio arrangements.

Darron Gee is an English former footballer and coach who worked mainly in non-league football. After playing for Hucknall Town, he entered management with Dunkirk and led the club to promotion in the mid-1990s. Gee later became assistant to manager Gary Mills at Grantham Town, King’s Lynn, and Tamworth. When he took charge of Tamworth, the club won the Southern League Premier Division and reached the final of the FA Trophy before securing its place in the Football Conference. Gee returned to assistant-management roles with Mills at Notts County and Alfreton Town and followed him back to Tamworth. The pair won the Conference North title in 2009 and moved to York City the following year. At York, they achieved promotion through the Conference Premier play-offs and won the FA Trophy. Gee left the club in 2013 and later worked in coaching and scouting.

Ovation Hollywood is a shopping, dining, and entertainment complex at the intersection of Hollywood Boulevard and Highland Avenue in Los Angeles. Formerly known as Hollywood & Highland, it includes the TCL Chinese Theatre, the Dolby Theatre, and a range of restaurants, shops, cinemas, and public spaces. The Dolby Theatre hosts the Academy Awards and other large televised ceremonies, while the Chinese Theatre remains associated with film premieres and the handprints and footprints of actors. The complex stands on the former site of the Hollywood Hotel and forms part of the Hollywood Walk of Fame’s main tourist area. Its central courtyard was inspired by the Babylon set in D. W. Griffith’s film Intolerance and includes monumental arches and elephant sculptures. Upper terraces provide views toward the Hollywood Sign, the Santa Monica Mountains, and downtown Los Angeles.

The Red River Jig is a fiddle tune and social dance associated with the Métis of the Canadian Prairies and with neighboring First Nations communities. Its history reflects the meeting of Indigenous, French Canadian, Scottish, English, and Orcadian traditions during the nineteenth-century fur trade. The name refers to the Red River, which runs north from the United States through Manitoba toward Hudson Bay. Dancers commonly combine quick footwork, heel-and-toe steps, turns, and gestures that can be performed by one person or by a pair. Regional versions differ in tempo and sequence, and the dance is often taught at community gatherings, festivals, and cultural workshops. Although the melody is called a jig, its rhythmic structure is closer to a reel. Fiddlers may add variations while dancers improvise steps within a shared pattern.

Brennan Howard is an American actor, writer, producer, and director. He has appeared in independent films and television projects and has written, produced, or directed several low-budget features. His early credits include a comedy about a fictional advertising executive and a fantasy film set in an imagined museum, followed by a political satire released in the early 2000s. Howard also performed voice work for an animated children’s program and briefly hosted a television show about video games. His first feature as director, Quiet Hours, premiered at a regional independent-film festival and received praise for its restrained performances, dark humor, and careful pacing. Howard works through a small production company that also serves as a repertory acting troupe, allowing him to develop projects with a recurring group of performers and technicians.

Maya L. Rivers is an American dancer, choreographer, director, and teacher. She founded Rivers Movement and has created commissioned works for modern-dance companies, universities, music festivals, and Broadway productions. Rivers began her performing career with a New York repertory company and later appeared as a guest artist with ensembles specializing in hip-hop, African diasporic dance, and contemporary ballet. Her choreography for the stage has included revivals, new musicals, and dance-driven concert pieces, while her film and television work has explored the relationship between movement, memory, and public history. Rivers teaches workshops and gives lectures at colleges and arts organizations throughout the United States. Her company partnered with a digital-arts project to create an online series about Black history through choreography, combining archival images with filmed performances in museums and historic buildings.

The McLaren MP4-15 was the car used by the McLaren Formula One team during the 2000 World Championship. It was driven by Mika Häkkinen, the reigning champion, and David Coulthard, who had been with the team for several seasons. The car was developed after a change in the technical department and the departure of several engineers who had helped create McLaren’s earlier championship winners. It used a Mercedes-Benz engine and retained the team’s silver-and-black color scheme, but introduced revised aerodynamic sidepods, a narrower rear body, and a new electronic traction-control system. Reliability problems affected the opening races, and the team spent much of the season pursuing Ferrari in the constructors’ standings. Häkkinen won several Grands Prix, while Coulthard’s consistent finishes helped McLaren remain in contention until the final rounds.

Thomas Edward Abernathy was an American professional baseball pitcher whose career included parts of three seasons in Major League Baseball during the 1940s. He appeared for the Philadelphia Athletics, recording a 1–4 record and a high earned-run average in a small number of games. Abernathy batted and threw right-handed and spent most of his career in the minor leagues. He played for clubs in Delaware, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Virginia and won 82 games against 70 losses in 250 minor-league appearances. His best season came with a Double-A team in Memphis, where he combined a sinking fastball with a curve and completed several games. Abernathy also managed two minor-league clubs during the 1948 season, balancing pitching with lineup and roster decisions. He left professional baseball after the following year and returned to work in a family business.

George Ezekiel Kerr was a Jamaican middle-distance runner who competed in the 400 and 800 metres. He won bronze medals in the 800 metres and 4×400-metre relay at the 1960 Olympic Games while representing the British West Indies. Two years later he won both events at the Central American and Caribbean Games in Kingston, becoming the first Jamaican athlete to have the national flag raised for an individual victory at that competition. At the 1964 Olympics he represented independent Jamaica and finished fourth in the 800 metres and in the relay. Kerr set an Olympic record in his semifinal but narrowly missed the medal in the final, running the fastest time of his career. He was known for a strong finish and for alternating between the two events during a meet. After retiring, he coached young runners and worked in Jamaican athletics administration.

Earle Mankey is an American guitarist, record producer, and audio engineer. He helped form the band Halfnelson, later known as Sparks, and engineered some of its earliest demonstration recordings. Mankey’s studio career expanded as he produced and recorded Los Angeles-area groups working in punk, power pop, new wave, and alternative rock. His credits include records by The Pop, 20/20, The Runaways, Concrete Blonde, The Long Ryders, and The Three O’Clock. Before gaining access to professional studios, Mankey built tracks at home with two small reel-to-reel tape machines. He recorded a part onto one machine, played it back into the second while adding another instrument, and repeated the process until a backing track was complete. The method introduced tape hiss and generation loss but allowed the young band to create dense arrangements with limited equipment. Mankey’s brother James later became a guitarist in Concrete Blonde.

Paul St. Pierre was a Canadian journalist, novelist, and politician from British Columbia. He represented the riding of Coast Chilcotin in the House of Commons from 1968 to 1972 and lost his seat in a close three-way election. St. Pierre became best known for humorous stories about life in the Chilcotin and Cariboo regions and for a long-running newspaper column about local characters, travel, and politics. One of his novellas was adapted into a feature film starring Glenn Ford and Chief Dan George, who also appeared in a television series based on St. Pierre’s regional stories. He maintained homes in the Chilcotin, the Fraser Valley, and Mexico and continued writing after leaving Parliament. His work combined documentary observation with fictional exaggeration and helped popularize the landscape and communities of interior British Columbia.

Marchantiophyta is a division of nonvascular land plants commonly called liverworts. Liverworts have a life cycle dominated by the gametophyte generation, meaning that the familiar green plant carries a single set of chromosomes while the short-lived sporophyte grows from it. Some species form broad, flattened thalli, but many have leafy shoots that resemble small mosses. Leafy liverworts can often be recognized by their leaves arranged in two or three rows, their single-celled rhizoids, and the absence of a central costa in the leaves. Some have deeply divided leaves or delicate marginal cilia. The group includes thousands of species found in damp forests, wetlands, soil, rock, and tree bark. Their small size and dependence on moisture make them sensitive to drying, but spores and fragments allow many species to colonize shaded habitats.

Viatcheslav Mikhailovich Kharlamov is a Russian-French mathematician whose research combines real algebraic geometry, topology, and the study of four-dimensional manifolds. He studied mathematics at Leningrad State University and completed a doctoral thesis on inequalities involving the Euler characteristic of real algebraic varieties. While conducting research, he taught at a secondary school and later held professorships in northern Russia and at a technical institute in Leningrad. Kharlamov received a higher doctoral degree for work on surfaces and algebraic constructions in three-dimensional space. He moved to France in the early 1990s and became a professor at the University of Strasbourg, where he joined the Institute for Advanced Mathematical Research. His publications examine the topology of real and complex varieties, algebraic surfaces, and the ways in which geometric structures constrain numerical invariants.

The Joseph R. Biden Railroad Station, commonly called Wilmington station, is a passenger railway station in Wilmington, Delaware. It lies on Amtrak’s Northeast Corridor and is served by intercity trains, SEPTA commuter services, local buses, and intercity coaches. The station opened in the early twentieth century as Pennsylvania Station and contains a waiting hall, ticket offices, shops, restrooms, and access to elevated platforms above the concourse. It was renamed in honor of Joe Biden, a longtime Delaware senator who regularly traveled by train between Wilmington and Washington. Biden used the station for campaign events and public appearances, including the announcement of an unsuccessful presidential campaign. The building is one of the busiest rail stops in Delaware and remains an important link between the state’s largest city, Philadelphia, Baltimore, and Washington.

Antaeotricha rubrogrisea is a moth in the family Depressariidae recorded from French Guiana. Its wingspan is about 22 mm. The forewings are pale grey-ochre with a slight pink cast and a wash of greenish grey across the disc. The costal edge is yellowish from the base to the middle, interrupted by a dark rust-colored dash above the center. Two dark discal spots are present, the second larger and set at an angle. A series of indistinct reddish marks runs from the costa toward the second stigma and then descends to the dorsum. Another slender streak follows the outer costal curve, while cloudy dots form an arc from the upper margin toward the lower edge before the tornus. Small dark points continue around the apical margin. The hindwings are grey and contain a deep groove near the middle that encloses a long, expandable hair pencil of pale ochre scales.

Hugo Baum was a German botanist who collected plants and animals in southern Africa and Mexico. He joined an expedition to the Cunene and Zambezi regions at the turn of the twentieth century, documenting the economic potential of southern Angola while assembling extensive botanical and zoological collections. After returning to Germany, Baum settled in Rostock and worked at the university’s botanical garden. He helped develop the institution despite limited resources and introduced specimens collected during his African travels. In his late fifties he undertook a second major journey to Mexico, where he described additional plants and contributed to the study of regional flora. Several genera and species were named in his honor, including a mushroom genus, a flowering-plant genus, a butterfly, and two ants. Baum’s notebooks and preserved specimens remained useful to later researchers studying the distribution of tropical and subtropical plants.

The Robinson was a Brass Era automobile manufactured in Massachusetts by the Robinson Motor Vehicle Company. The firm developed from a machinery business that had experimented with small three-wheeled cars before producing automobiles under the Robinson name. It joined the Pope group of companies in 1902, but production ended two years later. The 1904 Robinson touring car carried five passengers in an open tonneau body and sold for approximately $5,000. It used a front-mounted, water-cooled four-cylinder engine producing about 24 horsepower, a three-speed sliding-gear transmission, and a channel-steel frame. The car’s radiator and chassis followed the contemporary Panhard layout and were marketed as evidence of modern engineering. Its price placed it in competition with expensive European automobiles, but the limited production run and the consolidation of the Pope companies prevented the model from developing a lasting market.

Corin Braga is a Romanian scholar, novelist, and professor of comparative literature. He teaches at Babeș-Bolyai University in Cluj-Napoca, where he has served as dean of the Faculty of Letters and directs a center devoted to the study of imagination. He also edits an academic journal concerned with comparative literature and cultural myth. Braga’s fiction includes a series of novels written in the Romanian Oniric tradition, a style that uses dream structures, unstable identities, and transitions between waking and imagined worlds. Three volumes of the series appeared during the 1990s and 2010s, with a fourth announced for later publication. He has published studies of utopian literature, dream diaries, and the history of Romanian literary movements. One of his collections of dreams received a national literature festival’s grand prize, and he has held leadership roles in Romanian and international organizations devoted to comparative literature.

The Index Translationum is a UNESCO bibliographic database recording translations of books published around the world. An international register was begun under the League of Nations in the 1930s and transferred to UNESCO after the Second World War. The records were converted to computerized form near the end of the twentieth century and can be searched by author, title, language, subject, and country of publication. Because the database counts translated editions rather than unique literary works, rankings require interpretation. An author with many books translated a few times may appear above an author with one book translated into many languages. Corporate names, pseudonyms, and authors with similar spellings can also be grouped inconsistently. The Index is therefore useful for tracing patterns in international publishing but should not be treated as a precise measure of literary influence or the number of languages represented by a single work.

Fallingwater is a house designed by the American architect Frank Lloyd Wright for the Kaufmann family near Mill Run, Pennsylvania. Constructed between 1936 and 1939, it is built above a waterfall rather than facing it from a distant overlook. Reinforced-concrete terraces project over the stream, while local stone walls connect the house to the surrounding forest and rock ledges. Wright designed the building as an example of organic architecture, using horizontal lines, cantilevered forms, and large windows to make the interior feel continuous with the landscape. Fallingwater became one of his most celebrated works and influenced later architects interested in integrating buildings with natural sites. The house is now operated as a museum and receives visitors for guided tours, exhibitions, and educational programs. In 2019 it was included with several other Wright buildings on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

Class-size reduction is an educational policy intended to increase the amount of individual attention a teacher can give each student. Supporters argue that smaller classes improve participation, classroom management, early literacy, and the ability to identify learning difficulties. Critics emphasize the expense of hiring additional teachers, constructing classrooms, and maintaining lower enrollment in each section, and some studies have found only modest effects when reductions are too small or poorly implemented. The best-known research includes Tennessee’s Project STAR and later experiments in Wisconsin and other states. Results from these projects suggested that large reductions in the first years of schooling could improve later academic outcomes, including advanced-course enrollment and college attendance. Effects vary according to grade level, teacher quality, class composition, and whether schools use the additional capacity for individualized instruction rather than simply placing the same lessons in a smaller room.

The Euphiletos Painter was an Attic black-figure vase painter active in Athens during the second half of the sixth century BCE. He is best known for Panathenaic prize amphorae, which depict Athena on one side and an athletic contest on the other. His early figures are often stiff and arranged in poses that do not fully correspond to the movement they are meant to show, but later works display greater control of anatomy, clothing, and internal detail. Shield devices, runners, wrestlers, and chariot teams provided opportunities for increasingly complex decoration. The painter also produced ordinary amphorae and other vessels, although these are generally considered less accomplished and often repeat popular scenes of racing. His style developed while red-figure painting was becoming dominant, and some of his later work shows an awareness of the new technique. He collaborated with potters including Pamphaios.

The Fizeau experiment was performed in 1851 to determine whether moving water changed the measured speed of light passing through it. Hippolyte Fizeau sent light through a flowing column of water and used an interferometer to compare the returning beams. A simple theory in which the water completely carried the light along predicted a larger shift than the one observed. Fizeau detected a partial dragging effect, approximately matching a correction proposed by the physicist Augustin-Louis Cauchy, while a repetition using air produced no measurable result. The experiment was difficult to interpret within nineteenth-century theories of the ether and led to extended debate about how motion affected light in a transparent medium. Special relativity later explained the result through its rule for adding velocities. Einstein cited the experiment as an important predecessor to the modern understanding of light propagation.

The concept of a national treasure belongs to the language of romantic nationalism, which treats a nation as a community bound by shared history, language, artistic traditions, and symbols. A national treasure may be a building, manuscript, painting, song, landscape, craft, or living person whose importance is understood to exceed private ownership or market price. Governments often create legal categories to protect such objects, restrict their export, or fund their conservation. Japan designates especially significant cultural properties as National Treasures, while South Korea maintains a comparable register of artifacts, sites, and buildings. The phrase can also be used informally for an admired performer, athlete, teacher, or craftsperson whose knowledge is considered part of the public heritage. National-treasure programs preserve culture, but they also reflect decisions about which communities and traditions a state chooses to represent.

Oakland University is a public research university in the suburbs north of Detroit, Michigan. It operates campuses in Rochester Hills and Auburn Hills and offers undergraduate, graduate, professional, and doctoral programs in the arts, sciences, engineering, business, education, and health professions. The university began in 1957 when philanthropists Matilda and Alfred Wilson donated their estate and a substantial endowment to Michigan State University for the creation of a regional campus. The former estate included Meadow Brook Hall, a Tudor Revival mansion that remains one of the centerpieces of the campus and is open as a historic house museum. Oakland later became an independent university and expanded its research institutes, residence halls, athletic facilities, and medical partnerships. It is classified among American doctoral universities with high research activity and is one of the largest public institutions in the Detroit metropolitan area.

William Wilfred Cobey was an American university administrator who served as athletic director at the University of Maryland during the 1950s and 1960s. Born in Florida, he attended Maryland and played on the freshman lacrosse team before earning a degree from the university’s College of Arts and Sciences. He worked in athletic administration and became graduate manager before being appointed director in 1956. Cobey supervised the hiring and dismissal of coaches in football, baseball, and track and oversaw the expansion of Maryland’s intercollegiate program. During his tenure the university changed football coaches several times, including appointments of Lou Saban and Bob Ward, while baseball coach Jack Jackson established a long-running program. Cobey retired from the athletic-director position in the late 1960s and was succeeded by a track coach who had served on the university staff.

The Metre Convention is an international treaty concerning standards of measurement. It was signed in Paris in 1875 by representatives of seventeen countries and created the International Bureau of Weights and Measures. The agreement established a permanent framework through which governments could cooperate on the definition, comparison, and dissemination of units used in science, trade, and industry. The bureau maintains reference standards, coordinates international experiments, and supports the work of the General Conference on Weights and Measures and the International Committee for Weights and Measures. The treaty also specifies how member states contribute to the organization and participate in decisions about metrology. Although the metric system existed before the convention, the agreement gave it an enduring international administrative structure and helped make measurements comparable across national borders.

The McLaren F1 is a British three-seat sports car produced during the 1990s by McLaren Cars. It was designed as a road-going expression of the company’s racing experience, with a central driving position, a lightweight carbon-fiber monocoque, and a naturally aspirated V12 engine. The car’s development was led by Gordon Murray, who emphasized low mass, compact dimensions, and direct driver involvement rather than electronic assistance. A prototype and racing version competed in endurance events, and a modified F1 GTR won the 24 Hours of Le Mans in 1995. The road car set speed records during testing and was briefly recognized as the world’s fastest production automobile. Production was limited to a small number of road cars, long-tail models, and racing derivatives. Its combination of engineering innovation, scarcity, and high price made it one of the most influential supercars of its era.

The Great Rift is a broad lane of dark interstellar dust that obscures much of the Milky Way when viewed from Earth. It extends across the sky between the Solar System and the inner regions of the galaxy, where dense clouds lie along the plane of the galactic disk. At dark-sky locations the rift appears as a broken black band cutting through the brighter haze of the Milky Way. The dust absorbs and scatters visible light from millions of background stars, while infrared and radio observations reveal structures hidden behind it. Individual clouds within the rift contain cold gas, dust, and sites where new stars may eventually form. The apparent darkness is therefore not an empty gap but the result of material between the observer and the luminous central regions of the galaxy. The feature is easiest to see during summer nights in the Northern Hemisphere.

A jog dial is a control used to move slowly and precisely through recorded audio or video, while a shuttle control moves rapidly through the material in either direction. The device may be a freely rotating wheel, a ring around another control, or a spring-loaded dial with fixed positions for several speeds. In an incremental design, the electronics measure the direction and rate at which the wheel turns and translate that movement into frame-by-frame stepping, fast-forwarding, or rewinding. A spring-centered design returns to a neutral position when released and may pause playback or resume normal speed. Jog and shuttle controls are common on professional video recorders, editing consoles, DJ equipment, and some older compact-disc players. Similar behavior appears in the scroll wheels and rotary encoders used by computers and handheld devices.

Hampden County is a county in western Massachusetts, United States, centered on the lower Connecticut River Valley. Its traditional county seat is Springfield, the largest city in the region and a major center for education, health care, manufacturing, and culture. The county was created from Hampshire County in 1812 after Springfield and neighboring towns had grown into an urban and commercial district separate from Northampton. It was named for the English parliamentarian John Hampden. Hampden County borders Hampshire, Berkshire, and Worcester counties in Massachusetts and several counties in Connecticut. The area includes dense urban neighborhoods, former mill towns, suburban communities, and rural hills. It forms part of the Springfield metropolitan area and of the broader Knowledge Corridor linking western Massachusetts with Hartford, Connecticut. County government was abolished, but the county name remains in use for courts, public services, and regional institutions.

Q.931 is an ITU-T signaling protocol used by Integrated Services Digital Network systems to establish, maintain, and release circuit-switched calls. It operates on the D channel and exchanges messages between network terminals and switching equipment, identifying events such as call setup, alerting, connection, clearing, and release. The protocol includes a state machine that describes how a device responds to each message and transition. Q.931 normally carries control information rather than the user’s voice or data and assumes that lower layers provide reliable transmission. ISDN allocates bearer channels in fixed units, commonly 64 kbit/s, so Q.931 does not perform the kind of congestion control or retransmission associated with Internet transport protocols. Variants of the signaling system were later incorporated into H.323 voice-over-IP networks, mobile telephone systems, and some asynchronous-transfer-mode equipment.

Andrew John Procter is an English cricketer who represented Devon in minor counties and one-day cricket. A right-handed batsman and right-arm off-break bowler, he was born in Preston and made his first appearance for Devon against Herefordshire in 1996. Procter returned to the county in 2000 and played in championship, knockout, and List A matches over the following seasons. He appeared in ten List A games, scoring 114 runs at an average of 28.50 and making a highest score of 29 not out. With the ball he took 14 wickets, including figures of three for 26. His final List A appearance came against Essex in a domestic cup match at Exmouth in 2005. Procter continued to play club cricket and contributed to the development of younger players in Devon after leaving the county side.

The piccolo is a small transverse flute belonging to the woodwind family. It has fingering patterns similar to those of the concert flute but sounds one octave above the written notes. The instrument is usually made of wood, resin, or metal and may have a conical or cylindrical bore depending on the model. In an orchestra, the piccolo can reinforce violin or flute lines, add brilliance to climaxes, or imitate birds and other high sounds. Because its tone carries strongly over large ensembles, the player must control intonation and volume carefully. Some orchestral parts are assigned to a combined third-flute and piccolo player, while large wind bands normally include a separate piccolo part. Italian scores may call the instrument ottavino, meaning “little octave.” Its small size makes it portable, but the high register can be demanding to play accurately.

Klingon is a constructed language created for the fictional Klingon people in the Star Trek universe. Linguist Marc Okrand developed its grammar and vocabulary for film and television productions, shaping the language to sound unlike the major natural languages spoken by the actors. Klingon uses a distinctive word order, a system of suffixes attached to nouns and verbs, and sounds chosen to give the speech a harsh, unfamiliar quality. Early appearances used only a small number of phrases, but later publications expanded the vocabulary and described the grammar in enough detail for fans to study and use it. The language has inspired dictionaries, translations, clubs, online courses, theatrical performances, and original songs. Although it was designed for a fictional culture, speakers have used Klingon in conversation and correspondence outside the Star Trek productions.

The Way of Faith is a Christian devotional book written by the American religious teacher Clara M. Hart. First published in 1898, it was issued by a Protestant publishing house and later acquired by the author’s denomination for wider distribution. A revised opening chapter was added for a British edition, after which the book was printed in numerous languages and circulated through churches, schools, and missionary organizations. The text presents a practical account of conversion and religious life, discussing repentance, confession, trust, prayer, spiritual growth, and the believer’s relationship with Jesus. Rather than offering a systematic theological treatise, Hart writes in short chapters intended for personal reading and reflection. The book became her best-known work and was repeatedly reprinted in inexpensive editions. It continues to be used as an introductory devotional text within the denomination and among readers interested in nineteenth-century Protestant spirituality.

The Stefan problem is a mathematical model for a moving boundary between phases, especially the interface between ice and water during freezing or melting. It describes heat diffusion in the regions occupied by the solid and liquid and imposes a condition at the boundary that relates the speed of the interface to the latent heat released or absorbed during the phase change. The boundary is not known in advance; its position must be solved along with the temperature field. The problem takes its name from Josef Stefan, who studied the growth of ice and the thickness of frozen ground in the nineteenth century. Variants are used to model crystal growth, alloy solidification, snow formation, melting glaciers, and industrial casting. The equations are difficult because the domain changes with time and because the temperature and heat flux must satisfy conditions on an unknown surface.

Eutorna aurantivitta is a species of moth in the family Depressariidae endemic to New Zealand. Its wingspan is about 12 mm. The forewings are deep reddish brown with a curved yellow-white streak running from the base toward the middle of the disc. The lower edge of this streak is bordered in black, while brighter ochre scales extend upward toward the costa. A narrow white diagonal mark begins near the outer costa and ends in the central disc, enclosing a triangular patch of purple-grey and pale scales. A dark spot at two-thirds of the wing is surrounded by a yellowish ring. Additional purple scales occur along the inner margin, and a small white costal mark near the apex is followed by a dark suffusion. The hindmargin carries an irregular pale streak and scattered black scales. The hindwings are dark bronze-fuscous.

Record A.E.B.E. was a Greek manufacturer of agricultural machinery and small utility vehicles founded in Heraklion, Crete, during the 1950s. The company began with walking tractors and later built three-wheeled machines that combined the functions of a light truck and a farm tractor. It introduced conventional tractors during the 1970s and expanded into four-wheeled utility vehicles and mechanical components such as clutches, transmissions, and gearboxes. Most products were sold in Greece, although some walking tractors were exported to neighboring countries. Annual production reached several hundred vehicles in the late 1970s and early 1980s. Its most powerful tractor used a small diesel engine, while a later fiberglass-bodied truck carried approximately two tonnes and used a Peugeot diesel engine. The company ceased operations near the end of the twentieth century.

The Fujifilm FinePix S5 Pro is a digital single-lens reflex camera introduced in 2006 and later discontinued. It uses the Nikon F mount and is built around a body derived from the Nikon D200, providing an eleven-point autofocus system, i-TTL flash control, a larger rear display, and a rechargeable lithium-ion battery. Its Super CCD sensor combines high- and low-sensitivity photodiodes to produce a wider dynamic range than many cameras of the same period. The camera offers sensitivity settings extending to ISO 3200, face detection during image review, and a live-view mode for composing or focusing without the optical viewfinder. It can be operated while tethered to a computer and supports accessories such as barcode readers and wired or wireless network links. The S5 Pro was marketed especially to portrait and wedding photographers who valued its skin tones and highlight detail.

The Hundred of Axminster was a historic administrative division in Devon, England, whose origins lay in the Anglo-Saxon period. A hundred combined several ancient parishes for judicial, fiscal, and military purposes, and its court handled disputes, land matters, and the enforcement of the frankpledge system. Local residents could also be called into the fyrd, the territorial defense force. The hundred took its name from the town of Axminster, where meetings were held and records were presented. It included the parishes of Axminster, Membury, Chardstock, Hawkchurch, Seaton, Shute, Stockland, Kilmington, Dalwood, and neighboring rural settlements. By the nineteenth century the hundred court had lost most of its practical authority as county and parish institutions took over its functions. The name survived in legal, historical, and antiquarian descriptions of the district.

The Pine Ridge Formation is a Late Triassic geological unit exposed in the Deep River Basin of North Carolina. It forms one of the upper parts of the basin’s Mesozoic sequence and lies above darker lake and swamp deposits assigned to an older formation. The unit consists chiefly of coarse red conglomerate, sandstone, and mudstone deposited by rivers and temporary floodplains. Pebbles of schist and slate are common in the conglomerates, while larger granite blocks occur in some channels. The formation is broadly correlated with Triassic strata in the Newark Basin of the northeastern United States. Fossils are scarce in the main Sanford sub-basin but become more common in equivalent layers farther north, where plant fragments, trace fossils, and small vertebrate remains have been recovered. Differences in grain size and fossil abundance reflect changes in the ancient basin’s waterways and lake margins.

A phase-change incubator is a low-cost device for holding microbiological cultures at a nearly constant temperature without electricity. It contains a material that melts when heated and then releases stored heat gradually while returning to a solid state. Once warmed, the phase-change pack is placed in an insulated container with test bottles or culture tubes and can maintain a temperature near 37 °C for roughly a day. The method allows health workers to test water for indicator bacteria in villages, clinics, and other locations without a laboratory incubator or reliable power supply. Engineers have developed versions using reusable waxes and other compounds whose melting points are selected for the desired test. The device was created as part of efforts to make water-quality testing affordable in poor and remote communities. Related designs have been explored for keeping premature infants warm and for transporting temperature-sensitive materials.

The Mansfield Art Center is a community arts organization in Mansfield, Ohio, operated by a nonprofit guild founded in the 1940s. Before it had a permanent building, the guild held exhibitions and classes in libraries, hotels, schools, and other borrowed spaces. Growing enrollment led the organization to appoint a full-time director and seek a dedicated museum and teaching facility. The present building opened in the early 1970s and was designed by architect Don Hisaka, receiving a national architecture citation soon afterward. The center contains galleries, studios, classrooms, and spaces for demonstrations in ceramics, textiles, painting, woodworking, and other crafts. It presents juried exhibitions, hosts visiting artists, and works with local schools and historical organizations. Programs often connect contemporary art with the industrial and social history of the Mansfield area.

The Saskatchewan Huskies football team represents the University of Saskatchewan in U Sports competition. It plays in the Canada West conference and has won the Vanier Cup national championship three times. The Huskies have also claimed more Hardy Trophy conference titles than any other team in Canada West. Saskatchewan reached the national final in three consecutive seasons during the 2000s but lost each game, despite the university hosting one of those championships. The program combines a long-standing varsity tradition with a large community of alumni, coaches, and local supporters. Home games are played in Saskatoon, and the team’s facilities have hosted playoff contests and national events. Saskatchewan was the first western Canadian university to stage the Vanier Cup, and its history includes numerous players who went on to professional football in Canada.

In computing and telecommunications, a control character is a code value that directs a device or software system to perform an action rather than display a visible symbol. In ASCII, the codes below 32 include characters used for line breaks, carriage returns, tabs, alerts, and communication control. The delete code is also traditionally classified as a control character. Extended character sets introduced additional control ranges, including the C1 set, although many of those values have been assigned inconsistently across systems. Control characters may be transmitted in the same stream as ordinary text and are interpreted by the receiving terminal, printer, protocol, or application. A modern text format may replace them with visible escape sequences or restrict them for security reasons. The distinction between control and printable characters depends on the character encoding and the context in which the bytes are processed.

The Belford Historic District is a residential historic district in Georgetown, Texas. It covers several blocks near the older center of town and contains houses built mainly during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Much of the construction was associated with Charles S. Belford, a local lumberman and builder whose work included Queen Anne residences, Prairie-style houses, bungalows, and modified L-plan homes. Of the district’s roughly eighty buildings, most are considered contributing structures because they retain their historic form and materials. Belford’s own Queen Anne house is among the most prominent properties, while other homes were occupied by merchants, judges, and former mayors. The district’s tree-lined streets and varied domestic architecture illustrate the growth of Georgetown as a regional commercial center. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places for its concentration of intact residences.

Lillestrøm Station is a railway station in the town of Lillestrøm, Norway, northeast of Oslo. It lies at the junction of the main line toward Kongsvinger, the Gardermoen line to Oslo Airport, and the route toward the eastern districts. Local, regional, and airport express trains serve the station, which also functions as a major bus interchange. The original station opened in the nineteenth century as part of the railway from Oslo toward the Swedish border. Its early timber building was replaced as traffic increased, and the line was converted to standard gauge and electrified during the twentieth century. The modern station has several platforms, a footbridge, ticket facilities, shops, and a covered bus terminal. Additional tracks and upgraded signaling were installed when high-speed airport services began. Thousands of passengers use the station on weekdays.

The European Animal Welfare Forum is a Brussels-based advocacy organization that campaigns for stronger protections for farmed, companion, laboratory, and wild animals. It represents national animal-protection groups across most European Union member states and maintains contacts with organizations in neighboring countries. The forum supplies research and policy advice to the European Commission, the Council, and the European Parliament and participates in consultations concerning transport, agriculture, scientific testing, and wildlife conservation. Its work emphasizes the recognition of animals as sentient beings and the inclusion of welfare requirements in European legislation. The organization also coordinates a parliamentary group whose members meet regularly to discuss animal protection and conservation. Campaigns have addressed cage systems, long-distance transport, slaughter standards, and the use of animals in research.

Philippe Gilbert is a Belgian professional road cyclist known for success in one-day classics and hilly stage races. He won the world road race championship in 2012 and became one of the few riders to win the three Ardennes classics in a single season. Gilbert has also won the Amstel Gold Race several times, as well as the Tour of Flanders, Paris–Roubaix, Paris–Tours, the Giro di Lombardia, and the Clásica de San Sebastián. He completed a season as overall winner of the UCI World Tour and has frequently been recognized for his ability to attack on steep final climbs. In 2017 he became one of the few riders to win both the Tour of Flanders and Amstel Gold Race in the same year. Gilbert’s career has included victories for several major European teams and a long rivalry with other specialists in one-day racing.

Chris Cagle is an American country singer and songwriter who first gained attention by writing songs for another country performer. He signed with a Nashville label in 2000 and released the album Play It Loud, whose singles included “My Love Goes On and On,” “Laredo,” and a number-one hit about breathing in and out. The album received gold certification, and his next self-titled record produced the top-five songs “What a Beautiful Day” and “Chicks Dig It.” Cagle followed it with Anywhere but Here and My Life’s Been a Country Song, which included the charting single “What Kinda Gone.” After leaving his second major label, he signed with an independent music company and continued touring. Cagle announced his retirement from recording in the mid-2010s, citing family commitments and the demands of life on the road.

The President’s Daily Brief is a classified intelligence report prepared for the president of the United States and a limited group of senior officials. It summarizes information from agencies including the Central Intelligence Agency, the Defense Intelligence Agency, the National Security Agency, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Department of Homeland Security, and allied intelligence services. The brief may describe foreign military activity, terrorism, political developments, covert operations, cyber threats, and urgent risks to American personnel. Analysts combine reports from human sources, signals intelligence, imagery, and diplomatic channels before preparing the document or briefing. Access is controlled by the president and is limited according to security clearance and need to know. A president-elect may receive selected briefings during the transition period, while former presidents may receive access under specific arrangements. The format and delivery method have changed across administrations.

Bowenfels Station is a heritage-listed former railway station on the Main Western line near Lithgow, New South Wales. The sandstone station building and stationmaster’s residence were constructed in 1869 as the railway crossed the Blue Mountains and entered the western interior. The line was electrified during the 1950s as part of the Blue Mountains electrification program, although the planned extension farther west was not completed. Staff were withdrawn in the 1970s, passenger services were reduced, and the station closed after the last remaining service was cut back to Lithgow. The buildings were later restored and adapted as a visitor center and restaurant. The station complex was added to the New South Wales State Heritage Register for its early railway architecture and association with the expansion of transport across the mountains.

The Hickox Apartments are a historic apartment complex in Springfield, Illinois, built in several stages between 1920 and 1929. The development includes row apartments, detached low-rise buildings arranged around courtyards, and larger suburban-style blocks designed for upper-middle-class tenants. It stands near the Illinois Executive Mansion in the Aristocracy Hill neighborhood, an area associated with Springfield’s political and professional elite. Developer Harris Hickox promoted the complex as a prestigious alternative to the city’s more modest rental housing and provided elaborate amenities, lobby attendants, and domestic services. The buildings were among the first local apartments deliberately marketed to wealthy families rather than to workers or students. Their varied plans illustrate the transition from private houses to apartment living during the early twentieth century. The complex was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in the 1980s.

Dwight Le Merton Bolinger was an American linguist and professor of Romance languages and literature at Harvard University. He began his career as an editor of the “Among the New Words” feature in American Speech and later served as president of the American Association of Teachers of Spanish and Portuguese. Bolinger’s research ranged across semantics, intonation, sound symbolism, and the politics of language. His book The Phrasal Verb in English argued that combinations traditionally treated as minor teaching problems deserved systematic linguistic analysis. In Meaning and Form he developed the principle that differences in grammatical form normally correspond to differences in perceived meaning. Bolinger was also known for advising younger scholars and for testing linguistic theories against spoken language rather than relying only on abstract examples. His work influenced the study of English grammar, meaning, and discourse.

Stephen Michael Huntz was an American professional baseball infielder who played in the major leagues for the St. Louis Cardinals, Chicago White Sox, and San Diego Padres. He batted and threw right-handed and attended Villanova University before beginning a professional career that lasted more than a decade. Huntz spent most of his time in the minor leagues, appearing in more than 1,000 Triple-A games and playing primarily in the Pacific Coast League. In the majors he served as a utility infielder, filling in at second base, shortstop, and third base. He was traded by Chicago in a deal involving pitcher Tommy John and later returned to the majors with San Diego after two seasons with the Dodgers’ Albuquerque affiliate. Huntz was valued for his defensive flexibility and steady approach, even though he never became an everyday player.

WSRN-FM is a noncommercial college radio station operated by Swarthmore College in Pennsylvania. It broadcasts from the borough of Swarthmore and serves the campus and surrounding communities. The station began as a carrier-current service heard mainly through college buildings and moved to an FM license in the 1970s. Student organizers later secured permission to increase its power and build a directional transmission system. WSRN’s programming is eclectic, with music shows devoted to world music, hip-hop, blues, folk, rock, pop, rhythm and blues, classical music, and experimental recordings. Students also produce talk, comedy, public-affairs, and specialty programs, especially on weekends and during late-night hours. The station provides training in broadcasting, music programming, engineering, and audio production and has remained an important outlet for local and independent performers.

Louis Jean Jacques Angely was a German playwright, actor, and theatre director who wrote farces and vaudevilles adapted from French models for German audiences. He was born in Leipzig to a family connected with the French Reformed Church and made his stage debut in Stettin in 1808. Angely performed comic roles in Riga, Tallinn, and Jelgava before joining the German court theatre in St. Petersburg. After returning to central Europe, he became an actor-director at Berlin’s Königstädter Theater. He left regular performance in 1830 but continued writing plays and operated an inn in Berlin. His most successful work was the Berlin farce The Craftsmen’s Festival, in which he created the comic role of Foreman Kluck. Angely’s plays were known for topical humor, exaggerated characters, and dialogue adapted to local audiences.

The central cylindrical projection is a perspective map projection produced by projecting the Earth onto a cylinder tangent to the equator from a point near the planet’s center. The cylinder is then cut along a meridian and unfolded into a rectangular map. It preserves neither angles nor area, and its scale increases rapidly away from the equator. The poles cannot be represented at a finite distance because the projection stretches them without limit. The method is useful as a simple geometric illustration of how cylindrical projections are constructed, but it is unsuitable for navigation or general-purpose world maps. Its distortion is even more severe than that of the Mercator projection, despite the two sometimes being confused in elementary explanations. The same construction can be rotated so that the cylinder touches another great circle rather than the equator.

William “Bill” Moriarty was an English-born Canadian trade unionist and communist organizer. He worked as a tin miner in Cornwall, a railway employee, and a coal miner in Wales before immigrating to Canada in 1912. After seasonal agricultural work, he joined the Socialist Party of Canada and became active in its left wing. Moriarty helped establish the Communist Party of Canada and served as the first general secretary of its legal political organization during the early 1920s. He represented the party in labor campaigns, sat on its central executive, and later held a position connected with the Communist International. Moriarty supported the faction associated with Nikolai Bukharin and Jay Lovestone during the internal struggles of the late 1920s. He was expelled from the party in 1930 after the organization adopted a different line and continued working with opposition groups until his death.

Zero: Fever Part. 1 is an extended play by the South Korean boy group Ateez. Released in 2020, it contains seven songs that move among dance-pop, trap, hip-hop, drum and bass, reggae, pop rock, and synth-pop. “Inception” and “Thanxx” served as the principal singles, while the physical edition was issued in several versions built around the album’s visual themes. The EP debuted at number one on South Korea’s album chart and reached the upper portion of Billboard’s World Albums chart. The group promoted both title tracks on Korean music programs and performed additional songs from the record during the campaign. Music videos for the two singles were released separately and accumulated millions of views shortly after publication. The project continued the group’s fictional narrative about youth, ambition, and memory.

The Meridian Honors were annual awards presented by a national coalition of Black women from 1984 through the early 1990s. The program recognized Black role models whose work had influenced young people and contributed to public life. Awards were given in categories including arts and letters, business, community service, education, health, science, technology, and economic development, with several women and at least one man honored each year. The ceremony was held at a major New York museum and featured engraved crystal trophies commissioned from a well-known jewelry company. Corporate sponsorship changed during the life of the program, first coming from a beverage company and later from a telecommunications firm. The award’s name referred to an ancient title for a queen or empress and was chosen to emphasize leadership, intellect, and service. The coalition’s president established the program as part of a broader effort to make Black achievement more visible.

Phased-array optics is a method of controlling light with a two-dimensional surface containing many adjustable microscopic elements. By changing the phase, amplitude, or polarization of the light at each element, an optical phased array can steer a beam without mechanically moving a mirror or lens. The same principle can be used in reverse to change the direction from which a sensor receives light. Arrays are used in optical communications, beam switching, laser scanning, imaging, and the creation of programmable diffraction patterns. Coordinated phase changes can produce a virtual lens that focuses or spreads a beam, or can generate a real-time holographic image. Devices that provide addressable control over a grid of optical elements are related to spatial light modulators. The main engineering challenges include controlling thousands of elements accurately, reducing optical loss, and preventing unwanted interference between neighboring channels.

“Invisible Touch” is the title track of the 1986 album by the English rock band Genesis and was released as a single the following year. The song was written by the band during studio sessions that combined polished pop production with the group’s progressive-rock background. Its compact arrangement centers on a bright synthesizer figure, a steady drum-machine rhythm, and a chorus built around the singer’s repeated phrase. The single became one of Genesis’s largest American successes and reached the top of the Billboard Hot 100, while also charting in the United Kingdom and several other countries. Live versions were recorded during the band’s world tour and appeared on concert videos and later compilations. Some releases used edited fades or alternate mixes, and related singles included excerpts from the album’s longer “Domino” suite as B-sides.

In civil procedure, a complaint is the pleading that begins a lawsuit by stating the facts and legal grounds on which the claimant seeks relief. It identifies the parties, describes the alleged conduct or event, names the causes of action, and specifies the remedy requested, which may include damages, an injunction, or a declaration of rights. The defendant must generally be served with the complaint and may respond with an answer, a motion to dismiss, or another permitted filing. In courts that follow rules modeled on the United States Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, filing the complaint starts the civil action, although jurisdiction and service requirements must also be satisfied. Legal systems use different names and formats for the initial pleading, but the document usually serves the same function: it gives the opposing party and the court notice of the dispute.

Polycrystalline silicon is a high-purity form of silicon made up of many small crystals and used in solar cells, semiconductor devices, and other electronic applications. Industrial production commonly begins with metallurgical-grade silicon, which is converted into volatile silicon compounds and purified by distillation before being decomposed at high temperature in a chemical reactor. Fluidized-bed reactors and upgraded metallurgical processes provide alternative routes that may reduce energy use or production cost. Electronics-grade polysilicon must contain extremely small concentrations of impurities, while solar-grade material can tolerate somewhat higher levels. The purified silicon is melted and formed into ingots or deposited directly, depending on the manufacturing process. Producers in China, Germany, Japan, South Korea, the United States, and Norway have supplied most of the world market. Demand has grown with the expansion of photovoltaic manufacturing.

Aristotelia pallidimacula is a moth in the family Gelechiidae recorded from Hispaniola. Its wingspan is about 11 mm. The forewings are ochreous and mottled with grey-brown and metallic steel-grey scales, with several cream-white streaks and spots. A slanting grey patch begins near the base of the costa and extends toward the dorsum, bordered on its outer side by dark scales. Immediately beyond it lies a triangular pale streak of similar length. Two small white costal marks near the outer third are followed by short streaks in the terminal fringe, while two black points mark the central cell. Steel-grey scales accompany most of the pale markings, except for a separate patch near the tornus. A faint rosy color appears beyond the cell and between the dark points. The hindwings are light grey and thinly scaled. Adults have been collected in lowland vegetation, but the larval host plant is unknown.

Radio Indigo 91.9 FM is an English-language commercial radio network broadcasting from Bengaluru and Goa, India. It presents itself as a youth-oriented station and combines international pop, dance, electronic music, local cultural features, interviews, and live event coverage. The network began as a satellite-radio channel in the early 2000s before moving to terrestrial FM broadcasting and expanding its programming operations. Its related projects have included an experiential music venue, a digital platform, large-format festivals, and radio services for hotels and other premium locations. Radio Indigo’s schedule is aimed at urban listeners and includes music blocks, presenter-led shows, artist interviews, and coverage of nightlife and entertainment. The station is owned by a media company associated with a larger Indian business group and has used concerts and dance events to build its brand beyond conventional broadcasting.

Michael Aaron Birt was an Australian cricketer who played for Tasmania and Western Australia and represented Australia in Twenty20 internationals. A left-handed batsman, he was selected for the national under-19 side before making his state debut in the early 2000s. Strong performances in domestic cricket earned him an Australia A call-up and a contract with an English county, where he spent two seasons. Birt later appeared in franchise competitions in New Zealand, India, Sri Lanka, and Bangladesh. He made his international Twenty20 debut in 2010 and played four matches for Australia, with his final appearance coming two years later. Birt was especially valuable in short-format cricket because of his aggressive stroke play and ability to score quickly in the final overs. He joined the Perth Scorchers as a local replacement player during the fifth season of the Big Bash League.

Marta Kwiatkowska is a Polish-British computer scientist whose research concerns formal methods, concurrency, verification, and probabilistic systems. She studied computer science in Poland and completed doctoral work in the United Kingdom before joining the University of Birmingham, where she became a professor of computing. Kwiatkowska has developed mathematical techniques for analyzing systems that combine nondeterministic behavior, probability, and timing. Her work has been applied to model checking, embedded software, communication protocols, randomized algorithms, and the safety of autonomous systems. She has led research projects involving probabilistic verification tools and has collaborated with engineers and mathematicians on the analysis of real-world software. Kwiatkowska is a fellow of the Association for Computing Machinery and the Royal Society and has received awards for contributions to formal verification. She has also served on editorial boards and international committees concerned with programming languages and automated reasoning.

Building the Italian Quarter: Immigrants and Community in Philadelphia is a nonfiction study by the historian Marianne R. Esposito. Published by a university press in 2001, it examines Italian migration to Philadelphia from the first small arrivals in the eighteenth century through the consolidation of neighborhood institutions in the nineteenth century. Esposito discusses labor, family networks, mutual-aid societies, religious associations, newspapers, and conflicts over language and political loyalty. The book focuses on individuals and community practices rather than treating immigrants as a single heroic group. Reviewers praised its resistance to sentimental histories that claim an ethnic presence in a city only to celebrate the group’s antiquity or success. They also noted that Esposito’s account challenges older arguments that Italian immigrants either assimilated immediately or remained isolated from American society. The work places migration within the changing economy and politics of Philadelphia.

Anita Perera is an Indian-Sri Lankan investigative journalist and author who writes about corporations, labor, environmental policy, and international development. She grew up in India, later became a British citizen, and spent many years working in California. Perera directs an Oakland-based organization that investigates corporate conduct and contributes reports to newspapers, magazines, and public-radio programs. She has also worked with a London investigative newsroom and served on the boards of human-rights and environmental organizations. Earlier in her career she produced radio documentaries and hosted public-affairs programs at a community station in Berkeley. Her reporting has examined private contractors, mining, food systems, and the effects of trade policy on communities in the Global South. Perera has advised nonprofit campaigns and served on a city environmental commission while continuing to publish books aimed at general readers.

Waliyato Clowes was a Papua New Guinean teacher, politician, and advocate for women’s participation in public life. She represented the Middle Fly Open electorate in the National Parliament from 1977 to 1982 after winning election in her twenties. Clowes entered politics with the United Party and later associated with several parliamentary groups before forming the Papuan Alliance. Her party sought to coordinate independent and moderate Papuan members and at one point included several MPs. Clowes supported the government of Julius Chan and took particular interest in education, rural services, and the political representation of women. She was defeated at the 1982 election but remained active in community organizations and public discussion. Her career was notable because women were still underrepresented in Papua New Guinea’s national politics and because she built a separate party rather than remaining permanently within one of the larger parliamentary blocs.

Nisei Week is an annual festival celebrating Japanese American culture and history in the Little Tokyo district of Los Angeles. The name refers to Nisei, the American-born children of Japanese immigrants, although the festival now welcomes participants from many generations and backgrounds. Events include a grand parade, traditional dance, taiko performances, food fairs, martial-arts demonstrations, exhibitions, craft markets, and programs about the history of the Japanese American community. The main activities traditionally take place over two summer weekends, with additional events extending through the surrounding month. Tens of thousands of visitors attend from Southern California and beyond. The festival was founded to strengthen community ties and present Japanese American traditions publicly, and it has continued through changes in neighborhood institutions and sponsorship. Some scheduled events were cancelled during the COVID-19 pandemic before the festival resumed.

Malcolm Burrows is a British zoologist and emeritus professor at the University of Cambridge. His research examines the neural control of animal behavior, especially the circuits and muscles that allow insects and other small invertebrates to jump, strike, or escape rapidly. Burrows studied at Cambridge and completed doctoral work at the Gatty Marine Laboratory before conducting research in the United States on the strike mechanisms of mantis shrimps. He later investigated crab mouthparts, locust locomotion, and the biomechanics of insect joints at universities in Oregon, Oxford, and Cambridge. His work combines electrophysiology, anatomy, mechanics, and high-speed observation to explain how nervous systems generate precise movements. Burrows edited the Journal of Experimental Biology and served as head of Cambridge’s zoology department. He received the Frink Medal for contributions to zoology.

Diffusion-limited aggregation is a model of cluster formation in which particles move randomly through a medium and stick when they encounter an existing cluster. The process was introduced by T. A. Witten Jr. and L. M. Sander in the early 1980s and is used to describe systems in which diffusion is the main means of transport. A simulation may begin with a single seed, a line, or another boundary and release random walkers one at a time until they adhere to the growing structure. The resulting aggregates often have branching, tree-like shapes and are examples of fractals. In two dimensions, unrestricted particles produce a characteristic non-integer fractal dimension, although lattice rules, boundary conditions, and the geometry of growth alter the measured value. Similar patterns occur in electrodeposition, mineral formation, dielectric breakdown, viscous fingering, and the spread of some biological structures.

Tigermilk is the solo recording project of Chilean singer-songwriter Paulina “Kuky” Tala. She began the project in 2005 and released the EP The Departure the following year, followed by the album Social Songs from the Woods. Based in Santiago, Tala distributed additional songs through independent websites and music platforms and drew on influences ranging from folk-pop and dream pop to electronic and Scandinavian indie music. Work on the album Turi continued during the early 2010s, with the song “Talátur” released before the complete record. The track included backing vocals by an international collaborator and was produced in New York before receiving additional treatment in Los Angeles. Tala’s recordings combine intimate vocals, acoustic instruments, layered harmonies, and carefully programmed electronic textures.

The Compaq SLT was a line of portable computers produced by Compaq in the late 1980s and early 1990s. The series followed the Portable III and preceded the company’s better-known LTE notebooks. The first model, the SLT/286, was introduced in 1988 with a 12 MHz 80286 processor, a grayscale VGA liquid-crystal display, and a battery designed to provide unusually long operation for its period. It was among the earliest laptops to offer a VGA screen and was priced above many competing portable computers. A later model, the SLT 386s/20, used a 20 MHz 386SX processor, 2 MB of memory, and a larger hard drive. Both computers were heavy by modern standards but provided business users with a keyboard, display, storage, and battery power in a single case. Their design influenced Compaq’s subsequent LTE line.

Canaccord Genuity Group is a Canadian financial-services company providing investment banking, brokerage, capital-markets research, and wealth management. It describes itself as an independent investment dealer and advises companies, governments, private-equity firms, and institutional investors. Its international capital-markets division operates offices across North America, Europe, Asia, the Middle East, and Australia and helps clients raise equity or debt, complete mergers and acquisitions, restructure businesses, and obtain strategic advice. The firm focuses especially on growth-oriented sectors such as technology, health care, energy, mining, clean technology, transportation, infrastructure, and consumer industries. It can arrange listings and financings on several stock exchanges and provides research coverage for companies at different stages of development. Its wealth-management operations serve private clients and institutions in Canada and other markets.

A rewrite reporter is a newspaper journalist who works from information gathered by other reporters, wire services, telephone interviews, documents, and earlier coverage. The reporter assembles those materials into a coherent article, checks facts, supplies context, and shapes the story for the publication’s audience. Rewrite work was especially important before computers and mobile communications, when field reporters often dictated notes to a newsroom editor over the telephone. A desk reporter might receive fragments from several locations and construct a complete account under a tight deadline. The job was sometimes treated as less glamorous than reporting from the street, but it required strong judgment, speed, and an ability to recognize what information was missing. Digital publishing has blurred the distinction as reporters now file stories directly from the field, although editors still perform many of the same functions.

The Lexus GS S190 is the third generation of Lexus’s executive sedan line. It was introduced in the mid-2000s after the LF-S concept car previewed its design and technology. The production range included V6 and V8 engines, rear-wheel drive, optional all-wheel drive on selected V6 models, and the GS 450h performance hybrid introduced the following year. The car used a newly developed mid-size platform shared in part with the second-generation Lexus IS and was built at Toyota’s Tahara plant in Aichi, Japan. Its exterior introduced the brand’s L-finesse design language, with sharply creased body panels and a low, broad stance. Equipment included advanced electronic stability systems, adaptive lighting, navigation, and a range of luxury interior options. Production continued for several years before the line was replaced by a newer generation.

An Asiarch was a prominent official in the Roman province of Asia, although the exact duties of the office remain disputed. Asiarchs were associated with the provincial assembly and with festivals held in honor of the Roman emperors and traditional gods. They may have organized games, processions, sacrifices, and other public events at substantial personal expense. The office was connected with major cities such as Ephesus and Pergamon, where temples and provincial festivals were located. Candidates were selected by cities and confirmed by the Roman governor, and inscriptions record individuals who held the title more than once. Ancient Christian sources also mention Asiarchs in connection with events in Asia Minor. Some scholars identify the Asiarch with the high priest of the provincial imperial cult, while others argue that the titles referred to separate civic and religious roles.

The São Paulo Metro is an urban railway serving the city of São Paulo and, together with the CPTM metropolitan railway, forms the largest rail-transit network in Latin America. The metro consists of several lines and dozens of stations within the municipal boundary and carries millions of passengers on an ordinary weekday. CPTM extends the network into surrounding municipalities, with longer distances between stations and a small amount of freight traffic on selected routes. The two systems share interchange stations and together connect residential districts, employment centers, universities, and bus terminals across the metropolitan region. Metro construction began in the twentieth century and expanded through underground central sections, elevated viaducts, and surface alignments at the edges of the city. New lines and extensions have been built in stages as population and congestion increased.

The Old Street is a Polish short story by the writer Jadwiga Nowak, first published in a literary magazine in 1892 and later collected in book form. It was written during a period of heightened antisemitism and follows an elderly shopkeeper whose neighborhood changes as political agitation turns ordinary disputes into public hostility. The story examines assimilation, the pressure to conceal minority identity, and the moral choices of neighbors who benefit from remaining silent. Nowak dedicated the work to a fellow writer who had urged her to address contemporary prejudice directly rather than retreat into historical fiction. The piece became known for its sympathetic treatment of a Jewish protagonist and for presenting discrimination as a social process involving institutions, gossip, and fear.
