It has been included in anthologies of Polish realist literature and adapted for radio and the stage.

Hachijō is a Japonic language spoken on Hachijō-jima, Aogashima, and several communities in the Daitō Islands of Japan. Linguists disagree about whether it should be treated as the most divergent variety of Japanese or as a separate branch of the Japonic family. The language preserves grammatical and phonetic features associated with Eastern Old Japanese and shares some vocabulary with Kyushu and the Ryukyuan languages. These similarities may reflect ancient retentions, migration, or contact among sailors and island communities. Hachijō was formerly spoken on Hachijō-kojima, an island that is now uninhabited, and its number of speakers has declined as younger residents shift toward standard Japanese. Local researchers and cultural organizations have documented pronunciation, vocabulary, songs, and oral histories in an effort to preserve the language.

Kalyan Kumar was an Indian actor, director, and producer who worked primarily in Kannada and Tamil cinema. He made his screen debut in a mythological drama during the 1950s and appeared in more than 200 films over a career lasting several decades. Kumar became one of the leading actors of Kannada cinema during the 1960s and 1970s and was also successful in Tamil-language productions. He played romantic, historical, and dramatic roles and was among the first Kannada performers to appear as a leading actor in a color film. Along with Rajkumar and Udayakumar, he was regarded as part of the “Kumar trio” that dominated the industry during the period. Kumar occasionally directed and produced films and remained active in cinema after younger stars began to replace him in leading roles.

Beth “Bijie” Martin was an American fashion director, writer, and actress. She was born in New York to opera singers and spent her childhood moving between New York, Paris, and Italy as her parents pursued theatrical work. Although Martin developed an early interest in acting, she chose dramatic theatre rather than the vocal career associated with her family. Her stage appearances during the 1920s received favorable reviews, and she became friends with Tallulah Bankhead after meeting her in London. The two women shared an interest in clothing, travel, and unconventional social life. Martin’s acting opportunities diminished by the end of the decade, and she left the stage to live in Paris with her mother. She later wrote about fashion and worked as an adviser and editor for publications serving theatrical and artistic communities.

Makoto Douglas Sakamoto is a Japanese-born American gymnast and coach. He competed for the United States at the 1964 and 1972 Olympic Games, with his best individual result coming on the parallel bars. Before entering international competition, Sakamoto won national amateur titles in the all-around, horizontal bar, and other events. His family moved from Tokyo to California during his childhood, and he later earned undergraduate and graduate degrees in coaching. Sakamoto became an assistant coach at UCLA and worked with gymnasts who later represented the United States at the Olympics. He coached in Australia for several years before becoming head coach at Brigham Young University. He also served as an assistant coach for American teams at Olympic and world championships. Sakamoto was inducted into the U.S. Gymnastics Hall of Fame in the 1980s.

Thomas Antony Olajide is a Canadian actor from Vancouver, British Columbia. He received a Canadian Screen Award nomination for his leading performance in the film Learn to Swim, which follows a jazz musician coping with grief, artistic ambition, and a difficult relationship. Olajide also co-created Black Boys, a theatrical work about Black Canadian LGBTQ+ identities staged at a Toronto theatre. The production’s ensemble received a Dora Mavor Moore Award nomination. His other stage credits include Shakespeare productions at the Stratford Festival and performances in The Winter’s Tale, King Lear, A Midsummer Night’s Dream, and Love’s Labour’s Lost. He has also appeared in contemporary plays presented by Canadian Stage, the Belfry Theatre, and the National Arts Centre. Olajide’s work spans film, television, and experimental theatre.

Giovanni Battista Beccaria was an Italian physicist and teacher born in Mondovì in 1716. He entered the Piarist order as a young man, studied mathematics and natural philosophy, and taught grammar before turning increasingly to experimental science. Beccaria became professor of physics at Palermo and Rome and in 1748 accepted a chair at Turin, where he spent most of the rest of his career. He instructed members of the royal family and carried out experiments on electricity, atmospheric phenomena, and the properties of materials. His papers were published by the Royal Society of London, which elected him a fellow in 1755. The Sardinian king later commissioned Beccaria to measure the length of a meridian arc through Piedmont, contributing to the broader eighteenth-century effort to establish accurate geographic measurements.

Kinetic fractionation is the separation of isotopes caused by differences in reaction or transport rates. In a one-way process, lighter molecules often move or react slightly more readily than heavier molecules, leaving the product enriched in the lighter isotope and the remaining material relatively enriched in the heavier one. Biological reactions provide common examples because organisms selectively absorb some isotopic forms of carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, or nitrogen. Photosynthesis generally favors carbon-12 over carbon-13, so plant material and fossil fuels are often depleted in carbon-13 compared with inorganic carbon. Evaporation can produce a similar effect when water vapor moves rapidly into dry air: molecules containing oxygen-16 escape somewhat more easily than those containing oxygen-18. The difference is stronger when the process is effectively unidirectional and weaker when material can exchange freely in both directions and approach isotopic equilibrium.

François Girard is a French-Canadian filmmaker, screenwriter, and theatre director. He began on Montreal’s experimental video and art scene before producing his first feature film in the early 1990s. International attention followed with a film constructed from short episodes about the life and music of a famous pianist. Girard later wrote and directed The Red Violin, a historical drama tracing the ownership of a violin across several centuries. The film won an Academy Award for its original score and received numerous Canadian film prizes. Girard has also directed stage and concert works involving Stravinsky, Sophocles, Kafka, and modern chamber music. His theatre projects have been presented at festivals in Edinburgh, Lyon, Toronto, Ottawa, and New York. He directed a major Cirque du Soleil production in Tokyo and later created a show for Radio City Music Hall.

RX Telescopii is an irregular variable star in the constellation Telescopium. It is a luminous red supergiant whose brightness changes over time between approximately sixth and eighth magnitude, making it near the limit of naked-eye visibility under dark skies. The star is classified as an intermediate-luminosity M-type supergiant and has a cool, extended atmosphere. Its distance is uncertain because measurements from stellar parallax are affected by large astrometric noise. One interpretation would place the star far enough away to give it an enormous radius, while later catalog data imply a considerably smaller value. Estimates based on angular diameter therefore remain provisional. If the larger estimate were correct, the star’s outer atmosphere would extend beyond the orbit of Jupiter if it replaced the Sun. Astronomers continue to use variable brightness, spectroscopy, and improved astrometry to refine its properties.

Hyperpolarization is a change in a cell’s membrane voltage that makes the inside more negative relative to the outside. It commonly follows an action potential when potassium ions leave a neuron through open channels or chloride ions enter through chloride channels. Because the membrane potential is moved farther from the threshold required to trigger another action potential, hyperpolarization generally reduces excitability. The opposite condition, depolarization, brings the membrane potential toward threshold. A neuron enters a brief refractory period after firing, during which hyperpolarization and channel inactivation make a second impulse difficult or impossible. Sodium-potassium pumps and passive ion movement gradually restore the resting distribution of ions, bringing the membrane toward its usual potential of roughly –70 millivolts. Other cells can also hyperpolarize when voltage-gated channels or inhibitory neurotransmitter receptors alter ion flow.

Sindlesham is a village and estate settlement in Berkshire, England, southeast of Reading and near the town of Bracknell. It lies south of Winnersh, separated from that village by the M4 motorway, and the River Loddon passes along its western side. A chapel was recorded there in the thirteenth century, while later development included a watermill, estate houses, schools, and parish facilities. The large nineteenth-century residence of Bearwood House was built for a newspaper proprietor and is now used as an independent school. Other local institutions include a primary school, a church, a parish office, the National Grid’s United Kingdom control center, and a Masonic center. Recreational facilities include a golf course and a health spa. The village combines historic estate buildings with modern offices and residential areas.

Trevor Lee is an Australian architect and energy-policy adviser who has worked on reducing energy use in buildings since graduating from the University of Melbourne in the 1970s. He served as a senior architect for energy management in the federal construction department and later edited a quarterly journal published by the Australian and New Zealand Solar Energy Society. Lee chaired that organization and helped establish a sustainable-energy industry association that later merged into a national business council. He has advised governments, builders, and utilities on passive solar design, renewable generation, building efficiency, and energy markets. Lee also served as an executive director of an ethical investment company managing superannuation and unit funds. Through a consulting partnership formed in the 1990s, he continued to develop strategies for lowering energy demand in the built environment.

In library catalogues, a preferred title brings together editions of a work whose wording, language, or publication history has produced several different titles. The record may display the title found on a particular edition, while the authorized form supplies a stable point for searching and grouping related records. This is especially useful for works transmitted without a single original title, such as religious writings, traditional narratives, and anonymous poems. Music presents another common case: a symphony, opera, or song cycle may be identified by a number, key, nickname, or translated title in different sources. Cataloguers may add dates, language qualifiers, or other distinguishing information when two works share the same name. The resulting access point does not replace the titles printed on individual copies. Instead, it gives the catalogue a consistent structure through which users can discover translations, adaptations, arrangements, and alternate editions of what is understood to be one work.

SMART Project Space was an Amsterdam arts centre known for exhibitions, screenings, performances, and studio activity. It began in the 1990s in a former industrial district and developed a programme that connected emerging artists with curators, filmmakers, musicians, designers, and local residents. Rather than concentrating on a single medium, the organization treated the building as a changing workshop. Galleries might contain an installation one month, a film programme the next, and a public research project after that. Its exhibitions often emphasized experimentation over finished presentation, giving artists room to test ambitious or unfinished ideas. The centre also supported production through workspaces and short-term residencies. Although its original exhibition programme later ended, the name continued to be associated with artist studios and creative-enterprise initiatives. Former participants have described the project as an informal meeting place where professional networks formed across disciplines that were rarely brought together by conventional museums.

The ski-jumping complex at Le Praz, in Courchevel, contains several hills arranged around a Nordic sports centre. Its principal ramp is designed for long-distance competition, while smaller hills provide facilities for developing jumpers and for training in different wind conditions. A cross-country course beside the ramps allows the site to host events combining jumping with distance skiing. The first hill was built during the Second World War, but the present complex was largely reconstructed for the 1992 Winter Olympics. Olympic competition brought new landing slopes, spectator areas, and a separate normal hill to the valley. Since then, the venue has been used for international summer competitions as well as winter training. Records on the large and normal hills have changed as equipment and track profiles have improved. The two smallest ramps were added later, giving local clubs a progression from beginner practice to elite competition. Le Praz remains one of the best-known ski-jumping sites in the French Alps.

BlackBox Component Builder is a programming environment for creating applications from reusable software components. It combines a compiler, a component library, visual development tools, and a runtime system in one package. The environment is written in Component Pascal, a strongly typed language descended from the Pascal and Oberon families. Programs are organized as modules that can be compiled separately and linked dynamically, allowing a developer to replace one part of an application without rebuilding the entire system. Component contracts may include assertions describing conditions that must hold before or after an operation. These checks are intended to catch errors while a program is being developed. Automatic memory management removes the need for most explicit deallocation, while the language’s type system prevents many incompatible values from being passed between modules. The same component model is used by the editor, compiler, libraries, and runtime, so the tools serve as examples of the programming architecture they provide to users.

Pennsylvania Route 532 is a north–south highway connecting the northeastern part of Philadelphia with communities in Bucks County. At its southern end, the road leaves the city near a junction with U.S. Route 1 and follows an established urban avenue before entering lower-density commercial and residential districts. North of the Philadelphia boundary, it passes through Feasterville and Holland and continues toward Newtown and the Delaware River. Several sections began as nineteenth-century turnpike roads, whose tolls helped finance construction and maintenance between older settlements. The present route number was assigned during the early state-highway system and has been altered several times as nearby roads were renumbered. A bypass around Newtown removed through traffic from the borough’s centre and later became part of the route. The highway terminates near Washington Crossing, where roads and historic sites overlook the river. Although it is not a limited-access motorway, PA 532 serves both local travel and regional connections between Philadelphia and central Bucks County.

Change UK was a short-lived British political party formed by members of Parliament who had left the Labour and Conservative parties over Brexit and the direction of national politics. The group first appeared in the House of Commons as an independent parliamentary faction before adopting a formal party name in advance of the 2019 European elections. Its platform called for the United Kingdom to remain closely connected to the European Union and supported holding another public vote on the withdrawal agreement. The party also presented itself as socially liberal and economically moderate, hoping to attract voters dissatisfied with both major parties. Several prominent MPs joined at its launch, but disagreements over leadership, branding, and electoral strategy quickly became public. In the general election later that year, the party failed to retain any of the seats held by its founders. It was subsequently wound up, with some former members returning to established parties and others remaining politically independent.

Syncro-Vox is a limited-animation process in which a moving mouth is placed over an otherwise still picture. The image may be a photograph, drawing, puppet, or painted figure, while the lips are supplied by a filmed performer speaking the dialogue. Because only a small portion of the image moves, the technique can produce a complete scene with far less animation than a conventional cartoon requires. It was developed for inexpensive television production during the 1950s and became especially recognizable in programs made by Cambria Studios. The method was useful for talking animals and imaginary characters that would have been costly to animate frame by frame. Its jerky appearance eventually became part of its appeal, and later filmmakers used it deliberately as a visual joke or a reference to early television. Syncro-Vox should not be confused with ordinary cutout animation: the defining feature is the photographic or drawn still image combined with separately filmed moving lips.

Vironniemi is the historic central district of Helsinki, occupying the waterfront area around the city’s principal civic institutions. Government offices, banks, museums, churches, shops, and transport terminals are concentrated within a relatively small area, making the district both an administrative centre and a major destination for visitors. Senate Square forms one of its best-known spaces, with the cathedral and former government buildings arranged around the open plaza. Nearby, the Presidential Palace and the offices of the Council of State face the harbour. The district also contains the main campus buildings of the University of Helsinki, the Central railway station, and several national cultural institutions. Large department stores and newspaper offices reflect its commercial importance, while the National Library, Finnish National Theatre, Ateneum, Kiasma, and the Helsinki Music Centre give the area a prominent cultural role. Although Vironniemi is heavily built up, its streets connect directly with the waterfront and several public squares.

An open platform in computing is a system designed so that outside developers can connect to it through documented rules and interfaces. Those interfaces may permit programs to exchange data, add functions, or control selected operations without altering the platform’s internal source code. Openness therefore concerns access and interoperability rather than ownership. A company may publish an API while keeping the underlying software proprietary, just as an open-source project may restrict certain interfaces. Open standards make it easier for different implementations to communicate, which can reduce dependence on a single vendor. Web servers, operating systems, payment services, and mobile applications commonly use this model. The term is also relative: a platform may expose one open layer while keeping other components private or closed. Developers evaluating an “open” product therefore examine its documentation, licensing, compatibility requirements, and limits on what third-party software is allowed to do.

Francesco Gabrielli was an Italian performer of the early seventeenth century who worked in the commedia dell’arte tradition. He was remembered not only for acting but also for unusual skill as an instrumentalist, reportedly playing a wide variety of instruments. Gabrielli is frequently associated with the servant character Scapino, though the role’s authorship is uncertain and may have belonged to an earlier performer. Surviving records place him with several important companies, including the Accesi, the Confidenti, and the Fedeli. His career took him across northern Italy and to Paris, where he worked under the direction of Giovan Battista Andreini. A letter written while Gabrielli was trying to organize a company for the court at Mantua offers a glimpse into the practical business of theatre. It discusses recruiting performers, balancing specialties, arranging family members, and managing rivalries among actors. The document makes Gabrielli valuable to historians even where details of his performances have disappeared.

Bruce is a small settlement in South Australia’s Mid North, established during the expansion of farming and railway transport across the interior. The township was surveyed in the late nineteenth century on land associated with the Hundred of Willochra and was formally proclaimed soon afterward. A station on the Peterborough–Quorn railway connected Bruce with larger regional centres, carrying passengers, livestock, grain, and supplies. The line remained an important local service for much of the twentieth century before operations were discontinued. Bruce also had a post office and school, although both institutions eventually closed as the population declined and services became concentrated in nearby towns. The former town site now lies within a locality whose boundaries were defined in the 1990s. The origin of the name is uncertain: accounts variously connect it with a prominent landholder or with a personal choice made by a colonial governor. Sparse buildings and transport remnants mark the settlement’s earlier role.

Augsburg is a major city in Bavaria situated between the rivers Lech and Wertach. Its central district preserves a mixture of Roman foundations, medieval streets, Renaissance civic buildings, and later industrial architecture. The city began as a Roman settlement and became an important trading centre during the Middle Ages. Merchant families, especially the Fugger and Welser houses, helped make Augsburg one of Europe’s significant financial cities in the sixteenth century. Its religious history is equally prominent. The Augsburg Confession was presented there in 1530, and the Peace of Augsburg established a temporary legal arrangement between Catholic and Lutheran territories in 1555. Today the city serves as the administrative centre of the Swabian region and includes a university, theatres, museums, and manufacturing districts. The Fuggerei, a walled residential complex founded for poor citizens, remains one of its most distinctive landmarks. Modern Augsburg extends well beyond the old city but continues to organize public life around its historic centre.

Cricket in Finland developed from informal matches played by expatriates and international communities before becoming a nationally organized sport. Helsinki was the earliest major centre, with clubs forming in the capital region and in nearby Espoo. Teams also arranged occasional fixtures with diplomatic and foreign communities in other European cities. A national cricket association was established at the end of the twentieth century to coordinate competitions, train players, and introduce the game to Finnish schools and recreation clubs. The domestic programme later divided into a premier competition and a lower league, with promotion linking the two. Matches have been played in several formats, including longer limited-overs games, twenty-over tournaments, and indoor cricket during the winter. The association’s competitions provide opportunities for both experienced international players and Finnish beginners, while the short summer season encourages clubs to share grounds. Helsinki remains the centre of organized cricket, although teams now play in several Finnish cities.

The Moab Cabin is a small log building in Moab, Utah, preserved as evidence of the settlement’s early domestic and economic history. Its walls were made from roughly shaped logs fitted together with irregular corner joints and packed with mud. The roof used parallel logs covered by brush and earth, a construction method suited to a place where manufactured materials were scarce. Built in the late nineteenth century, the cabin passed through several periods in the town’s development. Mormon settlers used buildings of this kind during the first agricultural phase; later residents connected with cattle work, forestry, prospecting, and mining occupied the structure. Its survival is unusual because modest cabins were often dismantled, enlarged, or lost as Moab grew. The building was placed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1980. Its importance lies less in architectural grandeur than in the way a single, humble dwelling records changing work and settlement patterns in southeastern Utah.

The South Carolina Senate is the upper chamber of the state legislature. Its members represent individual districts and serve four-year terms, with elections held during the presidential cycle. The chamber’s present structure emerged after federal court decisions required South Carolina to replace its earlier county-based arrangement with districts of roughly equal population. Before reapportionment, every county had a senator, a system that gave rural counties influence far beyond their population. Legislative changes during the 1960s and 1970s gradually moved the Senate toward its current single-member districts. Senators introduce bills, confirm or reject certain appointments, approve the state budget with the House, and serve on standing committees that examine proposed legislation. The presiding officer is the lieutenant governor, although much of the chamber’s daily work is directed by the Senate president and committee chairs. Debate takes place in the State House in Columbia, where the Senate shares responsibility for state lawmaking with the House of Representatives.

Fused filament fabrication is an additive-manufacturing method in which a printer builds an object by laying down a melted plastic thread. A motor pushes filament from a spool into a heated nozzle, and computer-controlled movements trace the shape of each layer. Once a layer cools enough to support the next one, the print head rises or the platform lowers by a small increment. The process can pause extrusion while the head travels, which helps prevent unwanted strands between separate parts. Common materials include polylactic acid, ABS, nylon, and flexible thermoplastics, each of which has different requirements for temperature and cooling. The method is inexpensive and easy to adapt, making it common in schools, workshops, and home studios. It generally produces visible layer lines and may be weaker between layers than parts made by industrial processes. The term FFF is often preferred in open-source communities because the better-known alternative is a trademarked name.

The Armidale School is an Anglican independent school in Armidale, New South Wales, serving students from early childhood through the final years of secondary education. It began in the nineteenth century as a private school for the New England region and later developed into a co-educational day and boarding institution. Students are organized into junior, middle, and senior divisions, with boarders forming a substantial part of the older school. The campus combines classrooms, sporting grounds, residences, music facilities, and spaces for outdoor education. The school’s location on the tablelands gives it a different climate and landscape from the coastal cities of New South Wales. Its curriculum includes the state requirements alongside international programmes in some year levels. The institution has also promoted technological access and was an early Australian school to provide students with internet connectivity. Graduates have entered universities, the armed forces, public service, business, and the arts. Boarding remains central to the school’s identity and connects it with families across rural Australia.

Pong is a two-player arcade game in which each player moves a vertical paddle to return a square ball across a black screen. Its rules are simple: miss the ball and the opponent scores. Yet the limited interaction gives the game a steadily increasing tension as rallies become faster and angles become harder to predict. Atari released the machine in the early 1970s after engineer Allan Alcorn developed a working prototype as an exercise. A test cabinet placed in a California bar attracted so much attention that its coin box reportedly filled quickly, encouraging the company to manufacture the game. Pong’s success helped persuade businesses that video games could operate as commercial amusement machines rather than technical novelties. Competitors produced numerous variations, while home versions later brought the same idea into living rooms. The game also became the subject of a patent dispute involving the electronic tennis game demonstrated by Magnavox. Its paddle-and-ball design remains one of the most recognizable forms in early video-game history.

A cross-bolted bearing is an engine bearing cap reinforced by bolts that run sideways through the crankcase instead of only along the usual vertical fastening line. The additional hardware links the two sides of the lower engine structure and can reduce movement when the crankshaft is subjected to heavy loads. It also helps keep the cap seated against forces transmitted from the connecting rods and pistons. In a conventional arrangement, the main-bearing bolts are aligned with the cylinder axis or with a line passing through the angle of a V engine. Cross bolts are placed at right angles to that arrangement. Some designs use one long bolt extending through the block, while others use separate bolts threaded into each side of the cap. The technique is most useful in engines where stiffness and resistance to crankcase distortion are important, including high-output racing and heavy-duty applications. It adds machining and assembly complexity, so manufacturers use it when the structural benefit justifies the extra cost.

Richard Zarou is an American composer whose work includes concert pieces, electronic music, and scores for film. He studied composition in Virginia before completing graduate degrees at Florida State University, where he earned both a master’s degree and a doctorate. His music has been performed at university concerts, specialist new-music festivals, and professional events in the United States and abroad. Zarou often combines acoustic instruments with recorded or electronically processed sound. One of his works for bass trombone and fixed media places a solo performer against an intentionally unstable recorded environment, creating a dialogue between live gesture and studio manipulation. His compositions have appeared on programmes organized by the Society of Composers, the College Music Society, and festivals devoted to electroacoustic music. He has also hosted a podcast about contemporary composition, using interviews and discussion to introduce listeners to unfamiliar repertory. His career connects academic composition with public-facing work about new music.

Aristotelia roseosuffusella is a small North American gelechiid moth commonly known by names referring to its pink-washed wings and association with clover. The forewings are chiefly brown or dark ochre, but pale markings and rosy suffusion break up the surface. A light spot near the base, an angled band, and a larger mark near the middle are among the features used to distinguish the species. Additional pale and pinkish marks occur toward the wing tip. The hindwings are darker and more uniformly grey-brown, with similarly coloured fringes. Adults have a wingspan of roughly a centimetre and have been recorded in eastern and central parts of North America. The species was described in the nineteenth century from material collected in the United States. Like many small micro-moths, it is more likely to be noticed by specialists examining vegetation or light-trap samples than by casual observers. Its common names reflect both its colour pattern and the plants among which its larvae may be found.

Francis Wheeler Loomis was an American physicist who spent most of his career building the physics department at the University of Illinois. Born in West Virginia, he studied at Harvard and completed a doctorate on measurements involving mercury and thermodynamic properties. His research interests later included spectroscopy, low-temperature phenomena, and the precision measurement of physical constants. Loomis became head of the Illinois department in 1929 and held the position for nearly three decades. Recruiting leading scientists to a university far from the established northeastern centres was one of his principal administrative challenges. During his tenure, the department gained an international reputation and attracted researchers who would later receive major scientific honours. Loomis also supported graduate training and helped create laboratory facilities suited to modern experimental physics. He served as president of the American Physical Society and was elected to the National Academy of Sciences. His influence was therefore institutional as well as scientific: much of his legacy rests in the department he shaped and the physicists it trained.

Bafoussam is the principal city of Cameroon’s western highlands and the administrative capital of the West Region. The city lies among the Bamboutos Mountains and serves as a commercial meeting point for surrounding farming communities. Coffee, maize, beans, and potatoes are produced in the region, while local factories process agricultural goods and supply the urban market. Bafoussam is also an important centre of Bamiléké culture and is associated with a traditional chiefdom whose palace is one of the city’s notable landmarks. Municipal administration is divided among several communes, including Bafoussam I, Bafoussam II, and Bafoussam III, each containing numerous neighbourhoods and smaller settlements. Markets, breweries, workshops, schools, and transport businesses have expanded as the population has grown. The city’s roads connect it with Yaoundé, Douala, and other towns in the western plateau. Bafoussam’s role is therefore both regional and cultural: it functions as a financial centre while remaining closely tied to the agricultural villages around it.

Before the spread of Christianity, Slavic-speaking communities followed local religious traditions that varied across regions and changed over time. Their beliefs were expressed through seasonal festivals, household rites, sacred places, stories about supernatural beings, and customs connected with farming and the dead. No single surviving text records the whole religion, and later Christian writers often described earlier practices selectively or gave them new interpretations. Names associated with thunder, fertility, the underworld, the sun, and household protection appear in medieval sources, but their importance differed among East, West, and South Slavic peoples. Christianization was not a single event. Some rulers adopted the new religion and encouraged its institutions, while rural communities continued older ceremonies for generations. In the Balkans, Byzantine missions helped introduce Christianity; among eastern peoples, the conversion of Kievan Rus’ became a major political turning point. Western communities experienced influence from both Rome and neighbouring German territories. Modern reconstructions of Slavic paganism therefore combine archaeology, linguistics, folklore, and cautious reading of medieval accounts.

Moira Marti Geoffrion is an American sculptor and educator whose career has included studio work, teaching, professional service, and exhibitions. She grew up in Maryland in a large family and was the daughter of philosopher Fritz Marti. Geoffrion studied fine art at Boston University, continued her education at Indiana University, and completed a master of fine arts degree at Southern Illinois University Edwardsville. Her sculpture has appeared in solo and group exhibitions and is held by public collections in the American Midwest. Grants from arts organizations and research foundations supported different stages of her work, including awards from the National Endowment for the Arts and a Fulbright-related programme. Geoffrion has taught at universities including Notre Dame and the University of Arizona. She also held leadership roles in organizations concerned with college art education and administration. Her professional activities show the multiple paths followed by many academic artists, whose careers combine making objects, mentoring students, serving institutions, and participating in national arts networks.

Freeze-casting is a method for manufacturing porous ceramics by turning the freezing pattern of a liquid into a structural template. A suspension of ceramic particles is cooled from one direction, causing solvent crystals—usually ice—to form at the cold boundary and advance through the mixture. As the crystals grow, they push particles into the spaces between them. The frozen body is then dried under reduced pressure so that the crystals leave without melting, preserving channels in their former positions. After drying, the fragile particle framework is heated in a kiln to bond the ceramic walls. The result contains long, directionally arranged pores rather than the more random voids produced by ordinary foaming. Pore size and orientation can be adjusted through the cooling rate, particle concentration, and composition of the slurry. Such materials are studied for filters, catalyst supports, lightweight structures, and implants in which fluid movement or controlled permeability is important. The process is also called ice templating because the temporary ice architecture determines the final ceramic geometry.

Ozie Boo! is a Chilean animated programme for preschool viewers featuring a group of young penguin characters. Episodes are short and use simple stories, songs, and classroom situations to introduce cooperation, emotional awareness, and everyday problem-solving. The series was produced in Santiago by Atiempo Studios and was later distributed to broadcasters in several countries. Its first seasons appeared on Chilean children’s television before being released through home-video and international programming arrangements. Different language versions allowed the show to circulate outside South America, including on children’s channels in Europe and French-speaking Canada. A later continuation, Ozie Boo!: Save the Planet, placed the penguins in lessons about environmental care under the guidance of a pelican teacher. The characters’ setting changed, but the programme retained its emphasis on brief educational stories. Episodes generally run for only a few minutes, making the series suitable for preschool blocks and repeated daily broadcasts.

The almude was a historical Portuguese measure for liquids and dry goods whose size varied according to time and place. Its name came through Portuguese from an Arabic term for a measure, with an older connection to the Roman modius. Medieval documents use the word in several regional systems, so the almude never represented one permanent volume throughout the Portuguese-speaking world. In some areas it was defined as a multiple of the alqueire; elsewhere local authorities assigned it a different capacity. Royal reforms attempted to make measures more consistent, but older values continued in markets and municipal records. Lisbon’s standard eventually became influential as administrative practice was extended across the kingdom. Colonial Brazil and other Portuguese territories also used the name, sometimes with local interpretations. Converting an old reference to modern litres therefore requires knowing the date, jurisdiction, and commodity involved. The almude illustrates a common problem in historical measurement: a familiar unit name could remain stable while the quantity it represented changed substantially.

The rivalry between the Boston Celtics and Los Angeles Lakers is one of the defining competitions in professional basketball. The teams represent opposite coasts and developed their strongest identities during different periods, yet their championship histories repeatedly brought them together. Boston and Los Angeles have met in the NBA Finals more often than any other pair of franchises. Their series have included the disciplined, defensive Celtics teams of the 1960s, the fast-paced Lakers groups of the 1980s, and later meetings shaped by a new generation of stars. The rivalry is also unusual because both clubs have spent long stretches near the top of the league rather than relying on a single era of success. Championships, retired numbers, famous coaches, and dramatic Finals games have supplied much of its mythology. Although the two teams play in different conferences and meet infrequently during the regular season, every encounter carries the memory of their earlier contests. Together they account for a large share of the league’s historical titles.

Sonja Barend is a Dutch broadcaster whose interview programmes helped establish the television talk show as a forum for public discussion in the Netherlands. She began working in television during the 1960s and later became the central figure in a weekly programme produced for VARA. The show’s title changed with its broadcast day, but its format remained recognizable: Barend questioned politicians, artists, specialists, and people whose experiences were rarely represented in formal public debate. Her interviews frequently addressed social questions and gave minority communities an opportunity to speak directly to a national audience. The programme depended on her conversational style and willingness to pursue uncomfortable subjects rather than on elaborate studio spectacle. Barend continued presenting programmes for decades and became one of the most familiar faces in Dutch broadcasting. A long collaboration with producer Ellen Blazer shaped many of her early series. Barend retired from television in the 2000s, leaving a body of work associated with open discussion and the expansion of whose stories could appear on Dutch television.

Highway 17B was the designation used for former sections of Ontario’s Highway 17 after bypasses redirected through traffic around several towns. The business routes typically followed older streets through communities that had once stood directly on the Trans-Canada corridor. Once a bypass opened, the province could remove the highway from the urban section or assign the 17B number while local traffic continued to use the road. Most of the routes were eventually transferred to municipal control, even where residents continued to call them Highway 17B. Remnants of the provincial designation survive in road names, historic signs, and local descriptions. North Bay retained one of the original routes for many years. A separate designation was created near Garden River after a disagreement over the status and maintenance of a connecting road. The history of 17B therefore reflects a common pattern in highway administration: a route can disappear from provincial maps while remaining an important commercial street and a recognizable part of local geography.

WiiWare was Nintendo’s digital distribution service for original games and applications made for the Wii. Users purchased software through the Wii Shop Channel, after which each title appeared as a channel on the console’s menu or on an attached memory card. The service differed from the Virtual Console, which concentrated on older games reproduced through emulation. WiiWare instead offered new, usually smaller projects that did not need the manufacturing, packaging, and retail distribution required for a disc release. This lowered the barrier for independent and experimental developers, although Nintendo still controlled approval, licensing, pricing, and access to development tools. Games often used the Wii’s motion-sensitive controllers in compact puzzle, arcade, strategy, and action designs. Storage limits and the closed nature of the shop shaped what developers could make and how players could obtain it. When Nintendo later discontinued the Wii Shop Channel, WiiWare became an example of an early console download service whose catalogue was tied closely to a particular generation of hardware.

Toby Borland was an American right-handed relief pitcher who moved between Major League Baseball and the minor leagues during a professional career lasting more than a decade. He reached the majors with Philadelphia in the mid-1990s and later appeared for the Mets, Red Sox, Angels, and Marlins. Borland’s role was generally that of a middle reliever, entering games after the starting pitcher and working through difficult portions of the opposing lineup. His most productive season came with Philadelphia, when he appeared in dozens of games, completed a career high in innings, and recorded his best strikeout total. Injuries, roster changes, and opportunities in other organizations led to several returns and transfers rather than a single uninterrupted major-league tenure. Borland threw and batted right-handed and was known for his willingness to take on frequent appearances. He also wore number 42 for Philadelphia late in the period before the number was retired throughout professional baseball in honour of Jackie Robinson.

Robert Muczynski’s Three Preludes for Unaccompanied Flute is a compact work in which a solo instrument must create contrast without harmonic support from a piano or ensemble. Written in the early 1960s, the pieces were intended to function effectively as short concert encores rather than as a large-scale sonata. Their moods change quickly: one movement has a lively, sharply articulated character, another suggests the quiet concentration of night, and the last moves with a more independent, improvisatory energy. The writing tests the flutist’s control of rhythm, attack, breath, and changing colour. Although each prelude is brief, the set requires the performer to make its phrases sound purposeful and to distinguish the three atmospheres clearly. Muczynski’s description of the pieces emphasizes passing impressions rather than literal stories. The work is therefore less a narrative sequence than a series of concise studies in movement, darkness, and freedom.

Francisco Carmelo Camet was an Argentine fencer who represented his country at the 1900 Olympic Games in Paris. He had studied and trained in France, where the international competition was being held, and entered the épée tournament against a large field of European competitors. The event proceeded through several rounds of pools rather than a single elimination bracket. Camet advanced from the opening group and again survived the next stage, placing high enough to continue when the field was reduced. In the semifinal he finished among the qualifiers, becoming the first Argentine fencer to reach an Olympic fencing final. The final round contained nine competitors, and Camet won two of his five bouts. He ended the tournament in fifth place, a notable result in a competition dominated by French fencers. His Olympic appearance was important not only for the individual placing but also for the early international history of Argentine sport.

Gustav Strube was a German-born conductor, violinist, and composer who became an important musical figure in Baltimore. He studied at the Leipzig Conservatory and performed with the Gewandhaus Orchestra before joining the Boston Symphony Orchestra after moving to the United States. His early career combined orchestral playing with teaching and the performance of dance music, work that helped support him while he established himself professionally. In Baltimore, Strube taught at the Peabody Institute and in 1916 became the first conductor of the Baltimore Symphony Orchestra. He shaped the ensemble’s early programming and helped establish regular orchestral concerts in the city. Strube also wrote operas, including Ramona and The Captive, the latter of which was staged in Baltimore during the 1930s. His circle included journalists, musicians, and other members of the city’s Saturday Night Club. Strube remained active as a teacher and composer after leaving the orchestra, and his career linked the German musical tradition with the developing American concert institutions of the early twentieth century.

Nonuniversal theory describes cognitive development as a set of pathways that may differ from one area of ability to another. A child can therefore be advanced in language, inexperienced in mathematics, and developing at an intermediate level in music without passing through one identical sequence in every domain. David Henry Feldman’s model uses a progression of labels beginning with novice and moving through apprentice, journeyman, craftsman, expert, and master. Movement between stages is not simply the accumulation of more facts. A learner first consolidates existing abilities, then expands the repertoire with new skills. Periods of relative stability may follow, until an especially advanced ability appears and changes the organization of the rest. That emerging strength can draw weaker skills forward before another cycle begins. The theory contrasts with developmental accounts that assign the same stages and ages to all forms of knowledge. It is particularly useful for describing expertise in specialized fields, where progress depends on opportunities, instruction, motivation, and the structure of the domain.

El Chavo Animado is an animated Mexican comedy series adapted from the live-action programme El Chavo del Ocho. The cartoon retains the familiar courtyard setting and its group of children and adults, but uses digital animation to enlarge the physical comedy and reproduce situations that had become well known from the original show. Televisa and Ánima Estudios produced the series, which first appeared on Mexican television in the mid-2000s and was later shown elsewhere in Latin America. Many episodes reworked stories from the earlier programme, while the animated format allowed characters to move through exaggerated environments and visual gags. The launch was accompanied by a merchandising campaign and promotional events designed to connect the new series with the older audience. More than a hundred episodes were broadcast over several seasons. Repeats remained part of children’s programming after the initial run ended, and the series extended the franchise to viewers who encountered El Chavo through animation rather than through the original live-action broadcasts.

Maxwell is a graphics-processing architecture developed by Nvidia after Kepler. It was designed to improve performance per watt and appeared first in mid-range GeForce cards before being expanded to more powerful products. The initial chips, identified by the GM107 designation, powered the GeForce GTX 750 and GTX 750 Ti. A later generation used GM20x processors in cards such as the GTX 970, GTX 980, GTX 960, Titan X, and GTX 980 Ti. Maxwell products were manufactured on a 28-nanometre process and were also used in mobile graphics, professional Quadro boards, and selected embedded systems. Architectural changes included redesigned streaming multiprocessors and improvements to memory compression, allowing the processors to make more effective use of available bandwidth. The company marketed Maxwell as a substantial efficiency improvement rather than simply a larger version of the preceding design. It occupied the period between Kepler and Pascal and supported gaming, workstation, and mobile products across several product families.

Panackelty is a slow-cooked meat and vegetable dish associated with northeastern England. The basic preparation uses beef or lamb with potatoes, onions, and carrots, although families have traditionally altered the ingredients according to what was available. Corned beef is common in some versions, especially when the dish is made from leftovers. Everything is placed in a heavy pot and cooked gently for several hours so that the meat softens and the vegetables absorb its stock. Some cooks arrange sliced potatoes across the top, allowing them to brown while the lower layers simmer. The dish may be prepared in an oven, on a stovetop, or in a large frying pan, and a looser version can be served almost like soup. Local spellings and names include panacalty, panack, tatey pot, and corned beef and tatey pot. Its regional variations are less a matter of a fixed recipe than of household practice, with the central idea being economical use of simple ingredients.

Heywood railway station is a heritage railway station serving the town of Heywood in Greater Manchester. The original station opened in the nineteenth century on the Manchester and Leeds Railway and was later moved when the line was extended toward Bury. Passenger services ended in 1970, after which the railway buildings and track ceased to function as part of the national network. The East Lancashire Railway reopened the site in 2003 as part of its preserved line between Heywood and Bury Bolton Street. Steam and heritage diesel trains now use the station during operating seasons, making it a starting point for visitors exploring the former industrial railway. Proposals have periodically suggested reconnecting Heywood with the national network through Castleton, which would permit direct services toward Manchester. Funding and planning difficulties have prevented that project from proceeding. Even without the connection, the station contributes to local tourism and has been discussed as part of broader plans for the redevelopment of the surrounding area.

Talking Heads were a New York band whose music joined the nervous energy of punk with the precision of art rock, funk, and African-influenced rhythms. David Byrne, Chris Frantz, Tina Weymouth, and Jerry Harrison formed the core lineup, although their records and concerts increasingly involved additional musicians. Their first album introduced short, tightly arranged songs shaped by Byrne’s uneasy vocals and the rhythm section’s spare, propulsive playing. Working with Brian Eno on later albums, the band expanded its sound through layered percussion, synthesizers, and repeated patterns. Remain in Light was especially important for its use of interlocking grooves and contributions from musicians associated with funk and Afrobeat. Onstage, the group moved from a minimal quartet toward a large ensemble that included guitarists, keyboard players, singers, and percussionists. Talking Heads ended their active career in the early 1990s, but their combination of dance music, experimental production, and art-school theatricality continued to influence alternative and popular music.

The iPhone XR is a smartphone released by Apple in 2018 alongside the iPhone XS and XS Max. It used the same A12 Bionic processor as the more expensive models, but reduced the price through a different display, an aluminium frame, and a single rear camera. Its 6.1-inch screen was an LCD panel marketed as Liquid Retina rather than the OLED display used in the XS line. Face ID, wireless charging, and the gesture-based interface were retained, while the colourful glass back was offered in several finishes. The camera software used the processor to provide portrait effects even though the phone lacked the second telephoto lens found on Apple’s premium models. Battery life was a major selling point, exceeding that of the earlier iPhone 8 Plus under Apple’s testing conditions. The XR was positioned as a mainstream flagship: it provided the company’s current processor and most of its interface features without the highest price associated with the OLED models.

Jack Eagle was an American performer who moved from music and comedy into television advertising. He played trumpet during the big-band era and later worked as a comedian in the resorts of New York’s Catskill Mountains. His best-known character was Brother Dominic, a cheerful monk who appeared in a series of Xerox commercials beginning in the 1970s. The campaign presented the fictional monk as a user of the company’s copying machines and made Eagle’s face familiar to a national audience. Brother Dominic became a recurring corporate mascot, and Eagle spent years appearing at promotional events for the company as well as in filmed advertisements. He later estimated that the commercial work earned him more during a short period than his earlier entertainment career had produced. Eagle also played other advertising characters, including a figure used to promote margarine and cholesterol-conscious eating. His career illustrates how an actor’s association with one memorable advertising role can become more enduring than a conventional film or television credit.

Rødkleiva is a winter-sports hill in Oslo’s Nordmarka forest. It became a venue for alpine skiing in the years after the Second World War and was repeatedly included in the Holmenkollen Ski Festival’s combined events. During the 1952 Winter Olympics, thousands of spectators watched the slalom competition on the hillside. The course later deteriorated and was closed in the 1980s. Rødkleiva has also attracted proposals for a ski-jumping facility. Ideas for a jump at the site appeared as early as the 1910s and returned whenever Oslo’s existing ramps required replacement or expansion. Supporters argued that the hill could provide a new normal or flying hill close to the capital, but construction would have required substantial public investment and approval from local authorities. Competing plans at other Norwegian venues, together with the cost of the project, prevented the proposals from reaching construction. Rødkleiva is now remembered both for its Olympic history and for the series of unrealized jumping schemes attached to it.

The Indianist movement was a tendency in American concert music that sought to create a national style by incorporating imagined or collected Native American materials into European-derived composition. It reached its greatest visibility between the late nineteenth century and the early decades of the twentieth. Composers such as Arthur Farwell, Charles Wakefield Cadman, Charles Sanford Skilton, and Arthur Nevin wrote orchestral, chamber, vocal, and piano works described as Indianist. Some used melodies gathered from Indigenous communities, while others invented themes according to contemporary ideas about the “Indian” sound. The movement reflected a broader interest in American folk traditions, but it also carried the racial assumptions and romantic stereotypes of its period. Later scholars have questioned whether Indianism formed a coherent school at all or whether the label grouped together composers whose approaches differed considerably. Its history is therefore studied both as an attempt to define American musical identity and as an example of how classical composers appropriated Indigenous culture for a national artistic project.

Public Health England was an executive agency created in 2013 to coordinate health protection and improve population health in England. It absorbed responsibilities from the former Health Protection Agency and from several organizations concerned with treatment, prevention, and health information. The agency monitored infectious diseases, investigated outbreaks, advised on environmental hazards, supported vaccination programmes, and produced evidence for reducing health inequalities. Although it operated within the Department of Health and Social Care, it had its own staff and operational structure. The COVID-19 pandemic placed its testing, surveillance, and communications functions under unusually intense public scrutiny. In 2021 the government abolished Public Health England and divided its responsibilities among new and existing bodies. The United Kingdom Health Security Agency took responsibility for health protection and emergency preparedness, while health-improvement work moved to the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities and other parts of the health service. The agency’s brief existence reflected continuing debate about how public health should be organized nationally.

Dayspring Christian Academy is a private Christian school in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, serving children from preschool through the end of secondary school. Its educational programme combines conventional academic subjects with a classical curriculum that emphasizes history, languages, literature, mathematics, science, logic, rhetoric, and the arts. Latin and Greek are included in the language programme, while biblical teaching is treated as a framework connecting the different fields of study. The school offers advanced and dual-credit courses for older students and maintains extracurricular activities in athletics and the arts. It is accredited by Christian-school associations and has received recognition in local school rankings. Dayspring describes its model as a revival of forms of education used in the early United States, adapted for contemporary classrooms. Students remain in a single institution across multiple age levels, allowing the school to organize its curriculum as a continuous progression from early learning to college preparation.

Mandatory is a display typeface derived from the lettering used on British vehicle registration plates. Its heavy, uncomplicated characters are intended to remain readable at a distance and difficult to alter by adding strokes or changing individual digits. The design includes deliberate distinctions in letters such as M, W, and Q, as well as controlled spacing between characters. British registration plates have been required to use the approved form since the early 2000s, together with rules governing character height, width, margins, reflectivity, and plate construction. The typeface has also appeared in other countries’ registration systems, although local regulations may prescribe different sizes or layouts. Brazil used a related form during an earlier period before adopting the Mercosur plate design. Digital copies of Mandatory are available for some personal uses, but reproducing it on a legal vehicle plate does not by itself satisfy registration requirements. The font’s primary purpose is functional legibility rather than decorative display.

The Elephant 6 Recording Company is a network of American musicians and bands associated with psychedelic pop and home-recording experimentation. It was never a conventional label with a fixed roster. Instead, the name described friendships, shared equipment, collaborative projects, and a common enthusiasm for the bright harmonies and studio imagination of 1960s pop. The Apples in Stereo, Olivia Tremor Control, Neutral Milk Hotel, Beulah, Elf Power, of Montreal, the Minders, and Circulatory System are among the groups linked with the network. Its origins lay in recordings made by a few friends in Louisiana, after which members relocated and established active scenes in Athens, Georgia, and Denver. Some releases used deliberately rough or homemade production, while others employed elaborate arrangements and analogue effects. The collective’s most visible period came during the 1990s, when its records reached audiences far beyond the small communities in which they were made. Elephant 6 is remembered less for a single sound than for an unusually cooperative approach to independent music.

Debu is an Indonesian-based musical group whose songs combine Islamic devotional themes with an international ensemble. The group began in the early 2000s among teachers and students connected with a university in Makassar before moving its base to Jakarta. Its members have come from several countries, but the group presents that diversity as secondary to the spiritual message of its music. The name Debu, meaning “dust” in Indonesian, refers to the insignificance of individual performers when compared with God and the purpose of the songs. Concerts may include percussion, strings, keyboards, and vocal harmonies, with lyrics devoted to prayer, humility, and the movement of human life toward its source. The group has recorded and performed for audiences in Indonesia and abroad, using popular musical forms to communicate religious ideas. Public descriptions of Debu often emphasize that the musicians are not meant to become the focus of attention; the music is intended to direct listeners toward remembrance and devotion.

Busfest is an annual gathering for owners and enthusiasts of Volkswagen camper vans held at the Three Counties Showground in Malvern, Worcestershire. The event began in the 1990s under another name and developed into a large international meeting for vehicles ranging from restored early Transporters to modern camper conversions. Visitors may camp beside their vans, browse parts and accessories, attend technical demonstrations, and compare customized interiors and paintwork. Trade stalls occupy a substantial part of the showground, while arenas host music, talks, vehicle displays, and competitions. Families can also use fairground rides and other entertainment areas, so the festival functions as a general camping weekend as well as a specialist motor event. Participants arrive from Britain and continental Europe, with smaller groups travelling from farther overseas. Volunteers help manage the campsites and traffic alongside the professional production staff. The combination of practical advice, collecting, and social camping has made Busfest one of the largest events devoted to the Volkswagen Transporter.

The Federal Street District is a historic neighbourhood in Salem, Massachusetts, centred on a block of Federal Street between Washington and North Streets. It contains civic buildings, churches, houses, and former commercial structures that illustrate the city’s development from the eighteenth through the nineteenth century. The earliest courthouse on the site was built in 1785. Later public buildings include an 1840s granite courthouse designed in the Greek Revival manner and a Superior Court building erected two decades later. The latter was subsequently altered, giving it features associated with the Richardsonian Romanesque style. The district was first recognized through a National Register listing for the county court buildings and was expanded in the 1980s to include the surrounding block and the Tabernacle Church on Washington Street. Newer courthouse construction nearby has changed the area’s institutional setting, but the older buildings remain important landmarks. Their close arrangement makes the district a compact record of changing ideas about public architecture and local government.

Christopher Watson is a British tenor whose repertory ranges from medieval and Renaissance music to Baroque works and contemporary composition. He studied music at the University of Exeter after first learning the tuba and sang in the university chapel choir and at Exeter Cathedral. His early professional appointments included lay-clerk positions at Durham Cathedral, Christ Church Cathedral in Oxford, and Westminster Cathedral. Watson later moved to Australia, where he became director of music for the choir of Trinity College at the University of Melbourne. As a singer, he has worked both as a soloist and as a member of specialist ensembles. His collaborations have included The Tallis Scholars, Alamire, Gallicantus, Collegium Vocale, Tenebrae, and Theatre of Voices. He has also conducted chamber and collegiate choirs in Britain. Watson’s career combines the disciplined daily work of cathedral music with the international touring and recording demands of early-music performance.

Check Point GO was a portable security system designed to give a user a protected work environment on a Windows computer. The product combined a USB flash drive with encryption, virtualization, and secure network access. After the device was connected, it could launch an isolated desktop whose files and applications were separated from the host machine. This arrangement was intended for employees working from hotel computers, conference centres, or other machines outside the organization’s direct control. Credentials and documents stored within the workspace were encrypted, and access could be governed by password rules, certificates, tokens, and policies delivered through the company’s security infrastructure. A lost drive was therefore supposed to reveal neither the user’s files nor the corporate network to an unauthorized finder. The system was aimed at organizations that needed a controlled remote desktop without issuing a complete laptop to every travelling employee.

Colombia’s telecommunications industry expanded rapidly after reforms opened the sector to greater competition in the early 1990s. New investment supported mobile services, internet access, international links, and improvements to the fixed-line network. Growth was uneven, however, and the financial crisis around the turn of the century placed heavy pressure on the state telephone company. The government eventually liquidated the indebted Empresa Nacional de Telecomunicaciones and created Colombia Telecomunicaciones as its successor. A later strategic investment by Telefónica brought additional capital and management expertise while leaving the company in a more competitive market. Telecommunications became an increasingly important part of the national economy, although high-quality service remained concentrated in major cities and towns. Colombia’s international connections included submarine cables, satellite earth stations, and microwave links that extended service across difficult terrain. The sector’s development therefore involved both privatization and infrastructure building, with the benefits of modernization reaching urban users sooner than remote communities.

The Sutton Community Hall is a small historic meeting building in the Sutton area of Alaska. Its earliest purpose was not civic: it was constructed in the 1920s as lodging for workers involved in the development of the Eklutna power project. The wood-frame structure was later moved to its present site, where it became a gathering place for residents of the unincorporated community. A shallow metal roof covers the single-storey building, whose exterior combines board-and-batten siding with other forms of cladding added or altered over time. Entrances on several sides allowed the hall to serve different events and made it accessible from the surrounding settlement. For about four decades it hosted meetings, social occasions, and local activities that would otherwise have required travel to a larger town. By the time it was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, the hall was no longer in regular use and needed substantial care. Its significance comes from both its movable construction history and its role in Sutton’s community life.

The Philips PM5544 is a television test-pattern generator associated with the circular Philips pattern once broadcast by stations during periods when no programme was on air. The design places a large circle within a grid of geometric lines, colour fields, alignment marks, and identification information. Engineers used these elements to judge picture geometry, convergence, aspect ratio, colour reproduction, and signal stability. The pattern was developed at the Philips laboratory in Copenhagen in the late 1960s by a team led by Finn Hendil under the supervision of Erik Helmer Nielsen. Hardware capable of producing it entered service shortly afterward. Because the image exposed several kinds of distortion at once, technicians could diagnose a receiver or transmission chain by examining the shape and position of its features. Related Philips generators produced other national and regional patterns, but the PM5544 design became recognizable to television viewers in many countries. It remains a familiar emblem of analogue broadcasting.

Photoactivatable probes are research tools that remain inactive until a scientist exposes them to a selected wavelength of light. A light-sensitive chemical group may be attached to a small molecule, protein, or nucleic acid, temporarily blocking its activity. Illumination removes or changes that group and releases the probe at a chosen time and place. Researchers can therefore observe what happens when a signal, drug, enzyme, or gene-related process begins inside a cell. Lasers and ultraviolet lamps are commonly used as triggers, and a microscope can often provide both the illumination and the imaging. The method offers fine control over timing and location: one region of a cell may be activated while a neighbouring region is left untreated. Probe design must account for light penetration, unintended chemical reactions, and possible damage from ultraviolet exposure. Despite these limitations, caged compounds have become valuable for studying rapid biological events in cultured cells, tissues, and some living organisms.

Frozen is a Disney entertainment franchise that grew from the success of the animated film released in 2013. The film reimagined elements of Hans Christian Andersen’s The Snow Queen through the relationship between sisters Elsa and Anna, combining fantasy adventure with musical storytelling. Its songs, characters, and visual design quickly moved beyond the cinema into a broad range of products and experiences. Disney developed a sequel, short films, books, stage productions, touring ice shows, video games, and attractions for its theme parks. Merchandise featuring the sisters, Olaf, and other characters became a major part of the brand’s international presence. The Broadway musical translated the film’s songs and plot into a live theatrical form, while theme-park installations allowed visitors to enter versions of its fictional kingdom. Frozen is therefore treated not simply as a pair of films but as a long-term franchise whose characters support recurring releases across several entertainment industries.

Toronto’s Chinatowns are neighbourhoods shaped by Chinese immigration, commerce, community organizations, and changing patterns of urban development. The downtown Chinatown along Spadina Avenue and Dundas Street West is the best-known example, but it is not the only one. An earlier Chinese district grew in the area known as the Ward before redevelopment and displacement moved the community westward. Later residents and businesses established another concentration near Broadview Avenue and Gerrard Street, often called East Chinatown. Suburban districts in Scarborough and North York developed as immigration increased and Chinese families moved beyond the central city. Markham, Richmond Hill, and Mississauga also contain major Chinese commercial areas, with restaurants, groceries, professional services, schools, and cultural associations. These districts are not identical: some retain dense street-front markets, while others are organized around plazas and suburban roads. Together they form a network linking Toronto’s Chinese-Canadian communities across the metropolitan region.

The Phuket Big Buddha is a large seated image of Gautama Buddha on Nakkerd Hill overlooking southern Phuket. Its formal name is Phra Phutta Ming Mongkol Eknakiri, although visitors generally use the shorter name. Construction began in the early twenty-first century as a religious and landmark project associated with Wat Kitthi Sankaram, also known as Wat Kata. The concrete statue is faced with white marble and is positioned so that it looks toward Ao Chalong Bay. From the hilltop, visitors can see much of the surrounding coastline and nearby settlements. Work on the base and surrounding facilities continued for years after the principal figure had been erected, reflecting the project’s gradual construction and funding. The statue was recognized by Thailand’s senior Buddhist leadership as an important religious monument. Its combination of pilgrimage site, viewpoint, and tourist attraction has made it one of Phuket’s most visible contemporary landmarks.

Noah was the performance name of Danish singer and songwriter Troels Gustavsen during the period when he recorded with Lasse Dyrholm. The pair met at school and began posting songs online before signing with Copenhagen Records. Their first single for the label, “Alt er forbi,” entered the Danish singles chart, and the duo released a self-titled album in 2013. Their songs used polished pop arrangements and direct Danish-language lyrics, helping them build an audience beyond the school-age circle in which they had started. Dyrholm left the project at the end of 2015 to pursue other creative work. Gustavsen continued under the Noah name for a time, releasing “Vi brænder” as the first single of the new phase and later seeing the song selected as Denmark’s official Olympic song for the Rio Games. From 2020 onward he performed under his own name, marking a transition from the group identity to a solo career.

Active Desktop was a Windows feature that treated the computer desktop as a place for live web content rather than only a background image and collection of icons. Introduced with the Windows Desktop Update associated with Internet Explorer 4, it allowed users to place HTML material directly on the desktop or inside movable, resizable items. A stock ticker, news panel, weather display, or other web page could update itself through the network without the user opening a browser window. The feature appeared in Windows 95 as an optional component and was included in later consumer editions, including Windows 98 and some 32-bit versions of Windows XP. Microsoft removed it from later systems and from certain 64-bit releases. Active Desktop reflected an era when software companies imagined the desktop and the World Wide Web becoming a single interface. Its automatic synchronization was convenient, but the feature also consumed system resources and raised security and reliability concerns as web content became more complex.

Uma2rman is a Russian pop-rock group formed by brothers Sergei and Vladimir Kristovsky. The band began releasing music in the early 2000s and gained attention with songs that combined accessible rock arrangements, humorous writing, and a distinctly Russian pop sensibility. Their first full-length album appeared in 2004, after which the brothers expanded the project for concerts with keyboardists, drummers, and guitarists. The group received a nomination at the 2004 MTV Europe Music Awards in the Russian-group category. Its work has also been used in film, including music connected with the Russian production Passenger. Uma2rman’s name has appeared in several spellings as the group’s releases circulated internationally. The band’s songs often move between light comedy and dramatic storytelling, and its live identity depends on the contrast between the two brothers’ songwriting and the larger touring ensemble. The group remained active after its initial breakthrough, with changing supporting musicians around the Kristovsky partnership.
