Mark Van Doren was an American poet, critic, and teacher whose long career at Columbia University made him an influential figure in twentieth-century literary education. He taught English for nearly four decades and was known for treating poetry and literature as living forms of thought rather than as subjects to be reduced to historical information. Among the writers he encouraged or influenced were Thomas Merton, John Berryman, Robert Lax, Whittaker Chambers, and members of the Beat generation. Van Doren also worked as an editor and critic for The Nation, reviewing both books and films. His Collected Poems 1922–1938 received the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1940. Other publications included studies of Dryden, Shakespeare, Hawthorne, and American and British literature, as well as narrative poems and verse drama. His writing moved between scholarly criticism and accessible literary appreciation. Van Doren’s reputation rests on both the books he published and the generations of students and authors who remembered his classroom influence.

The Common Final Examination is the national examination taken by candidates seeking the Chartered Professional Accountant designation in Canada. It is written over three consecutive days after the candidate has completed the CPA Professional Education Program and the required preparatory coursework. Rather than testing isolated formulas, the examination presents integrated business cases that require candidates to identify issues, analyze evidence, choose among possible actions, and justify professional conclusions. Financial reporting, assurance, taxation, finance, strategy, governance, and performance management may all appear in the cases. Candidates must also demonstrate communication and professional judgment under time limits. The CFE replaced the earlier examinations associated with the separate Canadian accounting designations after the CA, CMA, and CGA organizations were unified. Passing the examination is one step in the qualification process; candidates must also complete an approved period of practical experience before receiving the CPA designation. The exam is administered nationally and delivered through regional professional bodies.

The Luleå algorithm is a compact data structure for finding the longest matching prefix in an Internet routing table. A router must compare an incoming IPv4 address with stored network prefixes and select the most specific entry that applies. A straightforward binary trie represents one node for each successive bit, but a large routing table can make that structure expensive in memory and require many pointer traversals. The Luleå method reduces the cost by retaining carefully chosen information from only selected levels of the trie. Tables and compressed representations allow the search to skip groups of addresses while still recovering the correct prefix. The approach was developed by researchers associated with Luleå University of Technology and became influential in discussions of high-speed routing. Its name was adopted in correspondence about the work rather than from the title of the original paper. The algorithm is an example of how a specialized representation can make a familiar tree-search problem practical for large network systems.

Buddha-nature is a Mahayana Buddhist concept used to explain how beings who are not yet enlightened can nevertheless become Buddhas. Related Sanskrit terms include tathāgatagarbha, often translated through images of a womb, embryo, or seed of the Buddha, and buddhadhātu, which can refer to a Buddha realm or underlying Buddha element. Texts presenting the idea appeared in India during the centuries when Mahayana thought was developing in new directions. Some passages describe an awakened potential hidden beneath confusion and destructive habits; others speak as though an aspect of Buddhahood is already present within every sentient being. Buddhist schools have not interpreted these statements identically. For some, Buddha-nature is a way of describing the mind’s capacity for transformation, while for others it suggests a deeper, enduring principle. The doctrine addresses a central question of Mahayana practice: if ordinary beings are caught in ignorance, what makes liberation possible? Its language of seeds, wombs, and inner nature answers that question in symbolic rather than purely psychological terms.

Kevin Michael Ward was an American baseball player who reached Major League Baseball as an outfielder with the San Diego Padres. He grew up in Pennsylvania and played both football and baseball at the University of Arizona. Ward began college as a quarterback, later moved to receiver, and continued to develop as a baseball player under coach Jerry Kindall. During the 1982 season he led his university team in batting average, runs batted in, and stolen bases, earning recognition from the All-Pac-10 South selectors. He also spent a summer playing for the Harwich Mariners in the Cape Cod Baseball League, a competition that has served as a proving ground for many college players. His professional career included time in the Padres organization and an appearance in the major leagues. Ward’s path from a multi-sport college athlete to professional baseball reflected the uncertainty of early specialization, especially for players who had competed at a high level in more than one sport.

Pneumonia was the final studio album by Whiskeytown, released by Lost Highway Records in 2001 after a long and unsettled production history. The band recorded a large amount of material while its lineup and record-company situation were changing. A corporate merger disrupted the group’s original release plans, and the finished album remained unreleased for an extended period. During that time, unauthorized copies circulated among fans, giving the record the reputation of a missing or abandoned project. Its eventual appearance coincided with the growing solo career of songwriter Ryan Adams and was received partly as a closing statement from Whiskeytown. The album’s title suggested a slow illness, which Adams connected with the record’s themes of romantic exhaustion and emotional collapse. The songs retain the group’s mixture of country instrumentation, rock arrangements, and unstable intimacy, but the circumstances surrounding them lend the album a particularly final atmosphere. Pneumonia is therefore remembered both as a set of songs and as the document of a band coming apart.

Split Enz was a New Zealand rock group formed by Tim Finn and Phil Judd in the 1970s. The band’s membership changed repeatedly, but its music retained a taste for theatrical presentation, unusual melodies, and abrupt shifts between pop accessibility and art-rock eccentricity. After early experimental records, Split Enz reached a broad audience with the arrival of songs such as “I Got You,” “One Step Ahead,” “History Never Repeats,” and “Six Months in a Leaky Boat.” The group became particularly successful in New Zealand and Australia, where several albums reached the top of the charts during the early 1980s. Its records also attracted listeners in Britain, Canada, and the United States, although the band’s international success was less consistent. Split Enz’s catalogue has been influential in New Zealand popular music, and the group appears frequently in national lists of important songs. The band’s imaginative costumes and stage identities were as much a part of its public reputation as its melodic songwriting.

En Marea was a Galician political coalition that brought together Podemos, Anova, United Left, and several local citizen alliances. It emerged from municipal movements that had won support in cities such as A Coruña, Santiago de Compostela, and Ferrol, and it first contested national elections as an electoral confluence rather than as a single traditional party. Ballots used a combined name reflecting its agreements with Podemos and the other participating organizations. The coalition also received support from smaller environmental and left-wing groups, whose involvement varied between elections. Before the 2016 Galician regional contest, the partners decided to formalize En Marea as a political party. That change was intended to create a common organization, but it also exposed disagreements over leadership, internal democracy, and the balance between the coalition’s national and Galician identities. En Marea belongs to a wider wave of Spanish political alliances built from local anti-austerity movements and new left parties.

Nagnajiti is a figure in Vaishnavite tradition counted among Krishna’s eight principal queens. She is also called Satya, and in South Indian devotional literature a related figure appears under the name Nappinnai. Accounts identify her as the daughter of King Nagnajita of Kosala and connect her with the goddess Nila, regarded as a consort of Vishnu. In the story of her marriage, Krishna must complete a difficult contest involving seven powerful bulls. He subdues the animals and thereby wins the right to marry her. The episode is one of several marriage narratives that surround Krishna’s royal life and divine identity. Tamil devotional poetry gives Nappinnai a prominent place, and later interpreters connect that beloved figure with Nagnajiti even though the names and narrative settings differ across traditions. Her importance therefore lies not only in the episode of the bulls but also in the way regional devotional texts translate and reshape the identities of Krishna’s companions.

Heinrich Jacob Bashuysen was a German printer and scholar who specialized in Hebrew and rabbinical literature. Born in Hanau, he established a press there during the early eighteenth century and issued more than a hundred publications. His work combined printing with translation and editorial projects intended to make Jewish scholarship available to a wider learned audience. Bashuysen translated selections from rabbinical commentaries on the Psalms and prepared material from Maimonides’ Mishneh Torah. He also published Isaac Abravanel’s commentary on the Pentateuch and planned a larger edition of the complete work. Several of his projects were never finished, including proposed translations of a Hebrew grammar and an expanded history of the teachers of the Mishnah. Bashuysen’s interests extended beyond production: he corresponded with scholars, employed specialists in Hebrew, and used his press as a centre for Orientalist study. His surviving publications show how early modern printing houses could function simultaneously as businesses, research workshops, and institutions of learned exchange.

Benny Fields was an American singer who became famous in vaudeville and recordings as the partner of Blossom Seeley. Born Benjamin Geisenfeld in Milwaukee, he began performing in Chicago cafés, where his relaxed delivery and warm voice attracted attention. Seeley encountered him in 1921 while touring and initially engaged him to sing from offstage as accompaniment for her act. Audiences gradually began to notice Fields as much as the featured performer, and he became a full partner in the show. The two married the following year and developed a successful stage identity built on the contrast between Seeley’s exuberant style and Fields’s easygoing phrasing. They recorded together and appeared in short films made for the Vitaphone system during the late 1920s. Fields also worked in radio, including programmes connected with the Ziegfeld name. His career shows how vaudeville performers could move between theatre, records, film, and broadcasting while preserving a recognizable act across each medium.

Machir ben Judah was a Jewish scholar associated with northern France in the tenth or eleventh century and is traditionally described as a brother of Gershom ben Judah. His principal work was the Alfa Beta de-R. Makir, an alphabetical dictionary that no longer survives as an independent book. Later medieval commentators quoted it frequently, especially when explaining difficult words and passages in the Talmud. Rashi is among the writers who preserve evidence of Machir’s definitions, and other scholars of the Tosafist tradition also drew upon the work. Machir often followed interpretations associated with his brother, but the two did not agree on every term. In disputed cases, later authorities sometimes preferred Machir’s explanation. Because the dictionary is lost, its contents must be reconstructed from these scattered citations. The quotations suggest that it served primarily as a lexical aid, providing explanations of rare, technical, or obscure Talmudic language for readers who could not rely on a continuous translation.

Stephen Kipkoech Kibiwott is a Kenyan road runner who has competed internationally in the half marathon and marathon. He entered the European professional circuit after placing highly in a race in Eldoret and quickly collected victories in major city events. In 2006 he won the Prague Half Marathon and the Turin Marathon and also finished near the front at the Alexander the Great Marathon. The following season was difficult: he failed to complete the London and Prague Marathons and placed well back in Frankfurt. Kibiwott recovered in 2008, winning the Paris Half Marathon and returning to the top of the Turin race. A personal-best time of 59 minutes 44 seconds at Lille helped secure his place on Kenya’s team for the IAAF World Half Marathon Championships. He finished fourth in the individual contest and contributed to Kenya’s team gold medal. His career illustrates the uneven form common in road racing, where a runner may move from major victories to non-finishes and back again within a few seasons.

Kristiania Kommunale Sporveie was a municipal tram operator in Oslo that existed for only a few years at the beginning of the twentieth century. Commonly called the Red Tramway, it was created after the city council decided that local government should participate directly in public transport. The company opened routes serving Sagene, Rodeløkka, and Vippetangen, connecting them with tracks operated by the older private tram companies. Its fleet included motor trams supplied by Schuckert and matching trailers, while depots were built at Sagene and Rodeløkka. Service was generally frequent, with some lines running at ten-minute intervals, but the undertaking did not produce a profit. A change in the political balance of the municipal council weakened support for continued public ownership. In 1905 the council rejected the idea of purchasing the struggling company and instead approved its sale to Kristiania Sporveisselskab. The short experiment left a mark on Oslo’s transport history as an early attempt at municipal operation.

Max Leon Stibbe was a Dutch educator and anthroposophist who helped establish Waldorf education in the Netherlands. Born in the Dutch East Indies, he moved to the Netherlands as a teenager and initially studied law. After a brief period in legal employment, he changed direction and devoted himself to education. In 1923 he helped found De Vrije School in The Hague, the first Dutch school based on the Waldorf educational approach, and worked there as a teacher. Stibbe left Europe in 1939 because of his Jewish background and returned to Batavia, where he opened an educational consultancy. The Japanese occupation interrupted this work and led to his internment. After the war he resumed educational activity in the Netherlands and remained involved in anthroposophical organizations. His books and essays addressed teaching, European cultural character, human development, and the figure of Kaspar Hauser. Stibbe’s life was shaped by both educational conviction and the political upheavals that forced him to move between continents.

Udyan Express is a long-distance Indian Railways service linking Mumbai with Bengaluru. The train travels through Maharashtra and Karnataka, with an operational history that has also included service through neighbouring parts of the Deccan region. Its name comes from the Sanskrit-derived word for a garden and refers to Bengaluru’s reputation as India’s Garden City, associated with parks such as Lalbagh and Cubbon Park. The service operates in both directions under separate train numbers and has been renumbered during changes to the national timetable. Although it is marketed as an express, the route covers a substantial distance and serves passengers travelling between major urban centres as well as intermediate stations. The train’s rolling stock has at times been shared with another express service, and administrative responsibility has shifted within the railway system. Udyan Express is therefore both a passenger connection and an example of the way Indian Railways names long-distance services after the cities and regions they connect.

Paraspur is a rural town and administrative block in Gonda district, Uttar Pradesh. The block contains dozens of village councils and more than ninety villages, making it one of the larger local administrative units in the district. Its settlements are linked to nearby market towns by roads, while the railway station at Colonelganj provides access to the wider regional network. Lucknow lies considerably farther away and is the nearest major urban centre with an airport. Agriculture shapes the local economy and much of daily life, although literacy and access to services differ sharply between men and women in the available demographic descriptions. Paraspur is also situated near several places of religious or historical interest. Colonelganj is associated with the uprising of 1857, Rajapur is connected with the poet Tulsidas, and Paska is identified in local tradition with an important mythological site. The block’s importance therefore comes from its population and administrative reach as well as from the cultural landscape around it.

Fluid catalytic cracking is a refinery process that converts heavy petroleum fractions into lighter and more valuable products. The feed is usually heavy gas oil, a mixture of long-chain hydrocarbons with boiling points too high for direct use as gasoline. After heating, the oil meets a fine powdered catalyst in a reactor. The catalyst promotes reactions that break large molecules into shorter chains, producing gasoline-range compounds, olefin gases, and other streams used by the petrochemical industry. Catalyst particles move continuously between the reaction vessel and a regenerator, where deposits of coke are burned away and heat is restored. This circulation gives the process its “fluid” character. Compared with older thermal cracking, catalytic cracking can produce more high-octane gasoline and economically useful unsaturated gases. Operators adjust temperature, pressure, residence time, and catalyst composition to control the product mixture. FCC units are among the most visually distinctive and chemically important installations in a modern petroleum refinery.

Ardozyga voluta is an Australian gelechiid moth described by Edward Meyrick in the early twentieth century. The species has been recorded from New South Wales and is distinguished by a patterned forewing rather than by a conspicuous body marking. The forewing is pale, with a faint ochreous cast along the leading edge and scattered dark scales across the surface. A broad dark patch extends from the lower edge toward the centre, while a second band crosses the wing closer to the tip. Pale spots interrupt that band near the costa, and a narrow dark line follows the terminal edge. The hindwing is lighter at the base and becomes greyish toward the margin. As with many small moths, its adult appearance is described mainly through the placement, shape, and colour of wing markings used by taxonomists. Records from Australia remain geographically limited, and the species is more familiar in collections and identification literature than in general accounts of wildlife.

New Tampa is a rapidly developed area in the northern part of the Tampa metropolitan region. The name is used most precisely for a large Tampa neighbourhood annexed by the city in 1988, but residents and businesses sometimes apply it to adjoining unincorporated communities north of the city. Much of the incorporated district was rural before annexation. Since then, master-planned subdivisions, apartment complexes, schools, shopping centres, and major roads have transformed the landscape. Large retail developments followed the increase in households, while former pasture and wooded land was divided into residential tracts. The broader usage of “New Tampa” can include areas near Wesley Chapel even though those places lie outside Tampa’s legal boundaries. This creates a distinction between the official neighbourhood and the name used in everyday conversation. New Tampa’s growth has made it one of the city’s largest suburban-style districts and has also produced debates about traffic, public services, and the preservation of remaining open land.

George Meegan is a British adventurer known for walking the length of the Western Hemisphere. Beginning at the southern end of South America in the 1970s, he travelled north through the continent and eventually reached Prudhoe Bay in Alaska. The journey covered more than nineteen thousand miles and took several years, making it one of the longest continuous pedestrian expeditions recorded. Meegan carried supplies, crossed a wide range of climates, and relied on assistance from communities encountered along the route. He later described the experience in The Longest Walk and discussed it in television appearances and public lectures. Encounters with Indigenous communities influenced his later interests in education and cultural continuity. Meegan became concerned with ways that people could participate in modern technological life without abandoning local language or identity. His later writing extended that concern to children’s education, arguing for learning shaped by curiosity and personal purpose rather than by a single centralized system.

PictureBox was an independent publishing company in Brooklyn that produced books and projects spanning contemporary art, music, photography, comics, and design. Directed by Dan Nadel, the company treated publishing as a form of exhibition: books could document an artist’s work, gather material from an overlooked scene, or create an object whose packaging was part of the concept. Its catalogue included the journal The Ganzfeld, monographs on artists associated with Providence and New York, and books about experimental music and visual culture. PictureBox also collaborated with museums, galleries, and individual artists on projects designed for particular exhibitions. A cover created by Nadel and Peter Buchanan-Smith for a Wilco album won a Grammy for recording package design, bringing the company’s book-oriented sensibility into popular music. Nadel announced the end of regular publishing in 2013, after which he continued to curate exhibitions and edit art books. PictureBox’s brief existence reflected the role small presses can play in connecting niche artistic communities.

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld is an American scholar of management whose work focuses on corporate leadership, chief executives, and governance. He holds a professorship at Yale School of Management and has served as a senior associate dean responsible for leadership studies. Sonnenfeld founded the Chief Executive Leadership Institute, a nonprofit organization affiliated with Yale that brings business leaders together for research, teaching, and private discussion. The institute is known for meetings in which executives, public officials, academics, and other prominent participants exchange views under rules of confidentiality. Its programmes have been held in the United States and in international locations. Before joining Yale, Sonnenfeld taught at Harvard Business School and Emory University’s Goizueta Business School. His research and public commentary examine how leaders are selected, how corporate boards function, and how organizations respond to crises. Through the institute, he has helped make executive education a subject of study rather than treating it solely as a practical corporate activity.

Water trading is a system in which holders of legal rights to use water transfer those rights temporarily or permanently to other users. A farmer may lease part of an allocation during a wet season, while a city, industry, or neighbouring farm may purchase a long-term entitlement. The rules differ widely because water rights are defined by national law, state systems, river-basin agreements, and local customs. Supporters argue that a price can encourage water to move from activities producing less economic value to those producing more, especially during drought. Critics question whether markets protect ecosystems, small communities, and households that cannot compete with large buyers. Trading can also be difficult to monitor when the amount of water delivered depends on weather, storage, and river conditions. Formal schemes operate in parts of Australia, the western United States, Chile, South Africa, Spain, and elsewhere, while informal exchanges occur in regions without a regulated market. The central debate is whether a market can allocate a public necessity fairly.

Science International was a Canadian television programme about inventions, scientific developments, and unusual facts that later used the title What Will They Think of Next! Each episode was assembled from many short segments rather than one continuous documentary story. Some segments used filmed demonstrations or interviews, while others relied on limited animation to explain an eccentric invention or an unexpected scientific idea. Joseph Campanella narrated the early programmes, with Tiiu Leek and later Kerrie Keane also serving as hosts. Chromakey backgrounds placed the presenters in front of animated or illustrated scenes. The show was produced during the late 1970s and was later broadcast in the United States, especially through Nickelodeon. American broadcasts used the later title most of the time, although some retained Science International. Its quick succession of topics made the series suitable for younger viewers and for repeated educational programming blocks. The format combined the tone of a science magazine with the visual shortcuts of children’s television.

Circular reasoning is an argument that uses its conclusion, either directly or through an equivalent claim, as support for itself. In its simplest form, the pattern is “A is true because B is true, and B is true because A is true.” The statements may be logically compatible, but the argument has not supplied an independent reason for believing either one. This makes circularity a problem of justification and persuasion rather than merely a mistake in formal validity. A longer chain can hide the repetition: a person may defend one claim with a second, the second with a third, and eventually return to the original claim. The fallacy is closely associated with begging the question, although writers sometimes use that phrase more broadly for arguments that assume what they are supposed to establish. Detecting circular reasoning requires asking whether the evidence offered would convince someone who did not already accept the conclusion.

John Curley is an American newspaper executive and sports-journalism educator associated with Gannett and Penn State University. He began his career in local newspapers, working as an editor and publisher in Rochester, New York; Bridgewater, New Jersey; and Wilmington, Delaware. Curley later became the first editor of USA Today and led Gannett News Service, where the organization received a Pulitzer Prize for Public Service. He served on Gannett’s board and held the company’s chairmanship before retiring in 2001 after more than three decades in newspaper management. Curley also held national leadership roles in the newspaper industry, including the chairmanship of the Newspaper Association of America. After leaving corporate management, he joined Penn State as a professor and helped direct its Center for Sports Journalism. The centre was named in his honour, reflecting his work connecting newsroom practice with the teaching of sports reporting and media leadership.

K-152 is a two-lane state highway in eastern Kansas that crosses Linn County from the vicinity of Parker to U.S. Route 69 near La Cygne. The road passes through La Cygne and runs near Prairie View High School, but most of its route crosses rural farmland and wooded country. Its present number is the result of several changes made to avoid confusion with other highways. The road was originally designated K-35 in the 1920s and connected K-7 with routes that were later absorbed into the federal highway system. When Interstate 35 was constructed, the state renumbered K-35 as K-135. A later conflict with Interstate 135 led to another change, producing the K-152 designation used today. The highway has remained a relatively narrow local connector rather than a divided or limited-access route. Its history demonstrates how state highway numbers can change even when the physical road has been substantially retained.

Karen Rose is an American author of romantic suspense novels. Born Karen Rose Hafer in Maryland, she studied chemical engineering at the University of Maryland and initially worked in industry. During that career she received patents, but began writing fiction after ideas for scenes and characters repeatedly distracted her from technical work. Her first suspense novel, Don’t Tell, was published in 2003. Rose’s books combine crime investigations, danger, and romantic relationships, often using continuing characters and connected families across several novels. Her work has earned major recognition from romance readers, including a RITA Award, and has been published internationally. She has written more than a dozen novels as well as shorter works, with later releases expanding a catalogue that began with her transition from engineering to fiction. Rose lives and works as a full-time writer, drawing on the contrast between the structured problem-solving of her scientific training and the emotional unpredictability required by suspense storytelling.

“They-Say Vision” is a pop-rock single by the American singer Res from her debut album, How I Do. Released commercially in 2002, it presents a theme of refusing to conform through a production that combines rock instrumentation with the rhythmic and vocal elements of contemporary pop. The song was unusual enough to resist a single radio category, yet it reached a broad audience through club play and music television. It became Res’s first major commercial success in the United States, appearing on several Billboard charts and reaching the top of the Dance Club Songs listing. The track also entered the lower ranges of the pop and Hot 100-related charts. MTV and VH1 aired its accompanying video, increasing the song’s visibility beyond listeners who had already discovered the album. Interest in the single helped revive sales of How I Do nearly a year after its original release and established Res as an artist whose music could move between genre markets.
